modules.title: Getting Started with SQL
modules.summary: Tables and rows, your first queries, filtering and sorting, simple aggregates, and changing data safely.

lessons.title: Tables, rows and your first query
lessons.tldr: A relational database keeps data in **tables** of **rows** and named, typed **columns**, and `SELECT … FROM` is how you ask it for some of that data. Every report, screen and API you will build starts as a query like this, so knowing exactly what a query reads and returns is the first skill to learn.

visualizer.title: Anatomy of a table and a first SELECT
visualizer.interaction: Step through from the server down to one cell. Watch which columns each query reads, compare the result, and click any cell to inspect it.

presets.label: Everything
presets.lookFor: 9 rows, 5 columns. Two rows show **NULL** for stock: the value is unknown, not zero.

presets.label: Pick columns
presets.lookFor: Only the two columns you listed, in that order. Swap them and run again.

presets.label: Expressions and AS
presets.lookFor: `price * 1.2` returns `28.800`: three decimals. `stock * 2` has no alias, so its column is named `?column?`, and NULL stock stays NULL. `||` joins text.

presets.label: Table alias and comments
presets.lookFor: `p` is a short name for `products` in this one query. Comments are ignored by the server.

presets.label: Where am I?
presets.lookFor: You are in database `postgres`, schema `public`, as user `postgres`, on PostgreSQL 18.

presets.label: List my tables
presets.lookFor: The database describes itself with ordinary tables you can query. `stock` is the only nullable column.

production.title: An export that stops breaking
production.problem: A developer adds a `supplier_id` column between `category` and `price`. The next export shifts every column one place to the right, and the finance script reads supplier ids as prices.
production.outcome: The export keeps exactly 5 columns in a fixed order no matter how the table changes. New columns appear only when someone adds them to the query on purpose.

pitfalls.title: Assuming rows come back in insert order
pitfalls.fix: Add `ORDER BY` whenever order matters, for example `ORDER BY id`. The next lesson covers sorting.

pitfalls.title: SELECT * in application code
pitfalls.fix: Use `SELECT *` for exploring. In code, list the columns you need.

pitfalls.title: Double quotes around text values
pitfalls.fix: Write `'home'`. To put a quote inside text, double it: `'it''s'`.

pitfalls.title: The statement never runs
pitfalls.fix: Type `;` and press Enter. Ending every statement with `;` also lets you put several in one script.

keyPointers: Cluster → database → schema → table → row → column. A connection works in one database. New tables land in schema `public`.
`SELECT columns FROM table;` Use `*` to explore and named columns in real code.
Expressions in the select list compute new columns. Name them with `AS`, or they are called `?column?`.
Rows have **no order** unless you ask for one with `ORDER BY`. `NULL` means unknown, not zero or empty.
**Going deeper:** [What PostgreSQL is](/m1/what-is-postgres) follows one query from your client through the server and back.

lessons.title: Creating tables and inserting rows
lessons.tldr: `CREATE TABLE` defines a table once (its columns, their types and the rules each row must obey), and `INSERT` adds rows that PostgreSQL checks against those rules. Types and constraints such as `NOT NULL`, `PRIMARY KEY` and `DEFAULT` let the database itself reject bad data, so every program that writes to it gets the same protection.

visualizer.title: Build a table, one statement at a time
visualizer.interaction: Step through CREATE TABLE and six INSERTs. Watch defaults fill in, bad rows bounce off the constraints, and the identity counter skip a number.

presets.label: Create the table
presets.lookFor: The second query reads the table definition back. `id` shows no default: identity columns are generated, not defaulted.

presets.label: Insert one, RETURNING
presets.lookFor: You sent two values; the row came back complete. `id` = 1, `vip` = false, `credit` = 0.00, and today's date.

presets.label: Many rows, DEFAULT keyword
presets.lookFor: One statement, two rows, ids 2 and 3. `DEFAULT` inside VALUES asks for the column default.

presets.label: Rules that reject rows
presets.lookFor: Four different errors: **23502** NOT NULL, **428C9** identity, **22P02** bad input for a boolean, **42703** unknown column. Eve then gets id **5**: the first failed insert used up 4.

presets.label: INSERT … SELECT
presets.lookFor: Rows can come from a query instead of VALUES. `source = 'friend'` is a true/false expression, so Hana becomes a VIP.

presets.label: Quotes and names
presets.lookFor: Unquoted names are folded to lower case, so `Orders` means `orders` and is not found (**42P01**). Only `"Orders"` with quotes finds it. Stick to lower-case names.

presets.label: Drop a table
presets.lookFor: `DROP TABLE` removes the definition **and** all its rows at once. `IF EXISTS` turns "not found" into a notice instead of an error.

production.title: Sign-up in one round trip
production.problem: The first version inserted the row, then ran `SELECT max(id) FROM customers` to find it. Under load two sign-ups interleaved and one user got the other's id, so the coupon went to the wrong account.
production.outcome: Each sign-up costs one statement instead of two, and the id returned is always the row that statement inserted, however many sign-ups run at once.

pitfalls.title: Expecting ids without gaps
pitfalls.fix: Treat ids as unique labels, not counters. If you need a gapless sequence (invoice numbers), build it separately; to count rows, use `count(*)`.

pitfalls.title: Typing ids by hand into an identity column
pitfalls.fix: For a one-off load, write `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE` after the column list, then move the counter past the highest id. Otherwise omit the column.

pitfalls.title: Money in a float column
pitfalls.fix: Use `numeric(12,2)` (exact) for money and anything that must add up to the cent.

pitfalls.title: Mixed-case table names
pitfalls.fix: Use lower-case names with underscores (`order_items`). If one exists already, rename it: `ALTER TABLE "Orders" RENAME TO orders;`.

keyPointers: `CREATE TABLE t (col type constraints, …)`. Everyday types: `int`/`bigint`, `text`, `numeric(p,s)`, `boolean`, `date`, `timestamptz`.
`PRIMARY KEY` = unique + not null. `NOT NULL` forbids missing values. `DEFAULT` fills omitted columns.
`bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` numbers rows for you; numbers are unique but can have **gaps**.
`'single quotes'` are values, `"double quotes"` are names. `RETURNING` sends the inserted row back.
**Going deeper:** [Primitive types, alignment and padding](/m2/primitive-types) shows how each type is laid out in bytes on disk.

lessons.title: Filtering and sorting
lessons.tldr: `WHERE` keeps only the rows whose condition is **true**, `ORDER BY` sorts them, and `LIMIT` keeps the first few. Those three clauses turn "the whole table" into "the ten rows this screen needs", and the rules around `NULL`, operator precedence and ties decide whether you get the rows you meant.

visualizer.title: Filter lab: true, false and NULL
visualizer.interaction: Pick a WHERE condition and see each row's verdict. Then sort, move NULLs, and drag LIMIT. The table on the right shows how NULL combines with AND, OR and NOT.

presets.label: Compare
presets.lookFor: `<>` (or `!=`) means "not equal". Text comparisons are exact and case-sensitive: `category = 'Office'` would match nothing.

presets.label: AND / OR precedence
presets.lookFor: Five rows, then three. Without parentheses AND is applied first, so cheap kitchen items sneak in.

presets.label: IN, BETWEEN, LIKE
presets.lookFor: `BETWEEN` includes both ends: five rows, from 15.00 up to 45.00. `_` matches one character: names whose second letter is `e`.

presets.label: NULL traps
presets.lookFor: `stock < 10` misses the two unknowns; `= NULL` finds nothing; `IS NULL` finds them. `NULL = NULL` is itself NULL.

presets.label: Sort, NULLs first or last
presets.lookFor: NULLs sort as if larger than any value: last when ascending, first when descending, unless you say `NULLS FIRST/LAST`. The last query sorts by category, then by price within each category.

presets.label: LIMIT, OFFSET, WITH TIES
presets.lookFor: Pen set and Plant pot tie at 15.00. `LIMIT 3` picks one of them; `WITH TIES` returns both (4 rows); adding `id` as a tiebreaker makes `LIMIT 3` repeatable. `OFFSET 3` skips the first three.

presets.label: DISTINCT
presets.lookFor: `DISTINCT` removes duplicate result rows. Three categories out of nine rows.

production.title: A low-stock alert that missed items
production.problem: New products are created with `stock` NULL until the first stock count. They never appeared in the alert, because `NULL < 10` is not true, and some sold out before anyone noticed they had never been counted.
production.outcome: On the sample data the alert grows from 3 rows to 5: Teapot and Pen set, which have never been counted, now come first. The rows are in the same order every night.

pitfalls.title: col = NULL finds nothing
pitfalls.fix: Use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`. To compare two columns that may both be NULL, use `a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b`.

pitfalls.title: OR without parentheses
pitfalls.fix: Put parentheses around every OR group: `(a OR b) AND c`.

pitfalls.title: NOT IN with a NULL in the list
pitfalls.fix: Use `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)`, or filter NULLs out of the list.

pitfalls.title: LIMIT without a full ORDER BY
pitfalls.fix: Always sort by a unique tiebreaker last: `ORDER BY price, id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20`.

keyPointers: `WHERE` keeps rows whose condition is **true**. False and NULL (unknown) are both dropped.
Precedence: `NOT`, then `AND`, then `OR`. When mixing AND and OR, use parentheses.
`IN (…)`, `BETWEEN a AND b` (inclusive), `LIKE` (`%` any, `_` one; case-sensitive), `ILIKE` (any case), `IS [NOT] NULL`.
`ORDER BY a, b DESC`; NULLs are last ascending and first descending unless `NULLS FIRST/LAST`. Use a unique tiebreaker before `LIMIT`.
**Going deeper:** [Designing indexes](/m4/index-design) shows how an index can answer a WHERE and ORDER BY without reading the whole table.

lessons.title: Counting, summing and grouping
lessons.tldr: An **aggregate** such as `count`, `sum` or `avg` turns many rows into one value, and `GROUP BY` computes it once per group of rows that share a key. Most questions people ask of data ("how many", "how much", "per what") are aggregates, and knowing the order the clauses run in tells you where each filter belongs.

visualizer.title: How a grouped SELECT is evaluated
visualizer.interaction: Step through the clauses in the order they run. Watch rows drop at WHERE, fold into buckets at GROUP BY, and buckets drop at HAVING. Click a bucket name to see all its aggregates.

presets.label: count(*) vs count(col)
presets.lookFor: `count(*)` = 9 rows, `count(stock)` = 7: the two NULL stocks are skipped. `avg` prints 16 decimals (37.8888888888888889); `round(…, 2)` gives 37.89.

presets.label: GROUP BY
presets.lookFor: One output row per category. Each aggregate is computed over that category's rows only.

presets.label: The GROUP BY rule
presets.lookFor: Error **42803**: a bucket has many names, so `name` must be grouped or aggregated. `string_agg` is an aggregate that joins them into one text value.

presets.label: WHERE vs HAVING
presets.lookFor: Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE (**42803**): WHERE runs before groups exist. WHERE drops the Desk chair row; HAVING drops the office group (only 2 rows left).

presets.label: The full pipeline
presets.lookFor: The visualizer's query: **home | 3 | 33.00**. ORDER BY may use the alias `avg_price`, but HAVING may not (**42703**), because it runs before SELECT names the columns.

presets.label: Group by an expression
presets.lookFor: Any expression can be a group key. 5 products are under 20.00 and 4 are not; 2 have unknown stock.

presets.label: Aggregates over no rows
presets.lookFor: No garden products: `count` gives 0, but `sum` and `avg` give **NULL**. `coalesce(x, 0)` replaces NULL with 0.

production.title: A category summary for a dashboard
production.problem: The first version loaded every product into the app and counted in code. It sent every row over the network on each page view, and the "units" tile was wrong because the code added NULL stock as 0 and counted those products as stocked.
production.outcome: The app receives 3 rows instead of 9 (and the saving grows with the catalog: always one row per category). Kitchen and office each show 1 product as "not counted" (Teapot and Pen set) instead of hiding it.

pitfalls.title: A column that is neither grouped nor aggregated
pitfalls.fix: Add the column to GROUP BY if you want a row per value, or wrap it in an aggregate (`min(name)`, `string_agg(name, ', ')`).

pitfalls.title: count(col) when you meant count(*)
pitfalls.fix: Use `count(*)` to count rows. Use `count(col)` only when "rows that have a value" is what you mean.

pitfalls.title: Filtering groups in WHERE
pitfalls.fix: Filter rows in WHERE, and filter groups in HAVING: `HAVING count(*) >= 3`. Repeat the expression; HAVING cannot see SELECT aliases.

pitfalls.title: sum() of nothing is NULL, not 0
pitfalls.fix: Wrap it: `coalesce(sum(stock), 0)`.

keyPointers: `count(*)` counts rows; `count(col)` counts non-NULL values; `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max` skip NULLs and return NULL on zero rows.
With GROUP BY, every selected column must be in the GROUP BY or inside an aggregate.
WHERE filters **rows** before grouping. HAVING filters **groups** after. Aggregates belong in HAVING.
Run order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. WHERE and HAVING cannot use SELECT aliases; ORDER BY can.
**Going deeper:** [Aggregates, FILTER and GROUPING SETS](/m3/aggregates-grouping) adds subtotals and conditional counts; [From SQL text to rows](/m4/query-pipeline) shows the plan that runs a query.

lessons.title: Updating and deleting safely
lessons.tldr: `UPDATE` changes and `DELETE` removes every row its `WHERE` matches, and a transaction (`BEGIN` … `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`) lets you look at the result before it becomes permanent. A single missing `WHERE` changes the whole table with no warning, so a habit of preview, transaction, check and only then commit is the cheapest insurance you will ever buy.

visualizer.title: The safe-change routine
visualizer.interaction: Pick a scenario and step through it. Compare the safe UPDATE with the forgotten WHERE, and watch ROLLBACK put every value back.

presets.label: 1. Preview
presets.lookFor: Three rows, and the prices they would get. Nothing has changed yet.

presets.label: 2. Try it, then ROLLBACK
presets.lookFor: RETURNING shows 10.45, 49.50 and 19.80. After ROLLBACK the last query shows the original 9.50, 45.00 and 18.00 again.

presets.label: 3. Do it, then COMMIT
presets.lookFor: Same UPDATE, now committed: the three kitchen prices stay raised. Every other row is untouched.

presets.label: 4. The forgotten WHERE
presets.lookFor: `UPDATE` with no WHERE hits all **9** rows. Inside the transaction 9 products cost 0; after ROLLBACK, 0 do.

presets.label: 5. DELETE … RETURNING
presets.lookFor: Preview finds Chef knife; DELETE removes exactly that row and lists it. 8 products remain.

presets.label: 6. An error aborts the transaction
presets.lookFor: Here the helper catches the error, so the transaction survives. In psql, after a real error every later statement fails with **25P02** ("current transaction is aborted") until you run ROLLBACK.

presets.label: 7. TRUNCATE inside a transaction
presets.lookFor: TRUNCATE empties the table in one step (0 rows), and ROLLBACK brings every row back. Outside a transaction it would be final.

production.title: Fixing a mispriced category in production
production.problem: A plain `UPDATE` typed into a console commits the moment it finishes. A typo in the WHERE, or no WHERE at all, would reprice the whole store instantly and customers would see it.
production.outcome: The change is checked before anyone sees it: 3 rows previewed, 3 rows updated, then one commit makes all 3 visible together. A mistake costs one `ROLLBACK`, not a restore from backup.

pitfalls.title: UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE
pitfalls.fix: Write the WHERE first and test it in a SELECT. Run changes inside `BEGIN` and compare the tag with the preview before `COMMIT`. In psql, `\set AUTOCOMMIT off` makes psql issue `BEGIN` for you, so nothing is saved until you `COMMIT`.

pitfalls.title: A transaction left open
pitfalls.fix: Always finish with COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` so a forgotten session is ended automatically.

pitfalls.title: current transaction is aborted
pitfalls.fix: Run `ROLLBACK;` and start again. (A `SAVEPOINT` lets you undo just part of a transaction.)

pitfalls.title: TRUNCATE where DELETE was needed
pitfalls.fix: Use `DELETE … WHERE` to remove some rows or when triggers must run. Use `TRUNCATE` (with `RESTART IDENTITY` to reset ids) only to empty a table nobody is using.

keyPointers: `UPDATE t SET col = expr WHERE …` and `DELETE FROM t WHERE …`. No WHERE means **every row**.
Preview with a `SELECT` using the same WHERE. The number of rows it returns is the number the change will touch.
`BEGIN` → change → check the tag and `RETURNING` → `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`. Outside BEGIN, each statement commits by itself.
`TRUNCATE` empties a table fast and frees space at once, but locks it completely and skips DELETE triggers.
**Going deeper:** [ACID and transactions](/m5/acid-transactions) explains how COMMIT and ROLLBACK work; [INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE](/m3/dml-lifecycle) shows what UPDATE does to the stored rows.

modules.title: Working with Data
modules.summary: Text, numbers, dates and times, conditional logic and type conversion: the functions you use every day.

lessons.title: Text and strings
lessons.tldr: PostgreSQL ships dozens of **string functions** that join, measure, change case, trim, slice, search and rewrite text, plus **regular expressions** for patterns. Real data arrives messy, with stray spaces, mixed case and odd formats, so you clean and compare it in SQL instead of shipping every row to application code.

visualizer.title: String workbench: every character and its bytes
visualizer.interaction: Pick an input (or type your own) and step through the functions. Watch which characters are kept, removed or changed, and compare **length** with **octet_length**.

presets.label: Joining strings
presets.lookFor: Bob has no last name. With `||` one NULL makes the whole result NULL. `concat` and `concat_ws` skip NULLs, and `concat_ws` puts the separator only between real values.

presets.label: Characters vs bytes
presets.lookFor: `são paulo` is 9 characters but 10 bytes, because `ã` takes 2 bytes in UTF-8. The emoji string is 12 characters and 17 bytes.

presets.label: Clean up names
presets.lookFor: The brackets show the stray spaces around `ann`. `trim` removes them and `initcap` fixes the case: `LEE` → `Lee`, `o'neil` → `O'Neil`, `são paulo` → `São Paulo`.

presets.label: Slice and search
presets.lookFor: Positions start at 1. `split_part` with `-1` takes the last field. Row 4 has a trailing space, so its `tld` is `com ` (with a space): dirty data shows up as soon as you slice it.

presets.label: Regular expressions
presets.lookFor: `\D` = any non-digit. The second query returns rows only for customers whose phone contains a 4-digit group: `regexp_matches` silently **drops** rows with no match (ids 3 and 4 vanish).

presets.label: format() for messages and SQL
presets.lookFor: `%s` inserts a value, `%I` quotes an identifier only when needed (`"Customer List"`), `%L` quotes a literal safely. This is how dynamic SQL avoids injection.

presets.label: Case-insensitive matching
presets.lookFor: Plain `=` finds 1 row; normalising with `lower(trim(...))` finds both Ann rows. `ILIKE`, the `citext` type and a **nondeterministic collation** are three more ways to ignore case.

production.title: Duplicate sign-ups that differ only by case
production.problem: `Ann.Lee@Example.COM` and `ann.lee@example.com` are different strings, so the `UNIQUE (email)` constraint lets both in. Users get two copies of every mail, and unsubscribe only removes one.
production.outcome: In the playground data, step 1 finds one duplicate group (ids 1 and 6) and step 2 removes id 6. After the index exists, inserting `ANN.LEE@example.com` fails with a unique violation, and lookups written as `WHERE lower(email) = lower($1)` can use the index.

pitfalls.title: One NULL blanks the whole label
pitfalls.fix: Use `concat_ws(' ', first_name, last_name)` or wrap the nullable pieces in `coalesce(col, '')`.

pitfalls.title: Counting characters when the limit is in bytes
pitfalls.fix: Check `octet_length` when the limit is in bytes, for example `CHECK (octet_length(bio) <= 255)`.

pitfalls.title: regexp_matches silently drops rows
pitfalls.fix: Use `regexp_match` (one result or NULL) when you want the first match, or wrap it: `(SELECT regexp_matches(col, pat))`.

pitfalls.title: Case-insensitive search that scans the whole table
pitfalls.fix: Create an expression index on exactly the expression you filter by, or use the `citext` type.

keyPointers: `||` returns NULL if any piece is NULL. `concat` and `concat_ws` skip NULLs.
**length** counts characters and **octet_length** counts bytes. String positions start at **1**.
`~` matches a regex anywhere in the string. `LIKE` must match the whole string. Add `g` to `regexp_replace` to replace every match.
For case-insensitive equality, normalise with `lower()`, use `ILIKE`, the `citext` type or a nondeterministic collation. Back it with a matching index.
Going deeper: the Internals lesson [Designing indexes](/m4/index-design) shows how an expression index on `lower(email)` serves these lookups.

lessons.title: Numbers and arithmetic
lessons.tldr: PostgreSQL has three families of number types: **integers** (whole numbers), **numeric** (exact decimals) and **floating point** (fast binary approximations). The type decides what arithmetic means, so `7 / 2` is 3, `0.1 + 0.2` may not equal 0.3, and picking the right type keeps money and ratios correct.

visualizer.title: Three number experiments
visualizer.interaction: Divide integers and watch the fraction vanish, add 0.1 ten times in binary and in decimal, then squeeze values into a **numeric(p, s)** column.

presets.label: Integer division
presets.lookFor: `7 / 2` is **3** and `-7 / 2` is **-3**: integer division truncates toward zero. One decimal operand (`7.0`) switches to numeric division.

presets.label: What type is this?
presets.lookFor: A whole-number literal is `integer` (or `bigint` if it is too big), and any literal with a point or exponent is `numeric`. Mixing types promotes to the "wider" one.

presets.label: Float vs numeric
presets.lookFor: Floats are binary, so `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004` and ten 0.1s make `0.9999999999999999`. A `real` keeps about 6 digits: widening its sum shows `3.3000000193715096`.

presets.label: Rounding family
presets.lookFor: `round(2.5)` on numeric is **3** (ties away from zero), but on double precision it is **2** (ties to even). `trunc` cuts toward zero; `floor` always goes down.

presets.label: numeric(p, s) limits
presets.lookFor: Extra decimals are rounded, but too many digits before the point is an **error** (`numeric field overflow`). Try `SELECT 2147483647 + 1;` yourself: integers never wrap around silently.

presets.label: Money math
presets.lookFor: `discount_pct / 100` is integer division, so it is 0 for every row and `discount_wrong` is always 0.00. Multiply first or use `100.0`. Order 101 averages 4.5 items, not 4.

presets.label: Random numbers
presets.lookFor: `random()` returns a double in [0, 1). `random(1, 6)` includes both ends. After `setseed` the sequence repeats, which helps tests. It is not secure: use `gen_random_uuid()` or pgcrypto for tokens.

production.title: An invoice that is off by one cent
production.problem: The invoice shows each line rounded to cents, but the charge rounds only the final sum. With five lines at 8.25% tax the two disagree, and customers spot the difference.
production.outcome: On the playground data the printed lines add up to **174.96** while the rounded total is **174.95**, and the float total is `174.95365`. Charging `sum_of_rounded_lines` makes the invoice and the card charge match exactly.

pitfalls.title: Ratios that are always zero
pitfalls.fix: Make one side numeric before dividing: `100.0 * a / b` or `a::numeric / b`, then `round(..., 1)`.

pitfalls.title: Storing money in float
pitfalls.fix: Use `numeric(12,2)` (or integer cents) for money. Keep `real`/`double precision` for measurements where tiny errors do not matter.

pitfalls.title: Integer overflow on a growing counter
pitfalls.fix: Use `bigint` for ids and large counters. Cast before multiplying big values: `a::bigint * b`.

pitfalls.title: Comparing floats with =
pitfalls.fix: Compare with a tolerance (`abs(weight - 0.1) < 1e-6`) or store the value as `numeric` if exact equality matters.

keyPointers: **integer / integer** truncates toward zero. Add a decimal point or cast to get fractions.
**numeric** is exact and right for money. **real**/**double precision** are fast binary approximations.
`numeric(p, s)` rounds extra decimals but **errors** when the integer part is too long. Integer overflow is also an error.
`round` on numeric rounds ties away from zero; on double precision it usually rounds ties to even (the exact rule depends on the platform).
Going deeper: the Internals lesson [Primitive types, alignment and padding](/m2/primitive-types) shows how many bytes each number type takes on disk.

lessons.title: Dates, times and time zones
lessons.tldr: PostgreSQL has `date`, `timestamp` (wall-clock time), `timestamptz` (a real instant, stored in UTC) and `interval`, plus functions to truncate, extract, bucket and convert them. Time zones and daylight saving time make "the same time" ambiguous, so choosing **timestamptz** and **half-open ranges** keeps reports and schedules correct everywhere.

visualizer.title: One instant, many clocks
visualizer.interaction: Step through eight scenes. The x axis is real time; each lane is a local clock with its DST jumps. Switch the **session TimeZone** to see that only the display changes.

presets.label: TimeZone and now()
presets.lookFor: The same stored instant prints as `17:00:00+00` or `22:30:00+05:30`. Inside a transaction `now()` never moves; `clock_timestamp()` does (elapsed is about 0.2 s).

presets.label: timestamp vs timestamptz
presets.lookFor: A `timestamp` literal **silently drops** the `+02`. The timestamptz version converts it: 12:00 at +02 is 10:00 UTC.

presets.label: AT TIME ZONE
presets.lookFor: timestamptz → timestamp (wall clock) and timestamp → timestamptz (an instant). Careful: the text `'+05'` is a POSIX zone meaning **UTC−5** (07:00); the interval form means UTC+5 (17:00).

presets.label: DST arithmetic
presets.lookFor: 02:30 does not exist and becomes 03:30-04. `1 day` lands on 12:00 but `24 hours` on 13:00. The fall-back day lasts `1 day 01:00:00`: 25 hours.

presets.label: Dates, months and age
presets.lookFor: Adding a month clamps to the last day (Feb 28, or Feb 29 in 2024). `date + integer` adds days; `date - date` is an integer number of days.

presets.label: Truncate, extract, bin
presets.lookFor: `date_trunc('week')` snaps to Monday. `dow` counts Sunday as 0, `isodow` Monday as 1. 2027-01-01 belongs to ISO **week 53 of 2026**: always pair `week` with `isoyear`.

presets.label: Daily report, half-open
presets.lookFor: Each day is `[start, start + 1 day)`: every event lands in exactly one bucket. Grouped by New York days the counts shift, and the 2026-03-08 bucket starts at 05:00 UTC but the next at 04:00 UTC (a 23-hour day).

production.title: A daily revenue report that is off by a day
production.problem: The database session runs in UTC, so `::date` cuts days at midnight **UTC**, which is 19:00 or 20:00 in New York. Evening orders show up on the next day and the totals never match the till.
production.outcome: On the playground data the UTC report shows 2026-03-06 with 15 events and 110.00; the New York report shows 14 events and 115.00 for that day, plus 4 events from the evening of 2026-03-05 that the UTC report had moved forward.

pitfalls.title: Using timestamp for events
pitfalls.fix: Store real moments as **timestamptz**. Use `timestamp` only for wall-clock values such as "store opens at 09:00 local".

pitfalls.title: BETWEEN on dates misses the last day
pitfalls.fix: Use a **half-open range**: `>= start AND < next_start`. It never overlaps and never leaves a gap.

pitfalls.title: A DEFAULT frozen at table creation
pitfalls.fix: Use the function: `created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()`.

pitfalls.title: POSIX offsets point the wrong way
pitfalls.fix: Use a zone name (`'Asia/Karachi'`) or an interval (`AT TIME ZONE INTERVAL '+05:00'`).

keyPointers: **timestamptz** stores an instant (in UTC) and displays it in the session **TimeZone**. **timestamp** is wall-clock digits only.
`AT TIME ZONE` flips the type: timestamptz → timestamp (read a clock), timestamp → timestamptz (pin to a zone).
`+ interval '1 day'` keeps the local time of day; `+ interval '24 hours'` adds elapsed time. They differ across DST.
Filter time with **half-open ranges** `>= start AND < end`, and pass the business zone to `date_trunc`.
Going deeper: the Internals lesson [Declarative partitioning and pruning](/m7/partitioning) uses the same half-open bounds to split tables by time.

lessons.title: Conditional logic
lessons.tldr: `CASE`, `COALESCE`, `NULLIF`, `GREATEST`/`LEAST` and aggregate `FILTER` let one query choose a value per row, replace missing data and count different things in a single pass. They exist so that labels, defaults and guarded calculations such as division by zero live in SQL, right next to the data, instead of in a loop in application code.

visualizer.title: Evaluate a conditional expression row by row
visualizer.interaction: Choose an expression and press **Next row**. Branches light up in order: true, false, NULL or not evaluated at all. In **FILTER** mode, watch four aggregates fill up in one pass.

presets.label: Searched CASE
presets.lookFor: The first true branch wins. For Cy the comparisons are NULL (not true), so CASE falls through to `IS NULL`. Without that branch Cy would be `bronze`.

presets.label: Simple CASE and NULL
presets.lookFor: A simple CASE compares with `=`, and `NULL = NULL` is not true, so it does **not** match. A CASE with no ELSE and no true branch returns NULL.

presets.label: COALESCE, GREATEST, LEAST
presets.lookFor: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument. GREATEST and LEAST **ignore NULLs**, so Ann's best offer is 5.00, and they return NULL only when every argument is NULL.

presets.label: Safe division with NULLIF
presets.lookFor: Eve has `qty = 0`. `NULLIF(qty, 0)` returns NULL, so the division returns NULL instead of an error. Try `SELECT total / qty FROM orders;` to see the error it prevents.

presets.label: FILTER: many metrics, one pass
presets.lookFor: Five metrics from one scan. `sum` skips Cy's NULL total, so paid revenue is 170.00 from three paid orders.

presets.label: Booleans as columns
presets.lookFor: A comparison is a value of type boolean, so it can be a column. Cy's `big_order` is NULL, not false. A sum over zero rows is NULL; `coalesce(..., 0)` turns it into 0.

presets.label: CASE needs one result type
presets.lookFor: `1` and `2.5` unify to numeric. Mixing a number with a word does not: `CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 'n/a' END` fails, so cast the number to text first.

production.title: A KPI tile query that crashed on an empty day
production.problem: Four queries scanned the table four times, and right after midnight there were no orders: `refunded / count(*)` divided by zero and the whole dashboard showed an error.
production.outcome: On the playground data the query returns 5 orders, 170.00 paid revenue and a 20.0% refund rate. With a filter that matches no rows it returns 0, 0 and 0 instead of failing, and the dashboard needs one scan instead of four.

pitfalls.title: CASE branches in the wrong order
pitfalls.fix: Order WHEN branches from most specific to least specific, and test the edge values.

pitfalls.title: CASE x WHEN NULL never matches
pitfalls.fix: Use a searched CASE: `CASE WHEN status IS NULL THEN … END`.

pitfalls.title: Division by zero in a ratio
pitfalls.fix: Divide by `NULLIF(denominator, 0)` and wrap the result in `COALESCE` if you need a number.

pitfalls.title: A constant error inside an unused CASE branch
pitfalls.fix: Do not rely on CASE to hide constant errors; compute guarded values with NULLIF instead.

keyPointers: Searched **CASE** returns the first **true** branch. NULL is not true. No ELSE means NULL.
**COALESCE** picks the first non-NULL argument and stops there. **NULLIF(a, b)** turns a chosen value into NULL.
`x / NULLIF(y, 0)` is the standard guard against division by zero.
`count(*) FILTER (WHERE …)` computes many conditional metrics in one pass. Sums over no rows are NULL.

Going deeper: the Internals lesson [From SQL text to rows](/m4/query-pipeline) follows a query through parsing, rewriting and planning, the stages that run before the executor evaluates CASE row by row.

lessons.title: Type conversion
lessons.tldr: A **cast** converts a value from one type to another, written `CAST(x AS type)` or `x::type`, and functions like `to_char`, `to_number` and `to_date` handle custom formats. Data often arrives as text from forms and files, so you need to know which conversions succeed, which round, which fail, and how to test input before it breaks a whole load.

visualizer.title: The cast matrix
visualizer.interaction: Every cell is a real cast result. Click a cell for its SQL and error, or press **Next interesting cell** for a guided tour. Switch to **From a number** to compare numeric and double precision rounding.

presets.label: Three ways to cast
presets.lookFor: All three spellings do the same conversion. `::` is PostgreSQL shorthand; `CAST(… AS …)` is standard SQL.

presets.label: Literals adapt, columns do not
presets.lookFor: A quoted literal starts as type `unknown` and takes whatever type its neighbour needs. Two texts compare character by character, so `'10' < '9'` is true and text numbers sort 1, 10, 2, 9.

presets.label: What would fail?
presets.lookFor: `pg_input_is_valid` tests a value **without raising an error**. `pg_input_error_info` returns the message the cast would have raised: `four` and `''` are invalid syntax, `40000` is out of range.

presets.label: Rounding and truncation
presets.lookFor: Casting a number to integer **rounds**, it does not truncate: 3.99 becomes 4. numeric ties go away from zero (3), double ties go to even (2). An explicit cast to `varchar(3)` silently cuts the text.

presets.label: to_char, to_number, to_date
presets.lookFor: `to_char` formats numbers and dates as text; `FM` removes padding. A format too narrow prints `###`. `to_number` and `to_date` parse text that a plain cast rejects.

presets.label: Validate, then load
presets.lookFor: Only rows that pass every check are cast, so the INSERT cannot fail halfway. Lines 1, 2 and 3 load (line 3 via `to_number`). Lines 4 to 7 stay in staging for a human to fix.

presets.label: DateStyle and JSON values
presets.lookFor: The same `03/04/2026` is April 3 or March 4 depending on **DateStyle**: prefer ISO `YYYY-MM-DD`. `->>` always returns text, so cast it before doing arithmetic.

production.title: Importing a messy CSV without losing the good rows
production.problem: The first version ran `INSERT … SELECT raw_qty::smallint, …`. One cell with `four` raised `invalid input syntax for type smallint` and the **whole statement** rolled back: no orders loaded until someone found the bad row.
production.outcome: On the playground data 3 of 7 rows load and 5 problems in 4 rows are reported (line 5 has both an empty quantity and February 30). Before the change, one bad cell meant zero rows loaded.

pitfalls.title: One bad value aborts the whole load
pitfalls.fix: Filter with `pg_input_is_valid(value, 'type')` before casting, and route invalid rows to a review table.

pitfalls.title: Numbers stored as text sort wrongly
pitfalls.fix: Store numbers in numeric columns. As a stopgap, cast in the query: `ORDER BY code::int`.

pitfalls.title: Casting to integer rounds, and not always the same way
pitfalls.fix: Say what you mean before casting: `trunc(x)::int`, `floor(x)::int`, `ceil(x)::int` or `round(x)::int`.

pitfalls.title: Explicit varchar casts truncate silently
pitfalls.fix: Do not cast to a shorter length to "make it fit". Check `length(x)` first, or widen the column.

keyPointers: `CAST(x AS t)`, `x::t` and `t 'literal'` are the same conversion. Quoted literals start as `unknown` and adapt to their context.
Text → number accepts spaces but not decimal points (for integers), commas or empty strings. Out of range is an error, never a wrap.
Number → integer **rounds**: ties away from zero from numeric, to even from double precision. Be explicit with `trunc`/`round`.
Check input with `pg_input_is_valid` and `pg_input_error_info` before casting; use `to_char`/`to_number`/`to_date` for custom formats.
Going deeper: the Internals lesson [JSON vs JSONB](/m2/json-jsonb) shows how JSON values are stored and why `->>` hands you text.

lessons.title: Working with JSON
lessons.tldr: PostgreSQL can build JSON documents from ordinary rows, query them with path expressions, turn them back into rows, change parts of them and validate them with constraints. Applications speak JSON, so doing this shaping in one SQL statement replaces many round trips and loops in application code, as long as you pick the right function and the right index.

visualizer.title: Rows, paths and indexes
visualizer.interaction: **Rows → document**: press **Fold one level** and watch join rows nest into one document; switch the empty-group handling to see what a customer with no orders gets. **Path explorer**: click a node. **Index guide**: pick a query shape.

presets.label: Rows become JSON
presets.lookFor: `to_jsonb(row)` turns a whole row into an object keyed by column name. `jsonb_build_object` picks the keys, `jsonb_agg(… ORDER BY …)` folds rows into an ordered array, and `jsonb_object_agg(key, value)` folds rows into one object.

presets.label: Empty groups: [null], NULL or []
presets.lookFor: Dara has no orders. Plain `jsonb_agg` gives `[null]`, `FILTER` gives SQL NULL, and `COALESCE(…, '[]')` gives an empty array. `jsonb_agg_strict` skips NULL values but not an object full of nulls. A NULL **key** in `jsonb_object_agg` is an error; a NULL value is kept unless you use the `_strict` form.

presets.label: SQL/JSON standard functions
presets.lookFor: The standard constructors return `json` unless you say `RETURNING jsonb`. `JSON_OBJECT` keeps NULLs by default, `JSON_ARRAY` drops them. Inbox row 2 has `13/11/2026`, which is not a valid date: `JSON_VALUE … RETURNING date` quietly returns NULL, unless you give a `DEFAULT … ON ERROR`.

presets.label: Shred JSON into rows and load it
presets.lookFor: `jsonb_to_recordset` maps each array element to a typed row: the string `"3"` becomes the integer 3 and a missing `qty` becomes NULL. `WITH ORDINALITY` numbers the elements from 1. The `LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true` keeps inbox row 2, whose array is empty.

presets.label: Update toolkit
presets.lookFor: `||` adds or replaces top-level keys, `-` removes a key, `#-` removes whatever sits at a path. `jsonb_insert` inserts into arrays (and refuses to overwrite an existing object key). `jsonb_set` with a missing **parent** returns the document unchanged, with no error. Mind the parentheses: `-` binds tighter than `||`.

presets.label: Validate documents
presets.lookFor: `IS JSON` tests text without raising an error; `WITH UNIQUE KEYS` catches duplicate keys that jsonb would silently collapse. The CHECK constraints accept only the first cart: watch the notices for which constraint rejected each of the others.

presets.label: Index decision guide
presets.lookFor: Containment and `?` use the GIN indexes; `->>` equality, the numeric range and top-N need the B-tree expression indexes; the jsonpath range stays a Seq Scan. In the last two plans compare the `rows=` estimate: a guess of 100 for `->>` against 50 (the true count) for the promoted column.

production.title: One query for an account page, with no [null]
production.problem: The page made 1 + 4 + 4 = **9** round trips for the 4 customers here, and it grew with every order. A rewrite with `LEFT JOIN` and `jsonb_agg` cut that to one, but customers without orders came back as `"orders": [{"id": null, "items": null}]` and the mobile app crashed reading the fake order.
production.outcome: One statement replaces nine on the playground data, and the count no longer grows with the number of orders. Dara now gets `"orders": []`, which every client can loop over.

pitfalls.title: Customers with no children get [null]
pitfalls.fix: Filter the fake row and default the empty case: `COALESCE(jsonb_agg(x) FILTER (WHERE child.id IS NOT NULL), '[]')`, or aggregate in a correlated subquery, which sees no fake row but still needs `COALESCE(…, '[]')`.

pitfalls.title: JSON_VALUE turns bad data into NULL
pitfalls.fix: In loads, write `ERROR ON ERROR` so bad documents fail loudly, or `DEFAULT … ON ERROR` plus a check that counts the defaults. Use `ON EMPTY` for keys that may be missing.

pitfalls.title: jsonb_set silently does nothing
pitfalls.fix: Create the parent first: `jsonb_set(doc, '{meta}', COALESCE(doc -> 'meta', '{}') || '{"source": "web"}')`, or rebuild the sub-object with `||`.

pitfalls.title: Expecting one index to serve every JSON query
pitfalls.fix: Add a B-tree on the exact expression (`((attrs ->> 'sku'))`, `(((attrs ->> 'price')::numeric))`), or promote a hot key to a `STORED` generated column with its own index and statistics.

keyPointers: Build: `to_jsonb(row)`, `jsonb_build_object`, `jsonb_agg(x ORDER BY …)`, `jsonb_object_agg(k, v)`. Empty groups: `COALESCE(jsonb_agg(x) FILTER (WHERE … IS NOT NULL), '[]')`.

Query: `JSON_VALUE` for one scalar (`RETURNING` a type), `JSON_QUERY` for objects, arrays or several items (`WITH WRAPPER`), `JSON_EXISTS` for a yes/no. `JSON_VALUE` and `JSON_QUERY` return NULL on error and `JSON_EXISTS` returns false, unless told otherwise.
Shred with `jsonb_to_recordset` or `jsonb_array_elements … WITH ORDINALITY`; update with `||`, `-`, `#-`, `jsonb_insert`, `jsonb_set`; validate with `IS JSON` and CHECK constraints.
Index guide: GIN for `@>`, `?` and jsonpath equality; B-tree on the expression for `->>`, ranges and sorting; a stored generated column for keys you filter, join or group on all the time.
Going deeper: [JSON vs JSONB](/m2/json-jsonb) shows how jsonb is stored and the `jsonb_set` NULL trap, and [GIN indexes](/m4/gin) shows what the GIN opclasses actually store.

lessons.title: Ranges and other special types
lessons.tldr: A **range** stores an interval such as a booking time or a quantity band as one value with two bounds, and PostgreSQL also ships types for IP networks, geometry and your own composite records. These types let the database answer questions like "do these overlap?" or "which subnet holds this address?" with one operator and an index, and refuse bad data such as double bookings outright.

visualizer.title: Ranges, bookings and networks
visualizer.interaction: **Two ranges**: drag the dots, flip the brackets and pick an operation; **Next case** walks the key cases. **Bookings**: try inserts against an exclusion constraint. **IP networks**: pick an address and see which subnets contain it.

presets.label: Range basics: bounds and canonical form
presets.lookFor: `[` and `]` include a bound, `(` and `)` exclude it; the default is `[)`. Discrete ranges (int4range, int8range, daterange) are stored in canonical `[)` form, so `[1,10]` reads back as `[1,11)`. An omitted bound is **unbounded** (`upper_inf` true), which is not the same as the value `infinity`.

presets.label: Range operators and lookups
presets.lookFor: `@>` tests containment, `&&` overlap, `-|-` adjacency, `<<` "entirely left of". Half-open `[1,5)` and `[5,9)` do not overlap but are adjacent, so their union is one range. A quantity of 0 falls in no band; 150 falls in the unbounded `[100,)`.

presets.label: Multiranges and free time
presets.lookFor: A **multirange** is a sorted set of non-overlapping ranges. `range_agg` merges touching bookings, so Lisbon's 09:00 and 10:00 meetings become one busy block. Subtracting it from the working day gives the free slots, even when the result has holes.

presets.label: No double bookings
presets.lookFor: The two touching or other-room bookings are accepted; `sync` overlaps `review` in room 1 and the exclusion constraint rejects it (see the notice, SQLSTATE 23P01). `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` builds the same kind of GiST-backed rule into a primary key. The constraint's GiST index also serves `&&` searches.

presets.label: Network types: inet and cidr
presets.lookFor: **inet** holds a host address with an optional netmask; **cidr** holds a network and rejects host bits (`'192.168.1.5/24'::cidr` is an error). `>>=` is "contains or equals", and sorting by `masklen` finds the longest prefix. A GiST index with `inet_ops` serves `<<` and `>>=`. Text comparison gets the order of addresses wrong.

presets.label: Geometric types and nearest neighbours
presets.lookFor: `<->` is distance. A GiST index on a `point` column answers `ORDER BY loc <-> p LIMIT n` as an **index scan** that walks outward from p, without computing every distance. Points have no `=` operator; use `~=` ("same as").

presets.label: Composite types and xml
presets.lookFor: A **composite type** groups fields into one value. Read a field with `(column).field`: the parentheses stop PostgreSQL from reading `total` as a table name. In `SET`, write `total.amount` without them. Row comparison goes field by field, and NULL makes `=` unknown. `xml` values are checked for well-formedness; `xpath` and `XMLTABLE` pull data out.

production.title: Making double bookings impossible
production.problem: Two people booking the same slot at the same moment both saw "free" and both inserted: a classic race between check and insert. Separate start and end columns also invited off-by-one bugs with `<=` against `<`.
production.outcome: The check and the insert become one atomic step inside the database, so no interleaving of sessions can produce an overlap. In the playground the conflicting `sync` booking is rejected with SQLSTATE 23P01 while touching bookings are accepted.

pitfalls.title: Closed upper bounds make back-to-back bookings collide
pitfalls.fix: Use half-open `[)` bounds everywhere (the constructor default). Back-to-back ranges are then adjacent (`-|-`), not overlapping.

pitfalls.title: Exclusion constraint on an integer column fails to create
pitfalls.fix: Run `CREATE EXTENSION btree_gist;` first. It adds GiST operator classes for the scalar types.

pitfalls.title: Range union or difference raises an error
pitfalls.fix: Work with multiranges: `range_agg(r)` to merge many ranges, `multirange - multirange` for differences, and `unnest()` to list the pieces.

pitfalls.title: IP addresses stored as text
pitfalls.fix: Store addresses in `inet` and networks in `cidr`. Filter with `<<=` / `>>=`, sort natively, and index with `USING gist (col inet_ops)`.

keyPointers: Range bounds: `[` / `]` include, `(` / `)` exclude, default `[)`. Discrete ranges are stored canonically as `[)`. An omitted bound is unbounded; `empty` contains no points.
Operators: `@>` contains, `<@` contained by, `&&` overlaps, `-|-` adjacent, `<<` / `>>` strictly left / right, `+` `*` `-` union, intersection, difference.

Multiranges (`range_agg`, `unnest`) hold sets of ranges with gaps. `EXCLUDE USING gist (k WITH =, r WITH &&)` or `PRIMARY KEY (k, r WITHOUT OVERLAPS)` forbids overlaps; scalar columns need `btree_gist`.
`inet` = host plus netmask, `cidr` = network; use `>>=` and `masklen` for longest-prefix lookups. Geometric types measure with `<->`; composite fields read as `(col).field`.
Going deeper: [GiST and SP-GiST](/m4/gist-spgist) shows how the index behind ranges, exclusion constraints, `inet_ops` and nearest-neighbour search is organised.

modules.title: Designing a Database
modules.summary: Keys and relationships, constraints, a first look at indexes, views and identity columns, and changing schemas safely.

lessons.title: Keys and relationships
lessons.tldr: A **primary key** gives every row a unique, never-NULL identity, and a **foreign key** is a column whose value must match the primary key of the table it references. Together they let you split data into focused tables and still connect them reliably, because PostgreSQL refuses any row that would point at nothing.

visualizer.title: Four ways tables relate
visualizer.interaction: Switch between the shapes, click rows to follow the links, then use the lab buttons. In one-to-many, pick an **ON DELETE** action and delete an author.

presets.label: One-to-many join
presets.lookFor: Each author appears once per book. The join condition is simply **foreign key = primary key**.

presets.label: Many-to-many through the junction
presets.lookFor: Two joins: book to junction, junction to tag. `book_tags` holds nothing but pairs of ids.

presets.label: Rows that would point at nothing
presets.lookFor: `try()` runs a statement and returns its error instead of aborting. Look for **23503** (no such author), **23505** (pair already linked) and **23001** (RESTRICT blocks the delete).

presets.label: CASCADE on the junction
presets.lookFor: Book 2 had two tags. Its two `book_tags` rows vanished with it; the tags themselves are untouched.

presets.label: Self-reference: who reports to whom
presets.lookFor: Join the table to itself under two aliases. `LEFT JOIN` keeps Maya, whose `manager_id` is NULL.

presets.label: List every foreign key
presets.lookFor: Default names follow `<table>_<column>_fkey`. The self-reference shows `employees` on both sides.

production.title: Deleting one customer took 40 seconds
production.problem: Each delete hung for many seconds and sometimes timed out. Deleting a parent row makes PostgreSQL check the child table for rows that still reference it, and `invoices.customer_id` had **no index**. Every delete was a full scan of the invoices table.
production.outcome: The foreign-key check becomes a single index lookup touching a handful of pages, so the delete returns in milliseconds. Joins from customers to invoices get the same speed-up.

pitfalls.title: Foreign key without an index
pitfalls.fix: Index the referencing column on any child table that is large or whose parents get deleted.

pitfalls.title: CASCADE deletes more than you expected
pitfalls.fix: Use CASCADE for rows that truly belong to the parent (junction rows, order lines). Use `RESTRICT` or the default `NO ACTION` for anything with independent value, like invoices.

pitfalls.title: A nullable foreign key lets rows float free
pitfalls.fix: Declare the column `NOT NULL` unless "no parent" is a real state of your data.

pitfalls.title: Using a value that changes as the primary key
pitfalls.fix: Use a **surrogate key** (`bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` or `uuidv7()`) as the primary key, and keep the natural value as a separate `UNIQUE` column.

keyPointers: A **primary key** is UNIQUE plus NOT NULL, one per table, and it creates a unique index automatically.
The table on the **many** side holds the **foreign key**. Many-to-many needs a **junction table** with two foreign keys and a composite primary key.
One-to-one is a foreign key that is also **UNIQUE** (or the primary key). A self-reference points a column at its own table.
`ON DELETE` decides what happens to children: **NO ACTION** (default) or **RESTRICT** refuse, **CASCADE** deletes them, **SET NULL** detaches them. Index the foreign-key column yourself.
**Going deeper:** [Modelling data: normalization and constraints](/m1/normalization-constraints) shows how to decide which tables you need in the first place.

lessons.title: Constraints and defaults
lessons.tldr: **Constraints** are rules attached to a table (`NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK`, foreign keys) that PostgreSQL checks on every insert and update, and **defaults** fill in columns you leave out. They keep bad data out at the single place every application has to pass through, so one buggy client or a hand-typed query cannot corrupt the table.

visualizer.title: The constraint gatekeeper
visualizer.interaction: Pick a scenario or build a row, then press **Run INSERT** and watch which gate stops it. Notice the identity counter moves even when the row is rejected.

presets.label: Defaults fill the gaps
presets.lookFor: Only `email` was given. `plan` became **free**, `seats` became **1**, `created_at` got the current time, and `username` is NULL because it has no default.

presets.label: One rejection per gate
presets.lookFor: Each column shows a different SQLSTATE: **23502**, **23514**, **23505**, **23503**. The constraint name in each message tells you exactly which rule fired.

presets.label: Failed inserts still use ids
presets.lookFor: The four failed attempts each drew a value from the identity sequence. Expect **id 7**, not 3. Gaps are normal and harmless.

presets.label: NULLs and UNIQUE
presets.lookFor: A plain `UNIQUE` column accepts many NULLs, because NULL is never equal to NULL. `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` treats them as equal and rejects the second one.

presets.label: CHECK lets NULL through
presets.lookFor: A CHECK passes when its expression is **true or NULL**. NULL BETWEEN 0 AND 100 is NULL, so the NULL row is stored. Add `NOT NULL` if the value is required.

presets.label: Enum, domain, exclusion
presets.lookFor: An enum rejects unknown labels (**22P02**). A domain is a reusable type with its own CHECK (**23514**). An exclusion constraint rejects overlapping time ranges (**23P01**).

presets.label: See every constraint
presets.lookFor: In PostgreSQL 18, `NOT NULL` constraints are catalog entries with names too, such as `accounts_email_not_null`.

production.title: Negative balances from a race-prone app check
production.problem: Two withdrawals arriving at the same moment both read the old balance, both passed the app check, and both subtracted. Some wallets went negative, and nothing in the database noticed.
production.outcome: Overdrafts became impossible regardless of which service wrote the update. The app now catches SQLSTATE 23514 and shows "insufficient funds" instead of silently corrupting data.

pitfalls.title: Expecting UNIQUE to stop duplicate NULLs
pitfalls.fix: Declare `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` if only one NULL is allowed, or make the column `NOT NULL`.

pitfalls.title: A CHECK that NULL slips past
pitfalls.fix: Pair the CHECK with `NOT NULL`, or write the NULL case into the expression explicitly.

pitfalls.title: Unnamed constraints make errors cryptic
pitfalls.fix: Name every CHECK and UNIQUE with `CONSTRAINT <name>` so errors explain themselves and the app can map them to messages.

pitfalls.title: An enum you cannot shrink
pitfalls.fix: Use an enum only for small, stable sets. For lists that change, use a lookup table with a foreign key, or a `CHECK (status IN (…))` you can replace.

keyPointers: Order of checks on INSERT: **defaults** fill missing columns, then **NOT NULL**, **CHECK**, **UNIQUE**, and finally the **foreign key**.
SQLSTATEs to know: **23502** not null, **23514** check, **23505** unique, **23503** foreign key, **23P01** exclusion.
`CHECK` passes on NULL. Plain `UNIQUE` allows many NULLs unless you add `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`.

Fixed set of values: **enum** (compact, cannot drop labels), **lookup table + FK** (flexible, can carry extra columns) or **CHECK … IN** (simple). A **domain** packages a type with its rules for reuse.
**Going deeper:** [Modelling data: normalization and constraints](/m1/normalization-constraints) covers deferrable, temporal and not-enforced constraints.

lessons.title: Indexes for beginners
lessons.tldr: An **index** is a separate, sorted copy of one or more columns, with a pointer from each entry to its row, like the index at the back of a book. It lets PostgreSQL jump to the few rows a query needs instead of reading the whole table, at the price of extra disk space and slower writes.

visualizer.title: Reading the whole book vs using its index
visualizer.interaction: Step through the same 100,000-row table. Watch **Pages read** and **Rows thrown away** change as an index appears, and see when the planner decides not to use it.

presets.label: 1. No index: Seq Scan
presets.lookFor: Look for **Seq Scan**, **Rows Removed by Filter: 99999** and **Buffers: shared hit=935**: every page of the table was read to return one row.

presets.label: 2. Add an index
presets.lookFor: Now it says **Index Scan using customers_email_idx**, with an `Index Cond` instead of a `Filter`. Buffers drop from 935 to about 4, and the cost from 2185 to about 8.

presets.label: 3. Ranges and the tipping point
presets.lookFor: One day (about 55 rows) uses a **Bitmap Heap Scan** on the new index. Four years (80% of rows) goes back to a **Seq Scan**: reading everything is cheaper than jumping around.

presets.label: 4. Multicolumn: leading column first
presets.lookFor: With both columns, `Index Searches: 1`. With only `city`, PostgreSQL 18 skips through the index country by country, so **Index Searches** is much higher (14 here). Put the column you always filter on first.

presets.label: 5. Functions and expression indexes
presets.lookFor: The first plan is a Seq Scan: an index on `email` does not help `lower(email)`. After indexing the expression itself, the same query uses an **Index Scan**.

presets.label: 6. What the indexes cost
presets.lookFor: The five indexes together are bigger than the table itself. Every one of them must be updated on each INSERT, so add indexes for the queries you actually run.

production.title: An order-history page that slowed down every month
production.problem: Page loads crept from 20 ms to over a second. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` showed a **Seq Scan** on `orders` reading every page and removing millions of rows by filter, for every page view.
production.outcome: The plan reads one customer's newest 20 index entries and their rows, a few dozen pages, no matter how large the table grows. Load time no longer depends on total order count.

pitfalls.title: Indexing every column "just in case"
pitfalls.fix: Index for real queries you have looked at with EXPLAIN. Find indexes that are never scanned and drop them.

pitfalls.title: A function or cast on the indexed column
pitfalls.fix: Rewrite the condition to leave the column bare (`created_at >= $1 AND created_at < $1 + 1`) or create an index on the exact expression.

pitfalls.title: Expecting the index to always be used
pitfalls.fix: Check how many rows the query really returns. Make sure statistics are fresh with `ANALYZE`. A Seq Scan for a big result is correct, not a bug.

pitfalls.title: Plain CREATE INDEX on a busy table
pitfalls.fix: Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` in production. It takes longer but lets writes continue.

keyPointers: A **Seq Scan** reads every page; an **Index Scan** walks a B-tree (root → internal → leaf) and jumps to the matching rows.
An index pays off when a query needs a **small fraction** of the rows. For most of the table, a Seq Scan is cheaper and the planner picks it.
In EXPLAIN, `Index Cond` means the index did the filtering; `Filter` plus a big **Rows Removed by Filter** means rows were read and thrown away.
Multicolumn indexes are sorted by the **first column first**. Functions on a column need an **expression index**. Every index slows writes.
**Going deeper:** [Designing indexes](/m4/index-design) and [Reading EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)](/m4/explain-analyze).

lessons.title: Views, sequences and identity
lessons.tldr: A **view** is a named, saved query you can select from like a table, and a **sequence** is a counter that hands out unique numbers for id columns. Views give every query the same well-tested definition of things like "active products", and sequences let many sessions get unique ids at once without coordinating.

visualizer.title: Tickets from a counter, windows onto a table
visualizer.interaction: In the sequence lab, try a rollback and a failed insert and watch the gaps, then switch to `serial` and type an id by hand. In the view lab, write through the view with and without **WITH CHECK OPTION**.

presets.label: Identity: RETURNING the new id
presets.lookFor: The new row gets **id 5**. `RETURNING` gives it back without a second query. The identity column is filled from a sequence named `products_id_seq`.

presets.label: Gaps: rollbacks and failures
presets.lookFor: The rolled-back insert used **6** and the failed one used **7**, so Rug gets **8**. Sequence values are never handed back.

presets.label: serial vs GENERATED ALWAYS
presets.lookFor: Identity ALWAYS refuses a hand-typed id (**428C9**). `serial` accepts it, then the sequence later hands out the same 1 and collides (**23505**). The retry gets 2.

presets.label: A view is a saved query
presets.lookFor: The view has no data of its own. The UPDATE through it changed the row in `products`, because a view over one table with plain columns is **automatically updatable**.

presets.label: WITH CHECK OPTION
presets.lookFor: The first Sofa was stored in `products` but the view cannot show it (count 0). The checked view refuses it with **44000**.

presets.label: Not every view is updatable
presets.lookFor: Aggregates, `DISTINCT`, `GROUP BY`, joins and `LIMIT` make a view read-only (**55000**). It is still perfectly good for reading.

presets.label: Materialized view: a stored copy
presets.lookFor: A materialized view saves the result when created. It stays the same until `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` re-runs the query.

production.title: An integer id column about to run out
production.problem: At 2.1 billion rows the sequence would reach the limit, and every insert would fail with `nextval: reached maximum value of sequence` (SQLSTATE 2200H). Gaps from rollbacks and retries made it arrive sooner than the row count suggested.
production.outcome: A daily check on `pct_used` gives months of warning instead of an outage. A `bigint` identity allows about 9.2 quintillion values, far more than any table will need.

pitfalls.title: Expecting ids without gaps
pitfalls.fix: Never use a sequence id as a "no gaps" business number. If the law requires gapless numbers, keep a counter row and update it under a lock inside the same transaction, accepting that inserts queue up behind it.

pitfalls.title: Manual ids with serial
pitfalls.fix: After loading rows with explicit ids, move the sequence past the largest one. Prefer identity `ALWAYS`, which refuses manual ids unless you write `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`.

pitfalls.title: `SELECT *` in a view does not pick up new columns
pitfalls.fix: List columns explicitly, and recreate the view (`CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`) when you want a new column in it.

pitfalls.title: Reading stale numbers from a materialized view
pitfalls.fix: Refresh on a schedule that matches how fresh the data must be. Add a unique index so you can use `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY`, which does not block readers.

keyPointers: New tables: `id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY`. `serial` is the older shorthand and lets manual ids collide with the sequence.
`nextval()` is **never rolled back**, so ids have gaps. Use `INSERT … RETURNING id` to get the new id in one round trip.
A **view** stores a query, not data. Simple single-table views are **updatable**; add `WITH CHECK OPTION` to reject rows the view could not show.
A **materialized view** stores the result and needs `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` to catch up.
**Going deeper:** [Views and materialized views](/m6/views-matviews) shows how the rewriter turns a view into its query.

lessons.title: Changing a schema safely
lessons.tldr: Every `ALTER TABLE` takes a **lock** on the table, and some forms also **rewrite** or **scan** every row while holding it. Knowing which changes are instant, which ones block traffic, and the two-step recipes that avoid blocking lets you change a live database without an outage.

visualizer.title: What does this ALTER really do?
visualizer.interaction: In the planner, pick a change and compare **One statement** with the **Safe recipe**. Then open **Lock queue** to see how a quick ALTER can still stall a whole application.

presets.label: 1. Which lock does an ALTER take?
presets.lookFor: Run inside a transaction so the lock is still held when we look. `AccessExclusiveLock` blocks every other session, even plain SELECTs, until the transaction ends.

presets.label: 2. Rewrite or not?
presets.lookFor: The file number stays the same for the constant default: only the catalog changed. The volatile default gets a **new file number**, because every row was copied into a new file.

presets.label: 3. Type changes
presets.lookFor: Widening a `varchar` keeps the same file. `int` to `bigint` changes how every row is stored, so the table and its indexes are rewritten.

presets.label: 4. NOT NULL without a long lock
presets.lookFor: Step 1 is instant, and new rows with a NULL `status` are rejected from then on. Step 2 scans the table under **ShareUpdateExclusiveLock**, which lets reads and writes continue. `convalidated` goes from false to true: every old row is now proven.

presets.label: 5. Foreign key in two steps
presets.lookFor: `convalidated` goes from false to true. During validation, `orders` holds ShareUpdateExclusive and `customers` only light read locks (AccessShare, RowShare): no writes were blocked.

presets.label: 6. Index without blocking writes
presets.lookFor: `CONCURRENTLY` must run on its own, outside `BEGIN … COMMIT`. If it fails it leaves an index with `indisvalid = false` that you must drop and retry.

presets.label: 7. Guard rails for migrations
presets.lookFor: Put these at the top of every migration. A migration that cannot get its lock within 2 s fails fast (SQLSTATE **55P03**) instead of queueing the whole application behind it.

production.title: A one-line migration that took the API down
production.problem: A nightly analytics query was still reading `orders`. The ALTER waited for it, and every API request touching `orders` queued behind the waiting ALTER. For four minutes the connection pool was exhausted and the API returned errors.
production.outcome: Later migrations sometimes needed two or three attempts, but none stalled traffic for more than the 2-second timeout.

pitfalls.title: A quick ALTER behind a long transaction
pitfalls.fix: Always `SET lock_timeout` before DDL and retry on failure. Find blockers with `pg_blocking_pids()`.

pitfalls.title: A volatile default rewrites the table
pitfalls.fix: Add the column without a default, `SET DEFAULT` for new rows, then backfill old rows in batches.

pitfalls.title: A failed CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
pitfalls.fix: Check `pg_index.indisvalid`, drop the invalid index, fix the cause and build it again.

pitfalls.title: Renaming or dropping what running code still uses
pitfalls.fix: Expand, then contract: add the new column, deploy code that writes both and reads the new one, backfill, and only then drop the old column in a later release.

keyPointers: Most `ALTER TABLE` forms take **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE**, which blocks even SELECT. The danger is how *long* it is held, and how long it *waits*.

Instant (catalog only): add a nullable column, add a column with a **constant** default, widen `varchar`, drop or rename a column. Rewrites: **volatile** defaults, identity columns, most type changes.
For constraints on big tables: `ADD … NOT VALID`, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` (reads and writes continue). For indexes: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.
Start every migration with `SET lock_timeout`, keep each step small, and retry on SQLSTATE 55P03.
**Going deeper:** [Heavyweight locks and the conflict matrix](/m5/table-locks) explains every lock mode and which ones conflict.

modules.title: Querying & Data Manipulation
modules.summary: What INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE really do, and how joins, CTEs, window functions and LATERAL compose.

lessons.title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE: what really happens
lessons.tldr: Every write in PostgreSQL appends or stamps **row versions**: INSERT adds a tuple, DELETE sets its `xmax`, and UPDATE does both, while `RETURNING` hands the affected rows (old and new, in 18) straight back. Knowing this explains real behaviour you will meet: why updates bloat tables, why an upsert burns sequence values, and why MERGE and `ON CONFLICT` are not interchangeable.

visualizer.title: Eight statements, one heap page
visualizer.interaction: Step through real statements and watch row versions, the RETURNING output and the identity sequence. Click a version to inspect its `xmin`/`xmax`. Note the xids: one statement, one transaction, even when MERGE does three different things.

presets.label: UPDATE makes a new version
presets.lookFor: Three tuples for two rows. The old apple (lp 1) has `xmax` set and `t_ctid` pointing at its replacement, lp 3.

presets.label: RETURNING old and new
presets.lookFor: For UPDATE both sides are filled. `SET qty = qty` changes nothing, yet the row moves to a new ctid: every UPDATE writes a version. `WITH (OLD AS o, NEW AS n)` renames the qualifiers, which you need inside trigger functions. For DELETE `new.*` is NULL. Always alias `old.x` and `new.x`: two output columns both named `qty` collide in most clients.

presets.label: Upsert and the sequence gap
presets.lookFor: apple is updated (old values present), fig is inserted. The sequence advanced for both proposed rows, so fig gets a higher id than you might expect: one value was burned on apple. Both paths report `INSERT 0 n`; `old.id IS NOT NULL` tells them apart. Before 18 the usual trick was `xmax = 0`: an inserted row has no xmax, an updated one carries the upsert's lock.

presets.label: MERGE + merge_action()
presets.lookFor: One row per action taken. Rows that match no WHEN clause are silently skipped. After the earlier presets pear is already gone, so it shows up as NOT MATCHED and is skipped (its delta is negative).

presets.label: Cardinality violations
presets.lookFor: Both fail with SQLSTATE `21000`. DO UPDATE and MERGE refuse to change one row twice in a statement. `UPDATE … FROM` would silently apply just one match.

presets.label: One transaction, one xid, one clock
presets.lookFor: A read-only transaction has **no xid** (NULL) until its first write. Both rows share one `xmin`. `now()` is frozen at transaction start, so it repeats exactly in the second statement; only `clock_timestamp()` keeps moving. After ROLLBACK the rows are gone but the ids are not given back, and the failed CHECK insert burns one more.

presets.label: UPDATE … FROM and DELETE … USING
presets.lookFor: FROM and USING are the same idea: extra tables joined into the write. `SET i.qty = …` fails (`42703`) because a qualified name after SET means a field of a composite column; write `SET qty = …`. Rows with no match in the joined table are not touched. Forgetting the join condition would pair every target row with every source row.

presets.label: Move rows with a CTE
presets.lookFor: DELETE and INSERT run in **one statement and one transaction**. The archive only ever receives what RETURNING passed along.

production.title: Idempotent stock ingestion for a warehouse feed
production.problem: The first version ran SELECT, then INSERT or UPDATE, row by row. Two overlapping runs both saw "no row" for a new SKU and one failed with a unique violation. Feeds with the same SKU twice also crashed an `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` rewrite with `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time`.
production.outcome: One statement per batch, no read-then-write race (ON CONFLICT guarantees an atomic insert-or-update), and a complete audit trail. Expect gaps in `inventory.id`: every conflicting row still consumed a sequence value. That is harmless for a surrogate key.

pitfalls.title: Expecting gapless ids from a sequence
pitfalls.fix: Use identity/sequence values only as surrogate keys. If you need a gapless business number, allocate it from a counter row updated inside the same transaction (`UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1 … RETURNING n`), and accept that this serializes writers.

pitfalls.title: UPDATE … FROM silently picks one match
pitfalls.fix: Deduplicate the source first (`DISTINCT ON (sku) … ORDER BY sku, updated_at DESC`), or use MERGE, which raises a cardinality violation instead of guessing.

pitfalls.title: One huge UPDATE bloats the table
pitfalls.fix: Batch it: a CTE selects `ctid`s with `ORDER BY … FOR UPDATE LIMIT 5000`, the UPDATE joins on `ctid`, and the loop repeats with VACUUM between batches.

pitfalls.title: UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE
pitfalls.fix: Run ad-hoc fixes inside `BEGIN`, check the tag (and `RETURNING`), then COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Write the WHERE clause first.

pitfalls.title: Get-or-create with a no-op DO UPDATE
pitfalls.fix: Use `DO NOTHING RETURNING id` and fall back to a SELECT when nothing came back. Under concurrency the fallback SELECT can miss a row committed after the statement's snapshot, so retry once.

pitfalls.title: Treating MERGE as a concurrency-safe upsert
pitfalls.fix: Use `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` for concurrent upserts. Use MERGE for batch synchronisation, where you need DELETE or `NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE`.

keyPointers: INSERT writes a tuple, DELETE sets its **xmax**, UPDATE does both: the old version stays until VACUUM.
`RETURNING` works on all four commands; PostgreSQL 18 adds `old.*` and `new.*` (old is NULL for INSERT, new is NULL for DELETE).
`ON CONFLICT (cols)` infers its **arbiter** unique index; `EXCLUDED` is the proposed row; DO UPDATE never touches one row twice.
MERGE gives each candidate row one status and runs the **first** matching WHEN clause; `merge_action()` tells you which.
Sequences are **not gapless**: upserts, failed inserts and rollbacks all burn values.

lessons.title: Joins, visualized
lessons.tldr: A join pairs rows from two inputs wherever the **join condition is true**, and outer joins then add back the unmatched rows **NULL-extended**, while semi- and anti-joins only ask whether a match exists. Joins are how a normalized schema is read back, and the exact rules (NULL never equals NULL, ON filters before the join and WHERE after it) decide whether a report is right or silently wrong.

visualizer.title: The join matcher
visualizer.interaction: Pick a join type and a filter placement, then step through each left row. Badges show the ON condition in three-valued logic. Compare **LEFT + ON filter** (4 rows) with **LEFT + WHERE filter** (2 rows).

presets.label: Row counts per join type
presets.lookFor: 3, 5, 5, 7, 20: the same numbers the visualizer ends on. Dee and Eli (team_id NULL) never match, because `NULL = 1` is NULL, not true.

presets.label: ON vs WHERE
presets.lookFor: First query: 4 rows, Bears and Wolves kept with NULL players. Second: 2 rows. A WHERE test on the nullable side throws away the NULL-extended rows.

presets.label: Anti-join: find orphans
presets.lookFor: Both return Bears and Wolves, and the second plans as a **Hash Right Anti Join** (an anti-join that hashes the left side). Test a NOT NULL column (`p.id`) for IS NULL, never a nullable one.

presets.label: USING vs NATURAL
presets.lookFor: `USING (player_id)` prints the join column once. `NATURAL JOIN` joins on **every** same-named column: here `id = id AND name = name`, which never holds, so 0 rows. A column added later can change any NATURAL join silently.

presets.label: Self-join: mentors and teammates
presets.lookFor: The same table appears twice under two **aliases**. LEFT keeps Ana and Eli, who have no mentor. For pairs, `a.id <> b.id` returns (Ana, Ben) and (Ben, Ana); `a.id < b.id` keeps one of each.

presets.label: Fan-out double counting
presets.lookFor: The first query says Lions have 4 players: Ana is counted once per goal. The second gives 2 players and 3 goals.

presets.label: Diff two tables: EXCEPT vs FULL JOIN
presets.lookFor: EXCEPT compares whole rows and treats NULLs as **equal**: 4 rows (Ben's old and new version, Cy, Fay), and Dee (position NULL in both years) is not reported. The keyed FULL JOIN returns 3 rows: Ben changed, Cy removed, Fay added. Joining on all columns reports Dee twice, because `NULL = NULL` is not true. Only `IS DISTINCT FROM` compares NULLs the way EXCEPT does.

production.title: A churn report that lost every quiet customer
production.problem: Someone added `WHERE o.created_at >= date_trunc('month', now())` to restrict the month. The report dropped from 12,400 customers to 8,100. The 4,300 missing customers were exactly the ones with no orders, the at-risk group the report existed to find.
production.outcome: Every customer appears again, with 0 for the quiet ones. The rule to remember: a WHERE predicate that is not true for NULL turns a LEFT JOIN into an inner join.

pitfalls.title: Filtering the nullable side in WHERE
pitfalls.fix: Put right-side restrictions in the `ON` clause. Keep `WHERE` for left-side filters and for deliberate `IS NULL` anti-join tests.

pitfalls.title: NATURAL JOIN after a schema change
pitfalls.fix: Write `USING (col)` or an explicit `ON`. Both survive unrelated column additions.

pitfalls.title: Fan-out inflates aggregates
pitfalls.fix: Aggregate each child in a subquery or LATERAL first, then join the totals. Or use `count(DISTINCT …)` when that is truly what you mean.

pitfalls.title: Expecting NULL keys to match
pitfalls.fix: Use `a.region IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.region` if NULLs should pair up, knowing it cannot use a plain hash or merge join as efficiently.

pitfalls.title: Set operators without parentheses
pitfalls.fix: Parenthesize each side: `(A EXCEPT B) UNION ALL (C EXCEPT D)`. Use UNION ALL when the two halves cannot overlap.

pitfalls.title: A self-join that lists every pair twice
pitfalls.fix: Use `ON a.id < b.id` to keep each pair once (and never pair a row with itself).

keyPointers: INNER keeps pairs where ON is **true**; LEFT/RIGHT/FULL add unmatched rows **NULL-extended**; CROSS is N × M.
ON decides *matching*; WHERE filters *after* the join. They differ only for outer joins.
`NULL = NULL` is NULL, so NULL keys never join. Use `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` deliberately.
`EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS` are **semi- and anti-joins**: they never duplicate the left row.
Prefer `USING` or `ON` over `NATURAL`; join algorithms (nested loop, hash, merge) are covered in m4.

lessons.title: Subqueries: scalar, IN, EXISTS, ANY/ALL
lessons.tldr: A subquery is a query nested inside another: a **scalar** subquery yields one value, while `IN`, `EXISTS`, `ANY` and `ALL` turn a whole row set into a true, false or NULL test. They let you ask "is there a matching row?" directly, and the planner rewrites most of them into semi- and anti-joins, except `NOT IN`, whose NULL rules make it both slower and a classic source of empty results.

visualizer.title: NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS, one row at a time
visualizer.interaction: Pick an operator and step through the customers. Each comparison is shown in three-valued logic. Start with **NOT IN** and the NULL present, then flip to **NOT EXISTS**.
