presets.label: The NOT IN trap
presets.lookFor: 0 vs 1,713. One refund row with a NULL `customer_id` makes every NOT IN test NULL. Filtering the NULLs out, or using NOT EXISTS, gives the right answer.

presets.label: Three-valued truth table
presets.lookFor: NULL when nothing matches and a NULL is present; true or false when a match decides it. Against an empty set, IN and ANY are false and ALL is true, even for a NULL left side. EXISTS is true for a row of NULLs.

presets.label: Plans: semi, anti, SubPlan
presets.lookFor: IN becomes a **Semi Join**, NOT EXISTS an **Anti Join**. NOT IN stays a Filter with a hashed SubPlan, which the planner cannot reorder.

presets.label: Scalar subqueries
presets.lookFor: Ava gets NULL (no rows, not 0). A scalar subquery that returns 2+ rows fails with SQLSTATE `21000` only when it runs, so it can pass tests on small data.

presets.label: ANY / ALL with arrays
presets.lookFor: `= ANY(array)` is the parameter-friendly form of IN: one bind parameter instead of a list. `>= ALL` finds the rows that are at least every value.

presets.label: ANY / ALL are min / max in disguise
presets.lookFor: Managers earn 55,000 to 60,000. `> ALL` means above the **highest** (only Bob). `> ANY` means above the **lowest** (Bob, Liam, Jack). `= ANY` is IN (Charlie). `< ALL` is below the lowest (8 people), `< ANY` below the highest (11). `SOME` is a synonym for ANY.

presets.label: Correlated subquery vs window
presets.lookFor: The first plan shows `SubPlan 1` with `loops=287`, one per joined refund: the inner join and average run again for every row. The window version joins once, sorts once and computes every country average in one **WindowAgg**. Both return the same 143 rows.

presets.label: Subquery in FROM
presets.lookFor: A derived table: aggregate per customer first, then average per country. The planner may flatten simple FROM subqueries into the outer query.

production.title: A suppression list that suppressed everyone
production.problem: One day the campaign sent zero emails. A new import path had written a single unsubscribe row with `customer_id` NULL (the address could not be linked). From then on every `NOT IN` test was NULL, and the query returned nothing. No error and no warning.
production.outcome: Correct results whatever the list contains. The plan changes from a filter with a hashed SubPlan to a Hash Anti Join, which the planner can reorder and which does not degrade to a per-row SubPlan when the list outgrows `work_mem`. With 2,000 customers and one NULL row in the list, the old query returns 0 rows and the new one 1,713.

pitfalls.title: NOT IN with a nullable column
pitfalls.fix: Use `NOT EXISTS`, or add `WHERE col IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery, and declare the column NOT NULL if NULL has no meaning.

pitfalls.title: Scalar subquery returning several rows
pitfalls.fix: Make the subquery provably single-row (aggregate, `LIMIT 1` with an `ORDER BY`, or a unique key in the WHERE), or turn it into a join or LATERAL.

pitfalls.title: Correlated subquery in the select list on a big table
pitfalls.fix: Aggregate once and join (`LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, sum(amount) … GROUP BY 1)`), use a window function (`avg(x) OVER (PARTITION BY key)`), or index the correlation column. Check `loops=` in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

pitfalls.title: Side effects inside EXISTS
pitfalls.fix: Keep subqueries side-effect free. Do writes in data-modifying CTEs or separate statements.

keyPointers: `EXISTS` is true if at least one row comes back and is **never NULL**; the select list inside it does not matter.
`IN` = `= ANY`, `NOT IN` = `<> ALL`. With a NULL in the list and no match, both give **NULL**.
Empty subquery: `IN`/`ANY` → false, `NOT IN`/`ALL` → true.
A scalar subquery with 0 rows is NULL; with 2+ rows it is an **error**.
IN/EXISTS plan as **semi-joins**, NOT EXISTS as an **anti-join**; NOT IN stays a SubPlan filter.

lessons.title: CTEs: inlined vs MATERIALIZED
lessons.tldr: A **common table expression** (`WITH name AS (…)`) names a subquery for one statement, and since PostgreSQL 12 the planner **inlines** it when it is referenced once and has no side effects, otherwise it **materializes** it once. CTEs exist to make complex queries readable and to chain data-modifying steps in one statement, and the `MATERIALIZED` / `NOT MATERIALIZED` keywords let you decide when the planner may see through them.

visualizer.title: One CTE, five plans
visualizer.interaction: Step through the same CTE planned five ways, then a data-modifying CTE. Watch rows read and shared buffers per plan: the same 20,000-row table, five very different amounts of work.

presets.label: Inlined (default)
presets.lookFor: No CTE node at all: the plan is a Bitmap Index Scan, exactly as if you wrote `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42`.

presets.label: MATERIALIZED fence
presets.lookFor: A `CTE c` subplan scans all 20,000 rows into a tuplestore (`Storage: Memory`), then `CTE Scan` filters. Shared hits go from about 42 to 128.

presets.label: Two references
presets.lookFor: Default: CTE Scan twice over a materialized copy (128 buffers). NOT MATERIALIZED: a Nested Loop of two primary-key Index Scans (6 buffers).

presets.label: When materializing wins
presets.lookFor: The expensive aggregate runs **once** (one HashAggregate over 20,000 rows) and both references read the 500-row result. Inlining would aggregate twice.

presets.label: Same snapshot
presets.lookFor: Inside the statement the table still shows 1.99, RETURNING shows 3.98, and the next statement sees 3.98. Sub-statements cannot see each other's writes.

presets.label: Move rows atomically
presets.lookFor: DELETE and INSERT commit together or not at all. Seven days of orders move: 468 rows, leaving 19,532.

presets.label: Parent and children in one statement
presets.lookFor: The generated `invoice_id` flows from one INSERT to the next through RETURNING, never back to the client. The foreign keys are checked at the end of the statement, so the child rows may reference a parent inserted in a sibling CTE. If any part fails, nothing is written.

production.title: Removing CTE fences from a multi-tenant dashboard
production.problem: On PostgreSQL 11 every CTE was an optimization fence. Each request scanned and materialized all tenants' events, then threw away 99% of them. Someone had also added `MATERIALIZED` everywhere "for safety" while preparing the upgrade, which kept the old behaviour.
production.outcome: At 20,000 rows the gap is already 42 shared buffers inlined vs 128 materialized for one customer. The materialized cost grows with the whole table while the inlined cost grows only with one tenant's rows, so the saving grows with the number of tenants in the table.

pitfalls.title: Using a CTE as a "temporary table" for speed
pitfalls.fix: Decide with EXPLAIN. If you need computed-once semantics for an expensive or volatile expression, write `AS MATERIALIZED` explicitly.

pitfalls.title: A fence left behind by an old query
pitfalls.fix: Use `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` (if duplicated work is cheap), move the filter inside the CTE, or remove the volatile call.

pitfalls.title: Reading your own writes inside one statement
pitfalls.fix: Pass data along with `RETURNING` and select from the CTE name, not from the table. Never modify the same row in two sub-statements: which change wins is unspecified.

pitfalls.title: ORDER BY inside the CTE
pitfalls.fix: Sort in the outer query. Keep ORDER BY inside a CTE only where it feeds `LIMIT` or an order-sensitive step in that same CTE.

keyPointers: Default: a side-effect-free, non-recursive CTE referenced **once** is **inlined**; referenced 2+ times it is **materialized** once.
`AS MATERIALIZED` forces a fence; `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` forces inlining of every reference.
Volatile functions, data-modifying statements and recursion always materialize.
Data-modifying CTEs run once, to completion, on the **same snapshot**; use RETURNING to pass rows on.
In EXPLAIN, a `CTE Scan` node means materialized; no CTE node means inlined.

lessons.title: Recursive CTEs
lessons.tldr: A `WITH RECURSIVE` query is a non-recursive term `UNION [ALL]` a recursive term, evaluated **iteratively**: each pass feeds only the previous pass's new rows (the **working table**) back into the recursive term until no new rows appear. It is how SQL walks trees and graphs of unknown depth (org charts, bills of materials, routes) in one statement, and the `CYCLE` and `SEARCH` clauses make loops and ordering explicit.

visualizer.title: Working table, intermediate table, result
visualizer.interaction: Step through the algorithm one pass at a time. Start with the org chart, then switch to the graph and compare **UNION ALL** (runs forever), **UNION** and the **CYCLE** clause.

presets.label: Everyone under Raj
presets.lookFor: 6 rows in four passes: Raj (depth 0), Omar and Ivy, Zoe and Kai, then Noor. The fifth pass finds nobody and the loop stops.

presets.label: Self-join: one level per join
presets.lookFor: Two joins find Omar, Ivy, Zoe and Kai, and miss Noor on level 3. The recursive version adds 1, 2, 2, 1 rows per pass and stops when a pass adds nothing. In the plan, **Recursive Union** runs the recursive term against a **WorkTable Scan**: the previous pass's rows only.

presets.label: Path to the top
presets.lookFor: Walking **upwards** is the same algorithm with the join reversed: Noor → Zoe → Omar → Raj → Maya.

presets.label: SEARCH DEPTH / BREADTH FIRST
presets.lookFor: `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST` adds an `ord` column (the path of ids) to sort by, giving an indented outline. Use `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST` to order level by level. Never rely on the natural output order.

presets.label: CYCLE detection
presets.lookFor: 5 rows. The row that returns to A has `is_cycle = true` and is not expanded. Without the CYCLE clause this query never terminates.

presets.label: UNION vs UNION ALL
presets.lookFor: With only `node`, UNION discards the repeat of A and stops after 4 rows. Add `hops` and no row ever repeats, so UNION no longer protects you. The LIMIT works only because the outer query stops fetching.

presets.label: A calendar without gaps
presets.lookFor: A counter with a stop condition in WHERE. For plain series, `generate_series` is simpler and faster.

production.title: Expanding a bill of materials for a manufacturer
production.problem: The application walked the tree with one query per level. A deep product took 9 round trips, and a data-entry error that made an assembly contain itself sent the loop spinning until the request timed out.
production.outcome: One round trip whatever the depth, and a cyclic definition terminates with `is_cycle = true` rows that a check can alert on. Add an index on `parts(assembly_id)`: the recursive term joins the working table to it once per level.

pitfalls.title: Infinite recursion on cyclic data
pitfalls.fix: Add `CYCLE col SET is_cycle USING path`, or a depth limit in the recursive term (`WHERE depth < 20`). Do not rely on a LIMIT in the outer query: it stops working as soon as the outer query sorts or joins.

pitfalls.title: Relying on breadth-first output order
pitfalls.fix: Add `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY id SET ord` (or BREADTH FIRST) and `ORDER BY ord` in the outer query.

pitfalls.title: Expecting UNION to stop a loop
pitfalls.fix: Track visited nodes explicitly with `CYCLE`, or keep the CTE's columns to the node key only when that is all you need.

pitfalls.title: Anchor and recursive term with columns in a different order
pitfalls.fix: Name the CTE columns once (`WITH RECURSIVE sub(id, manager_id) AS …`) and list them in the same order in both terms.

keyPointers: Shape: **non-recursive term** `UNION [ALL]` **recursive term**; only the recursive term may reference the CTE, once.
Each pass reads only the **working table** (last pass's new rows); recursion ends when a pass produces nothing.
UNION drops rows that duplicate **any earlier row**; UNION ALL keeps everything.
`CYCLE col SET is_cycle USING path` stops loops; `SEARCH DEPTH|BREADTH FIRST BY col SET ord` gives a sortable order.
Recursive CTEs are always materialized; data-modifying statements cannot be recursive.

lessons.title: Window functions and frames
lessons.tldr: A **window function** computes a value for every row from a set of related rows (its partition, and for aggregates and value functions a **frame** inside it), without collapsing rows the way GROUP BY does. It answers "compared with its neighbours" questions in one pass: rankings, running totals, moving averages, previous-row deltas and top-N per group, where a self-join or correlated subquery would be slower and harder to read.

visualizer.title: The window frame explorer
visualizer.interaction: Click a row to make it current, then change mode, bounds, offset and EXCLUDE. Start with **Default frame** on Sony VAIO (a three-way tie at 700), then compare **Running total**.

presets.label: Rows stay, unlike GROUP BY
presets.lookFor: GROUP BY returns 3 rows. The window version returns all 11, each with its group's average attached (Laptop 850, Smartphone 500, Tablet 350).

presets.label: Ranking with ties
presets.lookFor: Lenovo and Sony tie at 700: row_number 1,2 (arbitrary order), rank 1,1,3,4 (gap), dense_rank 1,1,2,3 (no gap). `percent_rank` = (rank − 1) / (rows − 1), so the first row is always 0. `cume_dist` = rows up to the last peer / rows: 0.5 for both 700s. `ntile(3)` over 4 rows makes buckets of 2, 1, 1: bigger buckets come first.

presets.label: The default frame trap
presets.lookFor: All three 700 rows show `range_default` = 3550 (peers share the frame end), while `rows_running` differs across them, in an order PostgreSQL does not guarantee. `last_default` is just the current row's last peer; `last_whole` is HP Elite everywhere.

presets.label: Cheapest per group
presets.lookFor: Window functions run after WHERE, so filtering on the rank needs a subquery. dense_rank keeps **both** 700s in Laptop; row_number would silently pick one.

presets.label: LAG: year over year
presets.lookFor: The first year of each group has no previous row, so `lag` returns NULL (pass a third argument for a default). `lag` and `lead` ignore the frame. They look at the previous **row**, not the previous year: if 2019 were missing, 2020 would be compared with 2018. And with `ORDER BY year DESC`, `lag` returns the following year.

presets.label: Percent of total in one pass
presets.lookFor: `sum(…) OVER ()` puts the grand total (20.8) on every row, so no CROSS JOIN to a total subquery is needed. Changing only the window to `PARTITION BY band` switches the denominator to the band total: Stills is 30.3% of all earnings but 48.5% of CSNY. The second query works because windows run **after** GROUP BY: CSNY 62.5%, PPM 37.5%.

presets.label: Fill gaps: last known value
presets.lookFor: `count(temperature)` skips NULLs, so the running count only rises on a real reading: every NULL row inherits the group of the last reading. `first_value` within that group carries 22.50 forward twice and 23.10 once. A plain `lag` is no fix: after two NULLs in a row it returns NULL.

presets.label: Moving window: ROWS vs RANGE
presets.lookFor: Compare with the explorer's presets: ROWS counts rows, RANGE compares price values, GROUPS counts distinct prices.

production.title: Deduplicating a change-data feed: latest row per key
production.problem: The first query used a correlated subquery `WHERE changed_at = (SELECT max(changed_at) … WHERE customer_id = c.customer_id)`. It ran one subquery per row, and returned two rows when two changes shared a timestamp.
production.outcome: One scan and one sort instead of one subquery per row, and a deterministic answer when timestamps tie, thanks to the `change_id` tie-breaker. An index on `(customer_id, changed_at DESC, change_id DESC)` can provide the order and skip the sort.

pitfalls.title: last_value returns the current row
pitfalls.fix: Add `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`, or use `first_value(…)` with the ORDER BY reversed.

pitfalls.title: Running totals that jump on ties
pitfalls.fix: Use `ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` and add a unique tie-breaker to the ORDER BY (`ORDER BY booked_at, id`) so the order is deterministic.

pitfalls.title: Filtering on a window function in WHERE
pitfalls.fix: Compute the window function in a subquery or CTE, then filter in the outer query.

pitfalls.title: A ROWS window treated as a time window
pitfalls.fix: Use `RANGE BETWEEN interval '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` on a date column, or fill the gaps with `generate_series` first.

pitfalls.title: DISTINCT does not deduplicate a row_number()
pitfalls.fix: Deduplicate first, then number: `SELECT price, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY price) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT price FROM products) p` (8 rows instead of 11). Or use `dense_rank()`, which gives equal values the same number.

pitfalls.title: Top-N with LIMIT on a tie
pitfalls.fix: Add a unique tie-breaker (`ORDER BY price DESC, product_id`), or include every tie with `FETCH FIRST 4 ROWS WITH TIES` (6 rows here) or `rank() <= 4`.

keyPointers: Window functions run **after** WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING and never collapse rows.
**Peers** are rows equal under the window ORDER BY; rank functions give peers the same value.
Default frame with ORDER BY: `RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` to the current row's **last peer**; without ORDER BY: the whole partition.
`ROWS` counts rows, `RANGE` compares values (one ORDER BY column for offsets), `GROUPS` counts peer groups; `EXCLUDE` trims the result.
Frames matter for aggregates and `first_value`/`last_value`/`nth_value`, not for `row_number`, `rank`, `lag` or `lead`.

lessons.title: LATERAL joins
lessons.tldr: A `LATERAL` subquery in FROM may reference columns of the FROM items to its left, so it is evaluated **once per outer row**, like the body of a for-each loop. It exists for questions a plain join cannot express, such as "the latest N rows for each parent" or "expand this row's array", and with the right index it is often the fastest top-N-per-group plan.

visualizer.title: LATERAL as a for-each loop
visualizer.interaction: Step through the outer rows and watch the subquery re-run with each `a.id`. Compare **CROSS JOIN LATERAL** (5 rows) with **LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true** (6 rows), and try the plain JOIN to see the error.

presets.label: Without LATERAL: an error
presets.lookFor: `42P01: invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table "a"`. A plain FROM subquery cannot see its neighbours.

presets.label: Latest 2 per account
presets.lookFor: 5 rows. Umbrella has no purchases, so CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops it.

presets.label: Keep empty parents
presets.lookFor: 6 rows: Umbrella appears with NULLs. `ON true` is required syntax for LEFT JOIN; the real condition lives inside the subquery.

presets.label: loops=4 and the index
presets.lookFor: A **Nested Loop** whose inner side shows `loops=4`. With the index the inner side is an Index Scan that reads at most 2 entries per account, no sort.

presets.label: Functions are implicitly lateral
presets.lookFor: A set-returning function in FROM may always reference earlier items, with or without the keyword. `WITH ORDINALITY` adds a bigint position column. Initech has no tags: dropped by the comma form, kept by LEFT JOIN.

presets.label: Split a CSV column (and the text trap)
presets.lookFor: `string_to_array` returns `text[]`, so the first query compares **strings**: North's minimum is '-1' (true value −16) and West's maximum is '9' (true 16). Casting to `int[]` fixes it. The last query numbers each reading with `WITH ORDINALITY` and keeps the top one per station: hour 8 at West (16°), hour 7 at South (33°).

presets.label: LATERAL vs a window function
presets.lookFor: Same 5 rows. The window version numbers **every** purchase and then filters; LATERAL + LIMIT with an index reads only the rows it returns. With few parents and many children per parent, LATERAL wins.

production.title: An activity feed: latest 3 events per followed user
production.problem: The original query ranked all posts of all followed accounts with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY author_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)` and then filtered `rn <= 3`. For a user following prolific accounts it sorted hundreds of thousands of rows to return 600.
production.outcome: The plan becomes a Nested Loop with an Index Scan inside, `loops` = number of followed accounts, and at most 3 index entries read per loop: about 600 rows touched instead of every post of those authors.

pitfalls.title: CROSS JOIN LATERAL silently drops parents
pitfalls.fix: Use `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (…) p ON true` to keep every outer row, NULL-extended.

pitfalls.title: LATERAL without a supporting index
pitfalls.fix: Create an index on `(correlation_column, sort_column DESC)` so each loop is a short index scan, and check `loops=` in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

pitfalls.title: Referencing the right side from a RIGHT/FULL join
pitfalls.fix: Rewrite with the LATERAL item on the right side of an inner or LEFT join.

pitfalls.title: Max-then-join-back for "latest per group"
pitfalls.fix: Use LATERAL with `ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1`, or `DISTINCT ON (account_id) … ORDER BY account_id, created_at DESC, id DESC`. Both return exactly one row per key, with a deterministic tie-breaker.

keyPointers: `LATERAL` lets a FROM subquery reference columns of FROM items **to its left**; it runs once per outer row.
Set-returning functions in FROM are **implicitly lateral**; the keyword is optional there.
CROSS JOIN / comma LATERAL drops rows with an empty result; `LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true` keeps them.
Top-N per group: LATERAL + `ORDER BY … LIMIT n` + index on `(key, sort DESC)` → Nested Loop with Index Scan.
`WITH ORDINALITY` numbers the rows of a function in FROM (bigint, from 1).

lessons.title: Aggregates, FILTER and GROUPING SETS
lessons.tldr: An **aggregate** folds many input rows into one value per group, and `FILTER`, ordered-set aggregates and `GROUPING SETS` / `ROLLUP` / `CUBE` control which rows feed it and which groupings are produced. Together they turn a dozen report queries (totals, subtotals, conditional counts, medians) into one pass over the data, provided you respect the NULL rules that make `count(col)` differ from `count(*)` and `sum` of nothing NULL.

visualizer.title: Grouping sets, one set at a time
visualizer.interaction: Pick ROLLUP, CUBE or your own GROUPING SETS and step through each set. Watch which input rows fold together, and how `grouping()` tells a subtotal's NULL from Baz's real NULL size.

presets.label: CUBE and grouping()
presets.lookFor: 12 rows. Two rows read `NULL, NULL`: sum 8 with g = 2 (Baz's real NULL size, grouped by size) and sum 58 with g = 3 (the grand total).

presets.label: Four queries, or one GROUPING SETS
presets.lookFor: The UNION ALL plan is an **Append** of four aggregates, each over its own Seq Scan. GROUPING SETS returns the same 12 rows from one **MixedAggregate** (one Hash Key per set, `Group Key: ()` for the total) over a single scan. `CUBE (brand, size)` is shorthand for exactly these four sets.

presets.label: ROLLUP with labels
presets.lookFor: ROLLUP gives detail rows, a subtotal per brand and a grand total. The plan is one **MixedAggregate** with a Hash Key per set: a single scan.

presets.label: count(*) vs count(col)
presets.lookFor: `count(*)` counts rows, `count(col)` skips NULLs (40 orders have no amount, so `avg` ignores them: 104.63). Dividing `sum` by `count(*)` counts those 40 rows as zeros and gives 102.54. Over zero rows `sum` is **NULL**, not 0; only count returns 0.

presets.label: FILTER: one pass, many counts
presets.lookFor: Each aggregate sees only the rows its FILTER allows, all in a single scan. Clearer than `sum(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`, and it works with any aggregate: `array_agg(x) FILTER (…)` skips rows, while the CASE trick would collect NULLs. FILTER is standard SQL, not a PostgreSQL extension.

presets.label: Median and mode
presets.lookFor: Ordered-set aggregates sort their input. `percentile_cont` interpolates between the two middle values; `percentile_disc` returns an actual input value. There is no separate `median()`: `percentile_cont(0.5)` is the median.

presets.label: WHERE vs HAVING
presets.lookFor: Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE (`42803`): WHERE filters input rows, HAVING filters groups after aggregation. HAVING cannot use the output alias `total` either (`42703`), because the SELECT list is computed after HAVING. Logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. ORDER BY can use output names, and so can GROUP BY as a PostgreSQL extension; WHERE and HAVING cannot.

presets.label: DISTINCT ON: first row per key
presets.lookFor: One row per region: the first after sorting, here the largest order. The DISTINCT ON expressions must lead the ORDER BY; add a tie-breaker (`id`) for a deterministic pick.

production.title: A finance dashboard: from 9 queries to 1
production.problem: It ran 9 separate queries (one per breakdown and metric), each scanning the orders table, and the page took seconds. Subtotal rows were found with `WHERE month IS NULL`, which also caught orders whose month column was legitimately NULL.
production.outcome: One scan feeding one MixedAggregate instead of nine scans. For 4 regions and 2 months that is 4 × 2 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 rows. Subtotal rows are identified by `level`, so a real NULL can never be mistaken for a total.

pitfalls.title: sum() of no rows is NULL
pitfalls.fix: Wrap it: `coalesce(sum(amount), 0)`. For arrays, `coalesce(array_agg(x), '{}')`. The same applies to FILTER: a month with no matching rows gives `sum(x) FILTER (…)` = NULL, so a CASE or FILTER rewrite of a report that used to print 0 needs the COALESCE back.

pitfalls.title: count(col) where count(*) was meant
pitfalls.fix: Use `count(*)` to count rows; use `count(col)` only when "rows with a value" is what you mean.

pitfalls.title: Telling subtotals apart with IS NULL
pitfalls.fix: Use `grouping(col)`: 1 means the NULL is a subtotal placeholder, 0 means it is data.

pitfalls.title: Order-sensitive aggregates without ORDER BY
pitfalls.fix: Put the order inside the call: `string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)`, `array_agg(x ORDER BY ts)`.

pitfalls.title: BETWEEN on a timestamp drops the last day
pitfalls.fix: Use a half-open range: `created_at >= '2026-10-01' AND created_at < '2026-11-01'`. It is exact for dates and timestamps, never double-counts, and an index can use it.

pitfalls.title: Integer division in ratios
pitfalls.fix: Make one operand numeric first (`100.0 * count(*) FILTER (…) / count(*)`) and guard the denominator with `NULLIF(count(*), 0)`, which turns 0 into NULL so the ratio is NULL instead of an error.

keyPointers: `count(*)` counts rows; `count(col)` counts non-NULL values; every other aggregate returns **NULL** on no rows.
`agg(...) FILTER (WHERE ...)` restricts one aggregate's input; WHERE restricts all rows; HAVING filters groups.
`ROLLUP (a, b)` = (a,b), (a), (); `CUBE (a, b)` = all 4 subsets; all sets run in one scan.
`grouping(a, b)` is a bitmask: bit = 1 when that column is **not** grouped in the current row's set.
Ordered-set aggregates: `percentile_cont` interpolates, `percentile_disc` picks a value, `mode()` returns the most frequent.

modules.title: Practical SQL Patterns
modules.summary: Pagination, upserts, pivots, gaps and islands, hierarchies, search, job queues and a performance checklist.

lessons.title: Pagination: OFFSET vs keyset
lessons.tldr: **Keyset pagination** fetches the next page with `WHERE (created_at, id) < ($last_ts, $last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT n`, so it seeks to where the previous page ended instead of counting rows from the start. `OFFSET n` must produce and discard n rows on every request, so deep pages get linearly slower and shift when rows are inserted, while a keyset page costs the same at page 10 000 as at page 1.

visualizer.title: Skipping rows vs seeking to a key
visualizer.interaction: Press **Go deeper** to jump from page 1 to page 10 000, then switch to **Keyset** and compare rows read and buffers. Below, add a row between two page loads and watch OFFSET serve a duplicate.

presets.label: OFFSET: page 1 vs page 5 000
presets.lookFor: Both use the index in order. Page 1 touches about 4 buffers. Page 5 000 shows the Index Scan with **actual rows=50000** under a Limit that returns 10: every skipped row was fetched, about 600 buffers.

presets.label: Keyset: seek to the last row seen
presets.lookFor: The row comparison becomes an **Index Cond**: one descent, 10 rows, about 4 buffers. Same rows as OFFSET 49990, at roughly 1/150 of the work.

presets.label: Why the tiebreaker matters
presets.lookFor: The row comparison keeps **50 010** rows. `created_at` alone silently drops id 50010, which shares the cursor's timestamp, and the AND version drops it too (and, with other data, many more). Always end the sort key with a unique column, and compare with a row constructor, not with a hand-written AND.

presets.label: Previous page (seek backwards)
presets.lookFor: The inner query walks the same index **backward** (`Index Scan Backward`), so one index serves both directions. The outer sort only reorders 10 rows.

presets.label: Page drift with OFFSET
presets.lookFor: The first row of page 2 has `already_seen = true`: the insert pushed every row one position down. With deletes the opposite happens and a row is skipped. Keyset pages cannot drift.

presets.label: Totals: exact vs estimate
presets.lookFor: An exact `count(*)` reads the whole table or index on every request. `reltuples` is free and maintained by VACUUM and ANALYZE. Fetching `LIMIT n + 1` answers "has next" exactly: true in the middle of the feed, false on the last page (only ids 1 to 10 remain).

presets.label: Cursor (inside one transaction)
presets.lookFor: A cursor keeps its position on the server, so the second FETCH continues where the first stopped. Unless declared `WITH HOLD`, it lives only inside the transaction: good for exports and batch jobs, not for stateless web pages.

production.title: An activity feed API that timed out on deep pages
production.problem: Each deep page re-reads every row before it, so walking the feed is quadratic: a client fetching all 800 000 pages makes the server produce about 50 × 800 000² / 2 ≈ 16 trillion rows to deliver 40 million. Users also report duplicated and missing items, because new events shift OFFSET positions while they scroll.
production.outcome: Every page costs one index descent plus 51 rows, whatever its depth. On the playground table page 10 000 drops from 1 210 shared buffers to 4, and duplicated or skipped items disappear because the cursor names a row rather than a position.

pitfalls.title: A sort key that is not unique
pitfalls.fix: Append a unique column (the primary key) to both the ORDER BY and the cursor, and index the same columns in the same order.

pitfalls.title: Hand-expanding the row comparison
pitfalls.fix: Use the row constructor. It is also what lets the planner use the multicolumn index as a single range.

pitfalls.title: Mixed sort directions
pitfalls.fix: Pick one direction for all keyset columns when you can. Otherwise write the expanded `OR` form and index `(score DESC, id ASC)` to match.

pitfalls.title: An exact total on every request
pitfalls.fix: Show "more results" with `LIMIT n + 1`, or an estimate from `pg_class.reltuples` or `EXPLAIN`. Compute exact totals asynchronously if the product really needs them.

keyPointers: `OFFSET n` still **computes and discards** n rows. The cost grows with page depth.
Keyset = **unique sort key** + **row comparison** `(a, b) < ($1, $2)` + an **index in the same order**.
Offsets drift when rows are inserted or deleted between requests. A keyset cursor names a row and cannot drift.
Use `LIMIT n + 1` for "has next page", and `reltuples` for an approximate total.
Going deeper: [Index design](/m4/index-design) covers multicolumn order and why the index must match the ORDER BY.

lessons.title: Upserts and de-duplication
lessons.tldr: An **upsert** (`INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`) inserts a row or, if a unique index already holds its key, updates the existing row instead, atomically and in one statement. It needs a **unique index** to act as the arbiter, so cleaning existing duplicates (rank with `row_number()`, delete every rank above 1) and adding that index is usually the first step.

visualizer.title: One batch through ON CONFLICT, and a duplicate clean-up
visualizer.interaction: Step through a batch: each proposed row probes the unique index, then inserts, updates or is skipped. Switch to **Clean duplicates** to rank, delete and lock the door with an index.

presets.label: 1. Find duplicates
presets.lookFor: 2 240 rows but only 2 000 people. Raw `DISTINCT email` sees 2 200 values because case and spaces hide 200 of the 240 duplicates; the other 40 are exact copies.

presets.label: 2. Rank: who survives?
presets.lookFor: The newest row per person gets **rn = 1**. The `id DESC` tiebreaker makes the choice deterministic when timestamps tie. Change the ORDER BY to keep the oldest or the most complete row instead.

presets.label: 3. Delete the losers
presets.lookFor: `DELETE 240` leaves 2 000 rows for 2 000 people. On a table with no key, `ctid` (the physical row address) does the same job inside one statement. Never store a ctid: UPDATE and VACUUM FULL change it.

presets.label: 4. Lock the door
presets.lookFor: The unique **expression index** makes case-insensitive duplicates impossible: the insert fails with `23505 duplicate key value`. It is also the arbiter the next preset uses.

presets.label: 5. Upsert with RETURNING old/new
presets.lookFor: user1 is updated (`old_plan` pro, `new_plan` team), New.Person is inserted (`inserted` = true) and user2 returns nothing because its plan did not change. The sequence advanced by 3 for 3 proposed rows, although only one was inserted.

presets.label: 6. Same key twice in one statement
presets.lookFor: Two staging rows map to one key, so the first form fails with `21000: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time`. `DISTINCT ON` keeps the newest row per key and the statement succeeds.

presets.label: 7. MERGE: sync with delete
presets.lookFor: MERGE runs the **first** WHEN clause that matches for each row and can also delete target rows missing from the source (`NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE`). It does not have ON CONFLICT's guarantee against concurrent inserts, so prefer ON CONFLICT for plain upserts.

production.title: A nightly CRM import that kept creating duplicate customers
production.problem: Duplicates kept appearing: the check is case-sensitive, two tools send the same lead in one batch, and two import workers running in parallel both pass `NOT EXISTS` before either commits. Sales saw the same company twice, with split activity history.
production.outcome: The unique index makes a duplicate impossible, even with parallel workers: one worker inserts, the other takes the update path. On the playground data the clean-up removes 240 of 2 240 rows (11%), and later imports never add them back.

pitfalls.title: Check-then-insert races
pitfalls.fix: Use `INSERT … ON CONFLICT`, which turns a concurrent insert of the same key into the update (or no-op) path, backed by a unique index.

pitfalls.title: No arbiter index
pitfalls.fix: Write the same expression: `ON CONFLICT ((lower(email)))`, or create the matching unique index. Prefer inference over `ON CONSTRAINT name`, so the index can be swapped later.

pitfalls.title: Updating rows that did not change
pitfalls.fix: Add a WHERE to the update so unchanged rows are skipped. They are still locked, but no new version is written.

pitfalls.title: Gaps in ids after upserts
pitfalls.fix: This is harmless: ids are identifiers, not counters. If gaps really matter, filter known keys out of the batch first, and do not use ids for numbering visible to users.

keyPointers: `ON CONFLICT` needs a **unique index** whose columns or expression match the conflict target exactly.
`excluded` is the proposed row. A `DO UPDATE … WHERE` that is false skips the update but still locks the row.
A batch with the same key twice fails with **cannot affect row a second time**. De-duplicate with `DISTINCT ON` first.
Clean duplicates with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY keep_first)` and delete `rn > 1` by primary key (or `ctid` within one statement).
Going deeper: [INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE: what really happens](/m3/dml-lifecycle) shows the row versions each of these writes.

lessons.title: Pivots and reports
lessons.tldr: A **pivot** turns rows into columns: `sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'web')` per output column, over a **date spine** from `generate_series`, gives one report row per period with zeros where nothing happened. Reports go wrong in the gaps, so the spine, `coalesce`, window shares and `lag` over a complete series are what keep the totals, percentages and month-over-month changes honest.

visualizer.title: Build a monthly report, one SQL idea at a time
visualizer.interaction: Step from long GROUP BY rows to a pivot, then add the date spine, totals, shares and month-over-month change. The last step shows what `lag` does when the spine is missing. Click a cell to see what feeds it.

presets.label: 1. Pivot with FILTER
presets.lookFor: Six rows, one per month. April `store` is **NULL**: `sum` over zero rows is NULL. `count` is the only aggregate that returns 0 for no rows.

presets.label: 2. Missing rows vs the spine
presets.lookFor: Plain GROUP BY yields 17 groups, the spine 18. April store is there with `sales = 0` and `orders = 0`, so charts and averages see the closure instead of skipping it.

presets.label: 3. crosstab (tablefunc)
presets.lookFor: The two-argument form maps each value to its category column, so order within a month does not matter. Columns must still be declared by hand: crosstab cannot invent columns at run time.

presets.label: 4. Subtotals with ROLLUP
presets.lookFor: The extra row has `grouping(month) = 1`: it is the grand total, computed in the same pass. Labelling it with `grouping()` rather than `coalesce` keeps it apart from real NULL keys.

presets.label: 5. Percent of the month
presets.lookFor: Window aggregates compute the denominators without collapsing rows: `PARTITION BY month` for the month share, an empty `OVER ()` for the share of everything. Web is about 50% each month.

presets.label: 6. Month over month: the lag trap
presets.lookFor: With the spine, April shows `-13468` and May `+13739`. Without it there are only five rows and May shows **+271**: `lag` returned March, the previous *row*, and the closure vanished from the report.

production.title: A revenue dashboard that hid a lost channel
production.problem: One region stopped selling for two weeks after a payment outage. Those weeks produced no rows, so the chart joined the points on either side, the average per week went *up*, and `lag` compared the recovery week with the week before the outage, showing healthy growth.
production.outcome: The outage weeks show as zeros and the recovery week as a jump from 0. In the playground, the same mistake turns the store's real -13 468 / +13 739 swing into a quiet +271.

pitfalls.title: Missing periods silently disappear
pitfalls.fix: Build a spine with `generate_series` (cross joined with the dimension values) and LEFT JOIN the facts to it.

pitfalls.title: NULL where the report needs 0
pitfalls.fix: Wrap the aggregate: `coalesce(sum(amount), 0)`. Use `NULLIF(denominator, 0)` when dividing.

pitfalls.title: crosstab with the one-argument form
pitfalls.fix: Use the two-argument form `crosstab(source_sql, category_sql)`, or plain `FILTER` aggregates, which never shift.

pitfalls.title: Time-zone boundaries
pitfalls.fix: Set the reporting zone explicitly: `date_trunc('month', ordered_at, 'Europe/Berlin')`, or `SET TimeZone` in the reporting session.

keyPointers: Pivot with one `agg(...) FILTER (WHERE key = …)` per output column: one scan, no shifting columns.
Build a **date spine** with `generate_series`, cross join the dimensions, LEFT JOIN the facts, `coalesce` to 0.
`lag()` means the previous **row**. It is only "the previous period" over a complete spine.
Shares come from window aggregates: `x / sum(x) OVER (PARTITION BY period)`. Subtotals come from `ROLLUP` in the same pass.
Going deeper: [Aggregates, FILTER and GROUPING SETS](/m3/aggregates-grouping) and [Window functions and frames](/m3/window-functions).

lessons.title: Gaps and islands
lessons.tldr: **Gaps and islands** problems ask for runs of consecutive values (streaks, sessions, busy periods) and the holes between them, and window functions solve them in one pass. The tricks are `value − row_number()` (constant inside a run), `lag()` plus a running `sum` (a new group starts at every large gap), and `range_agg` for overlapping intervals.

visualizer.title: Streaks, sessions and merged ranges
visualizer.interaction: Step through the **row_number difference** trick on one user's login days. Then drag the session timeout and watch sessions split and merge, and toggle bookings to see `range_agg` fuse them.

presets.label: 1. Streaks: day − row_number
presets.lookFor: `grp` stays constant inside a run. Four streaks come out: 3, 2, 4 and 1 days, exactly the visualizer's islands. `date − integer` is a date, so the anchor is a date too.

presets.label: 2. Longest streak per user
presets.lookFor: `PARTITION BY user_id` restarts the numbering per user. `DISTINCT ON` keeps the longest run per user. One sort and one window pass over all 18 872 login rows; streak lengths vary from user to user.

presets.label: 3. Gaps: the days in between
presets.lookFor: `lead()` pairs each day with the next one, so a gap is any step larger than 1: 03-04, 03-07..08 and 03-13..14. The `EXCEPT` form lists the five missing days one by one.

presets.label: 4. Sessionize clicks (30 min)
presets.lookFor: The first click has a NULL gap, so the CASE falls through to 1. Five sessions, the same as the visualizer at 30 minutes. Try 10 or 60 minutes and compare with the slider.

presets.label: 5. Sessions per user, all users
presets.lookFor: The same two-step pattern over 5 014 clicks: flag with `lag`, number with a running `sum`, then aggregate per (user, session). Result: 655 sessions of 7.7 clicks on average, the longest 28 minutes. A named `WINDOW` keeps the two window calls consistent.

presets.label: 6. Merge overlapping bookings
presets.lookFor: Room A collapses to three busy blocks, as in the visualizer: 09:00 to 12:00 (booking 3 is only adjacent, yet merges), 13:00 to 14:00 and 15:30 to 16:30. The `&&` self-join finds the two overlapping pairs, `*` gives the overlap.

presets.label: 7. Forbid overlaps with EXCLUDE
presets.lookFor: With the overlaps removed, an **exclusion constraint** rejects any new booking that overlaps one in the same room (`23P01`). The adjacent slot is fine, because `[)` ranges that touch do not overlap. `btree_gist` provides `=` for the GiST index.

production.title: Streak badges and session analytics for a learning app
production.problem: The nightly job pulled 60 M activity rows over the network and took hours. A second job counted sessions with a fixed 30-minute window per hour bucket, which split sessions that crossed the hour and disagreed with the product definition.
production.outcome: Both jobs become one sort and one window pass per table, and only one row per user is transferred. Sessions now match the product rule exactly, because a session boundary is defined by the gap between events, not by the clock.

pitfalls.title: Duplicate values break the difference trick
pitfalls.fix: De-duplicate first (`SELECT DISTINCT user_id, day`), or use `dense_rank()` instead of `row_number()`.

pitfalls.title: Timestamps instead of days
pitfalls.fix: Reduce to the unit first: `ts::date` (or `date_trunc` in the user's time zone) and de-duplicate. For irregular events use the `lag` + running-sum pattern with a threshold.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting PARTITION BY
pitfalls.fix: Partition every window by the entity, and order by the time column plus a tiebreaker. A named `WINDOW w AS (…)` keeps them identical.

pitfalls.title: Merging ranges in application code
pitfalls.fix: Store `tstzrange` with `[)` bounds, merge with `range_agg`, and enforce "no overlap" with `EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)`.

keyPointers: Streaks: `value − row_number() OVER (ORDER BY value)` is constant inside a run. GROUP BY it.
Sessions: flag rows where `lag()` is NULL or too far back, then a running `sum(flag)` numbers the groups.
Gaps: `lead(value)` minus value > 1, or a `generate_series` EXCEPT the values present.
Intervals: `range_agg` fuses overlapping and adjacent ranges, and `EXCLUDE … WITH &&` forbids overlaps.
Going deeper: [Window functions and frames](/m3/window-functions) explains partitions, ordering and the running-sum frame.

lessons.title: Trees and graphs
lessons.tldr: A tree can be stored as an **adjacency list** (each row points to its parent), a **materialized path** (`ltree`: each row stores its whole path) or a **closure table** (one row per ancestor and descendant pair). They trade read cost against write cost: the adjacency list is trivial to change but needs a recursive query per level, while paths and closure rows answer "the whole subtree" with one index scan and must be rewritten when a subtree moves.

visualizer.title: One org chart, three storage models
visualizer.interaction: Click any node to fetch its subtree. In **Adjacency list** press Next iteration to watch the recursive CTE descend one level at a time. Switch models to compare one index scan, and the rows each model must rewrite to move the subtree.

presets.label: 1. Subtree with a recursive CTE
presets.lookFor: `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST` adds an ordering column so the output reads like an outline. The second query shows the levels: 1, 4, 16, 64, 256 = 341 people under n6.

presets.label: 2. What the recursion costs
presets.lookFor: A **Recursive Union** over a **WorkTable Scan**: the join runs `loops=5` (one per level) and probes `staff_parent` once per row, `Index Searches: 341`, about 770 buffers in total. Without the `parent_id` index every level would be a full scan.

presets.label: 3. Subtree with ltree
presets.lookFor: `<@` means "is a descendant of (or equal to)". One **Bitmap Index Scan** on the GiST index returns all 341 rows for about 16 buffers. ltree comparison sorts in tree order, so `ORDER BY path` is depth-first.

presets.label: 4. Ancestors and patterns (ltree)
presets.lookFor: `@>` finds ancestors, `~` matches an **lquery** pattern (`*{1}` = exactly one more label). Seven levels from 1 person to 4 096.

presets.label: 5. Closure table reads
presets.lookFor: 36 409 pairs for 5 461 people: about 6.7 rows per person, growing with depth. Both directions are one B-tree lookup (about 10 buffers), and `depth` comes for free.

presets.label: 6. Graphs: stop cycles with CYCLE
presets.lookFor: `a → b → c → a` is a loop. The **CYCLE** clause tracks visited `dst` values in `path` and marks the row that revisits one with `is_cycle = true`, so recursion stops instead of running forever.

presets.label: 7. Move a subtree in each model
presets.lookFor: Watch the row counts: `UPDATE 1` for the adjacency list, `UPDATE 341` for paths, and `DELETE 682` plus `INSERT 682` (2 ancestors × 341) for the closure table.

production.title: A product catalogue with deep category trees
production.problem: Each request ran a recursive CTE to collect descendant categories, then joined products. Top-level pages walked thousands of categories level by level, and the breadcrumb needed a second recursive query, together the slowest queries on the site.
production.outcome: On the playground tree the subtree read drops from about 770 buffers and 341 index probes to about 16 buffers in one scan. The cost moves to writes: a move rewrites every path in the moved subtree, which is acceptable for data that changes a few times a day.

pitfalls.title: No index on parent_id
pitfalls.fix: `CREATE INDEX ON staff (parent_id);` Foreign keys do not create this index for you.

pitfalls.title: Cycles in graph data
pitfalls.fix: Add `CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path`, or carry an array of visited ids and stop on `id = ANY(path)`. Add a depth limit as a safety net.

pitfalls.title: Paths and closure rows drift from the truth
pitfalls.fix: Change the parent and the derived rows in **one transaction**, ideally inside a trigger or a single function, and add a periodic consistency check.

pitfalls.title: ltree label rules
pitfalls.fix: Build paths from ids or slugs (`n42`, `garden_tools`), never from free-text names.

keyPointers: **Adjacency list**: one `parent_id` column, cheap writes, a recursive CTE per read (index `parent_id`).
**ltree**: `path <@ x` = subtree, `path @> x` = ancestors, GiST index, rewrite the subtree on a move.
**Closure table**: every ancestor/descendant pair with depth, B-tree lookups both ways, the most rows and the costliest moves.
For graphs with loops use the **CYCLE** clause, and `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST` for outline order.
Going deeper: [Recursive CTEs](/m3/recursive-ctes) shows the working table and termination rules step by step.

lessons.title: Searching text
lessons.tldr: Text search in PostgreSQL comes in three shapes: **prefix** matching (`LIKE 'abc%'`, a B-tree range), **substring and typo** matching (trigrams from `pg_trgm`, GIN or GiST), and **word** matching (full-text search with `tsvector` and `tsquery`). Each needs a different index, and the wrong pairing silently falls back to reading the whole table, so choosing the pattern first and the index second is the whole game.

visualizer.title: Trigrams, similarity, and which index serves which query
visualizer.interaction: Type a misspelled product name (or press **Next typo**) to see its trigrams and the similarity of each candidate. Then click cells in the matrix: every number is a measured buffer count with only that index present.

presets.label: 1. Prefix search and the collation trap
presets.lookFor: The column uses the **en_US** collation, whose sort order is not plain character order, so the ordinary B-tree cannot turn a prefix into a range: Seq Scan. The `text_pattern_ops` index compares character by character, and the plan shows `Index Cond: (name ~>=~ … AND name ~<~ …)`.

presets.label: 2. Substring search with trigrams
presets.lookFor: No B-tree can serve a leading `%`. The **GIN trigram** index looks up the trigrams of `impact driver` and intersects their posting lists: the scan drops from 323 to about 91 buffers, and the gap widens with selective terms.

presets.label: 3. ILIKE and regex reuse it
presets.lookFor: The same index serves `ILIKE` and POSIX regexes (trigrams are extracted from the pattern). A selective substring like `#1234` (11 rows) costs about 16 buffers instead of 323.

presets.label: 4. Typos: similarity and "did you mean"
presets.lookFor: `%` keeps words above `pg_trgm.similarity_threshold` (0.3); `<->` (1 − similarity) orders them nearest first. Ordering by distance with an index needs **GiST**: GIN cannot return rows in distance order.

presets.label: 5. Patterns an index cannot help
presets.lookFor: Inside `%xr%` the two letters never form a complete trigram, so the index has nothing selective to look up and the planner reads the table (about 320 buffers). With three letters (`gun`) the trigram index is usable again. Ask for at least three characters in search boxes.

presets.label: 6. Full-text search with ranking
presets.lookFor: Full-text search matches **words** after stemming, so `drills` would match `drill`. `websearch_to_tsquery` accepts search-box syntax (`-hammer` excludes). The GIN index on the stored `tsvector` serves `@@`.

production.title: A product search box that read the whole catalogue
production.problem: In production every keystroke of the type-ahead ran a full sequential scan. An ordinary B-tree on `name` was never used, because leading wildcards cannot use a B-tree. Users also got nothing back for small typos such as "drivr".
production.outcome: Substring searches stop scanning the table: on the playground a selective substring drops from 323 buffers to about 16, and the saving scales with the catalogue. Typos now return suggestions instead of an empty page.

pitfalls.title: LIKE prefix ignores the B-tree
pitfalls.fix: Add `CREATE INDEX … (name text_pattern_ops)` for pattern queries (keep the ordinary index for `<`, `>` and ORDER BY), or declare the column `COLLATE "C"` if linguistic sorting is not needed.

pitfalls.title: GIN where you need distance order
pitfalls.fix: Use `gist_trgm_ops` for nearest-neighbour queries, or filter with `%` on a GIN index and sort the (small) result.

pitfalls.title: Very short search terms
pitfalls.fix: Require a minimum of three characters, or use a prefix search on a `text_pattern_ops` B-tree for very short input.

pitfalls.title: Using LIKE for word search
pitfalls.fix: Use full-text search for natural-language queries: `to_tsvector('english', …) @@ websearch_to_tsquery(…)`, ranked with `ts_rank`.

keyPointers: **Prefix**: B-tree, with `text_pattern_ops` unless the column collation is C.
**Substring, ILIKE, regex**: `gin_trgm_ops`. Patterns need at least one full trigram to be selective.
**Typos**: `similarity()`, `%` (threshold 0.3) and `<->`. Distance ordering needs **GiST**.
**Words**: a stored `tsvector` with a GIN index, `@@ websearch_to_tsquery`, ranked by `ts_rank`.
Going deeper: [Full-text search](/m6/full-text-search) covers parsers, dictionaries and ranking.

lessons.title: Job queues and concurrency patterns
lessons.tldr: A **job queue** in PostgreSQL is a table plus one claim statement, `UPDATE … WHERE id = (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1)`, that lets many workers take different rows without waiting for each other. Around it sit the patterns that make concurrent writes safe: **leases** for crashed workers, **idempotency keys** for retries, **version columns** against lost updates, and **advisory locks** for work that has no row.

visualizer.title: Workers, leases and conflicts on a timeline
visualizer.interaction: Step through three workers claiming jobs with SKIP LOCKED, one crashing mid-job, and the retry that cannot double-charge. Switch to **Optimistic update** and **Singleton job** for the other two patterns.

presets.label: 1. Claim one job
presets.lookFor: The subquery picks and row-locks the oldest open job; the UPDATE turns it into a lease and the statement commits on its own. A second worker running the same statement at the same moment would skip this row and get the next one.

presets.label: 2. What the claim costs
presets.lookFor: The plan uses the small **partial index** `jobs_open`, which contains only the 100 open jobs, not the 49 900 finished ones. A **LockRows** node sits above the scan: that is where locked rows are skipped.

presets.label: 3. Claim a batch
presets.lookFor: Ten jobs per round trip. The locking clause goes **inside** the CTE: a `FOR UPDATE` on the outer query does not reach into WITH queries.

presets.label: 4. Idempotent side effects
presets.lookFor: The first insert returns an id, the retry returns **no row**: the unique key turned a double charge into a no-op the worker can detect. One payment exists.

presets.label: 5. Optimistic concurrency
presets.lookFor: Watch the command tags: `UPDATE 1`, then **`UPDATE 0`** for the stale version. The application must check the row count and retry. The final row is 110, version 9.

presets.label: 6. Advisory locks
presets.lookFor: The same session can take a lock it already holds; session locks **stack**, so two unlocks are needed. Another session would get `false`. The `xact` variant needs no unlock at all.

presets.label: 7. Wake workers with NOTIFY
presets.lookFor: A notification is delivered only when its transaction **commits**, so a worker can never be woken for a job it cannot see yet. Workers still poll occasionally: notifications are not stored for sessions that were not listening.

production.title: An email queue that stalled under load
production.problem: With 20 workers, all of them queued on the same first row: `FOR UPDATE` waits for the lock holder, so throughput was one email at a time. Every worker held a transaction open for the whole SMTP call, which also held back VACUUM, and a worker killed mid-send left an email that was sent twice after restart.
production.outcome: Workers no longer wait for each other, so throughput scales with the number of workers until the mail provider is the limit. No transaction outlives one short statement, and a crashed worker's job is retried after its lease expires without a duplicate email.

pitfalls.title: Holding the lock for the whole job
pitfalls.fix: Claim and commit in one statement, store a lease (`locked_until`), and finish the job with a separate short UPDATE.

pitfalls.title: Jobs that are never retried
pitfalls.fix: Let the claim query also take `running` rows whose lease has expired, count `attempts`, and move rows over a limit to `failed` for inspection.

pitfalls.title: Retries that repeat side effects
pitfalls.fix: Give every side effect an **idempotency key** with a unique index and `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING`. No row back means "already done".

pitfalls.title: Ignoring the row count of an optimistic update
pitfalls.fix: Check the affected row count in the application. On 0, reload, re-apply the change and retry, or show a conflict to the user.

keyPointers: Claim: `UPDATE … WHERE id = (SELECT id … ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING …`, then commit.
Index only open jobs with a **partial index**, use a **lease** for crashes and an **idempotency key** for retries.
Optimistic concurrency: `WHERE version = $read_version`; `UPDATE 0` means someone else won.
Advisory locks lock an idea: `pg_try_advisory_lock(key)` for singleton jobs; session locks stack, `xact` locks free themselves at commit.
Going deeper: [Row locks, SKIP LOCKED and advisory locks](/m5/row-locks-skip-locked) shows how row locks are stored and which modes conflict.

lessons.title: A query performance checklist
lessons.tldr: Most slow queries come from a short list of causes (functions or casts on indexed columns, stale statistics, memory spills and N+1 round trips) and each leaves a recognizable mark in `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` or `pg_stat_statements`. A checklist turns tuning from guesswork into a routine: find the top queries, read the plan for the smell, apply the matching fix, and measure buffers before and after.

visualizer.title: An EXPLAIN smell detector
visualizer.interaction: Pick a smell, read the flagged plan lines, then press **Apply the fix** to see the plan change and the buffer count drop. Every plan was measured on the playground schema.

presets.label: 1. Find the top queries
presets.lookFor: Five statements with different constants collapse into **one normalized entry** (`user_id = $1`, calls = 5). Sort by `total_exec_time` for what costs the most overall, and by `calls` to spot N+1 loops.

presets.label: 2. Function on an indexed column
presets.lookFor: Before: Seq Scan, **Rows Removed by Filter: 9999**, 84 buffers. After the expression index: a Bitmap Index Scan, 3 buffers. The plain `users_email` index never helped `lower(email)`.

presets.label: 3. Casts and type mismatches
presets.lookFor: The cast version filters 59 520 rows (500 buffers); the half-open range is an Index Only Scan (4 buffers). With `4242.0` the filter reads `(user_id)::numeric = 4242.0`: the column is converted, so `orders_user` cannot be used.

presets.label: 4. Stale statistics after a bulk load
presets.lookFor: Before ANALYZE the planner estimates **rows=1** for 20 000 actual rows and runs a Nested Loop with `loops=20000` (about 60 000 buffers). After ANALYZE: a Hash Join, about 270 buffers. Run ANALYZE after every bulk load.

presets.label: 5. Sort spilling to disk
presets.lookFor: At 64 kB the plan says **Sort Method: external merge** with temp read/written buffers. At 8 MB it is an in-memory quicksort. `work_mem` applies per sort or hash node, so raise it per session or per query, not globally.

presets.label: 6. Batch instead of N+1
presets.lookFor: One statement fetches all 50 users' orders: one round trip, one plan, and a single Bitmap Index Scan with `user_id = ANY(…)` that returns every matching row (400 after preset 4's import, 300 without it) for about 300 buffers, against about 500 for 50 separate queries. A join with GROUP BY replaces a per-row loop entirely.

presets.label: 7. Indexes that never get used
presets.lookFor: Indexes with `idx_scan = 0` after a representative workload cost writes and space for nothing (here `users_email`, made redundant by the `lower(email)` index). A primary key or unique index at 0 still enforces its constraint, so keep it. Check replicas too before dropping one.

production.title: A weekly tuning routine for an API database
production.problem: The top of `pg_stat_statements` held three kinds of trouble: a login lookup on `lower(email)` doing a sequential scan on every request, an ORM loop issuing 200 single-row queries per page, and a nightly import after which reports switched to nested loops until autovacuum next analyzed the table.
production.outcome: On the playground data the same three fixes cut the login lookup from 84 to 3 buffers, the report after a bulk load from about 60 000 to 270 buffers, and the page from 50 round trips to 1. The routine catches regressions while they are still small.

pitfalls.title: Tuning from EXPLAIN without ANALYZE
pitfalls.fix: Use `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and compare estimated with actual rows. Wrap writes in `BEGIN … ROLLBACK`, because ANALYZE really executes the statement.

pitfalls.title: Testing on tiny tables
pitfalls.fix: Test with production-sized data, or at least realistic row counts and distributions, and run ANALYZE before reading plans.

pitfalls.title: Raising work_mem globally
pitfalls.fix: Raise it only where needed: `SET LOCAL work_mem = '64MB'` inside the reporting transaction, or `ALTER ROLE reporting SET work_mem = …`.

pitfalls.title: Indexing every column
pitfalls.fix: Index for the queries you actually run (check `pg_stat_statements`), and drop indexes that stay at `idx_scan = 0`.

keyPointers: Find: `pg_stat_statements` sorted by **total time** and by **calls**.
Read: estimated vs **actual rows × loops**, **Rows Removed by Filter**, buffers, **external merge**.
Fix: expression index or half-open range for wrapped columns, matching parameter types, `ANALYZE` after loads, batch N+1.
Measure: compare **shared buffers** before and after; timings vary, buffer counts are stable.
Going deeper: [EXPLAIN ANALYZE](/m4/explain-analyze) and [Planner statistics](/m4/statistics) explain every number in a plan.

modules.title: Foundations & Process Architecture
modules.summary: One postmaster, one process per connection, a shared memory arena, and the helper processes that keep it healthy.

lessons.title: What PostgreSQL is: cluster, client/server, a query's round trip
lessons.tldr: PostgreSQL is a **client/server** database: one server instance manages a **cluster** of databases in a single data directory, and every client connection gets its own server process. Clients send SQL as **plain text** over a small message protocol, and the server parses, plans and executes it and streams rows back, so any language with a socket can talk to it.

visualizer.title: A query's round trip, byte by byte
visualizer.interaction: Step from TCP connect to Terminate. Click any message in the wire log to decode its bytes. Every length follows protocol 3.0 framing exactly.

presets.label: Who and where am I?
presets.lookFor: Every session is one backend process with its own PID, connected to exactly one database as one role. `inet_server_addr()` is NULL when the session did not arrive over TCP (a Unix socket, or this in-process sandbox). Uptime counts from the postmaster start.

presets.label: The query from the visualizer
presets.lookFor: Two rows, so the command tag is `SELECT 2`. In the wire protocol each value travels as text.

presets.label: What lives where
presets.lookFor: initdb creates three databases; `template0` refuses connections. Two tablespaces exist from the start: `pg_default` for database files and `pg_global` for the cluster-wide catalogs (roles, the database list). Schemas belong to one database: this list is only `postgres`'s.

presets.label: Tables are files
presets.lookFor: Each table lives in `base/<database oid>/<relfilenode>` under the data directory. Database `postgres` has OID 5.

presets.label: Describe a table without psql
presets.lookFor: There is no `SHOW TABLES` or `DESCRIBE`: client tools query `information_schema` and `pg_class`. `varchar(80)` reports as `character varying` with max length 80. Each small table is `heap` storage of exactly one 8 kB page; `p` = permanent.

presets.label: One statement, one transaction
presets.lookFor: Outside a block, every statement runs in its own transaction and gets a new xid. Inside BEGIN … COMMIT both reads share one xid.

presets.label: Statement time vs wall clock
presets.lookFor: `now()` is fixed at transaction start. `statement_timestamp()` moves when a new statement arrives. `clock_timestamp()` is the real wall clock.

presets.label: Connection settings
presets.lookFor: `context = postmaster` means the value is fixed at server start. These decide where the postmaster listens and how many backends it may fork.

production.title: The migration that ran against the wrong database
production.problem: A migration created its tables in database `postgres` instead of `app_staging`. The connection string had no database name, and libpq defaults the database to the user name. A later run then failed with `relation does not exist` in the right database.
production.outcome: Misrouted runs now stop on the first statement with a clear message, before any DDL. The stray objects in `postgres` were found with `\dt` and dropped.

pitfalls.title: Expecting cross-database joins
pitfalls.fix: Put related data in one database with several **schemas**. If two databases are truly needed, use `postgres_fdw` or `dblink`.

pitfalls.title: Leaving trust authentication after initdb
pitfalls.fix: Initialize with `initdb -A scram-sha-256 -W`, or edit `pg_hba.conf` before the first start and reload. Check the result in `pg_hba_file_rules`.

pitfalls.title: Remote clients cannot connect
pitfalls.fix: Bind the interface you need, then add the narrowest hba line with `scram-sha-256` and reload.

pitfalls.title: Assuming each line of a script is separate
pitfalls.fix: Send statements one at a time (psql does this), or wrap intentional units in explicit `BEGIN … COMMIT` blocks.

pitfalls.title: Dropping a database you are connected to
pitfalls.fix: Connect to another database such as `postgres`, then run `DROP DATABASE shop WITH (FORCE);` to terminate the remaining sessions.

keyPointers: A **cluster** is one data directory managed by one server instance. initdb creates `postgres`, `template1` and `template0`.
Hierarchy: **cluster → database → schema → object**. Roles and databases are cluster-wide; a connection sees one database.
One **postmaster** listens on port 5432 and forks one **backend** per connection.
Every message is **type byte + Int32 length + payload**. A simple query is `Q` → `T`, `D`…, `C`, `Z`.
Inside the backend a query goes **parse → rewrite → plan → execute**, reading pages through shared buffers.

lessons.title: The postmaster and one process per connection
lessons.tldr: The **postmaster** is the first process of an instance: it starts the auxiliary processes, and it **forks one backend process for every client connection**. Separate processes isolate sessions from each other, so a crashed backend cannot corrupt another one silently, and the postmaster can reset shared memory and restart cleanly.

visualizer.title: A live instance: fork, connect, crash, shut down
visualizer.interaction: Connect clients until the slots run out, leave one idle in a transaction, then **kill -9** a backend and watch the postmaster restart everything. Try the three shutdown modes.

presets.label: My backend in pg_stat_activity
presets.lookFor: This sandbox runs the whole server inside one process, so you see a single **standalone backend**. A normal server lists one row per client backend and per auxiliary process here.

presets.label: Label your session, then find slow ones
presets.lookFor: The second query is the long-running query finder: every non-idle backend, oldest first. Set `application_name` in every service so its rows say which pod they belong to. Here the only active backend is this one, running the finder itself.

presets.label: Every backend type
presets.lookFor: `pg_stat_io` keeps a row for each kind of server process: client backends, background writer, checkpointer, walwriter, autovacuum, the PG18 **io worker**, and more.

presets.label: Idle in transaction
presets.lookFor: Between statements the session is **idle in transaction**: it holds an xid and a `RowExclusiveLock` on `accounts` until COMMIT. Any other session that wants this row waits for it.

presets.label: What a backend costs
presets.lookFor: Each backend owns private memory contexts (catalog caches, plans, sort space). Multiply by the connection count to see why thousands of connections hurt.

presets.label: Which settings need a restart
presets.lookFor: `postmaster` context = set at server start only. `max_connections` sizes shared memory, so changing it needs a restart. `user` settings can be changed per session.

presets.label: Cancel vs terminate
presets.lookFor: Cancel stops the current query and keeps the session. Terminate sends SIGTERM and ends the backend. Without a timeout, `true` only means the signal was **sent**; with `timeout` (ms) it means the process actually exited.

presets.label: Wait events catalog
presets.lookFor: An idle backend waits on `ClientRead`: it is blocked reading the socket for the next Query message. Each auxiliary process has its own main-loop wait event.

production.title: Too many clients during an autoscaling event
production.problem: During a traffic spike the autoscaler added pods. New pods failed health checks with `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`. Most existing backends were **idle**, and a few were **idle in transaction**, holding locks.
production.outcome: With 40 pods sharing a pooler of, say, 120 server connections, the fleet can no longer exceed `max_connections`; abandoned transactions end after 30 seconds, and the superuser reserve stays free for on-call access during incidents.

pitfalls.title: Raising max_connections into the thousands
pitfalls.fix: Keep `max_connections` in the low hundreds and use a connection pooler. Size pools to the number of CPU cores and disks, not to the number of app threads.

pitfalls.title: Sessions left idle in transaction
pitfalls.fix: Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` per role, and find offenders by `xact_start` age.

pitfalls.title: Using kill -9 on a backend
pitfalls.fix: Use `pg_cancel_backend(pid)` to stop the current query, or `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` to end the session cleanly. Never SIGKILL the postmaster itself.

pitfalls.title: pg_terminate_backend returned true, but the session is still there
pitfalls.fix: Pass a timeout so the call waits for the exit, and check the result before the DDL.

pitfalls.title: The Linux OOM killer picks PostgreSQL
pitfalls.fix: Lower `work_mem` and `max_connections`, consider `vm.overcommit_memory = 2`, and protect the postmaster with `oom_score_adj = -1000` while `PG_OOM_ADJUST_FILE` resets children to 0.

keyPointers: **Postmaster** = first process. It forks a **backend** per connection and supervises the **auxiliary** processes.
`max_connections` (default 100) is fixed at start; `superuser_reserved_connections` (3) keeps slots for emergencies.
`pg_stat_activity.state`: **active**, **idle**, **idle in transaction**. The last one holds locks and blocks cleanup.
One backend crash makes the postmaster **terminate everyone and run crash recovery**.
Shutdown modes: **smart** (SIGTERM, wait), **fast** (SIGINT, abort transactions), **immediate** (SIGQUIT, recovery on next start). `pg_ctl restart` = fast stop + start.

lessons.title: Shared memory: buffers, WAL buffers and the commit log
lessons.tldr: At startup the postmaster allocates one **shared memory** segment that every process maps: the **shared buffer pool** of 8 kB pages, the **WAL buffers**, the **commit-log (pg_xact) cache** and the lock tables. Disk is slow and backends are separate processes, so they share one cache of hot pages and pick victims with a cheap **clock-sweep** algorithm instead of each keeping its own copy.

visualizer.title: The buffer pool and its clock sweep
visualizer.interaction: Read and update hot pages, then run a large sequential scan with the ring **off** and watch the hot set get evicted. Reset, scan with the ring **on**, and compare. Click a buffer to pin it.

presets.label: Buffer pool summary
presets.lookFor: 16384 buffers of 8 kB = 128 MB. Usage counts run from 0 to **5**. Most buffers are still unused in a fresh instance.

presets.label: First scan: reads from disk
presets.lookFor: The setup evicted `orders`, so all 192 pages are `shared read`. Each page now sits in a buffer with `usagecount = 1`.

presets.label: Second scan: all hits
presets.lookFor: Now `shared hit=192`. Every access bumped `usagecount` by one: this is the credit the clock sweep spends before evicting a page.

presets.label: UPDATE makes pages dirty
presets.lookFor: Changed pages are **dirty** in memory. The table file on disk is not touched yet; the WAL record is what makes the change durable.

presets.label: CHECKPOINT cleans them
presets.lookFor: The checkpoint wrote every dirty buffer. The pages stay cached, now clean, so the next read is still a hit.

presets.label: Evict and look again
presets.lookFor: Eviction drops the pages from shared buffers (a developer tool, new in 18). The next scan reads them back: `shared read` again.

presets.label: Hit ratio, computed honestly
presets.lookFor: The counters are bigint, so `hit / (hit + read)` truncates to **0**; multiply by `100.0` first. `nullif` avoids a division by zero on a table nobody has read yet. `pg_stat_io` shows the same ratio per process type and context.

presets.label: Shared memory map
presets.lookFor: `Buffer Blocks` is the page pool. `XLOG Ctl` holds the 4 MB of WAL buffers (auto = 1/32 of shared_buffers). `transaction` is the pg_xact commit-log cache.

production.title: A nightly report that flushed the cache
production.problem: Right after the job started, p95 latency of the order API tripled and `pg_stat_io` showed reads jumping for client backends. The report walked the archive through an **index scan**. Only large sequential scans get the bulk-read ring, so every archive page entered the pool like a normal page and the clock sweep pushed the hot set out.
production.outcome: With the report on a replica, the hot set stayed resident on the primary through the night, client-backend reads in `pg_stat_io` stayed flat, and the API latency spike disappeared.

pitfalls.title: Giving shared_buffers most of the RAM
pitfalls.fix: Start at **25% of RAM** on a dedicated server; going above 40% rarely helps. Raise `max_wal_size` with it, and enable huge pages for large pools.

pitfalls.title: work_mem multiplied by everything
pitfalls.fix: Keep the global value modest and raise it for the one query that needs it: `SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB'` inside its transaction.

pitfalls.title: Trusting one global hit ratio
pitfalls.fix: Look per query with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`, per backend type in `pg_stat_io`, and per statement in `pg_stat_statements` (`shared_blks_read`).

pitfalls.title: A hit-ratio query that lies
pitfalls.fix: Use `round(100.0 * hit / nullif(hit + read, 0), 1)`, and read it per table or per backend type rather than as one global number.

pitfalls.title: Transparent huge pages
pitfalls.fix: Disable THP, reserve huge pages with `vm.nr_hugepages` from `postgres -C shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages`, and set `huge_pages = on` to fail fast if they are missing.

keyPointers: `shared_buffers` (default 128MB) is a pool of 8 kB pages shared by all processes. Start at **25% of RAM**.
Each buffer has a descriptor: **tag, refcount (pins), usage_count 0–5, dirty flag**.
**Clock sweep**: skip pinned buffers, decrement usage counts, evict the first unpinned buffer at 0. A dirty victim must be written first.
Large scans, VACUUM and COPY use a small **buffer access strategy ring** so they cannot flush the cache.
Also in shared memory: **WAL buffers** (1/32 of shared_buffers, max 16 MB) and **SLRU caches** such as `pg_xact`. `work_mem` is per backend, not shared.

lessons.title: The background crew
lessons.tldr: Next to the client backends, an instance runs a crew of **background processes**: the walwriter, background writer, checkpointer, autovacuum, archiver, logger and, in PostgreSQL 18, **I/O workers**. They move slow work off the query path, so a commit only waits for one WAL flush while dirty pages, cleanup, statistics and archiving happen later and in bulk.

visualizer.title: Follow one UPDATE through the whole crew
visualizer.interaction: Step through an UPDATE from the first read to the archived WAL segment. Each step lights the process that acts and lists the settings and statistics views that belong to it.

presets.label: The crew and its settings
presets.lookFor: The defaults from the visualizer. This sandbox reports `io_method = sync` because the whole server runs in one process; a normal PostgreSQL 18 server defaults to `worker` with 3 `io_workers`.

presets.label: I/O by process type
presets.lookFor: `pg_stat_io` splits I/O by **process type**, object (relation, temp relation, wal) and context (normal, bulkread, bulkwrite, vacuum). Here one standalone backend does every job. The `wal` rows are new in 18.

presets.label: Who is doing I/O right now?
presets.lookFor: `pg_stat_get_backend_io(pid)` (new in 18) gives one backend's own I/O, in operations and in bytes. `io_combine_limit` (16 × 8 kB) caps how many adjacent blocks one read may merge. `pg_aios` lists I/Os in flight; with `sync` it stays empty.

presets.label: Make work for the crew
presets.lookFor: The first read still shows the old value: statistics lag until the backend flushes them. After the flush, 12,000 dead row versions are visible to autovacuum.

presets.label: Would autovacuum run?
presets.lookFor: Threshold = 50 + 0.2 × 50,000 = **10,050**. With 12,000 dead tuples the launcher would start a worker on its next wake-up.

presets.label: Run the checkpointer's job
presets.lookFor: `CHECKPOINT` forces what the checkpointer does on its timer. The new **redo point** is where crash recovery would start.

presets.label: WAL written so far
presets.lookFor: `wal_fpi` counts full-page images: the first change to a page after a checkpoint logs the whole page. `wal_buffers_full` > 0 would mean WAL buffers are too small.

presets.label: Vacuum by hand
presets.lookFor: This is what an autovacuum worker does for you. Afterwards `n_dead_tup` is back to 0 and the freed space is reusable.

production.title: Checkpoint spikes every few minutes
production.problem: `pg_stat_checkpointer` shows `num_requested` far above `num_timed`: checkpoints are triggered by WAL volume, not time. With `max_wal_size = 1GB` the service fills the allowance in about two minutes, and every checkpoint also restarts full-page writes, so WAL grows even faster.
