production.outcome: Requested checkpoints dropped to near zero, checkpoints ran every 5 minutes, and WAL volume fell because fewer full-page images were written after each checkpoint.

pitfalls.title: Turning autovacuum off
pitfalls.fix: Leave `autovacuum = on`. Tune busy tables with per-table settings such as `ALTER TABLE t SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02)`.

pitfalls.title: Backends doing the background writer's job
pitfalls.fix: Raise `bgwriter_lru_maxpages` and `bgwriter_lru_multiplier`, check checkpoint frequency, and size `shared_buffers` for the working set.

pitfalls.title: A failing archive_command fills the disk
pitfalls.fix: Monitor `pg_stat_archiver.failed_count` and `last_failed_wal`, fix the command, and make sure it returns non-zero exit status only on real failure.

pitfalls.title: Expecting asynchronous I/O to speed up writes
pitfalls.fix: Measure reads, not commits: compare `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` of a cold scan and `pg_stat_io` read times (`track_io_timing = on`). Tune `effective_io_concurrency` and `io_workers` for read-heavy workloads.

pitfalls.title: Expecting io_method to change on reload
pitfalls.fix: Restart the server. Check `SELECT name, setting, pending_restart FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'io_method'` afterwards.

keyPointers: Auxiliary processes: **checkpointer, background writer, walwriter, autovacuum launcher, archiver, logger, startup, walreceiver, walsummarizer**; plus PG18 **io workers**.
A COMMIT waits only for its **WAL flush**. Data pages are written later by the **bgwriter** and the **checkpointer**.
Checkpoints run every `checkpoint_timeout` (5min) or at `max_wal_size` (1GB), spread over `checkpoint_completion_target` (0.9).
Autovacuum: launcher every `autovacuum_naptime` (1min); VACUUM when dead tuples > **50 + 0.2 × reltuples**.
Watch them with `pg_stat_activity.backend_type`, `pg_stat_io`, `pg_stat_bgwriter`, `pg_stat_checkpointer`, `pg_stat_archiver`.

lessons.title: Databases, schemas, search_path and roles
lessons.tldr: A cluster holds isolated **databases**, each database holds **schemas** that act as namespaces, and **roles** are cluster-wide identities whose privileges and memberships decide what a session may touch. These layers let many applications and teams share one server safely, with `search_path` choosing which schema an unqualified name means and `pg_hba.conf` deciding who may connect at all.

visualizer.title: Name resolution, authentication and membership
visualizer.interaction: Resolve names as different roles and search paths, and create a temp table to shadow one. Switch modes to replay connection attempts against `pg_hba.conf`, and to walk the joe / admin / wheel / island membership chain.

presets.label: Databases, templates, per-database settings
presets.lookFor: `CREATE DATABASE` is a file-level copy of `template1` unless told otherwise; `template0` stays pristine and refuses connections. `ALTER DATABASE … SET` stores a default that every **new** session in `shop` picks up. A connection cannot see into `shop` from here.

presets.label: search_path as alice
presets.lookFor: `"$user"` expands to `alice`, which exists, so new tables land there. Since PostgreSQL 15, ordinary roles have **no CREATE on public**: SQLSTATE 42501.

presets.label: Same name, different table, then a temp table
presets.lookFor: alice has no USAGE on `sales`, so it is **silently dropped** from her path and `orders` means `public.orders` (2 rows). bob inherits USAGE from `sales_team` and gets `sales.orders` (5 rows). The temp schema is searched first for relations, so `orders` then hits the empty temp table.

presets.label: The permission ladder: schema, table, sequence
presets.lookFor: Each gate is checked in order: **USAGE** on the schema, then the table privilege. The identity insert works, but the `serial` table also needs **USAGE on its sequence** (42501). In `relacl`, `simon=ar/postgres` reads: simon may a(ppend = INSERT) and r(ead = SELECT), granted by postgres.

presets.label: Grants are snapshots; default privileges are not
presets.lookFor: `ON ALL TABLES` grants on the tables that exist **now**; `customers` was missed. Default privileges apply to tables created later, but only by the role in `for_objects_created_by`. The predefined `pg_read_all_data` covers every table and schema at once.

presets.label: INHERIT vs SET (joe, admin, wheel, island)
presets.lookFor: joe **inherits** admin and island but not wheel (admin→wheel has INHERIT FALSE). joe may **SET ROLE wheel** through the chain, but never island (SET FALSE). `session_user` stays joe while `current_user` changes.

presets.label: Drop a role that owns things
presets.lookFor: The first DROP fails with **2BP01** and the DETAIL lists every dependency: privileges on the schema and table, and the owned table. Both cleanup commands only act on the **current database**, so in production repeat them in each database.

presets.label: Who may connect: pg_hba.conf
presets.lookFor: This sandbox runs with a permissive `trust` file. In production this view is how you test edits before a reload. Schema ACLs: `=U/pg_database_owner` means PUBLIC has USAGE on `public`, but no `C`.

production.title: A read-only reporting role that stays read-only
production.problem: One mistaken `UPDATE` from a notebook changed live data. The application role also owns the tables, so per-table GRANTs drifted every time a migration created a new table.
production.outcome: New tables are readable without any GRANT, writes fail with SQLSTATE 25006 (read-only transaction) or 42501, and the reload-time `pg_hba_file_rules` check showed the `+analysts` line matched before the catch-all reject.

pitfalls.title: CREATE on public in an upgraded database
pitfalls.fix: Revoke it, and give each application its own schema.

pitfalls.title: search_path in SECURITY DEFINER functions
pitfalls.fix: Pin the path on the function and schema-qualify names: `ALTER FUNCTION f() SET search_path = pg_catalog, app;`.

pitfalls.title: pg_hba.conf lines in the wrong order
pitfalls.fix: Put narrow, strong lines first and broad `reject` lines last. Check `pg_hba_file_rules.error`, then `SELECT pg_reload_conf()`.

pitfalls.title: New tables are invisible to the read-only role
pitfalls.fix: Set default privileges **for the role that runs migrations**, or grant the predefined `pg_read_all_data`.

pitfalls.title: Passwords that leak or use MD5
pitfalls.fix: Use psql `\password dana`, which hashes on the client and sends only the SCRAM verifier. Re-set old MD5 passwords so they are stored as SCRAM, and use `scram-sha-256` in `pg_hba.conf`.

pitfalls.title: DROP ROLE fails: role owns objects
pitfalls.fix: In **every** database, run `REASSIGN OWNED BY dana TO app_owner;` then `DROP OWNED BY dana;`. Then `DROP ROLE dana;`. A non-superuser needs CREATEROLE **and** ADMIN OPTION on the role to drop it.

keyPointers: Cluster → **databases** (isolated, one per connection) → **schemas** (namespaces) → objects. **Roles** are cluster-wide.
`CREATE DATABASE` is a file copy of **template1** (no other session may be connected to the source); use **template0** for a new encoding or locale.
`search_path` default `"$user", public`. `pg_temp` (relations only) and `pg_catalog` are searched implicitly first; schemas without USAGE are **silently skipped**.
Since 15, PUBLIC has **no CREATE on public**. Membership has **INHERIT**, **SET** and **ADMIN** options; LOGIN, SUPERUSER, CREATEDB, CREATEROLE are never inherited.

`pg_hba.conf`: **first matching line wins**, no fall-through, no match = rejected; a reload applies edits. Gates for a query: CONNECT on the database, **USAGE** on the schema, then the object privilege.

lessons.title: Modelling data: normalization and constraints
lessons.tldr: **Normalization** splits data into tables so that every fact is stored exactly once, keyed by what determines it, and **constraints** make PostgreSQL enforce that shape on every write. Duplicated facts drift apart under concurrent updates, so a normalized schema with keys, foreign keys and checks turns whole classes of application bugs into immediate, well-defined errors.

visualizer.title: From a messy spreadsheet to 3NF, column by column
visualizer.interaction: Step through the decomposition. Watch each column move to the table of the key it depends on, then see which constraints guard the result. Colours show functional dependencies.

presets.label: The 3NF schema and its constraint names
presets.lookFor: Unnamed constraints get predictable names: `<table>_pkey`, `<table>_<col>_key`, `<table>_<col>_check`, `<table>_<col>_fkey`, `<table>_<col>_not_null`. `contype`: p, u, f, c, and **n** (NOT NULL is a catalog row in 18). Only PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE built an index; the foreign keys did not.

presets.label: Every constraint, fired once
presets.lookFor: Each failure has its own SQLSTATE: **23502** not-null, **23505** unique, **23514** check, **23503** foreign key, **428C9** writing an ALWAYS identity column. The text after `|` is the DETAIL line, which names the offending key or row.

presets.label: Foreign key actions: same data, one clause changed
presets.lookFor: NO ACTION fails with **23503** and names the still-referenced key. SET NULL keeps John and Jane with `client_id` NULL; they now sit at the **end of the heap** (new ctids), because an update writes new row versions. CASCADE deletes David with his client, and the command tag still says `DELETE 1`. RESTRICT fails with **23001**.

presets.label: NULL is not a violation
presets.lookFor: A CHECK passes when its expression is **NULL**, and UNIQUE treats NULLs as distinct by default. `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` makes a second NULL a duplicate.

presets.label: Identity BY DEFAULT and the duplicate-key trap
presets.lookFor: BY DEFAULT accepts a manual id, but the sequence does not see it, so the next default 2 collides (**23505**). The failed `Ox` insert still consumed 3: sequence values are never rolled back. After `setval`, Blue gets 3.

presets.label: Deferred foreign key
presets.lookFor: A deferred constraint is checked at **COMMIT**, so rows can arrive in any order within the transaction. Only UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, EXCLUDE and foreign keys can be deferrable.

presets.label: PG18: virtual columns and temporal keys
presets.lookFor: `attgenerated = v`: **virtual**, the default in 18, recomputed on every read and stored nowhere, so it cannot be written or indexed (**0A000**). The temporal key accepts back-to-back periods (`[)` bounds) and rejects an overlap with **23P01**, enforced by a GiST index.

presets.label: Adding rules to live data: NOT VALID
presets.lookFor: `NOT NULL … NOT VALID` guards new rows at once (**23502**) but skips the existing NULLs; VALIDATE fails until the backfill is done. Adding a NOT NULL column without a DEFAULT fails on a populated table. A **NOT ENFORCED** check is never verified at all.

production.title: Customer data that drifted across 4 million order rows
production.problem: Customers who changed their email kept old addresses on older orders. A marketing export de-duplicated by email and found many more "customers" than accounts, and support could not tell which city was current.
production.outcome: Each customer fact now lives in one row, so an email change is one UPDATE. The export count matches the account count, the orders table lost three wide text columns, and no step held a long table lock.

pitfalls.title: Foreign keys without an index on the referencing side
pitfalls.fix: Index foreign key columns that are not already the leading column of an index. Find candidates in the catalog.

pitfalls.title: CHECK constraints that let NULL through
pitfalls.fix: Add `NOT NULL` when a value is required, or write the intent explicitly: `CHECK (discount IS NOT NULL AND discount BETWEEN 0 AND 50)`.

pitfalls.title: UNIQUE on a nullable column
pitfalls.fix: Use `NOT NULL`, or declare `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` when at most one NULL is acceptable.

pitfalls.title: Duplicate key right after a data import
pitfalls.fix: Move the sequence past the data after every import, or use `GENERATED ALWAYS` so manual ids need an explicit `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`.

pitfalls.title: SET NOT NULL on a big table blocks it
pitfalls.fix: Add `NOT NULL col NOT VALID` (instant, guards new rows), backfill in batches, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`.

pitfalls.title: Treating NOT ENFORCED as a safety net
pitfalls.fix: Use it only for rules enforced elsewhere. For real protection, add the constraint `NOT VALID` and run `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` once existing data is clean.

keyPointers: **1NF**: one value per cell. **2NF**: no column depends on part of a composite key. **3NF**: no non-key column depends on another non-key column.
Store each fact once. A historical price on an order line is a different fact from today's list price.
**PRIMARY KEY** = UNIQUE + NOT NULL. **UNIQUE** allows many NULLs unless `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`. **CHECK** passes on NULL.
Foreign keys: NO ACTION (default, deferrable), RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT. Index the referencing columns yourself.

PG18: generated columns default to **VIRTUAL** (computed on read, not indexable), keys can be temporal with **WITHOUT OVERLAPS**, NOT NULL can be added **NOT VALID**, CHECK and FK can be **NOT ENFORCED**.

modules.title: Storage & Page Layout Internals
modules.summary: How rows become bytes: data types, 8 KB slotted pages, tuple headers, TOAST, and the free-space and visibility maps.

lessons.title: Primitive types, alignment and padding
lessons.tldr: Every column type has a fixed on-disk width (`typlen`) or is variable-length, plus an **alignment** (`typalign`) that forces it to start at a multiple of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes. Alignment lets the CPU read values in place, but it means **column order changes row size**: badly ordered columns leave padding holes in every row of the table.

visualizer.title: Column tetris: how order creates padding
visualizer.interaction: Press **Pack columns**, drag columns around, add types or toggle NULLs, and watch padding appear and disappear. The byte map follows the same rules `pg_column_size` applies.

presets.label: typlen & typalign
presets.lookFor: `typlen = -1` means variable length (varlena). `typalign` is c/s/i/d = 1/2/4/8 bytes. `timestamp` and `timestamptz` are both 8 bytes: the zone is never stored. `uuid` is 16 bytes but only char-aligned.

presets.label: Size of single values
presets.lookFor: Fixed types are exactly `typlen`. `numeric` is variable: 6, 10 and 12 bytes here, about 2 bytes per group of 4 decimal digits plus a small header. These are in-memory sizes; inside a row, short varlenas shrink to a 1-byte header.

presets.label: Same data, two orders
presets.lookFor: Identical values: **67 bytes** in the bad order, **54 bytes** packed, exactly what the visualizer shows. MAXALIGN rounds them to 72 and 56, so (8192 − 24) / (72 + 4) = **107** rows fit per page against (8192 − 24) / (56 + 4) = **136**.

presets.label: Exact vs inexact
presets.lookFor: Binary floats drift: three float4 additions of 0.0001 give `0.00029999999`. `numeric` is exact and rounds ties away from zero. `money` formats with `lc_monetary`. An interval stores **months, days and microseconds separately**: they compare as equal (30-day months) but add differently.

presets.label: Casts: what works, what fails
presets.lookFor: `pg_input_error_info` shows the error a cast would raise without aborting: out of range, bad syntax, `numeric(7,5)` overflowing at 100. A quoted literal is `unknown` until context picks a type, `9.99::int` **rounds** to 10, and the same `06/10/2001` is June or October depending on `DateStyle`.

presets.label: Fixed width, byte by byte
presets.lookFor: The integer-to-`bytea` casts are new in PostgreSQL 18. Width depends on the **type**, not the value: 123 is 2, 4 or 8 bytes, negatives are two's complement. The cast prints most significant byte first; on disk (little-endian here) `id = 1` is stored as `0100000000000000`.

presets.label: Enums, domains, composites
presets.lookFor: An **enum** is a 4-byte OID into `pg_enum`, sorted by `enumsortorder`, not alphabetically. A **domain** is its base type plus a CHECK, so it costs the same 4 bytes as `date`. A **composite** is a varlena with its own tuple header inside (41 bytes here).

presets.label: Generated: STORED vs VIRTUAL
presets.lookFor: PostgreSQL 18 adds **VIRTUAL** generated columns, and makes them the default. The STORED `total` occupies 8 bytes in every row (48 B). The VIRTUAL one is only a NULL bit (`t_bits` 1110…), so the row is 40 B, and it is recomputed on every read.

production.title: Reordering a 200 M-row metrics table before launch
production.problem: Columns were listed in the order the team thought of them. Each `bool` or `smallint` placed before an 8-byte column forces up to 7 padding bytes, so a row with 32 bytes of real data occupies **72 bytes** on the page.
production.outcome: Each row drops from 72 to 56 bytes (plus its 4-byte line pointer), which is 76 → 60 bytes per row: **21% less heap**, about 15.2 GB → 12.0 GB at 200 M rows. More rows per page also means fewer pages per sequential scan and a larger share of the table in cache.

pitfalls.title: Using float for money
pitfalls.fix: Use `numeric` (exact) or integer cents in `bigint`, and store the ISO currency code in its own column. Size the precision generously: `numeric(7,5)` cannot hold 100.00. Avoid the `money` type: it has no currency, and its output depends on `lc_monetary`, so dumps can fail to load under another locale.

pitfalls.title: char(n) for codes and names
pitfalls.fix: Use `text`, or `varchar(n)` when you want a length check. Add a `CHECK (length(code) = 3)` when the length must be exact.

pitfalls.title: Expecting reordering to always save space
pitfalls.fix: Compute both orders with `pg_column_size(ROW(...))` and round up to 8 before paying for a rewrite. Reordering pays off when it removes 8 or more bytes per row.

pitfalls.title: Choosing int4 keys for a fast-growing table
pitfalls.fix: Use `bigint` for surrogate keys of tables that can grow large. The 4 bytes `int4` saves are often eaten by alignment padding anyway (an `int4` before an 8-byte column is followed by 4 padding bytes), and they are small compared with a table rewrite under pressure.

pitfalls.title: timestamp without time zone for real instants
pitfalls.fix: Use `timestamptz` for anything that happened at an instant. Render in the user's zone with `AT TIME ZONE`, and keep plain `timestamp` for wall-clock values such as "opening hour 09:00".

pitfalls.title: Integer and numeric arithmetic in generated columns
pitfalls.fix: Use `EXTRACT(quarter FROM d)`, or cast before dividing: `(EXTRACT(month FROM d)::int - 1) / 3 + 1`. Check `pg_typeof()` of any expression feeding an integer column.

keyPointers: Fixed widths: **bool 1, int2 2, int4/date/float4 4, int8/float8/timestamptz 8, uuid/interval 16** bytes.
`typalign` c/s/i/d forces a start offset that is a multiple of **1/2/4/8**. Short varlenas (under 127 bytes) are not aligned.
Rows start with a 23-byte header padded to `t_hoff` = 24, and the whole row is padded to **8 bytes** on the page, plus a 4-byte line pointer.
Order columns **8-byte first, then 4, 2, 1, then variable-length** to remove padding; verify with `pg_column_size(ROW(...))`.
Use **numeric** for exact decimals, **float** for measurements, **bigint** for keys that can grow, and **timestamptz** for instants. VIRTUAL generated columns cost no row bytes; STORED ones do.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.tldr: A PostgreSQL array is one **varlena value** holding a small header (dimensions, lower bounds, element type, optional null bitmap) followed by the aligned elements. Arrays let you keep a short list inside a row and search it with **GIN**-indexable operators like `@>` and `&&`, without a separate join table.

visualizer.title: An array, byte by byte, and a GIN lookup
visualizer.interaction: In **Bytes on disk**, step through five arrays and click each field to see its little-endian bytes. Switch to **GIN lookup** to see how `@>`, `&&` and `= ANY` use, or fail to use, the index.

presets.label: Array sizes
presets.lookFor: The 16-byte header plus 8 bytes per dimension, then the data: 36, 40, 48, 16 and 48 bytes, the numbers in the visualizer.

presets.label: Dimensions & bounds
presets.lookFor: Arrays are **1-based** and out-of-range reads return NULL instead of an error. A custom lower bound is stored in the header.

presets.label: Operators
presets.lookFor: `@>` ignores order and duplicates. `&&` is true when any element is shared.

presets.label: GIN: @> vs = ANY
presets.lookFor: The containment query uses a **Bitmap Index Scan** on the GIN index. The `= ANY` form asks for the same rows but can only run as a **Seq Scan**.

presets.label: unnest & array_agg
presets.lookFor: `unnest` turns an array into rows; `WITH ORDINALITY` adds each element's position. `array_agg` folds rows back into an array.

presets.label: Strings to arrays: spot the bug
presets.lookFor: The first result looks plausible and is wrong: `string_to_array` returns `text[]`, so `max` compares strings and `'9'` beats `'16'`. Station North reports a minimum of -1 instead of **-16**. South happens to be right because all its readings have two digits. Casting to `int[]` fixes the rest.

presets.label: Sort, reverse, compare
presets.lookFor: `array_sort` and `array_reverse` are new in PostgreSQL 18; `array_reverse` flips only the first dimension. Arrays compare **element by element**, left to right, like strings: `{1,3} < {2,1}`, so `min` and `max` pick whole arrays by their first element.

presets.label: The normalized alternative
presets.lookFor: Both models find the same 266 posts. The array needs one GIN lookup; the join table needs `GROUP BY … HAVING count = 2` (one scan, better than one self-join per tag). The join table is larger here but gives foreign keys, per-tag columns and cheap single-tag updates.

production.title: Tag filtering on a content platform
production.problem: The team added a GIN index on `tags`, but the listing query still did a sequential scan and took seconds. `= ANY` is not an operator in the GIN `array_ops` class, so the index was never considered.
production.outcome: The plan switched from a Seq Scan to a Bitmap Index Scan, which the playground reproduces on 20k rows. The cost of a GIN lookup grows with the number of matching rows, not with table size, so rare tags become near-instant.

pitfalls.title: Writing = ANY against a GIN index
pitfalls.fix: Write `col @> ARRAY[value]` for "contains this element", or `col && ARRAY[a, b]` for "contains any of".

pitfalls.title: Updating one element rewrites the whole array
pitfalls.fix: Keep arrays short and mostly read-only. Move growing lists such as event logs or followers into a child table.

pitfalls.title: Concatenating NULL behaves differently from array_append
pitfalls.fix: Use `array_append` / `array_prepend` when adding single elements, and add `CHECK (array_position(tags, NULL) IS NULL)` if NULL elements are not allowed.

pitfalls.title: Treating arrays as sets
pitfalls.fix: Use a join table when you need foreign keys, per-element data or uniqueness. Keep arrays for small ordered values such as tags or coordinates.

pitfalls.title: Aggregating split strings as text
pitfalls.fix: Cast at the source: `string_to_array(col, ',')::int[]` or `unnest(...)::int`. Better, store numbers as `int[]` (or rows) so the type is enforced on write.

keyPointers: Header: **vl_len, ndim, dataoffset, elemtype** (16 bytes), then 8 bytes per dimension, then an optional null bitmap and the aligned elements.
`dataoffset = 0` means no NULLs. NULL elements cost **one bit**, no data bytes.
Arrays are **1-based**, out-of-range reads return NULL, and declared sizes like `int[3]` are not enforced.
GIN `array_ops` indexes `@>`, `<@`, `&&` and `=`. Rewrite `x = ANY(col)` as `col @> ARRAY[x]`.
Any change rewrites the whole array, so keep growing lists in a child table.

lessons.title: JSON vs JSONB
lessons.tldr: `json` stores the exact input text, while `jsonb` parses it once into a **binary tree** that drops whitespace, sorts keys and keeps only the last duplicate key. Paying that parsing cost on write makes every later read fast and lets **GIN indexes** answer containment and key-existence queries, which makes `jsonb` the right default for most applications.

visualizer.title: One document, two storage formats
visualizer.interaction: Pick a sample document and step through what `jsonb` does to it: parse, de-duplicate, sort and store. The last two steps show which items each GIN operator class extracts.

presets.label: Normalization & size
presets.lookFor: json keeps both `user` keys and the spacing. jsonb keeps the last `user`, puts `size` before `color` (shorter keys first) and prints numbers as `numeric`. For these small documents jsonb is about 40% **larger** (96 vs 134 bytes).

presets.label: -> vs ->>: the quotes tell the type
presets.lookFor: `->` returns **jsonb** (`"click"`, with quotes), `->>` returns **text** (`click`). JSON arrays are **0-based** and `-1` counts from the end, unlike SQL arrays. A missing key is SQL NULL, but a JSON `null` is a real jsonb value until `->>` turns it into SQL NULL.

presets.label: Operators
presets.lookFor: `?` only sees **top-level** keys: `plan` lives under `user`, so navigate first. `@>` tests containment. `||` is a shallow merge: the right-hand `a` replaces the whole left-hand object.

presets.label: Which queries use GIN?
presets.lookFor: `@>` and `?` use the GIN index. `doc ->> 'type' = …` applies an operator to an *expression*, so it cannot use an index on `doc`.

presets.label: Text is not a number
presets.lookFor: `->>` yields text, so `> '50'` compares strings and `'9.00'` wins: 7,560 rows instead of **12,980**. Cast first, or compare jsonb to jsonb. Comparing `->> 'type'` to text is fine, and a **B-tree expression index** on exactly that expression turns it into an index scan.

presets.label: jsonb_ops vs jsonb_path_ops
presets.lookFor: The path-hash index is smaller, and the planner picks it for `@>`. `?` still needs `events_doc_ops`.

presets.label: jsonb_set: new row, and the NULL trap
presets.lookFor: Changing one key wrote a **whole new row version** at a new ctid. And `jsonb_set(…, NULL)` returns SQL NULL for the entire document: in an UPDATE it wipes the column. `jsonb_set_lax` sets a JSON null or deletes the key instead.

presets.label: jsonpath & JSON_TABLE
presets.lookFor: Lax mode (the default) treats a scalar as a one-element array, so `plan[0]` works; strict mode raises an error there, which `silent => true` turns into an empty result. JSON_TABLE turns documents into rows, one per `NESTED PATH` element.

production.title: Making an event-attribute filter indexable
production.problem: A GIN index on `props` had been created, yet every dashboard query was a sequential scan. The `->>` comparison is not one of the GIN operators: the index only helps `@>`, `?`, `?|`, `?&`, `@?` and `@@` applied to the column itself.
production.outcome: The playground shows the change on 20k rows: Seq Scan before, Bitmap Index Scan on the GIN index after. In the playground the path-ops index is also about 19% smaller than jsonb_ops (792 kB vs 976 kB).

pitfalls.title: Expecting a GIN index to serve ->> comparisons
pitfalls.fix: Write `doc @> '{"type": "purchase"}'`, or create an expression index on `(doc ->> 'type')`.

pitfalls.title: Relying on key order or duplicate keys
pitfalls.fix: Store payloads that must be reproduced byte for byte (signatures, audit copies) in `json` or `text`, and a parsed `jsonb` copy for querying if needed.

pitfalls.title: Updating one key in a large document
pitfalls.fix: Keep frequently changing fields in ordinary columns, and keep documents small and mostly immutable.

pitfalls.title: Comparing ->> results to numbers
pitfalls.fix: Cast the extracted value: `(doc ->> 'amount')::numeric > 50`, or compare jsonb to jsonb with `doc -> 'amount' > '50'`. To index it, the index expression must match the cast exactly, and the cast must be immutable (text to `numeric` is; text to `timestamptz` is not).

pitfalls.title: jsonb_set with a NULL value
pitfalls.fix: Use `jsonb_set_lax`, which by default stores a JSON `null` (or can delete the key), or wrap the value in `COALESCE(to_jsonb($1), 'null')`. Add `CHECK (doc IS NOT NULL)` or `NOT NULL` on document columns.

pitfalls.title: Using jsonb_path_ops for key-existence queries
pitfalls.fix: Keep the default `jsonb_ops` index if you need `?`, `?|` or `?&`, or index the expression `((doc ? 'coupon'))` for a single hot key.

keyPointers: **json** = exact text, reparsed on every use, no GIN support. **jsonb** = parsed binary tree: no whitespace, keys sorted shorter-first, last duplicate wins.
jsonb is not smaller: small documents are often **larger** than json. Its advantage is speed and indexing.
`->` returns jsonb, `->>` returns **text** (cast before comparing numbers), `#>` / `#>>` take a path, `?` tests top-level keys, `@>` tests containment.
GIN **jsonb_ops** indexes keys and values (supports `?`); **jsonb_path_ops** hashes paths (only `@>`, `@?`, `@@`, smaller).
jsonpath runs in **lax** mode by default (auto-wraps and unwraps arrays); **strict** raises structural errors.

lessons.title: UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7
lessons.tldr: A `uuid` is a 16-byte value: **UUIDv4** is 122 random bits, while **UUIDv7** starts with a 48-bit millisecond timestamp, so new values sort after older ones. Random keys scatter inserts across a B-tree, while time-ordered keys append at its right edge, so PostgreSQL 18 added a native `uuidv7()` that keeps the global uniqueness of UUIDs with the index locality of a sequence.

visualizer.title: Inside a UUID, and what it does to an index
visualizer.interaction: Generate UUIDs and click each bit field to see what it encodes. Then switch to **Index locality** and insert v4 vs v7 keys to see which leaf pages every insert has to touch.

presets.label: Generate & decode
presets.lookFor: `gen_random_uuid()` is the same as `uuidv4()`. Only v7 (and v1) carry a timestamp; for v4 it is NULL.

presets.label: v7 is ordered
presets.lookFor: Within one millisecond the 4th group counts up (`7000`, `7001`, …): the sub-millisecond field keeps values increasing. Zero of 50,000 neighbours are out of order.

presets.label: Storage size & input forms
presets.lookFor: Native `uuid` is 16 bytes; the same value as `text` is 40. Input is forgiving (upper case, braces, no hyphens) and output is always the canonical lower-case form, so there is no reason to store UUIDs as text.

presets.label: Index size: bigint vs v7 vs v4
presets.lookFor: Same 50,000 rows. v7 is larger than bigint only because keys are 16 bytes instead of 8. v4 is about **40% larger again** than v7, purely from half-empty pages.

presets.label: Leaf fill
presets.lookFor: About 90% for bigint and v7 (right-edge appends respect fillfactor 90) versus about 63% for v4 (the exact figure varies a little per run, since the keys are random).

presets.label: WAL after a checkpoint
presets.lookFor: The first change to a page after a checkpoint writes a **full-page image** into WAL. 2,000 v7 keys touch a handful of right-edge leaves; 2,000 v4 keys touch hundreds of different leaves. Expect roughly **4 to 5 times more WAL** for v4 (about 1.7 MB against 0.3 to 0.4 MB; keys are random, so it varies).

presets.label: Shifted timestamps
presets.lookFor: `uuidv7(shift)` moves the embedded timestamp, which is useful for backfilling historical rows. Note that it reveals when a row was created.

production.title: Moving an orders table from UUIDv4 to UUIDv7 keys
production.problem: As the primary-key index outgrew memory, insert latency rose. Each random key landed on a different leaf page, most of which had to be read from disk, and mid-page splits left leaves about two-thirds full.
production.outcome: On 50,000 rows in the playground, the v4 index has about 275 pages at about 63% leaf fill (it varies slightly per run), the v7 index 194 pages at 90%. At production scale the larger win is that inserts touch one hot leaf instead of thousands of cold ones.

pitfalls.title: Storing UUIDs as text
pitfalls.fix: Use the `uuid` type. It accepts upper case, braces and missing hyphens on input and always prints the standard form.

pitfalls.title: Leaking creation time through UUIDv7
pitfalls.fix: Keep v7 as the internal primary key, and expose a separate random v4 (or another opaque token) where the creation time must stay private.

pitfalls.title: Assuming v7 values are globally ordered
pitfalls.fix: Use a `timestamptz` column (or a sequence) when you need exact ordering. Treat v7 order as "roughly by creation time", which is all an index needs.

pitfalls.title: Benchmarking v4 vs v7 with buffer statistics
pitfalls.fix: Compare what the key type actually changes: index size (`pg_relation_size`), leaf fill (`bt_page_stats`), and WAL volume per insert after a checkpoint (`pg_current_wal_lsn()` before and after).

keyPointers: `uuid` is **16 bytes**, compared byte by byte. Store it as `uuid`, never as text.
`gen_random_uuid()` = `uuidv4()` (random); `uuidv7([shift])` puts a **48-bit Unix-ms timestamp** first.
Decode with `uuid_extract_version()` and `uuid_extract_timestamp()` (v1 and v7 only).
Random keys scatter writes (more dirty pages, more full-page images in WAL) and leave B-tree leaves about **2/3 full**; v7 keys append at the right edge and fill leaves to **90%**.
v7 still takes **twice the space of bigint** per key: choose UUIDs for distributed id generation, not by default.

lessons.title: The 8 KB slotted page
lessons.tldr: Every table and index is an array of fixed **8 KB pages**, each with a 24-byte header, an array of 4-byte **line pointers** growing forward, and tuples growing backward from the end. The indirection through line pointers lets PostgreSQL move, prune and compact tuples inside a page without changing their address, the **ctid** `(block, item)` that indexes point to.

visualizer.title: Inside a heap page, byte by byte
visualizer.interaction: Step through eight operations. Click any line pointer or tuple to inspect its header fields and byte offsets.

presets.label: ctid & system columns
presets.lookFor: Every row has hidden system columns. `ctid` is (block, line pointer).

presets.label: Page header
presets.lookFor: `upper - lower` is the free space. `special` = 8192 because heap pages have no special space.

presets.label: Line pointers & tuples
presets.lookFor: Offsets decrease as rows are added: tuples are allocated from the end of the page.

presets.label: UPDATE → new version
presets.lookFor: lp 2 keeps its bytes but gets `t_xmax` and `t_ctid = (0,4)`. lp 4 is the new version, flagged `HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE`.

presets.label: DELETE + VACUUM
presets.lookFor: Run after the UPDATE preset. lp 2 becomes `lp_flags = 2` (redirect to lp 4), lp 3 becomes 0 (unused), and the survivors are compacted.

presets.label: Fill a page
presets.lookFor: Each 61-byte row needs 64 bytes plus a 4-byte line pointer, so about **120 rows fit per page**. Files grow in whole pages, so even a one-row table takes 8192 bytes.

presets.label: Heap order is not id order
presets.lookFor: No ORDER BY, so rows come back in **physical order**: 1, 4, 5, 3, 2. Each UPDATE wrote a new version at the next free slot, so 3 and 2 moved behind the others. Updating every row moves all five again, to (0,8)–(0,12), even though nothing was deleted.

presets.label: ctid inside one statement
presets.lookFor: A table with no key can still be de-duplicated: within one statement every row version has a distinct, stable ctid. Keeping the lowest ctid per fruit leaves (0,1), (0,3) and (0,6). Outside a single statement, ctid is not a safe identifier.

production.title: Sizing a 500 M-row events table before it ships
production.problem: A spreadsheet based on "8 + 8 + 2 + 8 = 26 bytes a row" predicted 13 GB. The real table was **2.3× larger**, and the hot set no longer fit in `shared_buffers`.
production.outcome: The measured ~60 bytes per row predicts about **30 GB** for 500 M rows, against the spreadsheet's 13 GB. The team sized storage and memory from the measured number. Reordering columns would not help here: with the `smallint` last the row is 50 bytes, which still rounds up to 56. Per-row overhead (header + line pointer + alignment) is a fixed cost to budget for, not a rounding error.

pitfalls.title: Expecting rows back in insertion or id order
pitfalls.fix: Write `ORDER BY` whenever order matters, with a unique tiebreaker such as the primary key. Never rely on the order of a plain `SELECT *`.

pitfalls.title: Using ctid as a row identifier
pitfalls.fix: Always identify rows by a primary key. Use ctid only inside one statement, for example de-duplicating with `DELETE … WHERE ctid NOT IN (…)`.

pitfalls.title: Expecting DELETE to shrink the file
pitfalls.fix: Plain `VACUUM` makes the space reusable. To return it to the OS, rebuild the table: `VACUUM FULL` takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock; `pg_repack` can do it online. Or partition the table and drop whole partitions instead of deleting rows.

pitfalls.title: Assuming the block size can be tuned
pitfalls.fix: Keep the default 8 KB. A different size means rebuilding PostgreSQL and reloading the data, so tune `fillfactor`, row width and TOAST instead.

keyPointers: A page is **24-byte header → line pointers (4 B each, growing up) → free space → tuples (growing down) → special space**.
Free space is exactly **`pd_upper - pd_lower`**. The page is full when they would meet.
A **ctid `(block, lp)`** names a line pointer, not a byte offset, so tuples can move inside the page without breaking index entries.
Each tuple carries a **23-byte header** (`t_xmin`, `t_xmax`, `t_cid`, `t_ctid`, `t_infomask2`, `t_infomask`, `t_hoff`), padded to 24 before the row data.
Line pointer states: **NORMAL**, **REDIRECT** (HOT chain root), **DEAD** (waiting for index cleanup), **UNUSED** (free for reuse).

lessons.title: The heap tuple header: xmin, xmax, ctid, infomask
lessons.tldr: Every row version starts with a **23-byte header**: who created it (`t_xmin`), who deleted or locked it (`t_xmax`), where its newer version lives (`t_ctid`), and two flag words, `t_infomask` and `t_infomask2`. MVCC visibility, row locks, HOT chains and freezing are all decided from these few bytes, and readers cache commit status in them as **hint bits** so later readers can skip the commit log.

visualizer.title: Flip the infomask bits, one statement at a time
visualizer.interaction: Step through eleven statements. Bits that change in a step pulse; click any bit for its meaning, or any tuple to inspect it. The values are what `heap_page_items` reports after each statement.

presets.label: Fresh insert
presets.lookFor: `HEAP_XMAX_INVALID` (not deleted) and `HEAP_HASNULL` with `t_bits = 11100000`: the 4th column is NULL. The view itself was created after the insert, so no reader has hinted the row yet.

presets.label: Read → hint bit
presets.lookFor: After one SELECT, `HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED` appears. Reading wrote to the page.

presets.label: Aborted insert
presets.lookFor: lp 2 is still physically on the page. The SELECT stamped it `HEAP_XMIN_INVALID`, so nobody will check its xid again.

presets.label: HOT update
presets.lookFor: The old version points at the new one through `t_ctid` and carries `HEAP_HOT_UPDATED`. The new version is a `HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE`.

presets.label: Row locks live in xmax
presets.lookFor: Inside the transaction, the live version has `t_xmax` = your xid plus `HEAP_XMAX_LOCK_ONLY` and `HEAP_XMAX_EXCL_LOCK`: a lock, not a delete.

presets.label: Null bitmap & t_hoff
presets.lookFor: A NULL costs **one bit** and no data bytes (28 B), while an empty string costs its 1-byte varlena header (29 B): NULL and `''` are different on disk too. With 9 columns and a NULL, the bitmap needs 2 bytes: 23 + 2 = 25, MAXALIGNed to **t_hoff = 32**.

presets.label: No-op updates & upserts
presets.lookFor: An UPDATE that changes nothing still writes a **new version** with a new ctid and xmin. In the upsert, PostgreSQL 18 `RETURNING old/new` says which rows were inserted (`old` is NULL). The older `xmax = 0` trick agrees here because the updated version carries the conflict lock in its xmax, but that is an implementation detail.

presets.label: Freeze
presets.lookFor: Dead versions are gone. The survivors (alice and carol) show `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN` in `combined_flags`: XMIN_COMMITTED and XMIN_INVALID set together.

production.title: A full-table read that writes gigabytes
production.problem: The first read after the load ran far longer than later identical reads, generated heavy write I/O and WAL on a server with checksums enabled, and the replica lagged behind. Nobody expected a SELECT to write.
production.outcome: The playground shows the mechanism directly: one SELECT changes `t_infomask` from 2051 to 2307. Moving that write to a planned VACUUM makes first-read latency match later reads, and `COPY … FREEZE` skips the extra rewrite entirely.

pitfalls.title: Assuming an UPDATE that changes nothing is free
pitfalls.fix: Filter out no-op rows: `UPDATE t SET col = $1 WHERE col IS DISTINCT FROM $1`. For row-by-row writes from applications, the built-in `suppress_redundant_updates_trigger()` can skip them.

pitfalls.title: Reading t_xmax as "deleted"
pitfalls.fix: Never infer liveness from raw xmax. Decode the flags with `heap_tuple_infomask_flags`, or rely on MVCC and count live rows with `count(*)`. For the same reason, prefer `RETURNING old IS NULL` (PostgreSQL 18) or `merge_action()` over the `xmax = 0` trick for telling inserts from updates in an upsert.

pitfalls.title: Many NULLable columns pushing t_hoff up
pitfalls.fix: Keep very wide sparse attributes in a `jsonb` column or a side table, and keep frequently NULL columns out of hot narrow tables.

pitfalls.title: Assuming row locks are cheap to hold
pitfalls.fix: Lock only the rows you need, in small batches, and prefer `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` when you do not change keys so foreign-key checks are not blocked.

keyPointers: Header = `t_xmin` 4 + `t_xmax` 4 + `t_cid` 4 + `t_ctid` 6 + `t_infomask2` 2 + `t_infomask` 2 + `t_hoff` 1 = **23 bytes**, data at `t_hoff` (24 without a long null bitmap).
**Hint bits** `XMIN_COMMITTED`, `XMIN_INVALID`, `XMAX_COMMITTED`, `XMAX_INVALID` cache commit-log answers; readers set them, so a SELECT can write.
`t_xmax` means "deleted" only without `XMAX_LOCK_ONLY`; row locks live in the tuple itself.
`t_infomask2` = attribute count (11 bits) + `HOT_UPDATED`, `HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE`, `KEYS_UPDATED`.
**Frozen** = `XMIN_COMMITTED | XMIN_INVALID`: visible to all, safe from xid wraparound.

lessons.title: TOAST: oversized attributes
lessons.tldr: **TOAST** (The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique) compresses large variable-length values and, if they are still too big, slices them into ~2 kB chunks stored in a separate `pg_toast` table. A row must fit on one 8 KB page, so TOAST is how PostgreSQL stores values of up to 1 GB while keeping the main table narrow and fast to scan.

visualizer.title: Follow a big value through the toaster
visualizer.interaction: Pick one of four inserts and step through compression, chunking and the 18-byte pointer that stays behind. Click the pointer bytes to decode them.

presets.label: What happened to each value
presets.lookFor: Row 1 is compressed inline (9000 → 122). Row 2 is out of line, uncompressed. Row 3 is untouched. Row 4 is compressed **and** out of line (1.2 MB → 13,745 bytes).

presets.label: The TOAST table
presets.lookFor: Every TOASTed table has its own hidden `pg_toast.pg_toast_<oid>` table. Chunks are at most **1996 bytes**; row 2 needs 5 chunks, row 4 (compressed) needs 7.

presets.label: Main row vs pointer
presets.lookFor: Rows 2 and 4 are tiny: `body` is an 18-byte pointer starting `0112` (external, tag 18). Row 1 holds 122 compressed bytes inline.

presets.label: Update without touching TOAST
presets.lookFor: Updating another column **reuses** the same chunk_id: the new row version copies only the 18-byte pointer. Changing `body` writes a whole new TOAST value.

presets.label: Where the bytes live
presets.lookFor: The main heap is a single 8 kB page even though it "holds" 1.2 MB of text. `pg_relation_size` counts only the main fork; `pg_table_size` adds TOAST and the FSM/VM forks; `pg_total_relation_size` adds every index, including the TOAST table's own index.

presets.label: bytea vs large objects
presets.lookFor: `bytea` is an ordinary varlena: 3 bytes stay inline, 6,400 bytes are TOASTed with the row. A **large object** lives in `pg_largeobject` as 2,048-byte pages, and the row holds only its OID. Writing that OID into a `bytea` column stores its digits (`3136…` = "16…"), not the file.

presets.label: Storage strategies
presets.lookFor: EXTERNAL stores the 9000 bytes out of line uncompressed. MAIN compresses and keeps it inline, moving out of line only as a last resort.

presets.label: toast_tuple_target
presets.lookFor: Both rows are about 2.4 kB, so the toaster runs. By default it moves one column out until the row fits 2032 bytes; with a target of 256 it keeps going and moves **both** out.

production.title: Wide product descriptions slowing every listing query
production.problem: Descriptions just under the 2 kB threshold are never TOASTed, so each row is about 1.6 kB and only 4–5 rows fit per page. Listing queries that never read `description` still scan pages full of it.
production.outcome: The playground shows the target behaviour: with `toast_tuple_target = 256` a 2.4 kB row moves both columns out of line instead of one. Note that the toaster only starts at about 2 kB, so values under that threshold stay inline whatever the target; for those rows, the side-table split is what improves scan density: a row of name, price and stock is under 80 bytes, so a page holds about 100 of them instead of 4–5.

pitfalls.title: Changing the strategy and expecting old rows to move
pitfalls.fix: Rewrite the affected rows (`UPDATE t SET col = col || ''` in batches) or the table (`VACUUM FULL`, `pg_repack`) when you need the new format everywhere.

pitfalls.title: Updating a large value in place, frequently
pitfalls.fix: Keep frequently changed fields out of big documents. Unchanged TOASTed columns cost nothing on UPDATE, so put the counters in their own columns.

pitfalls.title: Expecting lz4 everywhere
pitfalls.fix: Check `SHOW default_toast_compression;` and test `SET COMPRESSION lz4` on your build. lz4 is usually faster than pglz when available.

pitfalls.title: Storing a large object's OID in a bytea column
pitfalls.fix: Pick one design. Either a `bytea` column (simple, TOASTed, up to 1 GB, deleted with the row), or an `oid` column with the large-object API plus `lo_unlink` (or the `lo_manage` trigger from the `lo` module) when the row goes away.

pitfalls.title: Hitting the 1 GB value limit
pitfalls.fix: Store very large objects outside the row: in object storage with a reference, or chunked across rows yourself.

keyPointers: TOAST starts when a row exceeds **~2 kB** (2032 bytes) and works until it is under `toast_tuple_target` (default 2032).
Strategies: **PLAIN** (never), **EXTENDED** (compress, then out of line; default), **EXTERNAL** (out of line, no compression), **MAIN** (compress; out of line last).
Out-of-line values become **1996-byte chunks**, 4 per TOAST page, keyed by `(chunk_id, chunk_seq)`; the row keeps an **18-byte pointer**.
UPDATEs that do not change a TOASTed column **reuse** its chunks.
Inspect with `pg_column_size`, `pg_column_compression` and `pg_column_toast_chunk_id`. Max value size is **1 GB**.

lessons.title: Files, forks, the free space map and visibility map
lessons.tldr: Each table is a set of files named by its **relfilenode**, split into 1 GB segments, with up to four forks: the **main** data, the **free space map**, the **visibility map** and, for unlogged tables, an **init** fork. The FSM lets inserts find a page with room without scanning the table, and the VM lets VACUUM skip clean pages and index-only scans skip the heap.

visualizer.title: One table on disk: files, free space and visibility
visualizer.interaction: Step through nine statements and watch the fork files, each page's FSM value and VM bits change. Drag the slider under the FSM tree to see how an INSERT finds a page with enough room.

presets.label: Where is the file?
presets.lookFor: The path is `base/<database OID>/<relfilenode>`. The FSM fork already exists; the VM does not, because nothing has been vacuumed.

presets.label: VACUUM builds the VM
presets.lookFor: A VM fork appears with **all_visible** set for every page. `pg_freespace` reports free bytes in steps of 32.

presets.label: DELETE: VM cleared, FSM stale
presets.lookFor: Pages 0, 4 and 5 lose all_visible immediately. Their FSM values do not move: the dead rows still occupy the space until VACUUM.

presets.label: VACUUM updates the FSM
presets.lookFor: Pages 0, 4 and 5 now show thousands of free bytes. FSM block 2 is the leaf page: nodes 4095… are the per-page categories (bytes / 32), lower node numbers are the max-tree above them.

presets.label: Freeze & the all-frozen bit
presets.lookFor: After the freeze every page is all-visible and all-frozen. One UPDATE clears both bits on the page it touches.

presets.label: TRUNCATE gets a new file
presets.lookFor: TRUNCATE swaps in a fresh, empty relfilenode while the table OID stays the same. Never assume filenode = OID.

presets.label: Unlogged: the init fork
presets.lookFor: Unlogged relations get an `_init` fork: empty for the heap, one metapage (8192 bytes) for the B-tree. After a crash it is copied over the main fork, so the table comes back empty.

presets.label: Which ALTERs rewrite the file?
presets.lookFor: A new relfilenode means the whole table was copied under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. A constant DEFAULT is kept in the catalog (`attmissingval`), a VIRTUAL column and a longer varchar change only metadata, and DROP COLUMN just marks `attisdropped`. A STORED column and a type change rewrite every row.

production.title: Index-only scans that still read the heap
production.problem: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` reports a high **Heap Fetches** count. Autovacuum triggers on dead tuples, and an insert-only table produces almost none, so recently filled pages never had their **all-visible** bit set. Every row on those pages needed a heap visit.
production.outcome: After the vacuum the VM covers the table and Heap Fetches drops towards zero, so the query reads only index pages. The VM is tiny (2 bits per heap page: one 8 KB VM page covers about 255 MB of heap), so it stays cached.

pitfalls.title: Assuming the filenode equals the OID
pitfalls.fix: Always ask the server: `SELECT pg_relation_filepath('t');`. Never touch files in the data directory of a running server.

pitfalls.title: Expecting DELETE to free space immediately
pitfalls.fix: Run `VACUUM` (or let autovacuum run) after large deletes. For bulk purges, partition and `DROP` / `DETACH` whole partitions.

pitfalls.title: Treating TRUNCATE as a light, MVCC-safe DELETE
pitfalls.fix: Use TRUNCATE for tables nobody reads concurrently, with a short `lock_timeout` so it gives up instead of queueing behind long queries. For tables under live reads, `DELETE` in batches plus VACUUM, or swap partitions.

pitfalls.title: Using unlogged tables for data you cannot lose
pitfalls.fix: Use unlogged tables only for caches and staging data you can rebuild. Convert with `ALTER TABLE … SET LOGGED` before the data matters.

keyPointers: Path = `base/<db OID>/<relfilenode>`, plus `_fsm`, `_vm`, `_init` forks and `.1`, `.2` segments every **1 GB**. Look it up with `pg_relation_filepath()`.
**FSM**: one byte per page (free space / 32), organised as max-trees so a search is a short descent. Updated mainly by **VACUUM**.
**VM**: two bits per heap page, **all-visible** and **all-frozen**; set only by VACUUM, cleared by any change to the page. Indexes have no VM.
All-visible pages let **index-only scans** skip the heap; all-frozen pages let anti-wraparound VACUUM skip them.
TRUNCATE and VACUUM FULL write a **new relfilenode**; unlogged tables restore from the **init fork** after a crash.

modules.title: Query Planner, Optimizer & Indexing
modules.summary: From SQL text to a plan tree: costs, statistics, every index access method, and reading EXPLAIN like a pro.

lessons.title: From SQL text to rows: parse, analyze, rewrite, plan, execute
lessons.tldr: Every statement passes through five stages: a **parser** that knows only grammar, **analysis** that resolves names against the catalogs, a **rewriter** that expands views and rules, a **planner** that costs alternative paths, and an **executor** that pulls rows up a plan tree. Splitting the work this way lets PostgreSQL parse transaction commands without a transaction, reuse analyzed statements through **PREPARE**, and pick among many equivalent plans by estimated cost.

visualizer.title: Follow one query through the backend
visualizer.interaction: Step through a join against a view, from characters to tokens, trees, costed paths and finally rows pulled up the plan. Switch modes to watch the plan cache decide between custom and generic plans.

presets.label: The view is a rule
presets.lookFor: A view is stored as a `_RETURN` rule (`ev_type` 1 = SELECT). The rewriter pastes this definition into every query that names the view.

presets.label: The view disappears
presets.lookFor: The plan scans `public.orders` directly with the view's `amount > 900` filter. After rewriting and subquery pull-up, `big_orders` no longer exists.

presets.label: Three join paths
presets.lookFor: Disabling the winner reveals the runner-up paths the planner costed: merge join (about 2788), then nested loop with Memoize (about 3528). The hash join (about 2022) won.

presets.label: Demand-pull counts
presets.lookFor: Each node reports the rows it handed to its parent: customers 1250 (3750 removed), orders 9700 (90300 removed), join 2425.

presets.label: Subqueries become joins
presets.lookFor: The planner rewrites EXISTS into a join: here a Hash Join over the de-duplicated customer ids. NOT EXISTS becomes a **Hash Right Anti Join** estimated at 3974 rows. NOT IN cannot become an anti join, because one NULL in the subquery would make every row unknown. It stays a `hashed SubPlan` filter, with a blind 2500-row guess.

presets.label: CTE: inlined or materialized
presets.lookFor: A plain CTE used once is **inlined**: the outer filter joins it, and a BitmapAnd of two indexes finds 1 row (cost about 21). `MATERIALIZED` computes all 1027 pending rows first, then filters a `CTE Scan` (cost about 155).

presets.label: Custom → generic
presets.lookFor: Five custom plans, then the generic plan wins: `generic_plans = 1`. EXPLAIN shows `customer_id = $1`, a plan built without knowing the value.

presets.label: Skew keeps it custom
presets.lookFor: The generic plan assumes 50000 matching rows and costs far more than the custom plans, so `generic_plans` stays 0.

production.title: A prepared statement that turned slow on the sixth call
production.problem: Latency for small tenants jumped after a connection had served a few requests. The first five executions got custom plans. Then the cached **generic plan** won the cost comparison, and it was tuned for an average tenant, so it walked the big tenant's part of the index for everyone.
production.outcome: Every execution is planned with the real tenant id, so small tenants get an index scan on their own rows again. The cost is one planning pass per call, which `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` reports as Planning Time (about 0.1 to 0.9 ms in the playground).

pitfalls.title: Generic plans on skewed parameters
pitfalls.fix: Check `generic_plans` in `pg_prepared_statements` and compare `EXPLAIN EXECUTE` with `EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN)`. Set `plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan` for that workload.

pitfalls.title: Expecting a view to be cached
pitfalls.fix: Use a **materialized view** (refreshed explicitly) or a summary table when you need the result stored.

pitfalls.title: Big joins switch to GEQO
pitfalls.fix: Reduce the join count (pre-aggregate, split the query), or write joins in a good order and set `join_collapse_limit = 1` for that query. `geqo_seed` makes the choice repeatable.

pitfalls.title: Using a CTE as an optimization fence, or as a cache
pitfalls.fix: Write `AS MATERIALIZED` when you really want compute-once or a fence, and `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` to allow inlining of a CTE that is referenced several times. Check the plan for a `CTE Scan` node.

pitfalls.title: NOT IN over a nullable subquery
pitfalls.fix: Write `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE t.ref = x.id)`. It is NULL-safe and becomes an Anti Join.

keyPointers: Stages: **parser** (grammar only, no catalogs) → **analysis** (names, types, operators) → **rewriter** (views, rules) → **planner** (paths, costs) → **executor**.
The rewriter turns query trees into query trees. A view is a `_RETURN` rule expanded like a macro, then usually flattened into the outer query.
The planner costs **paths** for each relation, then join pairs, keeping the cheapest. Above `geqo_threshold` = 12 FROM items it switches to GEQO.
The executor is **demand-pull**: each node returns one row per call, or NULL when done. Hash and Sort must drain their input first.
**PREPARE** caches the analyzed tree. Five custom plans, then a generic plan if its cost is not much higher (`plan_cache_mode`).

lessons.title: The cost model
lessons.tldr: The planner prices every candidate plan in abstract **cost units**, where reading one page sequentially costs `seq_page_cost` = 1.0 and every random page, row, index entry and operator call has its own relative price. Comparing those totals is how PostgreSQL decides between a sequential scan, an index scan and a bitmap scan, so the constants (and the statistics they multiply) decide which plan you get.

visualizer.title: Where the sequential scan starts to win
visualizer.interaction: Drag the predicate wider and watch three real cost curves cross. Then make the column scattered, shrink the cache, and lower `random_page_cost` to see each factor move the crossover.

presets.label: Seq scan formula
presets.lookFor: 935 pages × 1.0 + 100000 rows × 0.01 = **1935**. Adding one filter adds 100000 × `cpu_operator_cost` 0.0025 = 250, giving **2185**.

presets.label: Cost constants
presets.lookFor: Defaults: random 4.0, tuple 0.01, index tuple 0.005, operator 0.0025. `effective_cache_size` is a hint for costing only: it allocates nothing.

presets.label: Correlation matters
presets.lookFor: Same 5% of rows. The correlated column gets a cheap Index Scan (about 193). The scattered one gets a Bitmap Heap Scan (about 1090), because those rows are spread over almost every page.

presets.label: Scattered rows, every page
presets.lookFor: `Heap Blocks: exact=934`: only 2% of the rows, but they live on 934 of the 935 pages. That is why the bitmap scan is nearly as expensive as a full scan.

presets.label: Tiny table, index ignored
presets.lookFor: 200 rows fit in **2 pages**. Reading both and testing 200 rows costs 2 + 2 + 0.5 = **4.50**. The index path costs 8.16, because it reads index pages and then a random heap page. At 20000 rows the same query switches to the Index Scan (8.30). An unused index on a tiny table is the planner working correctly.

presets.label: Startup cost and LIMIT
presets.lookFor: A Sort has a large **startup cost**: it must read everything before returning a row. The index scan under LIMIT starts at 0.29 and the Limit node charges only a fraction of the total.

presets.label: SSD pricing
presets.lookFor: At 1.1 the random heap fetches look almost as cheap as sequential ones, so the plan cost drops and index plans win over a wider range.

presets.label: enable_* only discourages
presets.lookFor: There is no index on `note`, so a seq scan is the only path and it is still used. PostgreSQL 18 marks it `Disabled: true`.

production.title: Moving a reporting database to NVMe without telling the planner
production.problem: Dashboards filtering on scattered columns kept choosing full sequential scans of large tables, even when the filter matched well under 1% of rows. The planner was still pricing every random read at four sequential reads and assumed almost nothing was cached.
production.outcome: On the playground table, at 1.1 the 1% scattered-column bitmap plan drops from cost 999 to 661, plain index scans win at 40–50% of the table, and the seq scan wins only from 70% instead of 50%. On a large table the same shift turns many seq scans into index plans. Check the slow queries with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` before and after.

pitfalls.title: Testing plans with enable_seqscan = off
pitfalls.fix: Use the flag only to see the alternative's cost. Then fix the inputs: statistics (`ANALYZE`, a higher statistics target) or cost constants. Compare `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` runs, not costs alone.

pitfalls.title: Comparing cost numbers across queries
pitfalls.fix: Rank queries by measured time and buffers (`pg_stat_statements`, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`). Use costs to understand why one plan beat another.

pitfalls.title: Leaving random_page_cost at the spinning-disk default
pitfalls.fix: Set `random_page_cost` close to `seq_page_cost` (1.1 is common for SSD) and size `effective_cache_size` honestly. Change one setting at a time and re-check key plans.

keyPointers: Unit: one sequential page = `seq_page_cost` **1.0**. Defaults: random page **4.0**, row **0.01**, index entry **0.005**, operator **0.0025**.
Seq scan = **pages × seq_page_cost + rows × cpu_tuple_cost**, plus `cpu_operator_cost` per qual per row. It does not depend on selectivity.
Index scans cost heap fetches between "sequential" and "random" depending on **correlation**. Bitmap scans read each heap page once, in physical order.
Every plan shows **startup..total** cost. LIMIT and EXISTS favour low startup cost.
`enable_*` flags only discourage a node (`Disabled: true`). `effective_cache_size` is a costing hint, not an allocation.

lessons.title: Planner statistics
lessons.tldr: `ANALYZE` samples each table and stores per-column **statistics** (null fraction, distinct count, most common values, an equal-frequency histogram and physical correlation) that the planner turns into row-count estimates. Every cost in a plan is multiplied by those estimates, so knowing how `eqsel` and `scalarltsel` read `pg_stats` (and where their independence assumption breaks) explains most bad plans.

visualizer.title: Estimate rows from a real pg_stats row
visualizer.interaction: Drag the constant and watch the MCV list and histogram produce the estimate, matched against PostgreSQL's own number and the true count. The third mode shows correlated columns and extended statistics.

presets.label: Before the first ANALYZE
presets.lookFor: Never analyzed: `reltuples = -1`, and the plan guesses **rows=8 width=240**. The width comes from the declared `varchar(50)` sizes, and the row count from a default selectivity. After ANALYZE: rows=25, width=15, and the real count is 25.

presets.label: Read pg_stats
presets.lookFor: `zone` (target 10): 10 MCVs covering 48.5% of rows and 11 histogram bounds. `id`: `n_distinct = -1` means "unique", and the histogram has 101 bounds at the default target of 100.

presets.label: Under the hood: pg_statistic
presets.lookFor: `pg_stats` is a readable view over this catalog. Each column has five slots; `stakind` says what a slot holds: **1** = most common values (frequencies in `stanumbers`), **2** = histogram bounds, **3** = correlation. A unique column has no MCV slot, so it starts with the histogram.

presets.label: Equality: MCV vs not
presets.lookFor: zone 7 is an MCV with frequency 0.2214, so the estimate is 4428. zone 99 is not, so it gets (1 − 0.48515) / 490 × 20000 = **21** rows.

presets.label: Range: MCV + histogram
presets.lookFor: MCVs 7, 3, 12 and 40 contribute 0.4753 exactly. The histogram adds one full bucket plus 9/54 of bucket 51–105, times the non-MCV share 0.515. Estimate **10686**, actual 10706.

presets.label: Independence assumption
presets.lookFor: zip determines city, but the planner multiplies their selectivities: **5** rows estimated vs 100 real, and 2000 groups vs 200.

presets.label: Extended statistics
presets.lookFor: `{"4 => 5": 1.000000}`: column 4 (zip) fully determines column 5 (city). Estimates become 100 rows and 200 groups. CREATE STATISTICS collects nothing until ANALYZE runs.

presets.label: Statistics target
presets.lookFor: With target 100 the MCV list grows to 100 entries and the histogram gets more bounds, so more values get exact frequencies instead of the uniform guess.

production.title: A nested loop over 50,000 "one row" matches
production.problem: The planner multiplied the two selectivities and estimated a handful of rows. It chose a nested loop that probed another large table once per row. The real count was tens of thousands, and the query ran for seconds.
production.outcome: In the playground's version of the same shape, the estimate goes from 5 rows to 100 (actual 100) and GROUP BY from 2000 groups to 200 (actual 200). With correct estimates the planner switches to a hash join on the real workload.

pitfalls.title: No statistics after a bulk load
pitfalls.fix: Run `ANALYZE` as the last step of every bulk load or migration, and after creating an **expression index** (its expression gets its own statistics).

pitfalls.title: Correlated columns
pitfalls.fix: Create extended statistics (`dependencies`, `ndistinct` or `mcv`) on the column group, then ANALYZE. Use `mcv` when value combinations matter or when filters are not plain equality.

pitfalls.title: n_distinct badly estimated from the sample
pitfalls.fix: Raise the target for that column, or pin the value: `ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET (n_distinct = -0.05)` (negative means a fraction of rows), then ANALYZE.

keyPointers: `pg_stats`: **null_frac**, **n_distinct** (positive count, negative fraction, −1 unique), **most_common_vals/freqs**, **histogram_bounds**, **correlation**.
`=` on an MCV uses its frequency. Otherwise **(1 − Σ mcv freqs − null_frac) / (n_distinct − #MCVs)**.
`<` sums matching MCV freqs exactly, then adds histogram buckets (linear inside a bucket) scaled by the non-MCV fraction.
ANDed predicates are **multiplied**. Correlated columns need `CREATE STATISTICS` (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv) plus ANALYZE.
`default_statistics_target` = **100** caps MCVs and histogram buckets. ANALYZE samples 300 × the largest target rows.

lessons.title: B-Tree internals: splits, high keys and right-links
lessons.tldr: PostgreSQL's default index is a **B+tree** whose pages are sibling-linked on every level, and every page except the rightmost carries a **high key**, the upper bound of the keys it may hold. Those two additions, from **Lehman & Yao**, let readers descend without locking parents: a reader that lands on a page split behind its back notices its key exceeds the high key and simply **moves right**.

visualizer.title: Grow a B-Tree, one key at a time
visualizer.interaction: Insert keys and watch descents and page splits. Then reset, switch to **random keys**, and compare page count and leaf fill. That gap is the UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7 story.

presets.label: Metapage
presets.lookFor: Block 0 is the **metapage**. `level` is the root height (0 = the root is a leaf). `allequalimage` = true means deduplication is safe.

presets.label: A leaf page
presets.lookFor: `btpo_prev`/`btpo_next` are the sibling links. **Item 1 is the high key**: it is the first key of the right sibling, not a row on this page.

presets.label: Root & downlinks
presets.lookFor: On internal pages, `ctid` holds `(child block, …)`: a downlink, not a heap row. The first item has no key and covers "minus infinity".

presets.label: v4 vs v7 vs bigint
presets.lookFor: Same row count. Random UUIDv4 keys split pages all over the index (about 23% more pages here). UUIDv7 and bigint append at the right edge and pack leaves to about 90%.

presets.label: Leaf fill %
presets.lookFor: Walks every leaf with `bt_page_stats`. Expect about 90% for sequential keys and about 70% for random ones. Random fill keeps drifting lower as the index grows.

presets.label: Index scan buffers
presets.lookFor: An equality lookup touches only a handful of buffers (metapage, root, leaf, heap page). `Index Searches: 1` (new in 18) counts descents of the tree.

production.title: Switching primary keys from UUIDv4 to UUIDv7
production.problem: Every insert landed on a **random leaf**. With the index larger than cache, most inserts first had to read a cold leaf from disk, and full leaves split down the middle, leaving pages about 65% full at scale. Checkpoints also had to write a full-page image for every scattered leaf they touched.
production.outcome: UUIDv4 needs 23% more index pages than UUIDv7 at 20k rows and 39% more at 100k rows (64.7% vs 89.8% leaf fill). In production the bigger win is locality: inserts touch one hot leaf instead of thousands of cold ones, so fewer reads and less full-page-image WAL.

pitfalls.title: Random keys on a large, write-heavy table
pitfalls.fix: Use time-ordered keys (`bigint` identity or `uuidv7()`). If a random id must be exposed externally, keep it as a secondary unique column and leave the primary key sequential.

pitfalls.title: Indexing values that are too large
pitfalls.fix: Index a hash or prefix instead: `CREATE INDEX ON docs (md5(body))` for equality lookups, a trigram GIN index for search, or a `left(col, 100)` expression index.

pitfalls.title: Bloat after mass deletes
pitfalls.fix: Run `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx;` (no long write lock), then check the size with `pg_relation_size`. For time-based purges, partition and drop whole partitions instead.

keyPointers: Block 0 is the **metapage**. The **root** can move up as the tree grows. Leaf and internal pages on each level form a **doubly-linked list**.
Every non-rightmost page stores a **high key**. If a reader's key is greater than it, the reader follows the **right-link**: that is the Lehman & Yao move-right rule.
When a page is full: try **deleting dead entries**, then **deduplicate** into posting lists, and only then **split**. Splits cascade upward, and a root split adds a level.
Appending new largest keys fills leaves to **fillfactor 90**; random keys split pages in half, leaving leaves only about 65–72% full.
Entries max out at about **1/3 page** (2704 bytes); index a hash or prefix of big values.

lessons.title: Hash indexes
lessons.tldr: A hash index stores only a **4-byte hash code** per row, grouped into **buckets** that a lookup reaches directly from the metapage, without descending a tree. That makes it compact for long keys and cheap for pure equality lookups, at the price of no ranges, no ordering, no uniqueness and no multicolumn support.

visualizer.title: Linear hashing, one bucket split at a time
visualizer.interaction: Insert keys and follow each hash code through the masks into a bucket. Watch exactly one bucket split when the fill factor is exceeded, then insert a duplicate key until it grows an overflow chain.

presets.label: Empty metapage
presets.lookFor: An empty int4 hash index already has **8 buckets** (`maxbucket` 7, `highmask` 15, `lowmask` 7), 10 pages counting the metapage and bitmap page. `ffactor` 307 is the target tuples per bucket.

presets.label: One bucket split
presets.lookFor: 2456 = 307 × 8 tuples fit. Row 2457 crosses the threshold, so `maxbucket` goes 7 → 8: exactly **one** bucket split.

presets.label: Page types
presets.lookFor: Block 0 is the **metapage**, then primary **bucket** pages, a **bitmap** page that tracks free overflow pages, and more buckets added in batches as the index grows.

presets.label: Only the hash is stored
presets.lookFor: Each item is a heap `ctid` plus a 32-bit hash code, sorted by hash within the page. The key itself is not stored, so every match is rechecked against the heap.

presets.label: Duplicates → overflow
presets.lookFor: 800 copies of one key all land in one bucket. Its primary page overflows into a chain of 2 overflow pages, and the Bitmap Index Scan reads all 3 pages of that bucket.

presets.label: Long keys: hash vs B-tree
presets.lookFor: For ~90-byte URLs the hash index is smaller than the B-tree (about 2.0 MB vs 2.4 MB) and a lookup reads about 3 buffers. For a 16-byte uuid the opposite happens: hash 1040 kB vs B-tree 632 kB at 20000 rows.

production.title: Deduplicating long URLs in a crawler
production.problem: A B-tree on `url` stored every full string, so the index was nearly as large as the table and lookups touched more pages than necessary. Very long URLs also risked the B-tree entry limit of about a third of a page.
production.outcome: In the playground, 20000 URLs of about 90 bytes give a 2.0 MB hash index against 2.4 MB for the B-tree, and a lookup reads 3 buffers. The gap grows with key length, because hash entries never get wider.

pitfalls.title: Many duplicates in one key
pitfalls.fix: Use hash indexes for unique or nearly unique columns. Exclude the hot values with a partial index (`WHERE status <> 'done'`), or use a B-tree, which deduplicates.

pitfalls.title: Expecting it to shrink or to be smaller
pitfalls.fix: Rebuild with `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. Measure with `pg_relation_size` before choosing hash over B-tree for short keys.

pitfalls.title: Using it for anything but =
pitfalls.fix: Keep hash indexes for equality-only access paths. Everything else needs a B-tree.

keyPointers: Stores a **4-byte hash** per row, sorted by hash within each page. Every match is **lossy** and rechecked against the heap.
bucket = **hash & highmask**, folded with **lowmask** if above `maxbucket`. The masks live in the metapage, cached by each backend.
Growth is **linear hashing**: when `ntuples > ffactor × buckets`, exactly one bucket splits, in the foreground.
Page kinds: **metapage**, **bucket**, **overflow** (chained duplicates), **bitmap** (free overflow pages).
`=` only, single column, no UNIQUE, never shrinks without REINDEX. Best for long, nearly unique keys.

lessons.title: GIN: inverted indexes
lessons.tldr: A GIN index stores each **key** that occurs inside a composite value (array element, jsonb path, text-search lexeme) exactly once, with a sorted **posting list** of the rows that contain it. That inverted layout makes "which rows contain these elements?" fast, and the **pending list** exists because a single row insert would otherwise touch one entry per element.

visualizer.title: Inside a GIN index on tags
visualizer.interaction: Insert rows and watch them queue in the pending list, then overflow it or VACUUM it into the entry tree. Popular keys outgrow their posting list into a posting tree. Run the search to see posting lists intersected and the pending list scanned.

presets.label: Entries and pages
presets.lookFor: 5000 rows but only **29 keys** (t0–t19, c0–c6, rare, common). `common` occurs in 4950 rows, too many for a posting list, so it has a **posting tree**: the `{data,leaf,compressed}` page.

presets.label: Containment search
presets.lookFor: GIN finds both keys and intersects their posting lists. GIN only supports **bitmap scans**, so a Bitmap Heap Scan rechecks the rows. The index part reads **5 buffers**.

presets.label: Pending list fills
presets.lookFor: 300 new rows sit in **2 pending pages**, not in the entry tree. The same search now also reads the pending pages: index buffers go from 5 to **7**.

presets.label: Flush the pending list
presets.lookFor: `gin_clean_pending_list` (or VACUUM, or autovacuum's analyze) moves pending entries into the main structure in one bulk pass and returns the number of pages flushed.

presets.label: jsonb_ops vs jsonb_path_ops
presets.lookFor: `jsonb_path_ops` hashes whole paths, so it is smaller but supports only `@>`, `@?` and `@@`. Neither GIN index helps `->> =`: that is a plain equality on an expression and needs a B-tree expression index.

presets.label: Fix ->> with a B-tree
presets.lookFor: Three ways to ask for one SKU. `->> =` is a Seq Scan (cost 172.50). Rewritten as containment it uses the GIN index (about 17). A **B-tree expression index** on `attrs ->> 'sku'` serves the original query as an Index Scan (8.30), and at 128 kB it is less than half the size of the `jsonb_path_ops` index.

presets.label: Substring search with trigrams
presets.lookFor: pg_trgm splits text into 3-character keys, so a GIN index can answer `LIKE '%…%'`, which no B-tree can. The bitmap scan rechecks rows because trigram matches are only candidates.

production.title: A product catalog with p99 insert spikes
production.problem: Most inserts were fast, but every so often one API call took seconds. Those were the inserts that pushed the **pending list** past `gin_pending_list_limit` (4MB) and had to merge it in the foreground. Searches also slowed down between autovacuum runs, because every search scanned the whole pending list.
production.outcome: Cleanup moves from user requests into autovacuum, so the occasional multi-second insert goes away and searches read a short pending list. In the playground, 300 pending rows add 2 buffer reads to every search (5 → 7) until the list is flushed.

pitfalls.title: Expecting GIN to speed up ->> equality
pitfalls.fix: Either rewrite the filter as containment (`data @> '{"email": "x"}'`) or add a B-tree expression index.

pitfalls.title: Reaching for GIN on range columns
pitfalls.fix: Index ranges with GiST (`USING gist (during)`) or SP-GiST. Both support `&&`, `@>` and `<@`, and GiST also backs exclusion constraints and `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` keys.

pitfalls.title: Occasional very slow inserts
pitfalls.fix: Make autovacuum visit the table more often, lower the per-index limit, or set `fastupdate = off` when steady latency matters more than insert throughput.

pitfalls.title: Building GIN indexes slowly
pitfalls.fix: Raise `maintenance_work_mem` for the build session. For bulk loads, drop the GIN index, load, then recreate it.

keyPointers: GIN = an **entry tree** (B-tree over keys) whose leaf entries hold a **posting list** of TIDs, or point to a **posting tree** when the list is too big.
Each key is stored **once**, so repeated elements compress well. GIN supports only **bitmap scans** and never index-only scans.
**fastupdate** (default on) appends new entries to an unsorted **pending list**. VACUUM, autoanalyze, `gin_clean_pending_list()` or exceeding `gin_pending_list_limit` (4MB) merges it.
Every search also scans the pending list. A big list slows reads, and the insert that overflows it pays for the merge.
Opclasses decide the keys: `array_ops`, `jsonb_ops` (default), `jsonb_path_ops` (smaller, `@>` only), `tsvector_ops`, `gin_trgm_ops`.

lessons.title: GiST and SP-GiST
lessons.tldr: **GiST** is a balanced tree whose entries are predicates such as bounding boxes, and **SP-GiST** is an unbalanced tree that splits space into non-overlapping parts such as quadrants, k-d halves or string prefixes. Both are frameworks where an operator class supplies the geometry, so one access method can serve overlap, containment, range, nearest-neighbour `<->` and exclusion-constraint queries that a B-tree cannot express.

visualizer.title: Nearest-neighbour search, box by box
visualizer.interaction: Step a 3-nearest-neighbour search through a GiST R-tree, then through an SP-GiST quad-tree over the same points. Click anywhere to move the query point and compare how many nodes each visits.

presets.label: KNN with GiST
presets.lookFor: `Order By: (loc <-> …)` inside the Index Scan: the index returns rows nearest-first, so 5 neighbours out of 50000 cost about **8 buffers**, with no sort.

presets.label: Box containment
