presets.lookFor: The `consistent` function prunes every subtree whose bounding box cannot intersect the query box. The bitmap scan reads only a handful of index pages.

presets.label: SP-GiST quad-tree
presets.lookFor: `quad_point_ops` is the default SP-GiST opclass for `point`. Same KNN plan shape; here it reads about 14 buffers, and the index is smaller (about 2.3 MB vs 3.3 MB for GiST).

presets.label: Exclusion constraint
presets.lookFor: No two rows may have equal `room` **and** overlapping `during`. `btree_gist` supplies GiST support for `=` on int. Back-to-back bookings are fine because `[)` ranges do not overlap. Try inserting 101 at 10:30 to see the conflict error.

presets.label: Temporal primary key (18)
presets.lookFor: PostgreSQL 18 `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` turns the primary key into "no two rows for the same product whose periods overlap". The backing index is a **GiST** index (`USING gist (product_id, valid)`), the same machinery as an exclusion constraint. Try `INSERT INTO prices VALUES (1, tstzrange('2025-06-01', '2025-09-01'), 31);`: it fails with SQLSTATE **23P01**, an exclusion violation, not 23505.

presets.label: Operator classes
presets.lookFor: For `point`: GiST `point_ops`, SP-GiST `quad_point_ops` (default) and `kd_point_ops`. Choosing an opclass chooses the tree shape.

production.title: Double-booked meeting rooms
production.problem: Two users clicking "book" at the same moment both passed the check, because neither saw the other's uncommitted row. The result was a few double bookings every week and support tickets to fix them by hand.
production.outcome: Overlapping inserts now fail with SQLSTATE `23P01` (exclusion_violation), which the app turns into a "slot just taken" message. The same index also speeds up "what is booked in this room this week" queries.

pitfalls.title: Ordering by distance without the index operator
pitfalls.fix: Write `ORDER BY loc <-> $1 LIMIT k` so EXPLAIN shows `Order By:` inside the index scan.

pitfalls.title: Missing btree_gist for mixed exclusion constraints
pitfalls.fix: `CREATE EXTENSION btree_gist;` then create the constraint.

pitfalls.title: Catching 23505 for a temporal or exclusion key
pitfalls.fix: Handle both codes. In PL/pgSQL, catch `exclusion_violation` alongside `unique_violation`. Temporal keys also reject empty ranges, so validate input ranges before inserting.

pitfalls.title: Assuming GiST behaves like a B-tree
pitfalls.fix: For point data that is partitioned naturally, try SP-GiST (no overlap). Compare buffers with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and rebuild with REINDEX after heavy churn.

keyPointers: **GiST**: balanced, entries are predicates (e.g. bounding boxes). Support functions: `consistent`, `union`, `penalty`, `picksplit`, `same`, plus optional `distance` for KNN.
**SP-GiST**: unbalanced space partitioning (quad-tree, k-d tree, radix tree). Regions never overlap. `quad_point_ops` is the default for point.
KNN: `ORDER BY col <-> value LIMIT k` walks the tree best-first with lower-bound distances, so it never sorts the table.
Exclusion constraints (`EXCLUDE USING gist (… WITH &&)`) generalise UNIQUE to "no two rows overlap". `btree_gist` adds `=` for scalars.
Both are lossy per opclass: `Recheck Cond` and `Rows Removed by Index Recheck` show rows re-tested against the heap.

lessons.title: BRIN for huge append-only tables
lessons.tldr: A BRIN index stores one tiny **summary** (such as the min and max value) per **block range** of consecutive heap pages, so it stays a few kilobytes even for a table of gigabytes. When a column follows the physical row order, as timestamps do in an append-only log, those summaries let a scan skip almost every block for the cost of reading a handful of index pages.

visualizer.title: Block ranges, summaries and what a query must read
visualizer.interaction: Slide the query window and watch which ranges are consistent with it. Then add outliers, shuffle the rows, change `pages_per_range`, append unsummarized blocks, and compare minmax with minmax-multi.

presets.label: Tiny index
presets.lookFor: 1082 heap pages need only **68** range summaries (16 pages each): 24 kB of BRIN against about 4.4 MB of B-tree. `correlation` is 1 for `readings` and close to 0 for `shuffled`.

presets.label: Read the summaries
presets.lookFor: Each tuple covers 16 blocks starting at `blknum`. In `readings` each summary spans about 8 hours. In `shuffled` every summary spans the whole 23 days, so it can never exclude anything.

presets.label: Lossy bitmap scan
presets.lookFor: `Heap Blocks: lossy=16`: one matching range, all 16 of its pages read. `Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 2600` are the rows on those pages outside the hour. About 21 buffers in total.

presets.label: Uncorrelated: useless
presets.lookFor: Same query, same index type, shuffled rows: every range matches, so the planner does a **Seq Scan** of all 1088 pages.

presets.label: New rows: unsummarized
presets.lookFor: Pages appended after the index was built have no summary until VACUUM, `autosummarize`, or `brin_summarize_new_values()` processes them. Until then every scan must read them. Here 68 summaries become **75**.

presets.label: minmax-multi and bloom
presets.lookFor: **minmax-multi** stores several intervals per range (good with outliers). **bloom** stores a Bloom filter for equality on values that are not ordered. Both are still lossy.

production.title: Indexing a 2-billion-row sensor table without doubling its size
production.problem: A B-tree on `ts` was larger than a fifth of the table, every insert had to update it, and it no longer fit in memory. Dropping it made window queries scan the whole table.
production.outcome: In the playground the BRIN index is 24 kB against 4.4 MB for a B-tree on the same 200000 rows (about 180× smaller), and a one-hour query reads 21 buffers instead of 1088. Inserts barely touch the index, because a range's summary changes only when a new value widens it.

pitfalls.title: BRIN on a column that does not follow physical order
pitfalls.fix: Check `correlation` in `pg_stats` (close to ±1 is good). Use BRIN only for append-mostly data, or physically order the table first (`CLUSTER` with a B-tree, then switch).

pitfalls.title: Freshly inserted ranges are never skipped
pitfalls.fix: Create the index `WITH (autosummarize = on)` or call `brin_summarize_new_values()` from your loader.

pitfalls.title: Outliers and backfills widen ranges
pitfalls.fix: Use `minmax-multi` opclasses, or `brin_desummarize_range()` plus re-summarize after fixing the data.

keyPointers: One index tuple per **block range** (`pages_per_range`, default **128** pages). Index size ≈ table pages / pages_per_range.
BRIN scans are always **bitmap** and always **lossy**: every page of a matching range is read and every row rechecked.
Useful only when values follow **physical order** (`pg_stats.correlation` near ±1): append-only logs, time series, IoT.
Opclass kinds: **minmax**, **minmax-multi** (outliers), **inclusion** (ranges, boxes, inet), **bloom** (equality).
New ranges stay unsummarized until VACUUM, `autosummarize = on` (default off) or `brin_summarize_new_values()`.

lessons.title: Designing indexes: multicolumn, partial, expression, covering
lessons.tldr: A good index matches how one important query filters and sorts: **equality columns first and the range column last**, a **predicate** for the rows you actually query, the **same expression** the WHERE clause uses, and **INCLUDE** columns so the heap is never read. Each extra index slows every write and can block HOT updates, so the goal is the smallest set of indexes that turns your hot queries into short, ordered index reads.

visualizer.title: Pick the index: five real queries
visualizer.interaction: For each query, choose one of three candidate indexes. The answer shows the real plan, buffers and index size PostgreSQL 18 produced for that index alone.

presets.label: Equality first, range last
presets.lookFor: Both conditions appear in `Index Cond`, and the scan reads only user 42's February entries: about 5 buffers.

presets.label: Skip scan (18)
presets.lookFor: Run 1 uses `(region, category, sale_date)` without any condition on `region`. That is a **skip scan**, new in PostgreSQL 18, and it shows `Index Searches: 7`. Run 2 names the three regions and needs only 3 searches. Run 3, with an index that leads with the filtered columns, needs 1. Skip scan rescues an index whose leading column has few distinct values. It does not replace the right column order.

presets.label: Partial index
presets.lookFor: 32 kB, ordered, and only pending rows. The planner uses it only when the query's WHERE **implies** the predicate: the `status = 'done'` query cannot use it.

presets.label: Expression index
presets.lookFor: Before: Seq Scan with a `lower()` Filter. After creating the index and running ANALYZE (which collects statistics for the expression), the row estimate is right and the index is used.

presets.label: A cast hides the index
presets.lookFor: `int = bigint` still uses the index, because both types belong to the same B-tree operator family. `42.0` is `numeric`, so PostgreSQL casts the **column**: `Filter: ((user_id)::numeric = 42.0)` and a Seq Scan costing 2531 instead of 76. Casting the column to text does the same thing. Match the literal to the column type.

presets.label: INCLUDE and heap fetches
presets.lookFor: First run: `Heap Fetches: 0`, 15 buffers. The UPDATE clears the all-visible bits of the pages it touched, so the second run visits the heap: **4120 heap fetches**, more than the 4020 rows, because the non-HOT update left old index entries pointing at dead versions. VACUUM fixes both.

presets.label: NULLS NOT DISTINCT
presets.lookFor: By default NULLs are distinct, so two `(1, NULL)` rows are allowed. With `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` a second `(1, NULL)` would violate the index. Try inserting it again.

presets.label: Unused indexes
presets.lookFor: Statistics are flushed lazily; the first call forces it. `idx_scan = 0` over a long period means the index costs write time and space without serving reads. Check replicas too before dropping it. The second query is the usual "index usage %" check. It needs `NULLIF` against division by zero, and `coalesce` because `idx_scan` is NULL for a table with no indexes. Only trust it on large tables: seq scans on tiny tables are correct.

production.title: A job queue that slowed down as it grew
production.problem: The only index was on `state`. Each poll found all queued rows, fetched them from the heap and sorted them to keep ten. A full index on `run_at` alone would have walked millions of finished jobs before finding queued ones.
production.outcome: In the playground's smaller version (500 pending of 100000 rows) the same change cuts the poll from 503 buffers with a sort to 12 buffers without one, using a 32 kB index instead of 700 kB.

pitfalls.title: Range column first in a composite index
pitfalls.fix: Order key columns as: equality columns, then at most one range or ORDER BY column. Verify with buffers in `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`.

pitfalls.title: Partial index never chosen with parameters
pitfalls.fix: Write the predicate as a literal in the query (`WHERE status = 'pending'`), or use custom plans (`plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan`).

pitfalls.title: CREATE INDEX on a busy table
pitfalls.fix: Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` outside a transaction block. On failure, `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` the invalid index or `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY` it.

pitfalls.title: Indexes that block HOT updates
pitfalls.fix: Avoid indexing columns that change constantly (counters, `updated_at`) unless a key query needs them. Watch `n_tup_hot_upd` in `pg_stat_user_tables`.

pitfalls.title: Assuming foreign keys are indexed
pitfalls.fix: Index the referencing columns of every foreign key that sees parent deletes or joins. This catalog query lists foreign keys whose first column leads no index.

pitfalls.title: Expression index on a cast that is not immutable
pitfalls.fix: Store the value in a real `timestamptz` column written by the application or a trigger (a generated column has the same immutability rule), or store an immutable form such as epoch seconds and index `((doc->>'ts')::float8)`. Then write the query with exactly the same expression.

keyPointers: B-tree rule: **equality on leading columns + one range** on the next column bound the scan. PostgreSQL 18 **skip scan** helps when a leading column has few distinct values.
**Partial** indexes need the query to imply the predicate at plan time. Great for queues, soft deletes and rare states.
**Expression** indexes match only the identical expression. Run ANALYZE after creating one.
**INCLUDE** columns enable index-only scans (needs all-visible pages, i.e. VACUUM). INCLUDE indexes are never deduplicated.
Unique indexes treat NULLs as distinct unless `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`. Build with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and check for INVALID leftovers.

lessons.title: Reading EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
lessons.tldr: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and prints the plan tree with each node's **estimated** cost and rows next to its **actual** time, rows, loops and (by default in PostgreSQL 18) **buffers**. Reading it bottom-up shows where time and I/O really go, and the gaps between estimates and reality point straight at the statistics, indexes or memory settings to fix.

visualizer.title: Click through seven real plans
visualizer.interaction: Pick a scenario and click any node, or press Next node to tour the tree. Compare the in-memory and spilled sort, 1 and 2 hash batches, and an index-only scan before and after VACUUM.

presets.label: Node anatomy
presets.lookFor: Read bottom-up: two scans feed a Hash Join, which feeds HashAggregate. Each line shows `(cost=… rows=…)` then `(actual time=… rows=… loops=…)`. Buffers appear without asking: BUFFERS is on by default with ANALYZE in 18.

presets.label: Filter becomes Index Cond
presets.lookFor: Before: `Seq Scan`, `Filter`, `Rows Removed by Filter: 4999`, cost 94.50 and 32 buffers. After: `Index Scan`, `Index Cond`, cost 8.30 and 3 buffers. A **Filter** is checked on every row after it is read. An **Index Cond** decides which rows are read at all. The IN list shows `Index Searches: 3`.

presets.label: Sort spill
presets.lookFor: `Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 2128kB` with `temp read/written` buffers, versus `quicksort  Memory: 5174kB`. The fix is memory for that query, not an index.

presets.label: Hash batches
presets.lookFor: `Batches: 2` on the Hash node: the inner side did not fit in `work_mem × hash_mem_multiplier` (2.0), so it went to temp files and was processed in two passes.

presets.label: Loops multiply
presets.lookFor: The inner Bitmap Heap Scan shows `rows=20.00 loops=3`: 60 rows in total. `Index Searches: 3` counts one descent per loop.

presets.label: Heap fetches → 0
presets.lookFor: Before VACUUM: `Heap Fetches: 6020` and about 6028 buffers. After VACUUM sets the visibility map: `Heap Fetches: 0` and 9 buffers. Same plan shape, a 600× difference in I/O.

presets.label: Misestimate
presets.lookFor: An expression the planner has no statistics for gets a default selectivity, here **10 rows estimated, 199 actual**. Compare the two `rows=` values on each line first: everything above a misestimate is planned on wrong numbers.

presets.label: JSON and settings
presets.lookFor: `SETTINGS` lists planner-relevant settings that differ from defaults: `work_mem`, and also `max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0`, which is why the playground never shows parallel plans. `FORMAT JSON` is what plan visualizers parse. The `Sort Method` is `top-N heapsort`: LIMIT keeps only 10 rows, so no spill.

production.title: A nightly report that took 40 minutes
production.problem: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` showed a Hash node with **Batches: 64** and gigabytes of temp writes, then a Sort with **external merge**. The server ran with the default `work_mem` of 4MB, so every hash and sort spilled to disk.
production.outcome: In the playground the same effect is visible at small scale: the sort goes from external merge with 1636 temp blocks to an in-memory quicksort, and the hash join from 2 batches to 1. Spill-free plans also stop competing for disk with daytime traffic.

pitfalls.title: Reading per-loop numbers as totals
pitfalls.fix: Multiply time and rows by `loops`. Look for the node whose time × loops dominates. Buffers, unlike rows, are already totals.

pitfalls.title: Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on writes
pitfalls.fix: Wrap it in a transaction and roll back.

pitfalls.title: Blaming the wrong node
pitfalls.fix: Subtract children's times to find each node's own work, or use a visualizer that does it. Start from the deepest node whose estimate first diverges from actual rows.

pitfalls.title: Index-only scans that are not
pitfalls.fix: VACUUM the table (or tune autovacuum for insert-heavy tables with `autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor`) so pages become all-visible.

pitfalls.title: Looking for EXPLAIN options that do not exist
pitfalls.fix: For I/O, read the `Buffers:` lines (automatic with ANALYZE in 18), and set `track_io_timing = on` to add `I/O Timings`. Use `BUFFERS OFF` to hide them. For CPU time, compare `actual time` with the I/O timings.

keyPointers: Each node: `(cost=startup..total rows= width=)` estimated, then `(actual time=first..last rows= loops=)` measured. **Compare the two rows values first.**
Actual rows and time are **per loop**; multiply by `loops`. A node's time includes its children.
**Buffers** (default with ANALYZE in 18): shared hit = cached, read = from OS, temp = spills. They include child nodes.
Red flags: `external merge Disk`, `Batches` > 1, `Heap Fetches` > 0, big `Rows Removed by Filter`, `lossy` heap blocks.
Not shown in the playground but common in production: `Gather` with `Workers Planned/Launched` for parallel query, and a `JIT:` block when the plan cost exceeds `jit_above_cost`.

modules.title: Concurrency, MVCC & Locking
modules.summary: Snapshots and visibility rules, HOT updates, isolation levels, and the lock hierarchy from spinlocks to table locks.

lessons.title: ACID and transactions
lessons.tldr: A **transaction** groups statements so they commit or vanish together, and PostgreSQL implements that by stamping every row version with an **xid** and recording one 2-bit status per xid in the commit log. Because rollback and crash recovery only have to flip or ignore that status, an abort is instant and PostgreSQL needs **no undo log**.

visualizer.title: A transfer with a savepoint, xid by xid
visualizer.interaction: Step through BEGIN, two UPDATEs, a SAVEPOINT and a ROLLBACK TO. Switch the ending to compare a clean COMMIT, a crash, and an error followed by COMMIT.

presets.label: Virtual vs real xid
presets.lookFor: Before the UPDATE the xid is **NULL**: only a virtual xid exists. After it, a `transactionid` lock on the new xid appears, held in the main lock table (`fastpath = false`).

presets.label: Savepoint = subtransaction
presets.lookFor: Two `transactionid` locks: the top xid and a **subxid** one higher. Bob's new version has `cmin = 1`. After `ROLLBACK TO`, bob's surviving row shows `xmax` = the aborted subxid, which readers ignore.

presets.label: Transfer: all or nothing
presets.lookFor: The first CALL commits inside the procedure: alice **70**, bob **80**. The negative transfer fails on the credit (**23514**) and alice's debit vanishes with it. Inside a transaction block the procedure may not COMMIT, so CALL fails with **2D000** `invalid transaction termination`.

presets.label: Transactional DDL
presets.lookFor: The third ALTER fails (**23502**: existing rows have no postal code), and the first two columns are rolled back with it: `new_columns = 0`. Schema changes are ordinary transactional writes to the catalogs.

presets.label: Read the commit log
presets.lookFor: Every version ever written is still on the page. `pg_xact_status` reads `pg_xact`: versions whose xmin is **aborted** are invisible forever, and an aborted xmax deletes nothing.

presets.label: Sequences ignore ROLLBACK
presets.lookFor: The rollback did not give back 1 and 2, and the failed INSERT used up **3** before its CHECK fired, so the first real invoice is number **4**. Sequences are non-transactional by design, which is what lets concurrent sessions take values without waiting.

presets.label: Cost of subtransactions
presets.lookFor: Each `BEGIN … EXCEPTION` block is a subtransaction, and each one that writes burns a **subxid**: the 500-row loop advances the counter by about 500. The set-based UPDATE uses one xid.

presets.label: Implicit transactions & 2PC
presets.lookFor: A plain read gets no xid (**NULL**). `txid_current()` forces one, and outside BEGIN each statement is its own transaction, so the two values differ by one. `max_prepared_transactions = 0` disables `PREPARE TRANSACTION`; production 2PC needs it raised.

production.title: A nightly job that burned half a million xids
production.problem: Every exception block is a **subtransaction**, and every one that writes gets its own subxid. One run over 500 k accounts assigns about 500 k subxids inside one top-level transaction. Past **64 cached subxids** per backend, other sessions' visibility checks must consult `pg_subtrans`, and the xid counter races toward the freeze thresholds.
production.outcome: On 500 rows the per-row exception loop advances the xid counter by **502**, the set-based UPDATE by **1**. The subxid cache can no longer overflow, and xid consumption drops by the row count.

pitfalls.title: Idle in transaction
pitfalls.fix: Commit or roll back after every unit of work (reads included), and set a server-side guard.

pitfalls.title: Subtransaction overflow
pitfalls.fix: Avoid per-row savepoints (ORM "nested transactions", PL/pgSQL EXCEPTION inside loops). Batch the work set-based, or commit in smaller transactions.

pitfalls.title: Carrying on after an error
pitfalls.fix: Check every statement result and ROLLBACK on error, then retry the unit of work. To survive an expected failure inside one transaction, set a SAVEPOINT before it and `ROLLBACK TO` it on error.

pitfalls.title: A procedure that COMMITs, called inside BEGIN
pitfalls.fix: Run such procedures in autocommit mode, as a top-level CALL. If the caller must own the transaction, remove COMMIT from the procedure and let the caller commit.

pitfalls.title: Expecting ROLLBACK to undo everything
pitfalls.fix: Never use a sequence as a gap-free counter. Use `pg_advisory_xact_lock` when the lock should end with the transaction.

pitfalls.title: Forgotten prepared transactions
pitfalls.fix: Leave `max_prepared_transactions = 0` unless you run a transaction manager, and alert on old rows in `pg_prepared_xacts`.

keyPointers: Every transaction has a **virtual xid**. A real **xid** (32-bit, wraps; `xid8` adds the epoch) is assigned only at the first write.
Commit and abort are a **2-bit status** per xid in `pg_xact`. Rows are never undone: aborted xmins are invisible and aborted xmaxes are ignored.
**SAVEPOINT** and PL/pgSQL **EXCEPTION** blocks are subtransactions with their own **subxids**. Only 64 are cached per backend.
Locks are held to **transaction end**, except those taken after a savepoint that is rolled back to.
**2PC**: `PREPARE TRANSACTION` → `COMMIT PREPARED` / `ROLLBACK PREPARED`; inspect `pg_prepared_xacts`.

lessons.title: Snapshots and tuple visibility
lessons.tldr: A **snapshot** is three numbers, `xmin:xmax:xip`, that classify every xid as finished, in progress, or not yet started, and a row version is visible when its inserting xid counts and its deleting xid does not. Snapshots let readers and writers work on the same rows at once without blocking, because each reader just ignores the versions its snapshot cannot see.

visualizer.title: Two sessions, one row, two isolation levels
visualizer.interaction: Step the timeline, then flip A to Repeatable Read and replay it. Below, edit a snapshot and click xids to see the visibility rule decide.

presets.label: Your snapshot
presets.lookFor: With only one session, nothing is in progress: `xmin = xmax` and `xip` is empty. `my_xid` is NULL because this read-only statement never needed an xid.

presets.label: UPDATE writes a new version
presets.lookFor: `SET price = price` changes nothing, yet a new version is written: `old` is the version at **(0,1)** that just received an `xmax`, `new` is the one at **(0,3)**. A SELECT without ORDER BY returns heap order, so the desk now comes back after the chair.

presets.label: Own xid vs own snapshot
presets.lookFor: The function says your own xid is **not** visible (it equals xmax), yet the SELECT shows price 11. Own changes are visible through a separate rule, by command id.

presets.label: Save a snapshot, then write
presets.lookFor: A `pg_snapshot` is an ordinary value: we stored the snapshot from before three later transactions. The next preset judges every version against it.

presets.label: Time travel with the rule
presets.lookFor: The visibility rule in SQL. The **t0** snapshot still sees the old desk price and the chair; **now** sees the new desk and the lamp. Every version is still on the page until VACUUM.

presets.label: Hint bits
presets.lookFor: Right after the INSERT the tuple has no `HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED`. The next reader looks up `pg_xact`, then caches the answer as a **hint bit** (and dirties the page).

presets.label: Repeatable Read snapshot
presets.lookFor: The transaction snapshot is taken at the **first statement** and reused. With concurrent writers, `later_stmt` would still equal `first_stmt` under RR, but would move under Read Committed.

production.title: One forgotten transaction bloats every table
production.problem: That transaction's snapshot has an old **xmin**. Every row version deleted after it might still be visible to it, so VACUUM on every table in the database must keep them. Hot tables bloat, and index scans slow down as they wade through dead versions.
production.outcome: VACUUM can again remove versions older than the next-oldest snapshot. `n_dead_tup` in `pg_stat_user_tables` falls on the next autovacuum pass, and a recurring offender is cut off after 5 minutes.

pitfalls.title: Long snapshots block cleanup everywhere
pitfalls.fix: Monitor `age(backend_xmin)` in `pg_stat_activity` and `pg_replication_slots.xmin`; set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` and `transaction_timeout`.

pitfalls.title: Relying on the order rows come back in
pitfalls.fix: Always add `ORDER BY` with a unique tiebreaker when order matters. Never read meaning into `ctid`: it changes on every update and after VACUUM FULL.

pitfalls.title: TRUNCATE empties the table for old snapshots
pitfalls.fix: Use DELETE when concurrent snapshot readers must see the old rows, or touch every table the export needs at its start, so the TRUNCATE waits for its ACCESS SHARE lock to go.

pitfalls.title: Read Committed reports that do not add up
pitfalls.fix: Run multi-statement reports as `BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY`, so every query shares one snapshot.

pitfalls.title: Comparing xid values directly
pitfalls.fix: Compare `xid8` values, or better use a `updated_at` column or logical decoding for change tracking.

keyPointers: Snapshot `xmin:xmax:xip`: below xmin = finished, at or above xmax = not started, xip = in progress.
A version is visible if its **xmin** committed before the snapshot and its **xmax** is 0, aborted, or not yet visible.
**Read Committed**: one snapshot per statement. **Repeatable Read** and Serializable: one per transaction, taken at the first statement.
**Hint bits** cache commit status on the tuple, so the first reader after a write may dirty the page.
Use `pg_current_snapshot()`, `pg_visible_in_snapshot()` and `pg_xact_status()` with **xid8** values.

lessons.title: HOT updates and fillfactor
lessons.tldr: A **heap-only tuple (HOT)** update writes the new row version on the same page and chains to it from the old one, so no index entry is added when no indexed column changed. It exists because every non-HOT update must insert into **every index** on the table, and leaving free space with **fillfactor** is how you make HOT the common case.

visualizer.title: HOT chains vs index churn
visualizer.interaction: Step through two HOT updates, a non-HOT update, an index scan and VACUUM. Then pick a fillfactor and a workload to see the HOT rate and index growth it produces.

presets.label: HOT update
presets.lookFor: lp 1 gets `HEAP_HOT_UPDATED` and `t_ctid = (0,4)`; lp 4 is `HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE`. The pkey index still has exactly three entries, all pointing at the original ctids.

presets.label: Chain a second HOT update
presets.lookFor: The chain is now lp 1 → 4 → 5. An index scan for id = 1 enters at lp 1 and walks the chain inside the page.

presets.label: Non-HOT: change an indexed column
presets.lookFor: Both indexes gain an entry pointing at (0,6), even `items_pkey` whose key did not change. The counters show 3 updates, 2 of them HOT.

presets.label: VACUUM: redirects
presets.lookFor: `lp_flags = 2` is a **redirect**: lp 1 now points to lp 5 (its `lp_off` holds the target). lp 2 and lp 4 are unused (0). The pkey entry for (0,2) is gone.

presets.label: fillfactor 100 vs 80
presets.lookFor: Same 2,000 updates. **ff80** does all of them HOT and the primary key stays the same size. **ff100** does none HOT and its primary key index nearly doubles from page splits.

presets.label: An index on the hot column
presets.lookFor: Free space no longer helps: `qty` is now indexed, so `n_tup_hot_upd` does not move. A BRIN index would not block HOT, because BRIN is a *summarizing* index.

presets.label: No-op updates are real writes
presets.lookFor: The first UPDATE changes no value but still moves alice from **(0,1)** to **(0,3)** and leaves a dead version. It is HOT, since no indexed value changed, yet it still costs a tuple, WAL and later VACUUM work. The guarded UPDATE reports **UPDATE 0** and writes nothing.

presets.label: Upsert: DO UPDATE vs DO NOTHING
presets.lookFor: A "no-op" `DO UPDATE` exists only to make RETURNING produce the row, and each run writes a new version: the ctid and xmin move every time. `DO NOTHING` writes nothing and returns no row. All three attempts still drew an identity value, so the sequence moved from 2 to **5**.

production.title: An index on last_seen_at killed HOT on a sessions table
production.problem: Every request now changes an indexed column, so **no update is HOT**. Each one inserts into all four indexes, and the table and indexes bloat between vacuums. WAL volume and checkpoint I/O rise with them.
production.outcome: On a 10,000-row table updating 20% of rows, fillfactor 100 gave **0% HOT** in the first round and grew the primary key from 30 to 57 pages; fillfactor 80 gave **100% HOT** with zero index growth, at the cost of 25% more heap pages up front.

pitfalls.title: Indexing a frequently updated column
pitfalls.fix: Keep volatile columns out of B-tree indexes, or use BRIN. Check the ratio per table.

pitfalls.title: Expecting ALTER TABLE … SET (fillfactor) to fix existing pages
pitfalls.fix: Rewrite the table once (`VACUUM FULL` or `pg_repack` during a maintenance window), or let churn redistribute rows over time.

pitfalls.title: Believing an unchanged UPDATE is free
pitfalls.fix: Filter out unchanged rows with `IS DISTINCT FROM`, or add the built-in `suppress_redundant_updates_trigger()` as a BEFORE UPDATE trigger. For get-or-create, use `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and read the existing row separately.

pitfalls.title: Pruning blocked by old snapshots
pitfalls.fix: Remove long transactions (see `backend_xmin` in `pg_stat_activity`), then pruning and HOT reuse resume on their own.

keyPointers: HOT needs both: **no indexed column changed** (BRIN excepted) and **room on the same page**.
A HOT update adds **no index entries**; index scans follow the `t_ctid` chain within the page.
Pruning turns the chain root into an **LP_REDIRECT** and frees intermediate versions, even during normal reads.
Tables default to **fillfactor 100**; 70–90 leaves room for HOT on update-heavy tables.
Monitor `n_tup_hot_upd` and `n_tup_newpage_upd` in `pg_stat_user_tables`.

lessons.title: Isolation levels: RC, RR, Serializable (SSI)
lessons.tldr: PostgreSQL offers **Read Committed** (a snapshot per statement, re-checking rows changed by others), **Repeatable Read** (one snapshot per transaction) and **Serializable** (Repeatable Read plus conflict tracking with SIRead locks). Each step up removes a class of anomalies at the cost of **serialization failures** (SQLSTATE `40001`) that the application must answer by retrying the whole transaction.

visualizer.title: Three classic races, replayed
visualizer.interaction: Pick a scenario and step through it. Watch wait bars, snapshots and row versions; in the SSI case, watch the rw-conflict edges close into a cycle.

presets.label: Levels you can ask for
presets.lookFor: You may request READ UNCOMMITTED, and it is reported back, but PostgreSQL runs it as **Read Committed**: dirty reads are never possible.

presets.label: Hits example, run serially
presets.lookFor: Run one after the other, the DELETE removes **id 1** (now 10). Run concurrently (the visualizer), the same two statements delete nothing. That gap is the RC anomaly.

presets.label: Race-free upsert
presets.lookFor: id 2 existed and took the UPDATE path (11 → 12), id 3 was inserted. Under Read Committed, a session that meets an uncommitted insert of the same key **waits** for it, then updates the committed row: it never fails with 23505 on the conflict key. `old IS NULL` (PG18) and the older `xmax = 0` trick both tell the two paths apart.

presets.label: SIRead locks: seq scan
presets.lookFor: The tiny table is read by a sequential scan, so the predicate lock covers the **whole relation**: any insert into mytab by another serializable transaction conflicts.

presets.label: SIRead locks: index scan
presets.lookFor: With an index scan the locks are fine-grained: two **tuple** locks on the heap and one **page** lock on `mytab_class_idx`. Fewer false conflicts, fewer needless 40001s.

presets.label: READ ONLY DEFERRABLE
presets.lookFor: A deferrable read-only transaction waits (if needed) for a **safe snapshot**, then reads with **no SIRead locks** and can never fail with 40001. Ideal for long reports.

production.title: On-call scheduling that let everyone go off call
production.problem: Two doctors press "go off call" at the same moment. Under Read Committed or Repeatable Read both transactions count **2**, both update their own row, and both commit. Neither update touched a row the other wrote, so no lock ever conflicted: **write skew**, and the shift has nobody.
production.outcome: The invariant holds under any interleaving, with no explicit locks. Retries are rare (only on true overlap); the tradeoff is the SSI bookkeeping overhead and a retry path that every writer must implement.

pitfalls.title: Retrying only the failed statement
pitfalls.fix: ROLLBACK and rerun the entire transaction from BEGIN, re-reading everything, with a bounded number of attempts.

pitfalls.title: Assuming Repeatable Read prevents write skew
pitfalls.fix: Use SERIALIZABLE for such transactions, or take explicit locks (`SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the rows the rule depends on).

pitfalls.title: Treating MERGE as an upsert
pitfalls.fix: Use `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` for single-table upserts. Keep MERGE for multi-action synchronisation, and retry it on 23505.

pitfalls.title: Get-or-create that returns nothing
pitfalls.fix: When the statement returns no row, run the SELECT again as a new statement (it gets a fresh snapshot in Read Committed), or loop in PL/pgSQL until one of the two paths returns the row.

pitfalls.title: Serializable with sequential scans
pitfalls.fix: Index the predicates serializable transactions filter on, keep them short, mark read-only ones `READ ONLY`, and raise `max_pred_locks_per_transaction` if promotion is frequent.

keyPointers: PostgreSQL has three real levels; **READ UNCOMMITTED = READ COMMITTED**, and its Repeatable Read also blocks phantoms.
**Read Committed**: snapshot per statement; a blocked UPDATE/DELETE re-checks its WHERE on the newest row version.
**Repeatable Read**: changing a row updated after your snapshot raises `40001` *could not serialize access due to concurrent update*.
**Serializable** (SSI): SIRead locks never block; a cycle of rw-conflicts aborts one transaction with `40001`.
Always retry the **whole transaction** on 40001 (and 40P01). Read-only transactions under RR never need to.

lessons.title: Heavyweight locks and the conflict matrix
lessons.tldr: PostgreSQL has **eight table lock modes** that commands take automatically, and two transactions can hold locks on the same table only if their modes do not conflict. The modes exist so reads, writes, VACUUM and schema changes can each run alongside exactly the operations that are safe, and the **lock queue** decides who waits when they are not.

visualizer.title: A migration stalls the whole table
visualizer.interaction: Step through the lock queue, then switch the migration to `lock_timeout = 2s` and replay it. Below, click cells or two modes in the matrix to test any pair.

presets.label: Locks a SELECT holds
presets.lookFor: **AccessShareLock** on the table and on every index the plan may use, all taken through the **fast path** (`fastpath = true`): weak locks skip the shared lock table.

presets.label: Locks an UPDATE holds
presets.lookFor: **RowExclusiveLock** on the table and its indexes, plus an ExclusiveLock on the new xid. The row lock itself is not in `pg_locks`: it lives in the tuple.

presets.label: ALTER TABLE lock levels
presets.lookFor: ADD COLUMN and ADD CONSTRAINT … NOT VALID take **AccessExclusive** but finish instantly. VALIDATE CONSTRAINT scans the table under the much weaker **ShareUpdateExclusive**, so writes continue. CREATE INDEX takes **Share**, which blocks writes.

presets.label: PG18: NOT NULL in two steps
presets.lookFor: The NOT VALID constraint is added under AccessExclusive but without a scan, and it rejects new NULLs at once (**23502**). VALIDATE fails while 400 old rows are NULL. After the backfill it scans the table under **ShareUpdateExclusive**, so writes keep flowing, and `convalidated` turns true.

presets.label: TRUNCATE vs DELETE
presets.lookFor: DELETE takes **RowExclusive** and stamps `xmax` on each row, so readers and other writers carry on. TRUNCATE takes **AccessExclusive**, which blocks even SELECT, and points the table at a brand-new empty file. It is still transactional: after ROLLBACK the old file and all 1,000 rows are back.

presets.label: A transaction never blocks itself
presets.lookFor: Share and AccessExclusive conflict, but **not with yourself**: both are granted. Strong modes always go to the main lock table (`fastpath = false`).

presets.label: Timeouts and NOWAIT
presets.lookFor: With another session holding a lock, `NOWAIT` would fail at once and `lock_timeout` after 2 s, both with **55P03**. Alone, the lock is granted and nobody blocks us (`{}`).

presets.label: Who is blocking whom
presets.lookFor: A waiting session has `wait_event_type = Lock` and a non-empty `blocked_by`; the oldest transaction is usually the root. `pg_cancel_backend` stops the running query, `pg_terminate_backend` ends the session and rolls back its transaction. With a timeout (ms) terminate returns true only once the process has exited. The lock table is sized by `max_locks_per_transaction` (objects, not rows).

production.title: A one-line migration that took the API down
production.problem: An analyst's session had run a SELECT on `orders` and stayed **idle in transaction**. The ALTER queued for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE behind it, and every API query on `orders` queued behind the ALTER. Connection pools filled and the API timed out, though no query was doing any work.
production.outcome: The worst stall an API query can see from the migration drops from "as long as the oldest open transaction" to the 2-second timeout, and the migration still lands on a later retry.

pitfalls.title: Assuming a waiting DDL is harmless
pitfalls.fix: Always set `lock_timeout` for DDL, and check for long transactions first.

pitfalls.title: CREATE INDEX blocks writes
pitfalls.fix: Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. It is not lock-free: it takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE (blocking other DDL and VACUUM), waits for every existing transaction that could modify or use the new index, and cannot run inside a transaction block. A failed concurrent build leaves an INVALID index you must drop; a failed plain CREATE INDEX rolls back completely. For a new unique constraint, build `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` first, then `ADD CONSTRAINT … UNIQUE USING INDEX`.

pitfalls.title: Assuming TRUNCATE needs only a light lock
pitfalls.fix: Run TRUNCATE with a short `lock_timeout` and retry. When readers must never block, DELETE in batches instead, or rotate partitions (DETACH, then DROP).

pitfalls.title: SET NOT NULL on a big table
pitfalls.fix: In PostgreSQL 18, add the constraint as `NOT NULL … NOT VALID` (instant), backfill in batches, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`, which scans under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE while writes continue.

pitfalls.title: Running out of lock table space
pitfalls.fix: Raise `max_locks_per_transaction` (server restart), and make sure partition pruning removes partitions at plan time.

keyPointers: Eight modes from **ACCESS SHARE** (SELECT) to **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE** (DROP, TRUNCATE, most ALTER TABLE). Only ACCESS EXCLUSIVE blocks a plain SELECT.
Locks are held to **transaction end**; a transaction never conflicts with its own locks.
Waiters queue in order: a strong waiting request blocks newcomers too. Use `lock_timeout` for DDL.
Find blockers with `pg_blocking_pids(pid)` and `pg_locks.granted = false`.
Weak locks (ACCESS SHARE, ROW SHARE, ROW EXCLUSIVE) use the per-backend **fast path** when nothing conflicts.

lessons.title: Row locks, SKIP LOCKED and advisory locks
lessons.tldr: Row locks (`FOR UPDATE`, `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, `FOR SHARE`, `FOR KEY SHARE`) are written into the tuple itself, in `t_xmax`, so PostgreSQL can lock any number of rows without memory limits. On top of them, **NOWAIT** and **SKIP LOCKED** let a worker refuse to wait, which turns a plain table into a concurrent job queue, while **advisory locks** lock ideas that are not rows at all.

visualizer.title: Three queue workers, two locking clauses
visualizer.interaction: Step through three workers claiming jobs with SKIP LOCKED, then switch to plain FOR UPDATE and watch them line up. Below, test any pair of row-lock modes.

presets.label: Claim a job
presets.lookFor: Only job 1 gets `xmax` = our xid. `pg_locks` shows a **RowShareLock** on the table and nothing per row: the row lock lives in the tuple.

presets.label: Lock bits in the tuple
presets.lookFor: Both rows carry our xid in `t_xmax`, with `HEAP_XMAX_LOCK_ONLY` (a lock, not a delete). The strength is in the flags: `HEAP_XMAX_EXCL_LOCK` vs `HEAP_XMAX_KEYSHR_LOCK`.

presets.label: Claim and start in one statement
presets.lookFor: The production pattern: the subquery picks and locks one unclaimed row, the UPDATE marks it, all in one round trip. Run it repeatedly: ids 1, 2, 3 …

presets.label: MultiXact: two lockers
presets.lookFor: `t_xmax` has room for one xid. With two lockers (here our xid and the savepoint's subxid) it holds a **MultiXact id** instead, whose members are listed in `pg_multixact`.

presets.label: Foreign keys take KEY SHARE
presets.lookFor: Inserting a child row locks the **referenced** customer `FOR KEY SHARE`. That blocks deleting the customer or changing its key, but not an ordinary UPDATE of its name.

presets.label: A hot counter row
presets.lookFor: The trigger updated the single `job_stats` row, so its current version carries **our xid** as `xmin`, and the old one has it as `xmax`. Until COMMIT, any other session inserting a job must update the same row and waits on our xid: all inserts into `jobs` now run one at a time.

presets.label: Advisory locks
presets.lookFor: Session locks stack (two locks need two unlocks) and **ignore ROLLBACK**: after it, the xact lock 7 is gone but the session lock from `pg_try_advisory_lock` is still held.

production.title: A job queue that stopped scaling at one worker
production.problem: Every worker's query targets the same oldest row. All but one block on its row lock, then re-check, then block on the next row. Adding workers added lock waits, not throughput, and `pg_stat_activity` showed most workers in `Lock: transactionid`.
production.outcome: Each worker claims a different row without waiting, so throughput grows with the number of workers until the database itself is the bottleneck. The order of processing becomes approximate, which a queue can accept.

pitfalls.title: SKIP LOCKED for general reads
pitfalls.fix: Use it only for queue-style claiming. Ordinary reads need no row locks at all under MVCC.

pitfalls.title: LIMIT and locking functions
pitfalls.fix: Apply the LIMIT in a subquery, then lock in the outer query.

pitfalls.title: Session advisory locks behind a pooler
pitfalls.fix: Behind transaction pooling use `pg_advisory_xact_lock`, which ends with the transaction.

pitfalls.title: A trigger-maintained counter row
pitfalls.fix: Compute the total on read, or spread the counter over several rows (`id = pid % 16`) and sum them, or append deltas and fold them in periodically. Create the summary row once with `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`.

pitfalls.title: MultiXact growth from FK-heavy workloads
pitfalls.fix: Monitor `mxid_age(datminmxid)`, keep autovacuum healthy, and avoid hot parent rows when you can.

keyPointers: Four row modes: **FOR UPDATE** > **FOR NO KEY UPDATE** > **FOR SHARE** > **FOR KEY SHARE**. A plain UPDATE takes NO KEY UPDATE unless it changes a key.
Row locks are stored in **`t_xmax` + infomask** (a **MultiXact** when shared); they appear in `pg_locks` only while someone waits.
**NOWAIT** errors at once (55P03); **SKIP LOCKED** silently skips. Both still take the ROW SHARE table lock normally.
Job queue: `UPDATE … WHERE id = (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1) RETURNING …`.
Advisory locks: **session** level (survive rollback, stack) vs **transaction** level (`pg_advisory_xact_lock`).

lessons.title: LWLocks, spinlocks and deadlock detection
lessons.tldr: PostgreSQL stacks three kinds of locks: **spinlocks** for a few instructions, **LWLocks** for shared-memory structures, and **heavyweight locks** for SQL objects, and only the last kind is checked for deadlocks. Deadlock detection is deferred until a waiter has slept for **deadlock_timeout**, because walking the waits-for graph is expensive and real deadlocks are rare.

visualizer.title: Two transfers, one deadlock
visualizer.interaction: Step through the classic two-account deadlock on a millisecond clock and watch the waits-for graph close. Switch to consistent lock order to see it disappear. Below, explore the lock hierarchy.

presets.label: Deadlock settings
presets.lookFor: `deadlock_timeout` = **1s**: a waiter sleeps that long before checking for a cycle. `pg_stat_database.deadlocks` counts every 40P01 in this database.

presets.label: Wait event families
presets.lookFor: Every wait a backend can report is listed. **LWLock** (84 names in 18) and **Lock** (12 heavyweight lock types) are the two lock families; `SpinDelay` hides under **Timeout**.

presets.label: The LWLocks you will meet
presets.lookFor: Hot LWLocks map to subsystems: buffer pages, WAL, the lock manager, snapshots (`ProcArray`), and the SLRU caches for commit status, subtransactions and MultiXacts.

presets.label: Heavyweight lock types
presets.lookFor: These are the `locktype` values of `pg_locks`. Row-lock waits show up as **transactionid** (waiting for the holder to finish) and **tuple** (queuing behind other waiters).

presets.label: Lock in a consistent order
presets.lookFor: Locking both rows up front in **acctnum order** means every transfer acquires its row locks in the same sequence, so no waits-for cycle can form, whatever order the UPDATEs run in.

presets.label: A transfer procedure that cannot deadlock
presets.lookFor: Without the `PERFORM … FOR UPDATE`, two opposite transfers running at once lock their sender first and deadlock. With it, both lock 11111 before 22222, so the second simply waits. Balances end at **630** and **370**.

presets.label: Tune detection for a session
presets.lookFor: Superusers can lower `deadlock_timeout` (fewer ms lost per real deadlock, more needless checks). The `pg_stat_activity` query is the one to run when sessions hang: look for `Lock` waits and their blockers.

production.title: Deadlocks between concurrent transfers
production.problem: Transfer X locks Alice then Bob; transfer Y locks Bob then Alice. Under load the logs fill with `ERROR: deadlock detected`, each one costing a retry and about **1 s** (`deadlock_timeout`) of latency for the surviving transaction.
production.outcome: With one lock order a waits-for cycle between transfers is impossible, so this path produces zero 40P01 errors; conflicting transfers now simply queue for a few milliseconds instead of stalling 1 s and retrying. Track `pg_stat_database.deadlocks` to confirm.

pitfalls.title: Opposite lock order in different code paths
pitfalls.fix: Sort keys before locking, take the strongest lock first, and retry on 40P01. The DETAIL line names both processes and lock targets.

pitfalls.title: Raising deadlock_timeout to "fix" deadlocks
pitfalls.fix: Leave it around 1 s (ideally above typical transaction time) and fix the lock order. Use `log_lock_waits = on` to log any wait longer than `deadlock_timeout`.

pitfalls.title: Treating LWLock waits as blocking
pitfalls.fix: Treat it as a capacity problem: reduce connections (pooling), add RAM for `shared_buffers`, batch WAL-heavy writes, or reduce subtransaction / MultiXact churn depending on the lock name.

keyPointers: Hierarchy: **spinlock** (instructions) → **LWLock** (shared memory structures, shared/exclusive) → **heavyweight lock** (SQL objects, 8 modes).
Only heavyweight locks have **deadlock detection**; LWLocks avoid deadlock by coding rules.
A waiter checks for deadlock after **deadlock_timeout** (default 1 s); a cycle aborts one transaction with **40P01**.
Prevent deadlocks with a **consistent lock order** (`ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE`) and retry the rare remainder.
Diagnose with `pg_stat_activity.wait_event_type` (`Lock` vs `LWLock`) and `pg_blocking_pids()`.

modules.title: Advanced Programmability & Extensions
modules.summary: Views, triggers, PL/pgSQL, the rule system, foreign data wrappers and the extensions everyone runs.

lessons.title: Views and materialized views
lessons.tldr: A **view** is a stored query that the rewriter splices into your query tree through an `ON SELECT DO INSTEAD` rule named `_RETURN`, while a **materialized view** runs that query once and keeps the result in a real heap. Views give you reusable, permission-controlled abstractions at zero runtime cost, and materialized views trade freshness for speed when the query is too expensive to run on every read.

visualizer.title: From view name to plan, and from matview to refresh
visualizer.interaction: Step through the rewriter expanding a view, then switch to **Materialized view** and watch REFRESH swap files while CONCURRENTLY patches one row. The numbers match what the playground presets print.

presets.label: The _RETURN rule
presets.lookFor: The view is a relation with `relkind = v` and `relfilenode = 0` (no file). Its query lives in `pg_rewrite` as the `_RETURN` rule, `ev_type = 1` (SELECT), `is_instead = t`.

presets.label: View vs subquery plan
presets.lookFor: Both plans are identical (`Hash Join cost=8.32..12.86`). The `id = 42` filter was pushed through the view down to `Index Scan using orders_pkey`.

presets.label: Matview goes stale
presets.lookFor: The matview still reports 2919.00 from 56 orders. The live view already sees 3084.00 from 57.

presets.label: REFRESH swaps the file
presets.lookFor: A plain REFRESH writes a brand new heap, so `relfilenode` changes. CONCURRENTLY is refused until the matview has a unique index. A matview created `WITH NO DATA` exists (`ispopulated = f`) but cannot be read at all until its first plain REFRESH.

presets.label: CONCURRENTLY patches rows
presets.lookFor: Run after the previous preset. The relfilenode does not change, and only **1 of 360** rows has the new xmin: the diff touched just the changed group.

presets.label: Updatable view + CHECK OPTION
presets.lookFor: `cheap_products` reads one table with a plain WHERE, so it is **automatically updatable**; `order_lines` (a join) is not. The second insert fails `WITH CHECK OPTION` because the row would be invisible through the view.

presets.label: Stacked views: LOCAL vs CASCADED
presets.lookFor: Without a check option, John Snow is inserted through `fte` and becomes invisible in it. **LOCAL** on `fte_1` rejects department 2 but lets contractor Mia in, because `fte`'s own filter is not checked. **CASCADED** (the default for a bare `WITH CHECK OPTION`) checks `fte` too: `new row violates check option for view "fte"`. `DELETE … WHERE id = 3` removes nothing: Bob is a contractor, so he is not a row of `fte`.

presets.label: Recursive view: org chart
presets.lookFor: `CREATE RECURSIVE VIEW` is shorthand for a view over `WITH RECURSIVE`; the column list is mandatory. Each pass joins the previous level: 1, 4, 10, then 5 people, then an empty working table ends it. The plan shows `Recursive Union` under a `CTE Scan` with `Filter: (employee_id = 10)` on top: the filter is applied **after** the whole tree is built, not pushed into the recursion.

production.title: A revenue dashboard that stopped melting the primary
production.problem: Each load scanned and aggregated the whole orders table. With dozens of viewers refreshing, the database spent most of its CPU on identical aggregates, and order inserts slowed down.
production.outcome: Dashboard reads became an index lookup on a table of a few thousand rows instead of a full aggregate. The trade-off is explicit: numbers can be up to five minutes old, and the page shows when the last refresh ran. In the playground, a concurrent refresh after one new order rewrote 1 of 360 rows.

pitfalls.title: CONCURRENTLY without a usable unique index
pitfalls.fix: Create a unique index on the natural grouping key. Populate once with a plain REFRESH if the matview was created `WITH NO DATA`.

pitfalls.title: `SELECT *` in a view freezes the column list
pitfalls.fix: List columns explicitly. After altering the base table, run `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` with the new column added **at the end** (replacing may add columns but not reorder, rename or drop them: `cannot drop columns from view`). To remove a column, drop and recreate the view, or `DROP … CASCADE` knowing which dependants go with it.

pitfalls.title: A view that hides rows leaks them anyway
pitfalls.fix: Declare the view `WITH (security_barrier)` so its quals run first, or use row-level security. Only **LEAKPROOF** functions may then be pushed below the barrier.

pitfalls.title: Base-table privileges checked as the view owner
pitfalls.fix: Set `security_invoker = true` on views that should run with the caller's rights and policies.

pitfalls.title: Blaming REFRESH for blocked order writes
pitfalls.fix: Use `REFRESH … CONCURRENTLY` with a unique index for matviews that are read during the day. Check the locks yourself inside a transaction.

pitfalls.title: Relying on the ORDER BY inside a matview
pitfalls.fix: Put the ORDER BY in the query that reads the matview, and index the sort column if the list is long.

keyPointers: A view is `relkind = v` plus a `_RETURN` rule in `pg_rewrite`. The rewriter substitutes it as a subquery before planning, and the planner usually flattens it away.

Auto-updatable views: **one FROM item**, no aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, LIMIT or set operations. Add `WITH CHECK OPTION` (CASCADED by default; LOCAL checks only the top view) so writes stay visible through the view.
A **materialized view** is a real heap filled by its query. It is stale until you REFRESH it.
**REFRESH** rewrites the whole file under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. **REFRESH CONCURRENTLY** needs a unique index, diffs rows, and lets readers continue.
Use `security_barrier` for row-filtering views and `security_invoker` when the caller's privileges and policies must apply.

lessons.title: Triggers
lessons.tldr: A **trigger** binds a function returning `trigger` to INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE on a table or view, firing BEFORE, AFTER or INSTEAD OF the change, once per row or once per statement. Triggers let the database itself enforce rules, stamp columns, write audit trails and maintain derived data, so every client gets the same behaviour no matter which code path issued the write.

visualizer.title: Every trigger for one UPDATE, in firing order
visualizer.interaction: Step through one UPDATE on three rows. Flip the toggles to skip a row, drop the WHEN clause, rename a trigger or change the statement, and watch the order change. With the default toggles the steps match, line for line, the `trigger_log` the first preset writes.

presets.label: Firing order log
presets.lookFor: Ten log lines: statement BEFORE, then b_touch and c_guard per row (alphabetical), the two queued `d_audit` events at the end, and finally `e_summary` with `old_rows=2 new_rows=2 delta=-10`. B-2 was skipped, so it keeps qty 3 and no `updated_at`.

presets.label: No-op and zero-row updates
presets.lookFor: The no-op update runs both BEFORE ROW triggers but `d_audit` never fires: its **WHEN** is false, so nothing was queued. The `WHERE false` update still fires both **statement** triggers, with empty transition tables.

presets.label: Trigger calls in EXPLAIN
presets.lookFor: EXPLAIN ANALYZE ends with one `Trigger …: calls=N` line per trigger. Row triggers show calls=3; statement triggers show calls=1.

presets.label: Catalog: pg_trigger
presets.lookFor: `tgtype` is a bitmask: 1 = ROW, 2 = BEFORE, 16 = UPDATE. So 19 = BEFORE UPDATE FOR EACH ROW, 17 = AFTER ROW, 18 = BEFORE STATEMENT, 16 = AFTER STATEMENT.

presets.label: INSTEAD OF on a join view
presets.lookFor: A join view is not auto-updatable, so the **INSTEAD OF** row trigger decides what an INSERT means. Version 1 does the work but returns NULL: the insert reports **0 rows** and `RETURNING` comes back empty. Version 2 returns NEW (with the new id filled in), so the row counts and `RETURNING` shows it. Both moves landed in the view, and the UPDATE inside also fired every inventory trigger.

presets.label: Gatekeeper: soft delete, no TRUNCATE
presets.lookFor: A BEFORE ROW trigger is a **gatekeeper**: raise to abort, edit NEW to transform, or return NULL to skip. Here the DELETE returns **no rows** and Kettle stays, marked inactive. TRUNCATE never visits rows, so it fires no DELETE triggers; only a **statement-level** TRUNCATE trigger (BEFORE or AFTER) can stop it.

presets.label: Catalog peek: hidden FK triggers
presets.lookFor: The `stock_moves.sku` foreign key is enforced by four internal **RI_ConstraintTrigger** rows (`tgisinternal = true`), two on each table. `ALTER TABLE … DISABLE TRIGGER ALL` switches those off too; `DISABLE TRIGGER USER` leaves them on. `information_schema.triggers` has one row per event and does not list TRUNCATE triggers at all.

presets.label: Event trigger on DDL
presets.lookFor: Event triggers are per database and fire on **DDL**, not DML. `ddl_command_end` sees the finished command through `pg_event_trigger_ddl_commands()`.

production.title: Auditing a bulk price update without one call per row
production.problem: A nightly job updated millions of prices in one statement. The row trigger queued one AFTER event per row in memory, then ran its INSERT once per row, one function call and one plan execution each. The job time grew far beyond the UPDATE itself.
production.outcome: On 100,000 rows the bare UPDATE took 386 ms, with the row trigger 937 ms, with the statement trigger 527 ms, writing the same 100,000 audit rows. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows why: `Trigger audit_prices: calls=1` instead of `calls=100000`. Single-row updates from the app are still audited by the same trigger.

pitfalls.title: An AFTER trigger that updates its own table
pitfalls.fix: Change the row in a **BEFORE** trigger by editing NEW (no extra UPDATE at all). If you must cascade, guard with `pg_trigger_depth()` or a WHEN clause that becomes false after the first pass.

pitfalls.title: A BEFORE trigger that forgets to return NEW
pitfalls.fix: Return NEW for INSERT/UPDATE and OLD for DELETE on every path. Reserve `RETURN NULL` for rows you really mean to drop, and log when you do.

pitfalls.title: Relying on creation order
pitfalls.fix: Encode the order in the names, for example `10_normalize`, `20_validate`, `90_audit`.

pitfalls.title: Row triggers on bulk loads
pitfalls.fix: Use statement triggers with transition tables, add `WHEN` to AFTER ROW triggers, or disable non-essential triggers for the load with `ALTER TABLE … DISABLE TRIGGER name` or `DISABLE TRIGGER USER`. `DISABLE TRIGGER ALL` also switches off the internal foreign-key triggers, so rows that break the FK load silently.

pitfalls.title: An INSTEAD OF trigger that returns NULL
pitfalls.fix: Return NEW for INSERT and UPDATE (fill generated keys into NEW first) and OLD for DELETE. Also match the full key in UPDATE and DELETE branches, or one view row changes several base rows.

pitfalls.title: A per-row trigger that maintains a summary row
pitfalls.fix: Make the write a single upsert, and gate repeat work with WHEN so re-running the same UPDATE does not double-count. Every writer then serialises on that one summary row, so keep the trigger short.

keyPointers: Order for one statement: **BEFORE STATEMENT → per row (BEFORE ROW in name order → write → queue AFTER) → AFTER ROW queue → AFTER STATEMENT**.
BEFORE ROW can **edit NEW** or **return NULL to skip** the row. AFTER return values are ignored.
Statement triggers fire **once per SQL statement** (not per transaction), **even when zero rows match**. The default granularity is FOR EACH STATEMENT.
AFTER-trigger **WHEN** runs at write time and decides whether an event is queued at all: free filtering for bulk statements.
**Transition tables** (`REFERENCING OLD TABLE … NEW TABLE …`) give AFTER triggers the whole changed set for set-based work.

lessons.title: PL/pgSQL functions and procedures
lessons.tldr: **PL/pgSQL** is the built-in procedural language: blocks of variables, loops and conditionals around embedded SQL, compiled on first call and run inside the server next to the data. It exists so logic that needs many dependent queries runs without a network round trip per statement, and so triggers, checks and batch jobs can live in the database itself.

visualizer.title: An EXCEPTION block is a subtransaction
visualizer.interaction: Step through one call and watch xids, row versions and variables. Switch to **Without EXCEPTION clause** to see the same error abort everything.

presets.label: Run demo()
presets.lookFor: The function reports its xid and the caught error (x = 2: variables keep their values). Both audit rows have that same xmin, and account 1 is still alice. `pageinspect` shows the rolled-back `Joe` version at lp 3 with the **subtransaction's own xid** (top xid + 1) as `t_xmin`.

presets.label: Error kata: INTO, FOUND, CASE, ASSERT
presets.lookFor: `INTO STRICT` raises **P0002** for no row and **P0003** for two; plain `INTO` silently keeps the first row. `SELECT sum(…) INTO` always returns one row, so **FOUND is true** even with no match and total NULL. A CASE statement with no match and no ELSE raises **20000**. ASSERT raises **P0004**, which `WHEN OTHERS` does not catch. RAISE uses a bare `%`, so `%s` prints "Brooklyn Desert**s**". A new RAISE EXCEPTION in a handler reports **P0001**; a bare `RAISE;` keeps the original **22012**.

presets.label: Cost of EXCEPTION blocks
presets.lookFor: Same loop, same work. Entering and leaving a block with an EXCEPTION clause costs a subtransaction every iteration, several times slower even when no error ever happens.

presets.label: One subxid per block
presets.lookFor: Plain inserts share the transaction's one xid. Each guarded insert ran in its own subtransaction, so 1000 rows carry **1000 different xmins**. Each one also consumed a transaction id.

presets.label: Procedure with COMMIT
presets.lookFor: A **procedure** called with CALL can end transactions. Only the even batches survive, each with its own xmin, because every COMMIT starts a new transaction. Called from inside a SELECT, or inside an explicit `BEGIN … COMMIT` block, the first COMMIT fails with **2D000 invalid transaction termination**.

presets.label: Overloads, defaults, OUT and INOUT
presets.lookFor: Overloads are chosen by their **IN argument types**; defaults are not part of the signature. `balance_of(1)` matches both functions, so it fails with **42725 is not unique**. `SELECT swap(…)` returns one **composite** value `(20,10)`; `SELECT * FROM swap(…)` expands it into columns. Procedures accept **OUT** parameters (since PostgreSQL 14); pass NULL for them in CALL. `$t$` does not close a `$T$` string.

presets.label: Dynamic SQL done safely
presets.lookFor: `regclass` validates the table name, `%I` quotes identifiers, `%L` quotes literals, and `USING` passes values as parameters. EXECUTE is re-planned on every call.

presets.label: STABLE now() vs VOLATILE clock
presets.lookFor: `now()` is **STABLE**: one value for the whole statement (in fact the whole transaction). `clock_timestamp()` is **VOLATILE** and changes per row. `provolatile` is `i`, `s` or `v`.

production.title: An upsert loop that burned through transaction ids
production.problem: Each call opened a subtransaction and, because it wrote, consumed its own transaction id. Batches of thousands of rows in one transaction overflowed the per-backend subtransaction cache (64 entries), so other sessions taking snapshots had to look subtransactions up in `pg_subtrans`. Xid consumption also brought anti-wraparound vacuums forward.
production.outcome: The batch now uses one xid instead of one per row (the "One subxid per block" preset shows 1000 xmins for 1000 guarded inserts versus 1 for plain ones), no subtransaction cache overflow, and one set-based statement instead of a per-row loop.

pitfalls.title: EXCEPTION blocks inside hot loops
pitfalls.fix: Put the EXCEPTION clause around the whole loop, not inside it, or avoid it: `ON CONFLICT`, `IF NOT FOUND`, and constraint checks before the write usually remove the need.

pitfalls.title: SQL injection through EXECUTE
pitfalls.fix: Take identifiers as `regclass`, quote with `format('%I')` and `%L`, and pass values with `EXECUTE … USING`.

pitfalls.title: A variable with the same name as a column
pitfalls.fix: Prefix variables (`v_owner`, `p_id`) or qualify (`accounts.owner`, `fn_name.param`). Turn on `plpgsql.extra_warnings = all` in development.

pitfalls.title: Marking a function IMMUTABLE when it is not
pitfalls.fix: Use **STABLE** for functions that read the database or settings within one statement, **VOLATILE** (the default) for anything with side effects or changing results.

pitfalls.title: Testing FOUND after an aggregate
pitfalls.fix: Test the value (`IF total IS NULL`), or check existence first with a non-aggregate query. Use `INTO STRICT` when exactly one row must exist: it raises `no_data_found` (P0002) or `too_many_rows` (P0003).

pitfalls.title: Re-raising an error under a new code
pitfalls.fix: Use a bare `RAISE;` to re-throw the caught error unchanged, or keep the code explicitly with `USING ERRCODE = SQLSTATE`. Add context with `DETAIL` or `HINT` instead of rewriting the message.

keyPointers: Block = `[DECLARE] BEGIN … [EXCEPTION WHEN … THEN …] END`. An EXCEPTION clause turns the block into a **subtransaction**.
On a caught error, **database changes in the block roll back** but **local variables keep their values**.
Code is compiled on first call; each SQL statement is **prepared on first execution** and may get a cached generic plan. `EXECUTE` re-plans every time.
**Procedures** (`CALL`) can `COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK`; functions cannot. Neither can end a transaction inside an EXCEPTION block.
Volatility: **IMMUTABLE** (pure), **STABLE** (fixed within a statement), **VOLATILE** (default, re-evaluated every call).

lessons.title: The rule system
lessons.tldr: The **rule system** is a query rewriter between the parser and the planner that turns one query tree into zero or more trees, using rules stored in `pg_rewrite`: it is how views work and how `CREATE RULE` adds or replaces commands. It exists to transform whole statements at once, which is powerful for views but surprising for data changes, so nearly all custom write logic today belongs in triggers instead.

visualizer.title: Rewriting an UPDATE with log_shoelace, step by step
visualizer.interaction: Follow the rewriter through its five steps for the `log_shoelace` rule. Switch statements to see a colour-only update log nothing and a multi-row update log 3 of 4 rows.

presets.label: Rules in pg_rewrite
presets.lookFor: The view `shoelace` has its `_RETURN` rule (ev_type 1 = SELECT, INSTEAD). `log_shoelace` is ev_type 2 = UPDATE and `is_instead = f`: an ALSO rule.

presets.label: One UPDATE, two plans
presets.lookFor: EXPLAIN prints **two plans**: first the rule's INSERT, with the substituted qual `Filter: (6 <> sl_avail)`, then the original UPDATE.

presets.label: Log a change
presets.lookFor: One log row, written by the extra INSERT that the rewriter generated.

presets.label: Colour change: no log
presets.lookFor: Still one log row. `NEW.sl_avail` was not assigned, so it was replaced by `shoelace_data.sl_avail` and the qual compared the column with itself.

presets.label: Multi-row: 4 updated, 3 logged
presets.lookFor: sl1, sl2 and sl4 are logged with one INSERT … SELECT; sl3 already had 0. The action ran **before** the UPDATE, so it still saw the old values.

presets.label: Volatile functions run twice
presets.lookFor: The copies have ids 3 and 4, not 1 and 2. `NEW.id` was replaced by the column default `nextval(…)`, which the rule action evaluated **again**. A trigger would see the real values.

presets.label: DO INSTEAD NOTHING
presets.lookFor: The rewriter returned **zero** query trees: the DELETE silently became nothing (`DELETE 0`), with no error. That silence is why rules make poor constraints.

production.title: Retiring an audit rule that logged the wrong ids
production.problem: Archive rows had ids that did not match any order: every insert consumed two sequence values and the archive got the second one. Bulk loads with `COPY` were not archived at all, because COPY does not invoke the rule system.
production.outcome: Archive ids match the source again, sequences advance once per row, and COPY loads are archived. The "Volatile functions run twice" preset reproduces the original bug: ids 1 and 2 in the table, 3 and 4 in the copy.

pitfalls.title: Volatile expressions evaluated more than once
pitfalls.fix: Use a trigger, which sees the final row values. Rules give surprising results with volatile functions, because each action re-evaluates the NEW expressions.

pitfalls.title: INSTEAD NOTHING hides failures
pitfalls.fix: To block writes, revoke privileges or use a BEFORE trigger that raises an exception, so callers see an error.

pitfalls.title: Rules and features they do not cover
pitfalls.fix: Move the logic to triggers, which run for INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE actions and COPY.

keyPointers: The rewriter runs **between parser and planner** and returns **zero or more** query trees. Views are `_RETURN` rules.
A rule action is a template: **NEW** becomes the original target-list expression (or OLD for unassigned UPDATE columns, NULL for INSERT), **OLD** becomes the result relation.
**ALSO** keeps the original query; **INSTEAD** replaces it; a qualified INSTEAD also adds the original with the negated qual.
For **ON UPDATE/DELETE** the actions run **before** the original; for **ON INSERT** after it.
Prefer **triggers** for data changes: rules re-evaluate volatile expressions, cannot raise errors, and skip COPY.

lessons.title: Foreign data wrappers
lessons.tldr: A **foreign data wrapper** is a C handler that lets a local table name stand in for data elsewhere, configured through a chain of SQL/MED objects: wrapper, server, user mapping and foreign table. It exists so you can query another database or a file with plain SQL, while the wrapper decides how much of each query (filters, joins, sorts, aggregates) to **push down** to the remote side instead of dragging every row across the network.

visualizer.title: What does postgres_fdw ship to the remote server?
visualizer.interaction: Click **Next scenario** or toggle clauses yourself. Watch the Remote SQL, the local Filter and the rows on the wire change. The remote table holds 1,000,000 orders.

presets.label: The SQL/MED chain
presets.lookFor: Wrapper → server → user mapping. `fdwhandler = -` (0): this wrapper has no handler. Connection details live on the server; credentials live on the **user mapping**, per local role.

presets.label: Foreign tables
presets.lookFor: `relkind = f` and **0 local bytes**: a foreign table is only a definition. The `column_name` option maps local `amount` to remote `total`; matching is by name, not position.

presets.label: Scanning needs a handler
presets.lookFor: Planning a scan calls the handler's `FdwRoutine` (GetForeignRelSize, GetForeignPaths, …), and IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA calls `ImportForeignSchema`. Without a handler both fail.

presets.label: What postgres_fdw would ship
presets.lookFor: postgres_fdw ships a clause only if every function in it is **built-in and IMMUTABLE** (or belongs to an extension listed in the server's `extensions` option). `now()` is STABLE; `risk_score` is IMMUTABLE but user-defined.

presets.label: No validator, no checks
presets.lookFor: The typo `fetch_sizee` is accepted because this wrapper has **no validator** function. postgres_fdw's validator would reject it at ALTER time.

presets.label: Tune options in place
presets.lookFor: Options are text key/value pairs on each object. For postgres_fdw, a table-level option overrides the server-level one.

production.title: A reporting query that copied a whole remote table
production.problem: `EXPLAIN VERBOSE` showed the Remote SQL carrying only `status = 'shipped'`. Because `now()` is STABLE, the date filter ran locally, and with a local filter present the LIMIT could not be shipped either. Every shipped order ever recorded crossed the network, 100 rows per FETCH, for each dashboard refresh.
production.outcome: The Remote SQL now contains both predicates, the ORDER BY and `LIMIT 50::bigint`, so 50 rows cross the network instead of every shipped order. In the visualizer, scenario 3 against scenario 4 shows the same effect on a 1,000,000-row remote table: 250,000 rows against 10.

pitfalls.title: Mutable functions block pushdown
pitfalls.fix: Pass constants from the application, rewrite with immutable built-ins, or list a shared extension in the server's `extensions` option. Always read the `Remote SQL:` line.

pitfalls.title: Type or collation mismatch with the remote column
pitfalls.fix: Declare columns with exactly the remote types and collations, or use `IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA`, which copies them.

pitfalls.title: Repeatable reads in a READ COMMITTED transaction
pitfalls.fix: Keep transactions that read foreign tables short, and do not rely on atomic commit across servers.

pitfalls.title: Tiny fetch batches over a slow link
pitfalls.fix: Raise them per server or per table.

keyPointers: SQL/MED chain: **wrapper** (handler + validator) → **server** (where) → **user mapping** (who) → **foreign table** (what).
The handler returns an **FdwRoutine** of callbacks: plan with GetForeignRelSize/Paths/Plan, execute with Begin/Iterate/ReScan/EndForeignScan.
postgres_fdw ships WHERE clauses only with **built-in, IMMUTABLE** functions and operators; joins only between tables on the **same server**.
Read pushdown in `EXPLAIN VERBOSE`: the `Remote SQL:` line is what the other server actually runs.
Remote transactions run at **REPEATABLE READ** or SERIALIZABLE, without two-phase commit.

lessons.title: Extensions everyone runs
lessons.tldr: An **extension** is a versioned package of SQL objects (types, functions, operators, index classes, often backed by a C library) that `CREATE EXTENSION` installs as one unit and `DROP EXTENSION` removes as one unit. Extensions are how PostgreSQL grows new capabilities, from query statistics to fuzzy text search to vector similarity, without forking the server or waiting for a core release.

visualizer.title: Inside two favourite extensions
visualizer.interaction: Type two strings and watch pg_trgm split them into trigrams and score their overlap. Then switch to **pgvector** and step through an HNSW search descending three graph layers.

presets.label: What is installed
presets.lookFor: Each row in `pg_extension` is one installed package and version. `plpgsql` itself is an extension, installed by default in `pg_catalog`.

presets.label: Trusted, versions, members
presets.lookFor: `trusted = t` (pg_trgm, pgcrypto) lets any role with CREATE on the database install it. pg_trgm 1.6 owns **47** member objects, tracked by `deptype = e` in `pg_depend`; that is how DROP EXTENSION finds them.

presets.label: Trigrams & similarity
presets.lookFor: 5 shared trigrams out of 12 distinct ones gives **0.416667**, above the 0.3 threshold, so `%` is true. `word_similarity` scores the best matching extent inside the second string.

presets.label: Trigram index for %…% search
presets.lookFor: A B-tree cannot help with an unanchored pattern; the trigram GIN index can. The plan switches from a Seq Scan to a **Bitmap Index Scan on products_name_trgm**, followed by a recheck of each candidate row.

presets.label: pgvector: HNSW index
presets.lookFor: `<=>` is cosine distance (`<->` is L2, `<#>` negative inner product). The plan is an **Index Scan … Order By**: an approximate nearest-neighbour search, not a sort of all 2000 rows.

presets.label: pg_stat_statements
presets.lookFor: Constants are replaced by `$1`, so both LIKE queries collapse into **one** normalized entry with `calls = 2`. The ranking query puts `pg_sleep($1)` on top with almost all of the execution time, while it used no CPU at all: `total_exec_time` is wall time, waits included. On a server the module must be in `shared_preload_libraries`.

presets.label: pgcrypto
presets.lookFor: `crypt` with a Blowfish salt produces a `$2a$08$…` hash. To check a password, hash the attempt using the stored hash as the salt and compare. New in PostgreSQL 18: `fips_mode()` reports whether OpenSSL runs in FIPS mode, and `pgcrypto.builtin_crypto_enabled` (`on`, `off` or `fips`) controls whether the built-in `gen_salt()` and `crypt()` work (`fips` disables them when OpenSSL is in FIPS mode).

presets.label: hstore: key/value in one column
presets.lookFor: **hstore** adds a type with operators: `->` (value), `?` (has key), `@>` (contains pair), `||` (add or overwrite), plus functions such as `each` and `akeys`. Keys and values are **text only** and there is no nesting, which is why new designs mostly use jsonb. `@>`, `?`, `?&` and `?|` are GIN-indexable, just like their jsonb counterparts.

production.title: Typo-tolerant product search without a search engine
