production.problem: Every search was a sequential scan of the whole table, and misspellings such as "caterpiler" found nothing at all.
production.outcome: In the playground the same change turns `Seq Scan on products` into `Bitmap Index Scan on products_name_trgm` for `ILIKE '%gres 12%'`, and `similarity('caterpillar', 'caterpiler')` scores well above the 0.3 threshold, so the misspelling now matches.

pitfalls.title: pg_stat_statements created but empty
pitfalls.fix: Add it to `shared_preload_libraries` and restart, then check that `compute_query_id` is `auto` or `on`.

pitfalls.title: Trigram search on very short patterns
pitfalls.fix: Require at least 3 characters before searching, or route very short inputs to a prefix B-tree index (`text_pattern_ops`).

pitfalls.title: Approximate vector search with filters returns too few rows
pitfalls.fix: Raise `hnsw.ef_search` for filtered queries, use pgvector's iterative scans if available in your version, or partition / partially index by the filter column.

pitfalls.title: Upgrading the package but not the extension
pitfalls.fix: Run `ALTER EXTENSION name UPDATE;` in every database, and check `pg_available_extensions` for `installed_version` versus `default_version`.

pitfalls.title: Reading execution-time share as CPU
pitfalls.fix: Call the column what it is, read `mean_exec_time` next to `calls`, and compare `shared_blks_read` and `shared_blks_hit` (plus I/O timing columns when `track_io_timing` is on) to tell waiting from computing. Then EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) the top entries.

keyPointers: An extension is a **control file + versioned SQL scripts** (+ shared library). Members are tracked in `pg_depend` with deptype `e`, and pg_dump emits only `CREATE EXTENSION`.
**Trusted** extensions can be installed by non-superusers with CREATE on the database. Check with `pg_available_extension_versions`.
**pg_stat_statements** needs `shared_preload_libraries`; it groups queries by normalized text into one row per query id, user and database.
**pg_trgm**: similarity = shared trigrams / union, threshold 0.3. GIN or GiST `*_trgm_ops` indexes speed up `%`, `LIKE`, `ILIKE` and regex, even unanchored.
**pgvector**: `<->` L2, `<=>` cosine, `<#>` inner product. HNSW (m=16, ef_construction=64, ef_search=40) gives approximate nearest neighbours.

lessons.title: Full-text search
lessons.tldr: **Full-text search** turns documents into a `tsvector` of normalized, positioned **lexemes** and queries into a `tsquery` of lexemes joined by AND, OR, NOT and FOLLOWED BY, then matches them with `@@`. It exists because `LIKE` and regular expressions know nothing about language: they cannot match "indexes" to "index", skip stop words, rank results, or use an index for word searches.

visualizer.title: From words to lexemes to a GIN lookup
visualizer.interaction: Pick a document to see the parser and dictionary at work, then click **Next query** to watch GIN combine posting lists. Every token, lexeme and position is exactly what `ts_debug` and `to_tsvector` return for these documents.

presets.label: Document → tsvector
presets.lookFor: `ts_debug` shows each token, its type, the dictionary that handled it and the lexemes produced. `{}` means **stop word**: `on` and `up` are dropped, yet positions skip them. `ts_stat` counts documents and occurrences per lexeme: `page` and `row` lead with 3 documents each, and `search` counts "Search", "searching" and "Searching" as one lexeme.

presets.label: Four ways to build a tsquery
presets.lookFor: `to_tsquery` needs operator syntax; `plainto` ANDs words; `phraseto` uses `<->`; `websearch_to_tsquery` understands quotes, `or` and `-` and never raises a syntax error.

presets.label: tsquery operators, and two that do not exist
presets.lookFor: `:*` is a **prefix** match (`plan` finds "planner"), `<->` is FOLLOWED BY, `!` is NOT. Double quotes and a leading `-` are **websearch** syntax only: `to_tsquery` rejects both with a syntax error.

presets.label: Match with the GIN index
presets.lookFor: A **Bitmap Index Scan on docs_tsv_gin** finds candidate rows; the `Recheck Cond` verifies them on the heap (needed here for the phrase positions).

presets.label: Ranking with weights
presets.lookFor: Both docs contain `index`, but doc 3 also has it in its **title** (weight A = 1.0 versus D = 0.1), so it ranks higher. Ranking reads every matching tsvector, so rank only what you filtered.

presets.label: Highlighting
presets.lookFor: `ts_headline` re-parses the **original text**, not the tsvector, so it is slow on long documents. Its output is not HTML-escaped.

presets.label: Expression index: error, then fix
presets.lookFor: The one-argument `to_tsvector` is only STABLE, so indexing it fails: **functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE**. With `'english'` it builds, but a query written with the one-argument form still runs a **Seq Scan**; only the identical expression gets the Bitmap Index Scan. An expression index saves the stored column but makes every query repeat the expression.

presets.label: Cast vs to_tsvector
presets.lookFor: A cast only splits on spaces: no stemming, so `rats` never equals `rat`. Always build tsvectors with `to_tsvector`.

production.title: Replacing ILIKE search in a help-center
production.problem: Every search scanned the whole table. A search for "indexes" missed articles that only said "index", and results came back in date order, not by relevance.
production.outcome: Searches use a Bitmap Index Scan on the GIN index instead of a full scan, stemming connects word forms, and title hits rank first. In the playground, the same pattern over 5,000 rows plans as `Bitmap Index Scan on docs_tsv_gin`, and the title-weighted doc 3 outranks doc 5 for "indexes".

pitfalls.title: The index is never used
pitfalls.fix: Write `to_tsvector('english', body)` in both the index and the query, or index a generated tsvector column and query that column.

pitfalls.title: Casting text to tsvector
pitfalls.fix: Build documents with `to_tsvector(config, text)` and queries with `websearch_to_tsquery` or `to_tsquery`.

pitfalls.title: Ranking every match
pitfalls.fix: Narrow first (date range, category), cap the candidate set in a subquery with LIMIT, or accept GIN order for very broad queries.

pitfalls.title: Language-specific stemming of names and codes
pitfalls.fix: Use the `simple` configuration for codes and names, or put a synonym dictionary before the stemmer for protected words.

pitfalls.title: Writing web-search syntax into to_tsquery
pitfalls.fix: Pass raw user input to `websearch_to_tsquery`, which never raises. Use `to_tsquery` only for queries your code builds, with `&`, `|`, `!`, `<->` and `:*`.

pitfalls.title: Leaving out STORED on the tsvector column
pitfalls.fix: Write `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (…) STORED` for a search column, or skip the column and index the expression `to_tsvector('english', body)` directly.

keyPointers: Pipeline: **parser** splits tokens → **dictionaries** normalize to lexemes and drop stop words → **tsvector** of sorted lexemes with positions.
Build queries with `websearch_to_tsquery` for user input: quotes → `<->`, `or` → `|`, `-` → `!`, no syntax errors.
Index with **GIN** (one entry per lexeme, posting lists) on a **stored generated tsvector column**, or on `to_tsvector('config', col)` with the same expression in queries.
**Weights** A–D (default 1.0, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1) let titles outrank bodies in `ts_rank` and `ts_rank_cd`.
Phrase (`<->`) and weighted queries need the row's tsvector, so GIN results are **rechecked**.

lessons.title: Row-level security
lessons.tldr: **Row-level security** attaches policies to a table, boolean expressions that PostgreSQL adds to every query so each role sees and changes only the rows the policies allow. It exists so tenant or user isolation is enforced by the database for every query and code path, instead of trusting each application query to remember its `WHERE tenant_id = …`.

visualizer.title: How policies combine into one filter
visualizer.interaction: Click **Next scenario**, or toggle policies, switch roles and change session settings. Watch the effective filter and each row's verdict, plus whether an INSERT passes WITH CHECK.

presets.label: Default deny
presets.lookFor: RLS is on and no policy exists, so `app_user` sees **0 rows** and gets no error. The playground runs as a superuser, which is why every preset switches with `SET ROLE`.

presets.label: Tenant isolation
presets.lookFor: One permissive policy, keyed on a **session setting** the application sets per connection or transaction. Tenant 1 sees tickets 1, 2 and 3.

presets.label: Add a restrictive policy
presets.lookFor: Restrictive policies are **ANDed**: ticket 3 disappears. The plan shows the policy quals placed **before** the user's `title ~~ 'L%'`, so non-leakproof user functions never see hidden rows.

presets.label: Permissive policies OR
presets.lookFor: `(tenant_isolation OR own_rows) AND hide_archived`: cho's open ticket 4 from tenant 2 now appears alongside tenant 1's open tickets.

presets.label: WITH CHECK and silent filtering
presets.lookFor: A new row that fails the policy is an **error** (WITH CHECK, here implied by USING). An UPDATE of a row you cannot see is **silently filtered**: 0 rows, no error.

presets.label: Owner bypass and FORCE
presets.lookFor: The **owner** bypasses policies (6 rows) until `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` (2 rows). Superusers and roles with **BYPASSRLS** bypass even FORCE.

presets.label: row_security = off for dumps
presets.lookFor: `row_security = off` does not bypass anything: a query that policies would filter **raises an error** instead, so a backup never silently misses rows. `pg_policies` lists every policy.

presets.label: Per-command policies (CRM)
presets.lookFor: `FOR INSERT … USING` is rejected: **only WITH CHECK expression allowed for INSERT**. With per-command policies, LexCorp's contacts are visible, the LEFT JOIN still lists Wayne and Queen with NULL contacts (RLS filters only `contacts`), the Joker insert fails WITH CHECK, and `DELETE` with no DELETE policy removes **0 rows** without an error. `set_config(…, true)` lasts only for the transaction; afterwards the setting reads as an **empty string**, which a bare `::int` cast turns into an error. `NULLIF(…, '')` makes it NULL, so the policy denies instead.

production.title: Multi-tenant isolation that does not depend on every query
production.problem: A new reporting endpoint forgot the predicate and showed one customer another customer's tickets. Code review could not guarantee that no other query would ever forget it.
production.outcome: A query that forgets the predicate now returns only the current tenant's rows, and a write tagged with another tenant fails with `new row violates row-level security policy`. The policy is just a qual, so the `tenant_id` index keeps it cheap. The presets reproduce each behaviour.

pitfalls.title: Testing as a superuser or the table owner
pitfalls.fix: Run the application and its tests as a dedicated non-owner role, and use `ALTER TABLE … FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` when the owner role also serves traffic.

pitfalls.title: A missing setting breaks every query
pitfalls.fix: Use `NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')`. An unset tenant then becomes NULL, the policy evaluates to NULL, which counts as false: no rows instead of an error.

pitfalls.title: Leaks through constraints and errors
pitfalls.fix: Include `tenant_id` in unique keys, use non-guessable ids, and do not expose raw constraint errors to end users.

pitfalls.title: Only restrictive policies
pitfalls.fix: Always have at least one permissive policy (even `USING (true)` for a role) and layer restrictive ones on top.

pitfalls.title: Writing an INSERT policy with USING
pitfalls.fix: Write `FOR INSERT … WITH CHECK (…)`, `FOR SELECT` and `FOR DELETE … USING (…)`, and `FOR UPDATE` with both. Check the result in `pg_policies`.

pitfalls.title: A session setting that outlives its request
pitfalls.fix: Set the tenant with `SET LOCAL` or `set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true)` inside each transaction, so it ends at COMMIT. Only let trusted application code issue the SET; untrusted users need their own database roles.

keyPointers: `ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` with no policy = **default deny**. Owners bypass unless **FORCE**; superusers and **BYPASSRLS** always bypass.
Filter = **(permissive OR permissive …) AND restrictive AND …**. No permissive policy means no rows.
**USING** silently filters existing rows; **WITH CHECK** raises an error for new or updated rows. FOR ALL without WITH CHECK reuses USING.
Policy quals run **before** user quals (except leakproof functions), so hidden rows never reach user code.
Key multi-tenant policies on `NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')` set with **SET LOCAL** per transaction. INSERT policies take only WITH CHECK.

modules.title: WAL, Replication, Vacuum & High Availability
modules.summary: Durability through the write-ahead log, vacuum and wraparound, replication, partitioning and pooling.

lessons.title: Write-ahead logging and LSNs
lessons.tldr: The **write-ahead log** is an append-only stream of change records, and every byte in it has an address called a **Log Sequence Number** (LSN). A change may reach a data file only after its WAL record is safely on disk, so a commit needs just one sequential WAL flush and a crash can always be repaired by replaying the log.

visualizer.title: Watch statements turn into WAL records
visualizer.interaction: Step through eight statements and watch the insert and flush pointers move. Click any record to decode its LSN into a segment file and offset. Then pick a `synchronous_commit` level below.

presets.label: Where is the WAL now?
presets.lookFor: An LSN is a byte offset. The file name is timeline (8 hex digits) + segment number, and the offset is the LSN modulo 16 MB.

presets.label: One INSERT, record by record
presets.lookFor: `Heap INSERT`, `Btree INSERT_LEAF` for the primary key and a 34-byte `Transaction COMMIT`. The first `Sequence LOG` appears because the identity sequence logs 32 values ahead. `end_lsn - start_lsn` is the length rounded up to 8 bytes.

presets.label: ROLLBACK, UPDATE and DELETE
presets.lookFor: The rolled-back INSERT is still in the WAL, followed by an `ABORT` record. The UPDATE is a single `HOT_UPDATE` with no index record. DELETE is just 54 bytes.

presets.label: LSN arithmetic
presets.lookFor: Subtracting LSNs gives bytes. Adding 16 MB moves exactly one segment file. Compare LSNs as `pg_lsn`, never as text: as text, `0/9` sorts after `0/10`.

presets.label: Async commit: the loss window
presets.lookFor: With `off`, COMMIT returns while its record is still only in WAL buffers. The next synchronous commit flushes everything. This single-process playground has no WAL writer, so the gap stays open until then; a server with a WAL writer closes it within about 600 ms.

presets.label: WAL volume by resource manager
presets.lookFor: About one Heap and one Btree record per row, a `Sequence LOG` every 32 ids, but a **single COMMIT** for the whole statement. The flush cost is paid once per transaction, not once per row.

presets.label: Sequences log 32 values ahead
presets.lookFor: 100 `nextval` calls wrote only **4** `Sequence LOG` records (at 1, 33, 65 and 97). Each record reserves the next 32 values, and `log_cnt` counts how many are left. After a crash the sequence restarts after the last reserved value, so up to 32 numbers are skipped.

presets.label: What skips the WAL: UNLOGGED and TEMP
presets.lookFor: The same 1,000 rows cost about **96 kB** of WAL in a normal table and **40 bytes** (just the COMMIT record) in an unlogged or temp table. `relpersistence` is `p`, `u` or `t`. No WAL also means no crash safety and no replication.

production.title: Ingesting telemetry without fsync-bound commits
production.problem: Write throughput flattened as threads were added. `pg_stat_io` showed WAL `fsyncs` climbing in step with commits: every reading waited for its own WAL flush, so the commit rate was bounded by flush latency, not CPU.
production.outcome: Telemetry commits stop waiting on flushes, so throughput is limited by CPU and WAL insertion instead. The risk is bounded: after a crash at most about 3 × `wal_writer_delay` (600 ms by default) of telemetry is missing, and the database is never corrupted. Billing durability is unchanged.

pitfalls.title: Turning off fsync to "speed up commits"
pitfalls.fix: Leave `fsync = on`. Use `synchronous_commit = off` per transaction (or per role) where losing the last fraction of a second is acceptable.

pitfalls.title: Comparing LSNs as text
pitfalls.fix: Cast to `pg_lsn` and subtract to get bytes, or use `pg_wal_lsn_diff()`.

pitfalls.title: Expecting remote_apply without a synchronous standby
pitfalls.fix: Name the standby in `synchronous_standby_names` (it must be streaming), or route read-your-writes queries to the primary.

pitfalls.title: UNLOGGED tables for data you cannot rebuild
pitfalls.fix: Use UNLOGGED only for data you can regenerate (caches, bulk-load staging). Make it durable with `ALTER TABLE … SET LOGGED`, which rewrites it through the WAL.

pitfalls.title: Expecting gapless sequence numbers
pitfalls.fix: Treat sequence values as unique, not consecutive. If gapless numbering is a legal requirement, keep a counter row updated inside the same transaction and accept that it serializes writers.

keyPointers: **WAL rule**: the WAL record must be flushed before the data page it describes may be written.
An **LSN** is a byte position; `lsn_a - lsn_b` is bytes; segment files are **16 MB**, named timeline + segment number.
COMMIT costs **one sequential flush**, and concurrent commits share it (**group commit**).
`synchronous_commit` is **per transaction**: `off` risks losing recent commits after a crash, never corruption.
Inspect real records with **`pg_walinspect`**: `pg_get_wal_records_info` and `pg_get_wal_stats`.

lessons.title: Checkpoints and full page writes
lessons.tldr: A **checkpoint** flushes every dirty page to the data files and records a **redo point** in `pg_control`, so crash recovery only has to replay WAL written after it. Because a page write can be torn by a power failure, the first change to each page after a checkpoint logs a **full page image**, which makes recovery safe and makes WAL volume spike after every checkpoint.

visualizer.title: One checkpoint cycle, then a crash
visualizer.interaction: Step through a checkpoint, three UPDATEs, a torn page and replay. Flip `wal_compression` to see the image sizes shrink.

presets.label: pg_control and the knobs
presets.lookFor: Defaults: a checkpoint every 300 s or before 1 GB of WAL, writes spread over 90% of the interval. `redo_lsn` is where crash recovery would start right now.

presets.label: CHECKPOINT and its records
presets.lookFor: `CHECKPOINT_REDO` marks the redo point, `RUNNING_XACTS` snapshots open transactions for standbys, and `CHECKPOINT_ONLINE` names the redo LSN in its description.

presets.label: First change after a checkpoint
presets.lookFor: The `HOT_UPDATE` is about 14.8 kB: `(FPW)` images of heap block 0 (8192 minus the free-space hole) and of the visibility-map page, whose all-visible bit the UPDATE cleared.

presets.label: Same page, next change
presets.lookFor: id 11 is on block 0, already imaged since the checkpoint: about 77 bytes. id 500 is on block 5: a new image of about 6.6 kB.

presets.label: Compress the page images
presets.lookFor: `block_ref` now reports `compression saved: … method: pglz`. Here the image rides in an `FPI_FOR_HINT` record: reading the page set hint bits first, and with data checksums on that change is imaged too. `lz4` and `zstd` work only on servers built with those libraries; this one has pglz only.

presets.label: A whole-table UPDATE, twice
presets.lookFor: The same statement writes far more WAL the first time after a checkpoint, because every page it touches is imaged once. Longer checkpoint intervals mean fewer images per hour.

production.title: Taming WAL spikes on a write-heavy IoT database
production.problem: WAL generation, network to replicas and archive cost all spiked right after each checkpoint. The server log showed `checkpoints are occurring too frequently` because `max_wal_size` (1 GB) was reached in under the 30 s `checkpoint_warning` window, so almost every update after a checkpoint paid for a full page image.
production.outcome: With one checkpoint per 15 minutes instead of one every few seconds, each hot page is imaged at most four times an hour. The FPI share of WAL (`wal_fpi` vs `wal_records`) dropped sharply, and so did replication and archive volume. The cost is longer crash recovery: up to one 15-minute cycle of WAL to replay, which the team measured and accepted.

pitfalls.title: Checkpoints driven by max_wal_size
pitfalls.fix: Raise `max_wal_size` until checkpoints are mostly timed. It is a soft limit, so leave disk headroom.

pitfalls.title: Turning off full_page_writes on ordinary storage
pitfalls.fix: Keep `full_page_writes = on` unless the storage guarantees atomic page writes (for example ZFS). Reduce the cost with longer checkpoint intervals and `wal_compression` instead.

pitfalls.title: checkpoint_completion_target = 1.0
pitfalls.fix: Keep the default 0.9. Spread writes further by lengthening `checkpoint_timeout`, not by raising the target.

keyPointers: Checkpoint = **redo record → flush all dirty pages → checkpoint record → pg_control**.
Triggered by **`checkpoint_timeout`** (5 min) or **`max_wal_size`** (1 GB, soft), writes spread by `checkpoint_completion_target` 0.9.
The **first change to a page after a checkpoint logs its full image**; later changes to that page log only the delta.
Recovery: read **pg_control**, jump to the checkpoint, **replay from the redo point** to the end of WAL.
Fewer checkpoints = less WAL but longer recovery; **`wal_compression`** shrinks the images.

lessons.title: VACUUM vs VACUUM FULL
lessons.tldr: **VACUUM** removes dead row versions so their space can be reused, updates the visibility and free space maps, and runs alongside normal reads and writes. **VACUUM FULL** instead rewrites the whole table into a new file to give space back to the operating system, at the price of an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the entire run.

visualizer.title: Vacuum a real table, phase by phase
visualizer.interaction: Step through the seven phases of `pg_stat_progress_vacuum` on 106 pages, then switch to **VACUUM FULL** and compare locks, files and results. All counts are from VACUUM VERBOSE on the playground table.

presets.label: Make dead rows
presets.lookFor: All 2,500 updates were **HOT** (fillfactor 70 left room). The table is still 106 pages: DELETE frees nothing by itself.

presets.label: Before VACUUM: maps
presets.lookFor: No page is all-visible: every page was modified. The FSM still reports only the fillfactor headroom, because the FSM is updated by VACUUM, not by DELETE.

presets.label: Run VACUUM
presets.lookFor: The 16 empty pages at the end were truncated: **106 → 90**. All remaining pages are all-visible, and `n_dead_tup` is back to 0.

presets.label: Free space after VACUUM
presets.lookFor: Each page now advertises its free bytes to the FSM, so the next INSERTs and non-HOT UPDATEs reuse them instead of growing the file.

presets.label: How VACUUM reads: its own ring
presets.lookFor: VACUUM's page accesses are counted under context **vacuum**: it reads through a small ring of buffers (`vacuum_buffer_usage_limit`, 2 MB) so a big table does not evict the hot working set. In 18, `io_method = worker` (the server default) lets VACUUM issue its reads ahead asynchronously; writes stay synchronous. This single-process build reports `sync`.

presets.label: TRUNCATE false keeps the tail
presets.lookFor: With `TRUNCATE false` the emptied tail pages stay (no ACCESS EXCLUSIVE needed). A later plain VACUUM gives them back.

presets.label: VACUUM FULL rewrites the file
presets.lookFor: A new `relfilenode` means a brand-new file. The index is rebuilt and smaller. In production this whole step holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.

presets.label: Emptying a table: DELETE vs TRUNCATE
presets.lookFor: DELETE left **5,000 dead rows** in 64 pages for VACUUM. TRUNCATE swapped in a new empty file (new filenode, 0 bytes) and left nothing to clean, but it holds **AccessExclusiveLock** until COMMIT. Roll it back and the old file comes back.

production.title: An audit table that was "fixed" nightly with VACUUM FULL
production.problem: VACUUM FULL took over 40 minutes and held ACCESS EXCLUSIVE the whole time, so every API call that wrote an audit row queued behind it and timed out. It also needed about 120 GB of free disk for the copy.
production.outcome: The table settles at its steady-state size (about 90 days of data plus one day of churn) without ever going offline. Plain VACUUM runs alongside writes, needs no extra disk, and with partitions the nightly purge becomes a metadata change.

pitfalls.title: Running VACUUM FULL in business hours
pitfalls.fix: Use plain VACUUM for routine work. If only the indexes are bloated, `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY` rebuilds one online under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE (if it fails, it leaves an INVALID index to drop). To shrink the table itself online, use an extension such as pg_repack, or rebuild into a new table and swap.

pitfalls.title: A long transaction makes VACUUM useless
pitfalls.fix: Find and end the oldest snapshot holders; set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`.

pitfalls.title: Expecting plain VACUUM to shrink the file
pitfalls.fix: That is usually what you want. If the table will stay small, rewrite it once in a maintenance window, or partition so you can drop whole chunks.

pitfalls.title: VACUUM from application code fails
pitfalls.fix: Switch that connection to autocommit before sending VACUUM, and never wrap it in BEGIN, a function or a DO block.

pitfalls.title: Treating TRUNCATE as a cheap DELETE
pitfalls.fix: Use TRUNCATE for tables nobody else is reading at that moment. Keep its transaction short, and set `lock_timeout` so it gives up instead of queueing everyone behind it.

keyPointers: Plain VACUUM: **SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE**, runs online, space is **reused**, only the empty tail goes back to the OS.
Phases: **scan heap (prune, collect dead TIDs) → vacuum indexes → vacuum heap → clean up indexes → truncate → final cleanup**.
Dead TIDs must fit in **`maintenance_work_mem`**, or indexes are scanned more than once.
VACUUM sets **all-visible / all-frozen** bits and fills the **FSM**; DELETE does neither.
VACUUM FULL: **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE**, new relfilenode, rebuilt indexes, needs disk for a full copy.

lessons.title: Tuning autovacuum
lessons.tldr: **Autovacuum** is a launcher plus a few worker processes that vacuum and analyze each table once its counts of dead, inserted or changed rows cross a threshold computed from the table size. The defaults suit small tables, so big or hot tables need per-table thresholds and a larger I/O budget, or dead rows pile up faster than the throttled workers can remove them.

visualizer.title: When autovacuum fires, and how fast it can work
visualizer.interaction: Pick a scenario or drag the sliders: the trigger formulas update, and a 24-hour simulation shows dead rows and runs. Switch to **How fast can it go?** for the cost-based throttle.

presets.label: The global knobs
presets.lookFor: New in 18: `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold` (100 M), and `autovacuum_worker_slots` (16) next to `autovacuum_max_workers` (3). Slots reserve shared memory and need a restart; `max_workers` is reloadable up to the slot count. `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = -1` means "use `vacuum_cost_limit`" (200).

presets.label: When will this table be vacuumed?
presets.lookFor: With 20,000 rows the dead-row trigger is 50 + 0.2 × 20,000 = **4,050**. The `av_status` view in the setup applies the trigger formulas, including per-table overrides.

presets.label: Churn rows past the trigger
presets.lookFor: 3,000 dead rows: not yet. 5,000: due. On a server the launcher would start a worker within `autovacuum_naptime` (1 min). This playground runs no autovacuum, so nothing happens by itself here.

presets.label: Per-table override
presets.lookFor: Now 1000 + 0.01 × 20,000 = **1,200**. Storage parameters beat the global settings for this table only.

presets.label: Insert-only tables and freezing
presets.lookFor: The insert trigger scales with the **unfrozen** share of the table. After VACUUM FREEZE every page is all-frozen, so the trigger falls to the base **1,000** instead of 1000 + 0.2 × 30,000 = 7,000. (`relpages` and `relallfrozen` refresh only at the next VACUUM or ANALYZE.)

presets.label: Throttle arithmetic
presets.lookFor: At defaults one worker can read about 390 MB/s from disk but only about 35 MB/s when it also dirties every page. That budget is shared by all running workers.

presets.label: Health check and 18's timing columns
presets.lookFor: The dead-row share uses `NULLIF` so an empty table does not divide by zero. The `total_*_time` columns (milliseconds, new in 18) show where vacuum time goes; `autovacuum_ms` stays 0 here because nothing runs automatically. A per-table `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold = 500` caps the trigger at **500** dead rows.

production.title: A 200 M-row orders table that bloated between vacuums
production.problem: With the default scale factor, autovacuum waited for 50 + 0.2 × 200 M = **40 M** dead rows. That took about 17 hours of updates to reach, so heap and indexes carried up to 20% dead rows between runs, and every run had 40 M index entries to remove. Queries slowed as scans read through dead rows.
production.outcome: The trigger drops from 40 M to about 2 M dead rows: roughly one run every 50 minutes at peak instead of one every 17 hours, and each run has 20× less to clean. Dead rows stay near 1% of the table.

pitfalls.title: Big tables wait for 20% of their rows to die
pitfalls.fix: Lower `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` per table (0.01 to 0.05 for big, hot tables), or lower `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold`.

pitfalls.title: Autovacuum keeps getting cancelled
pitfalls.fix: Stop the frequent conflicting command, or run a manual `VACUUM` in a quiet window. Check `pg_stat_user_tables.autovacuum_count` to confirm runs complete.

pitfalls.title: Adding workers does not make vacuum faster
pitfalls.fix: Raise `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` (or lower the delay) together with the worker count, within what the disks can sustain.

pitfalls.title: Partitioned parents are never auto-analyzed
pitfalls.fix: Run `ANALYZE parent_table` after large loads and on a schedule.

pitfalls.title: Hunting autovacuum workers by query text
pitfalls.fix: Filter on `backend_type`, grant the predefined role to the migration user, and remember that an anti-wraparound run will simply restart.

keyPointers: Vacuum when dead rows > **min(max_threshold, 50 + 0.2 × reltuples)**; max_threshold (100 M) is **new in 18**.
Insert-only tables: **1000 + 0.2 × reltuples × unfrozen share**; analyze: **50 + 0.1 × reltuples**.
Override per table with **storage parameters** (`ALTER TABLE … SET (autovacuum_…)`).
Throttle: **cost_limit 200** per **2 ms** delay, page hit 1 / miss 2 / dirty 20, **shared by all workers**.
Watch **`pg_stat_user_tables`**: `n_dead_tup`, `n_ins_since_vacuum`, `last_autovacuum`, `autovacuum_count`.

lessons.title: XID wraparound, freezing and MultiXacts
lessons.tldr: Transaction IDs are 32-bit counters compared modulo 2^32, so any row whose `xmin` falls more than about 2 billion transactions behind would suddenly look like it came from the future. VACUUM prevents that by **freezing** old rows, marking them older than every XID, and PostgreSQL escalates from aggressive vacuums to forced autovacuums to refusing new XIDs as a table approaches the limit.

visualizer.title: The XID circle
visualizer.interaction: Advance through each threshold and watch what the server does. Run VACUUM to freeze and pull `relfrozenxid` forward, then switch to **What if nothing froze?** and push past 2^31.

presets.label: How old is everything?
presets.lookFor: The three ages to monitor: per table, including its TOAST table, and per database. `pg_current_xact_id()` returns a 64-bit `xid8` (epoch + xid); the on-disk xmin is the low 32 bits.

presets.label: Which statements use an XID?
presets.lookFor: A transaction gets an XID only when it first **writes**: reads alone leave it NULL, so read traffic never ages the cluster. `txid_current()` and `pg_current_xact_id()` force one, so each probe call burns an XID (they differ by 1).

presets.label: Burn 100,000 XIDs
presets.lookFor: Each loop commits once, so each consumes one XID. `relfrozenxid` stays put and its age grows. Busy servers burn this many in seconds to minutes.

presets.label: Not frozen yet
presets.lookFor: Rows still carry their original xmin and no `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN` flag. No page is all-frozen.

presets.label: VACUUM (FREEZE)
presets.lookFor: `relfrozenxid` jumps forward and its age drops to almost 0. Each tuple shows `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN`, yet `t_xmin` keeps its original value: freezing sets flag bits, it no longer overwrites xmin.

presets.label: The freeze settings
presets.lookFor: 50 M, 150 M, 200 M and 1.6 B for XIDs; multixacts have their own, larger limits (5 M, 150 M, 400 M).

presets.label: Make a MultiXact
presets.lookFor: Two lockers on one row do not fit in `xmax`, so `xmax` holds a **MultiXact ID** (`HEAP_XMAX_IS_MULTI`) and its members live in `pg_multixact`. MultiXact IDs wrap around too.

production.title: A forgotten replication slot and the wraparound countdown
production.problem: Monitoring showed `age(datfrozenxid)` climbing past 1 billion although autovacuum ran constantly. The slot's `catalog_xmin` pinned the oldest XID that VACUUM could freeze past. At 3,000 XIDs/s, about 1.1 billion remaining XIDs is roughly 4 days until the 40 M warning zone.
production.outcome: Once the slot was dropped, the next aggressive vacuums advanced `relfrozenxid`, and `age(datfrozenxid)` fell back to around the 200 M `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` range. An alert on `age(datfrozenxid) > 500 M` and on inactive slots now catches this weeks earlier.

pitfalls.title: Panicking into single-user mode
pitfalls.fix: Stay online. Clear prepared transactions, long transactions and stale slots, then run a plain database-wide `VACUUM` as superuser. Do not use VACUUM FULL (it needs an XID) or VACUUM FREEZE (more work than needed).

pitfalls.title: An idle-in-transaction session blocks freezing
pitfalls.fix: Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` and alert on old `backend_xmin`.

pitfalls.title: Insert-only tables surprise you with a huge vacuum
pitfalls.fix: Let insert-triggered autovacuum freeze as you go (keep `autovacuum_vacuum_insert_threshold` enabled, consider a lower per-table `autovacuum_freeze_min_age`), or run `VACUUM (FREEZE)` after bulk loads.

pitfalls.title: A health check that burns XIDs
pitfalls.fix: Probe with `SELECT 1`, or read the current value without assigning one: `pg_current_snapshot()` or `pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned()`.

keyPointers: XIDs are **32-bit, compared modulo 2^32**: 2 billion in the past, 2 billion in the future.
**Freezing** marks a row older than every XID; `relfrozenxid` / `datfrozenxid` track the oldest unfrozen XID.
Ladder: **150 M** aggressive · **200 M** forced autovacuum · **1.6 B** failsafe · **40 M before wrap** warnings · **3 M before wrap** no new XIDs.
Recovery: end prepared/long transactions, drop stale slots, plain **VACUUM** as superuser; never single-user mode, FULL or FREEZE.
**MultiXacts** (several lockers in one `xmax`) age and wrap the same way: watch `mxid_age(relminmxid)`.

lessons.title: Physical streaming replication
lessons.tldr: A **standby** is a copy of the primary that stays in permanent recovery, receiving the primary's WAL over a replication connection and replaying it byte for byte. Streaming gives a second server for failover and read queries, and **synchronous replication** lets a COMMIT wait until a standby has written, flushed or replayed its WAL.

visualizer.title: A primary streaming to a hot standby
visualizer.interaction: Press **COMMIT** and watch WAL travel out and replies come back. Change the `synchronous_commit` level, the latency, cut the network, or start a long standby query. The standby is simulated: the playground database is a single process.

presets.label: Replication settings
presets.lookFor: `wal_level = replica` is enough for physical standbys. `max_slot_wal_keep_size = -1` means a slot may retain unlimited WAL. The standby-side settings are listed too; they only matter on a standby.

presets.label: Create a physical slot
presets.lookFor: The second argument reserves WAL immediately. A standby would use it with `primary_slot_name = 'standby_a'`.

presets.label: Write WAL nobody consumes
presets.lookFor: With no standby attached, `restart_lsn` never moves, so every byte written since is pinned in `pg_wal`. `safe_wal_size` is NULL because `max_slot_wal_keep_size` is unlimited.

presets.label: What a lag query computes
presets.lookFor: Each gap points at a different bottleneck: network, standby disk, or replay (often a query conflict). `write_lag`, `flush_lag` and `replay_lag` give the same stages as time.

presets.label: Recovery functions on a primary
presets.lookFor: On a primary the standby-side functions return NULL. On a standby, `now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()` is a common lag-in-time check.

presets.label: Drop the slot
presets.lookFor: Dropping an unused slot releases the retained WAL at the next checkpoint. Forgotten slots are the classic cause of a full `pg_wal`.

production.title: Synchronous replication without single-standby hangs
production.problem: They started with `synchronous_standby_names = 's1'`. During a routine restart of s1, every write transaction on the primary hung at COMMIT for the whole maintenance window, because the only synchronous standby was gone.
production.outcome: Either standby can now confirm a commit, so restarting one no longer blocks writes, and an acknowledged payment is still on durable storage in a second zone. Commit latency is one round trip to the nearest healthy standby plus its fsync.

pitfalls.title: An inactive slot fills pg_wal
pitfalls.fix: Alert on inactive slots and retained bytes, drop slots you no longer need, and set `max_slot_wal_keep_size` so a dead standby is invalidated instead of taking the primary down.

pitfalls.title: Standby queries cancelled with "conflict with recovery"
pitfalls.fix: Enable `hot_standby_feedback` (costs some bloat on the primary), raise `max_standby_streaming_delay` on reporting standbys, or move long reports to a dedicated delayed replica.

pitfalls.title: Both nodes think they are primary
pitfalls.fix: Fence the old primary (STONITH) before promoting, and use a cluster manager. Rejoin the old primary as a standby with `pg_rewind` instead of a full re-clone.

keyPointers: **walsender** (primary) streams WAL to the **walreceiver** (standby); the **startup process** replays it.
Positions: **sent → write → flush → replay**; `pg_stat_replication` shows each LSN and the matching **lag**.
Slots keep WAL (and with feedback, old rows) until the standby has it; cap with **`max_slot_wal_keep_size`**.
`synchronous_standby_names` = `FIRST n (…)` or `ANY n (…)`; `synchronous_commit` picks **remote_write / on / remote_apply**.
Hot standby is read-only; conflicts are resolved by **delaying replay** up to `max_standby_streaming_delay`, then cancelling.

lessons.title: Logical replication
lessons.tldr: **Logical replication** decodes the WAL back into row-level INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE messages and streams them, per table, from a **publication** to a **subscription** on another server. Unlike physical streaming it can replicate a subset of tables, rows and columns, across major versions and platforms, into a database that stays writable.

visualizer.title: From WAL records to filtered row changes
visualizer.interaction: Step through four interleaved transactions: decoding, the reorder buffer, commit order, an abort, and a publication with a row filter and column list. Then flip old and new values below.

presets.label: Publication with a row filter and column list
presets.lookFor: An INSERT-only publication may filter on any column. `total` and `card_last4` are not in the column list, so they never leave the publisher (but a column list is not a security boundary).

presets.label: Replica identity
presets.lookFor: UPDATE and DELETE messages identify the old row by its replica identity. `clicks` has no primary key, so its default identity is empty.

presets.label: Publishing UPDATEs needs an identity
presets.lookFor: The error is raised **on the publisher**, even with no subscriber attached. `FULL` fixes it, at the cost of logging whole old rows and slow row lookups on the subscriber.

presets.label: Row filters must use identity columns
presets.lookFor: A publication that sends UPDATEs must evaluate the filter on the old row, so it may only reference replica identity columns. Filtering on the primary key works.

presets.label: Generated columns (new in 18)
presets.lookFor: With `publish_generated_columns = stored` the stored `price_with_vat` is sent; the **virtual** `label` never is, because it has no stored value. Listing a stored generated column in a column list publishes it even with the default `none`. On the subscriber the target column must be an ordinary column.

presets.label: DDL is not replicated
presets.lookFor: The new column joins publications without a column list automatically, but the ALTER itself is not sent: the subscriber must add `coupon` first, or apply errors start.

presets.label: The WAL is the source
presets.lookFor: Logical decoding reads the same WAL as everything else; `pg_logical_emit_message` writes a record decoders pass through. Creating a logical slot needs `wal_level = logical`, which this playground runs without (it reports `replica`).

production.title: Upgrading a major version with near-zero downtime
production.problem: Physical replication cannot cross major versions, and a dump and restore of 2 TB takes many hours of read-only time.
production.outcome: The write freeze lasts as long as the final catch-up and the sequence sync, typically seconds to minutes instead of hours. Tables without a primary key were given one (or `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`) beforehand, because their UPDATEs would otherwise fail on the publisher.

pitfalls.title: UPDATE fails: "does not have a replica identity"
pitfalls.fix: Add a primary key, or `REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX` on a unique non-null index, or as a last resort `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`.

pitfalls.title: Replication stops on a conflict
pitfalls.fix: Fix the local data, or skip the remote transaction with `ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SKIP (lsn = ...)` using the finish LSN from the log (with the default `streaming = parallel` it can be missing; set streaming to `on` and let the error repeat). Skipping drops the whole transaction. In 18, per-type conflict counters show what keeps happening; the `*_origin_differs` ones need `track_commit_timestamp = on` on the subscriber.

pitfalls.title: A dropped subscription leaves its slot behind
pitfalls.fix: Check `pg_replication_slots` on the publisher and drop orphaned slots; cap retention with `max_slot_wal_keep_size`.

pitfalls.title: Sequences and DDL silently drift
pitfalls.fix: Apply schema changes to the subscriber first (additive changes), and run `setval` for every sequence before a switchover.

pitfalls.title: Publishing a generated column into a generated column
pitfalls.fix: Either leave the option at `none` and let the subscriber compute the column itself, or make the subscriber column an ordinary column. Virtual generated columns are never published.

keyPointers: **Publication** (what to send) on the publisher, **subscription** (where from) on the subscriber, one logical **slot** per subscription.
Decoding is in **commit order**; rolled-back transactions are **never sent**.
**Replica identity** (default: primary key) identifies old rows; without one, published UPDATE/DELETE fail on the publisher.
**Row filters** turn UPDATEs into INSERT/DELETE when rows cross the filter; **column lists** limit columns but are not security.
Not replicated: **DDL, sequences, large objects**. Initial data is copied by table-sync workers, then changes stream.

lessons.title: Declarative partitioning and pruning
lessons.tldr: A **partitioned table** has no storage of its own: each row is routed by its partition key to one partition, an ordinary table with its own heap, indexes and statistics. Queries that constrain the key touch only the relevant partitions through **partition pruning**, and old data leaves by dropping a whole partition instead of deleting rows.

visualizer.title: Which partitions does a query touch?
visualizer.interaction: Pick a query and see where pruning happens (plan time, executor start, or run time), next to its EXPLAIN output. Then route a few rows and compare DELETE with DROP for retention.

presets.label: Partitions and routing
presets.lookFor: The parent stores nothing (0 bytes). `tableoid` shows which partition each row was routed to.

presets.label: Plan-time pruning
presets.lookFor: With pruning only `events_2026_10` appears. Turn it off and the plan becomes an Append over all five partitions.

presets.label: Pruning at executor start
presets.lookFor: Look for **Subplans Removed: 4**: the generic plan kept every partition, and pruning ran when the parameter became known.

presets.label: Pruning during execution
presets.lookFor: Four subplans say **(never executed)**: the value came from an InitPlan, so the Append pruned at run time.

presets.label: Unique keys must include the partition key
presets.lookFor: Each partition enforces uniqueness only inside itself, so a primary key on `id` alone is rejected. With `created_at` added it works, and the parent's key creates one index per partition.

presets.label: Retention: DELETE vs DROP
presets.lookFor: DELETE logged every row (about 1.2 MB) and left 22,320 dead rows for VACUUM. DROP removed a month in a few kB of WAL and left nothing to clean.

presets.label: Add next month with ATTACH
presets.lookFor: ATTACH takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE on the parent. The matching CHECK constraint lets it skip the validation scan; the DEFAULT partition is still checked for December rows.

presets.label: DEFAULT partition traps
presets.lookFor: A late row lands in the DEFAULT partition, and then creating January **fails**: the new bounds would make that row belong elsewhere. Moving the rows out and attaching in one transaction fixes it. As long as `partdefid` is set, `DETACH … CONCURRENTLY` is refused too.

production.title: Monthly partitions for a 3-year event log
production.problem: The monthly `DELETE` produced tens of GB of WAL, saturated the replica link, and left a month of dead rows that autovacuum took days to clear. Recent-data queries still walked indexes covering three years.
production.outcome: Retention became a metadata operation of a few kB of WAL (dropping a 22,000-row month writes about 6 kB, deleting it about 1.2 MB), with no dead rows. Recent-data queries touch one month instead of 36, so their indexes are 36 times smaller and stay in cache.

pitfalls.title: Queries that do not mention the partition key
pitfalls.fix: Partition by the column most queries filter on, add the key to hot queries, or accept the fan-out for rare queries.

pitfalls.title: DETACH CONCURRENTLY refused
pitfalls.fix: Avoid a DEFAULT partition on tables you rotate (create future partitions ahead of time instead), or use a plain DETACH in a short maintenance window.

pitfalls.title: Too many partitions
pitfalls.fix: Keep partition counts in the hundreds to low thousands, choose coarser ranges, and make sure common queries prune.

pitfalls.title: A DEFAULT partition that quietly fills up
pitfalls.fix: Create partitions ahead of time and alert when the default holds any rows. To add a range, move its rows out of the default and ATTACH in one transaction (the last playground preset).

keyPointers: RANGE / LIST / HASH; range bounds are **inclusive below, exclusive above**; the parent has **no storage**.
Pruning at **plan time** (constants), **executor start** (`Subplans Removed`), and **run time** (`(never executed)`).
PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE must **include the partition key**; an index on the parent is created on every partition.
Retention: **DROP / DETACH a partition**, not DELETE; ATTACH with a matching CHECK to skip validation.
Autovacuum handles partitions, but **ANALYZE the parent** yourself.

lessons.title: Backups and point-in-time recovery
lessons.tldr: PostgreSQL backs up either **logically** with `pg_dump` (SQL or an archive of one database) or **physically** with a base backup of the whole cluster plus the continuous stream of archived WAL. Physical backups enable **point-in-time recovery**: restore the base backup and replay archived WAL up to any moment after it, such as one second before a destructive mistake.

visualizer.title: Recover to one minute before the mistake
visualizer.interaction: Step through a day with a base backup, archived WAL and a bad DROP, then recovery. Drag `recovery_target_time` to before 01:20, before 14:05, or after it and step again.

presets.label: What pg_dump does inside the server
presets.lookFor: A dump is one **REPEATABLE READ** transaction: every table is read in the same snapshot, so the output is consistent. It holds **AccessShareLock** on each table it dumps until the end, and no XID. `pg_export_snapshot()` is how `pg_dump -j` workers share that one snapshot.

presets.label: Archiving settings
presets.lookFor: This playground runs with archiving off. A PITR-ready server needs `wal_level` replica or higher, `archive_mode = on` and a working `archive_command` or `archive_library`.

presets.label: A low-level base backup
presets.lookFor: `labelfile` is the `backup_label` you must save with the copy: START WAL LOCATION and CHECKPOINT LOCATION tell recovery where to begin.

presets.label: Segment files and switches
presets.lookFor: `pg_switch_wal` closes the current segment so it can be archived now (what `archive_timeout` does on a timer). Every file is a full 16 MB.

presets.label: A named restore point
presets.lookFor: A `RESTORE_POINT` record sits in the WAL before the purge. Recovery could stop exactly there with `recovery_target_name = 'before_invoice_purge'`.

presets.label: Write the recovery settings
presets.lookFor: Targets can be a time, a restore point name, an LSN or an XID (one at a time). `pause` lets you check the data before ending recovery.

presets.label: Incremental backups need WAL summaries
presets.lookFor: `pg_basebackup --incremental` (17+) copies only blocks changed since a previous backup, using summaries written by the WAL summarizer. With `summarize_wal = off` there are none.

production.title: Undoing a bad migration with PITR
production.problem: A nightly `pg_dump` would restore last night's state and lose 13 hours of invoices. Restoring the base backup alone would do the same.
production.outcome: Data loss is bounded by the recovery target, one minute here, instead of 13 hours. Recovery time is dominated by replaying 13 hours of WAL; newer incremental backups (`pg_basebackup --incremental` + `pg_combinebackup`) or a more recent base backup shorten it.

pitfalls.title: An archive_command that lies
pitfalls.fix: Return 0 only after the file is durably stored, refuse to overwrite existing files, and test restores regularly. `pg_stat_archiver.failed_count` must stay flat.

pitfalls.title: Archiving silently stopped and pg_wal filled
pitfalls.fix: Alert on `failed_count` and on `pg_wal` size; fix the archive target. Never delete files from `pg_wal` by hand.

pitfalls.title: Treating pg_dump as the only backup
pitfalls.fix: Use base backups plus WAL archiving for recovery, and keep `pg_dump` for migrations, partial restores and cross-version moves. Verify base backups with `pg_verifybackup`.

pitfalls.title: pg_restore refuses the dump file
pitfalls.fix: Dump with `-Fc` or `-Fd` for anything you may restore selectively. Repeat `-t` / `-n` once per object (they do not take comma lists), use `-O` (`--no-owner`) when roles differ, and dump roles and tablespaces separately with `pg_dumpall --globals-only`, because `pg_dump` never includes them.

pitfalls.title: A long pg_dump blocks a migration and VACUUM
pitfalls.fix: Schedule DDL outside dump windows and set `lock_timeout` on migrations. Take large dumps from a standby, or rely on base backups and use `pg_dump` for smaller, targeted exports.

keyPointers: **pg_dump**: one database in one snapshot; plain SQL goes to **psql**, custom/directory archives to **pg_restore** (`-j`, `-L`); roles need **pg_dumpall --globals-only**.
**Base backup + archived WAL** = PITR; replay must start at the backup's `START WAL LOCATION`.
`restore_command` + `recovery.signal` + one **recovery_target_*** (time, name, lsn, xid, immediate).
Ending recovery starts a **new timeline**; `.history` files record branch points.
Incremental backups (17+) need **`summarize_wal`** and are rebuilt with **`pg_combinebackup`**.

lessons.title: Connection pooling
lessons.tldr: Every PostgreSQL connection is a separate backend process with its own memory and session state, so thousands of mostly idle connections waste RAM and slots up to `max_connections`. A **pooler** such as PgBouncer lets many clients share a few server connections, and its pooling mode decides which session features, such as `SET`, prepared statements, advisory locks and `LISTEN`, still behave correctly.

visualizer.title: Four clients, two server connections
visualizer.interaction: Step through the same client script in **transaction**, **session** and **statement** mode and watch where session state lands and what breaks.

presets.label: Session state a pooler can leak
presets.lookFor: All five live in **this backend**, not in the client. Under transaction pooling the next client on this server connection would inherit them, including the tenant_a search_path.

presets.label: DISCARD ALL wipes it
presets.lookFor: `DISCARD ALL` resets settings to their defaults, drops prepared statements and temp tables, releases session advisory locks and stops listening: every count is back to 0. Session-mode poolers run it between clients.

presets.label: Transaction-scoped alternatives
presets.lookFor: `SET LOCAL` and `pg_advisory_xact_lock` end with the transaction, so nothing survives COMMIT. This is what is safe under transaction pooling.

presets.label: Per-request context: set_config(…, true)
presets.lookFor: The third argument `true` makes the value transaction-local, like `SET LOCAL`, so a tenant id used by row-level security policies cannot leak to the next client on the connection. Afterwards the value is an **empty string**, not NULL. Without `missing_ok = true`, reading a name that was never set raises an error.

presets.label: What one connection costs
presets.lookFor: Even this idle backend holds about 2 MB in memory contexts (caches, plans), before any query runs, and each query can add `work_mem` per sort or hash node. The playground has one standalone backend; a server forks one process per connection.

presets.label: Timeouts that protect a pool
presets.lookFor: All are off (0) by default. `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` kills sessions that sit in an open transaction holding locks and an old snapshot; `idle_session_timeout` is dangerous behind a pooler, which keeps idle server connections on purpose.

presets.label: Idle in transaction holds an XID
presets.lookFor: While a transaction stays open its `backend_xid` and snapshot hold back VACUUM cluster-wide. A pooled client that forgets COMMIT pins a server connection and the cleanup horizon.

presets.label: Find the sessions that hog the pool
presets.lookFor: On a server, sort `idle in transaction` sessions by `xact_open_for` to find the ones holding connections and snapshots. `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` returns true once the signal is **sent**; with a `timeout` in ms it returns true only if the backend actually exited.

production.title: From 4,000 connections to 60
production.problem: The server needed `max_connections = 5000`; each backend kept its own caches and memory even when idle, connection storms during deploys forked hundreds of processes at once, and snapshot work grows with the number of backends.
production.outcome: The primary serves the same traffic with about 60 busy backends instead of 4,000 mostly idle ones, deploys no longer cause fork storms, and memory goes to `shared_buffers` and `work_mem` instead of idle processes. A sensible pool size is a small multiple of CPU cores, measured under load.

pitfalls.title: Session SET under transaction pooling
pitfalls.fix: Use `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction, or pass settings per role/database (`ALTER ROLE … SET`). Schema-qualify names instead of relying on `search_path`.

pitfalls.title: Session advisory locks that never unlock
pitfalls.fix: Use `pg_advisory_xact_lock` (released at COMMIT) or route lock holders through a session-mode pool.

pitfalls.title: Prepared statements "do not exist"
pitfalls.fix: Enable the pooler's prepared-statement support (PgBouncer 1.21+ `max_prepared_statements`) for protocol-level statements, or disable server-side prepares in the driver. SQL-level `PREPARE` is never safe in transaction mode.

pitfalls.title: A new connection for every query
pitfalls.fix: Create one pool per application process (the driver's built-in pool or a pool library) and borrow from it per request; add a server-side pooler when many processes connect.

pitfalls.title: Drivers that leave transactions open
pitfalls.fix: Use autocommit for read paths, always end transactions (commit or rollback in a `finally`), and set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` as a backstop.

keyPointers: One connection = **one backend process** with private memory; `max_connections` (100) sizes shared memory and slots.
**Session** mode: safe but no multiplexing. **Transaction** mode: multiplexes, breaks session state. **Statement** mode: autocommit only.
Session state lives in the backend: **SET, PREPARE, session advisory locks, LISTEN, temp tables**; `DISCARD ALL` resets it.
Transaction-safe forms: **`SET LOCAL`**, **`pg_advisory_xact_lock`**, schema-qualified names.
Guard the pool with **`idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`**; avoid `idle_session_timeout` behind a pooler.

modules.title: Vector Search with pgvector
modules.summary: Embeddings, distance metrics, exact and approximate search, HNSW and IVFFlat internals, filtering, hybrid search and scaling.

lessons.title: Embeddings and the vector type
lessons.tldr: An **embedding** is a fixed-length list of numbers that a model produces for a piece of text or an image, and pgvector stores it in a `vector(n)` column. Similar meanings land close together in that space, so storing embeddings next to your rows turns "find related things" into a plain SQL query.

visualizer.title: An embedding, from meaning to bytes
visualizer.interaction: Click a word (or **Next word**) to see its 8 numbers and its nearest neighbours. Switch the storage type to see the exact byte layout, then compare sizes at real model dimensions.

presets.label: Read vectors
presets.lookFor: The extension is called `vector` (version 0.8.7). A vector literal is a bracketed list. `vector_dims` gives the length of the list, `vector_norm` its geometric length.

presets.label: Nearest words
presets.lookFor: `<->` is the straight-line distance between two vectors. Lion and dog come first because their numbers are closest to wolf's. [Distance metrics](/e1/distance-and-exact-search) covers every operator.

presets.label: Errors you will meet
presets.lookFor: The type checks the dimension count on every value, rejects NaN and infinity, and caps storage at 16 000 dimensions. halfvec overflows above 65504.

presets.label: halfvec, sparsevec, bit
presets.lookFor: halfvec keeps about 3 significant digits: 0.1 becomes 0.099975586. The sparse form lists only non-zero positions (1-based). `binary_quantize` keeps only the sign of each element.

presets.label: Normalise and average
presets.lookFor: `l2_normalize` scales a vector to length 1 without changing its direction. `avg()` works on vectors element by element, which gives the centre of each group.

presets.label: Big vectors live in TOAST
presets.lookFor: Storage `e` (EXTERNAL) means out-of-line and uncompressed. A 6 KB vector is above the 2 KB TOAST threshold, so the main heap holds only small pointers (8 kB for 100 rows) and the vectors sit in the TOAST table.

production.title: Sizing an embeddings column before the first insert
production.problem: Nobody had sized the column. Stored as `vector(1536)`, each embedding is 6152 bytes, so the vectors alone are about 12.3 GB, more than the RAM of the instance they planned.
production.outcome: The arithmetic (2 M × 6152 B) settled the hardware question before launch. As `halfvec(1536)` the same data would be 2 M × 3080 B, about 6.2 GB.

pitfalls.title: Dimension does not match the model
pitfalls.fix: Treat a model change as a migration: add a new column (or a `model` key), re-embed every row, build its index, then switch reads over.

pitfalls.title: Expecting the database to make embeddings
pitfalls.fix: Call the model in your application or a job, then `INSERT` (or `COPY … FORMAT BINARY` for bulk loads) the resulting numbers.

pitfalls.title: Indexing vectors wider than 2000 dimensions
pitfalls.fix: Index a half-precision expression (up to 4000 dims) or binary-quantized bits (up to 64 000), as shown in [pgvector in production](/e1/pgvector-production).

keyPointers: `CREATE EXTENSION vector;` adds `vector`, `halfvec`, `sparsevec`, distance operators and two index types.
`vector(n)`: 4-byte floats, **4·n + 8** bytes, up to 16 000 dims stored and 2000 dims indexed.
`halfvec(n)`: **2·n + 8** bytes, about 3 significant digits, max value 65504, indexable to 4000 dims.
`sparsevec`: `{index:value,…}/dims`, 1-based, **8·nnz + 16** bytes. `bit(n)`: **n/8 + 8** bytes, from `binary_quantize()`.
Large vectors are stored out of line in TOAST without compression; random floats do not compress anyway.

lessons.title: Distance metrics and exact search
lessons.tldr: pgvector compares vectors with six distance operators: `<->` (L2), `<#>` (negative inner product), `<=>` (cosine), `<+>` (L1) for real-valued vectors, and `<~>` (Hamming) and `<%>` (Jaccard) for bits. Without an index, `ORDER BY embedding <-> $1 LIMIT k` is an **exact** search that computes every distance and keeps the best k, which is always correct but costs a full table scan.

visualizer.title: Rank 20 vectors four different ways
visualizer.interaction: Drag the query ✕ and switch operators: the same points rank differently. **Compare next row** steps the exact scan one row at a time, keeping a top-5 heap.

presets.label: Six operators
presets.lookFor: L2 = 2.449, the negative inner product = **−11** (the dot product is 11), cosine distance = 0.214, L1 = 4. Hamming counts differing bits (1). Jaccard = 1 − shared ones / all ones = 0.333.

presets.label: Similarity and edge cases
presets.lookFor: Cosine distance runs from 0 (same direction, any length) to 2 (opposite). A zero vector has no direction, so its cosine distance is **NaN**.

presets.label: Same query, four rankings
presets.lookFor: These are the visualizer's points and its starting query. L2 picks the nearby points, inner product prefers the long vectors 4 and 3, and cosine ranks by angle only.

presets.label: Exact k-NN plan
presets.lookFor: No index yet: **Seq Scan** reads all 10 000 rows, then **top-N heapsort** keeps only the best 10 in 17 kB of memory. This is exact search, with perfect recall.

presets.label: Neighbours of a row
presets.lookFor: "More like this" for an existing row: join to the row, exclude it, order by distance. All five neighbours share item 1's topic, because the data is clustered.

presets.label: Normalised: same order
presets.lookFor: For unit-length vectors the three metrics give the **same ranking**. Many embedding models return normalised vectors, so inner product (the cheapest) is a safe choice for them.

production.title: Picking the operator for a semantic search API
production.problem: The first version ranked with `ORDER BY 1 - (embedding <=> $1) DESC`, reading "highest similarity first". It returned correct rows, but it can never use a vector index, so every query scanned the whole table.
production.outcome: Rankings were unchanged (the "Normalised: same order" preset shows why). The query shape is now index-friendly, which [HNSW indexes](/e1/hnsw) turn into a speed-up.

pitfalls.title: Sorting by similarity instead of distance
pitfalls.fix: Order by the operator itself and compute similarity in the select list.

pitfalls.title: Reading <#> as a similarity
pitfalls.fix: Multiply by −1 for the real inner product, or call `inner_product(a, b)`.

pitfalls.title: Zero vectors in a cosine search
pitfalls.fix: Reject them at insert time with a check constraint.

keyPointers: `<->` L2, `<#>` **negative** inner product, `<=>` cosine distance (0 to 2), `<+>` L1, `<~>` Hamming and `<%>` Jaccard on `bit`.
Similarity: `1 - (a <=> b)` for cosine, `(a <#> b) * -1` for inner product.
Unit-length vectors rank identically under L2, cosine and inner product; prefer `<#>` for them.
Exact search = Seq Scan + top-N heapsort: perfect recall, cost linear in rows × dimensions.
Use the distance your embedding model was trained for; the model card says which.

lessons.title: HNSW indexes
lessons.tldr: An **HNSW** index is a layered proximity graph: a search drops in at a sparse top layer, walks greedily toward the query, and finishes with a beam search of width `hnsw.ef_search` on the bottom layer. It visits a small fraction of the rows, so k-NN queries get much faster in exchange for **approximate** results whose recall you tune with `m`, `ef_construction` and `ef_search`.

visualizer.title: Search a real HNSW graph, layer by layer
visualizer.interaction: Step through one query from the entry point down to layer 0. Then drag **ef_search** below **LIMIT** and watch the result count drop. The second tab shows which query shapes can use the index at all.

presets.label: Build the index
presets.lookFor: The build takes a second or two here (m = 16, ef_construction = 64). The plan is now an **Index Scan … Order By**, under a millisecond, versus about 6 ms for the exact scan. The index is larger than the table: it stores every vector plus its links.

presets.label: Recall vs ef_search
presets.lookFor: The `recall` view runs 20 queries with `LIMIT 10` and compares each with the exact answers stored in `truth`. At ef_search 5 you get only 5 rows, so recall is at most 0.5. At 10 it is about 0.98 and from 20 up it reaches 1.0 on this clustered data. The graph is built with random levels, so the third decimal varies between builds.

presets.label: ef_search caps LIMIT
presets.lookFor: `LIMIT 100` returns only **40 rows** at the default ef_search of 40, with no error or warning. `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction raises it for one query: now all 100 rows arrive.

presets.label: A thinner graph: m = 4
presets.lookFor: Fewer links and a narrow build beam make a smaller, faster-to-build index, but recall drops to about 0.4–0.5 at ef_search 10 and stays near 0.6 even at 100: a larger ef_search cannot fix it. The links are fixed at build time; ef_search only widens the walk over them.

presets.label: When the index is NOT used
presets.lookFor: Five shapes, five sequential scans: DESC, an expression around the operator, no LIMIT, the wrong operator for `vector_l2_ops`, and a distance predicate in WHERE.

presets.label: Zero vectors and NULLs
presets.lookFor: Through the cosine index only rows 2 and 4 come back: the zero vector cannot be normalised and NULLs are not indexed. The sequential scan returns all four, with NaN and NULL last.

production.title: A RAG pipeline that silently got 40 chunks
production.problem: After the index went in, answer quality dipped. The retrieval step was returning **40 rows**, never 50: the default `hnsw.ef_search` of 40 caps how many rows one HNSW scan can produce, and the re-ranker never saw chunks 41–50.
production.outcome: Every request now gets 50 candidates. On the playground data the same fix takes `LIMIT 100` from 40 rows to 100, and recall@10 is about 0.98 at ef_search 10 versus 0.5 at ef_search 5.

pitfalls.title: LIMIT larger than ef_search
pitfalls.fix: Keep ef_search ≥ LIMIT, per query with `SET LOCAL`, or enable iterative scans ([Filtering and hybrid search](/e1/filtering-and-hybrid)).

pitfalls.title: One index, several distance functions
pitfalls.fix: Create the index with the opclass that matches the operator the application uses (`vector_cosine_ops` for `<=>`, `vector_ip_ops` for `<#>`).

pitfalls.title: Slow builds on big tables
pitfalls.fix: Load the data first, raise `maintenance_work_mem` for the session (keep it well below RAM), add parallel workers, and build with `CONCURRENTLY` in production. Watch progress from a second session.

pitfalls.title: Turning m and ef_construction down to save time
pitfalls.fix: Start from the defaults (m = 16, ef_construction = 64, which must be at least 2·m) and raise them only when measured recall is too low.

keyPointers: Layers: every row on layer 0; each node is promoted with probability 1/m; one entry point on top.
Build: `WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64)`; no training step, so it can be created on an empty table.
Query: `hnsw.ef_search` (default 40, 1–1000) is the beam width and also the **maximum rows returned**.
Index use needs `ORDER BY embedding <op> $1 LIMIT n`, ascending, with the matching opclass.
Measure recall against exact search with `SET LOCAL enable_indexscan = off`.

lessons.title: IVFFlat indexes
lessons.tldr: An **IVFFlat** index runs k-means on the existing rows to find `lists` centroids, files every vector under its nearest centroid, and at query time scans only the `ivfflat.probes` closest lists. It builds far faster and smaller than HNSW, but its centroids are frozen at build time, so it needs data before it is created and periodic rebuilds as the data drifts.

visualizer.title: Voronoi cells, probes and recall
visualizer.interaction: Click to move the query and raise **probes** one list at a time: recall climbs as more cells are scanned. Then switch to **Built too early** to see what stale centroids do.

presets.label: Build with 100 lists
presets.lookFor: The build is roughly five to ten times faster than HNSW on the same table, and the index is about the size of the table. With the default `ivfflat.probes = 1` the scan touches about 15 buffers instead of the 224 of a sequential scan.

presets.label: Recall vs probes
presets.lookFor: probes = 1 misses neighbours that sit in an adjacent list (recall 0.6–0.7; k-means starts from a random sample, so it varies by build). Three probes bring it near 0.98. A starting point is **probes ≈ √lists** (10 here).

presets.label: Cost of more probes
presets.lookFor: Each probe reads one more list. Compare `Buffers: shared hit` between the two plans: about 15 at probes = 1 and about 40 at probes = 10. Every probed list adds its rows to the distance computations, so the work grows with probes.

presets.label: probes = lists
presets.lookFor: Probing every list would read the whole index, so the planner prefers an exact **Seq Scan + Sort**. At 50 probes it still uses the index.

presets.label: Built too early
presets.lookFor: Centroids trained on 4 topics cannot separate the other 36, so recall drops to about 0.6–0.7. `REINDEX` re-runs k-means on all rows and recall returns to about 0.99–1.0 (k-means starts from a random sample, so the exact figures vary by build).

presets.label: Empty table warning
presets.lookFor: Watch the messages: `ivfflat index created with little data`. It still builds, but its lists are meaningless. IVFFlat also rejects L1 and strict-order iterative scans. IVFFlat has 7 operator classes (L2, inner product, cosine for vector and halfvec, Hamming for bit); HNSW has 14.

production.title: An IVFFlat index created by the first migration
production.problem: Recall was poor and some queries returned fewer rows than their LIMIT. The centroids had been computed from an empty table, so millions of rows were filed under arbitrary lists, and a single probe often hit a nearly empty one.
production.outcome: The playground reproduces the effect at small scale: an index trained on 4 of 40 topics gives recall@10 of about 0.6–0.7; after `REINDEX` it is about 0.99–1.0.

pitfalls.title: Creating the index on an empty table
pitfalls.fix: Load data first, then build. If the table starts empty, use HNSW (no training step) or rebuild IVFFlat once data exists.

pitfalls.title: probes left at 1
pitfalls.fix: Start at probes ≈ √lists and measure. Set it per query with `SET LOCAL`, or per database.

pitfalls.title: Expecting IVFFlat to track new data
pitfalls.fix: Rebuild after big changes with `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, or prefer HNSW, whose graph is updated on every insert.

keyPointers: Build: k-means picks `lists` centroids (default 100); each row goes to its nearest list.
Sizing: lists ≈ rows/1000 up to 1M rows, √rows above; probes ≈ √lists to start.
`ivfflat.probes` (default 1) trades speed for recall; probes = lists makes the planner fall back to exact search.
Versus HNSW: faster, smaller build; worse speed/recall trade-off; needs data first; goes stale.
IVFFlat supports L2, inner product, cosine and Hamming, for `vector`, `halfvec` and `bit` (no `sparsevec`, no L1).

lessons.title: Filtering and hybrid search
lessons.tldr: An approximate index applies `WHERE` filters **after** it finds candidates, so a filtered k-NN query can return fewer rows than its LIMIT unless you use iterative scans, a B-tree path, partial indexes or partitions. **Hybrid search** runs a vector search and a full-text search side by side and merges them with **Reciprocal Rank Fusion**, so exact keywords and fuzzy meaning both count.

visualizer.title: Where filtered rows go, and how two rankings merge
visualizer.interaction: Pick a filter and an `ef_search`, then turn iterative scans on: watch rows returned and the measured recall. The second tab merges a semantic and a keyword ranking; drag **k** to see how RRF weighs ranks.

presets.label: Filter after the index
presets.lookFor: Look at the Index Scan node: `Filter: (category = 3)` and `Rows Removed by Filter: 39`. The scan produced its 40 candidates (ef_search) and only 1 matched, so `rows=1` for a LIMIT 10 query.

presets.label: Lost rows, lost recall
presets.lookFor: With a 10% filter, 40 candidates leave about **4 rows** on average (recall about 0.37). A larger ef_search helps, but only because it reads more candidates for every query.

presets.label: Iterative scans
presets.lookFor: The index now keeps scanning until 10 rows pass: `rows=10` with well over 100 rows removed by the filter. Recall returns to 1.0, at the default ef_search of 40.

presets.label: A filter against the clusters
presets.lookFor: Each query asks for rows from a region its own topic is not in. Off: **0 rows**. Iterative scans return 10 rows, but recall is only about 0.8 (strict) and just under 0.9 (relaxed), varying a little between builds, because the walk starts in the wrong place.

presets.label: Re-sort relaxed results
presets.lookFor: Relaxed order can be slightly out of order. Materialise the scan, then sort the 10 rows again. The `+ 0` stops PostgreSQL 17+ from assuming the CTE is already sorted.

presets.label: Selective filters: go exact
presets.lookFor: For a handful of matching rows the planner picks the B-tree (**Bitmap Index Scan**) and sorts them exactly: perfect recall, tiny cost. The partial HNSW index holds only category 3, so every candidate passes the filter and recall is about 1.0 without iterative scans.

presets.label: Hybrid search (RRF)
presets.lookFor: Rows found by both searches lead (1 and 7). "Recover a locked account" comes only from the vector side, "Reset the router" only from keywords. The FULL OUTER JOIN keeps both; `coalesce(…, 0)` scores a missing side as zero.

presets.label: Sparse vectors for exact codes
presets.lookFor: The parser turns `RTX-4090` into `rtx` and `-4090`, so the query "RTX 4090" misses it, while stemming makes "organization" match "organic". In the sparse vector the code is its own weighted dimension: the 4090 card scores **4.55**, the 3090 only **0.75** from the shared "gaming" term. Note the scales: an unbounded dot product next to a cosine distance between 0 and 2. `sparsevec` supports L2, inner product, cosine and L1 with HNSW only; Jaccard `<%>` exists only for `bit`.

production.title: Per-tenant search in a shared embeddings table
production.problem: Large tenants were fine, but small tenants (under 1% of rows) got 0–3 results for `LIMIT 10`: the 40 nearest candidates almost never belonged to them. Their vectors also shared one graph with everyone else's.
production.outcome: Every tenant gets full result lists. In the playground the same mechanisms take a 10% filter from about 4 rows (recall 0.37) to 10 rows (recall 1.0), and a 0.1% filter is answered exactly from the B-tree.

pitfalls.title: Filtered vector query returns too few rows
pitfalls.fix: Enable iterative scans (0.8.0+), or raise ef_search for that query.

pitfalls.title: Iterative scan over a very selective filter
pitfalls.fix: Add a B-tree on the filter column so the planner can choose an exact scan of the few matching rows, or use a partial index or partition for that value.

pitfalls.title: Adding vector distance and text rank directly
pitfalls.fix: Fuse by rank, not by score: Reciprocal Rank Fusion with k = 60, or re-rank the union with a cross-encoder. To trust one list more, multiply its `1/(k + rank)` term by a weight.

pitfalls.title: Ordering by the rank instead of the distance
pitfalls.fix: Order the branch by the distance operator itself (`ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 20`), or take the top 20 in a subquery and number them outside. Then the index scan feeds the window and stops after 20 rows.

keyPointers: Approximate indexes filter **after** the scan; with HNSW the result count is at most ef_search before filtering.
`hnsw.iterative_scan = strict_order | relaxed_order` (HNSW) and `ivfflat.iterative_scan = relaxed_order` keep scanning until LIMIT is met.
Selective filter: B-tree exact path. Few hot values: partial index. Many tenants: `PARTITION BY LIST`.
Re-sort relaxed results with a `MATERIALIZED` CTE and `ORDER BY distance + 0`.

RRF: score = Σ 1/(60 + rank) across lists, joined with `FULL OUTER JOIN`. For exact codes, a learned **sparsevec** gives each term its own weighted dimension, scored with `<#>` (HNSW indexes at most 1000 non-zeros per row).

lessons.title: pgvector in production
lessons.tldr: In production the questions are memory, build time and recall: keep full vectors in the table, index a smaller form (`halfvec` or binary bits), and re-rank with exact distances. Sizing `maintenance_work_mem` for builds, checking recall against exact search, and knowing when a dedicated vector database is worth it keep a pgvector deployment fast as it grows.

visualizer.title: Smaller indexes, measured
visualizer.interaction: Step through the four index strategies and compare bytes, index size and recall, all measured on the playground table. For **bit + re-rank**, change the candidate count. The second tab sizes a real deployment.

presets.label: Bytes per row
