presets.lookFor: A 256-d vector takes 4·256 + 8 = **1032 bytes**, half precision 520, and the bit form 40. The vectors are small enough to stay inline in the heap.

presets.label: Full-precision HNSW
presets.lookFor: The baseline: an index somewhat larger than the table, with recall 1.0 on this data.

presets.label: Half-precision index
presets.lookFor: The table keeps full precision; only the index is float16. The query must repeat the **same expression** (`::halfvec(256)`) or the index is ignored. Recall is unchanged at about 60% of the index size. (Building the float16 index is slower than the full-precision one in this in-browser database; build speed on a native server can differ, so measure on your own hardware.)

presets.label: Binary quantization
presets.lookFor: A quarter of the size, but sign bits alone are a blunt instrument: recall is below 0.5.

presets.label: Re-rank the bits
presets.lookFor: Fetch N candidates by Hamming distance, then sort them by exact `<->` on the full vectors. 100 candidates recover about 0.93, 200 about 0.96. ef_search is raised to match each inner LIMIT.

presets.label: Build memory
presets.lookFor: Watch the messages: `hnsw graph no longer fits into maintenance_work_mem after … tuples`, and compare the run time with the "Full-precision HNSW" preset: roughly three to four times slower. This in-browser server has no parallel workers (0); a real server defaults to 2.

presets.label: Deletes and REINDEX
presets.lookFor: VACUUM repairs the graph and marks space reusable but does not shrink the file. `REINDEX … CONCURRENTLY` rebuilds it at about half the size without blocking writes.

production.title: Fitting 20 million 1536-d chunks on one server
production.problem: Raw vectors are 20 M × 6152 B ≈ 123 GB. A full-precision HNSW index is larger again, so neither fits in RAM, builds spill out of `maintenance_work_mem`, and queries hit disk.
production.outcome: The index shrinks by roughly 30× in vector bytes (200 B instead of 6152 B per row) and fits in memory. The playground shows the recall trade on 256-d data: bits alone about 0.44, with 200-candidate re-ranking about 0.96. High-dimensional text embeddings usually quantize well; low-dimensional ones do not, so measure first.

pitfalls.title: Binary quantization without re-ranking
pitfalls.fix: Always re-rank a larger candidate set by the full vectors, and set `hnsw.ef_search` at least as large as that candidate LIMIT.

pitfalls.title: Expression index never used
pitfalls.fix: Write the query with the same expression as the index.

pitfalls.title: HNSW vacuum taking hours
pitfalls.fix: Rebuild first, then vacuum. Run pgvector 0.8.4 or later, which fixed HNSW vacuum bugs.

pitfalls.title: Never measuring recall
pitfalls.fix: Periodically replay a sample of real queries with `SET LOCAL enable_indexscan = off` and compare the top-k overlap with the indexed results.

keyPointers: Store `vector`, index `halfvec` (same recall, about half the size) or bits (with re-ranking).
Re-rank: inner `LIMIT N` by `<~>` on bits, outer `ORDER BY` exact distance; ef_search ≥ N.
Builds: load first, `maintenance_work_mem` big enough for the graph, `max_parallel_maintenance_workers`, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.
Maintenance: `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY` then `VACUUM` after large deletes; stay on 0.8.4+.

Stay in PostgreSQL while vectors share rows, filters, transactions and backups with the rest of your data; consider a dedicated engine only when one node can no longer hold the index in memory and sharding is not an option.

lessons.title: pgvector in the browser
lessons.tldr: **PGlite** is PostgreSQL compiled to WebAssembly: with the `vector` extension it runs pgvector, HNSW indexes included, inside a browser tab, and it stores its files in IndexedDB or OPFS. Paired with an embedding model running in a Web Worker, it gives semantic search that works offline and never sends the user's text or vectors to a server.

visualizer.title: The browser stack, byte by byte
visualizer.interaction: Step through one search from first download to result, then flip to **Return visit**. **Two tabs** shows how PGliteWorker shares one database. The two live views write to IndexedDB and load a real model, only when you click.

presets.label: What is running here
presets.lookFor: PostgreSQL 18.6 on **wasm32-unknown-emscripten**, pgvector 0.8.7, and exactly one `standalone backend`: no postmaster, no other connections, no parallel workers. This is the database running in this tab.

presets.label: 384-d unit vectors
presets.lookFor: Each embedding is **1544 bytes** (4 × 384 + 8) and has length exactly 1, like `normalize: true` output. A thousand of them take 1.6 MB.

presets.label: <#> and <=> agree
presets.lookFor: For unit vectors `<=>` is `1 + <#>`: the difference column is under 0.000001 (float32 rounding) and all 8 top-10 lists match. So use `<#>` with `vector_ip_ops`: it skips the norm computation.

presets.label: Exact search is already fast
presets.lookFor: Without an index the plan is a **Seq Scan** plus a top-N heapsort over 1 000 rows, in a couple of milliseconds. Many on-device datasets are this small: measure before adding an index.

presets.label: HNSW on 384 dimensions
presets.lookFor: Note the build time in the status bar: one backend, no parallel workers. The index is about **2008 kB**, larger than the 1600 kB heap. On 1 000 rows the planner still prefers the seq scan, so the transaction switches it off to show the **Index Scan … Order By: (embedding <#> …)**.

presets.label: Wrong operator, no index
presets.lookFor: Same ranking, but `<=>` belongs to `vector_cosine_ops`, not `vector_ip_ops`: the plan falls back to a sort over a disabled seq scan. The query operator must match the index operator class.

presets.label: What gets persisted
presets.lookFor: With `idb://` every one of these files lives in IndexedDB: the system catalogs and template databases of a fresh cluster come first, then your tables and indexes. That is why the first open of a new name is several times slower than a reopen.

production.title: A private, offline notes search
production.problem: A server-side vector database means sending every note and query to the backend, a network round trip per search, and no search offline. A naive in-browser version froze typing while the model ran and lost the index on every reload.
production.outcome: The first visit downloads about 5 MB of compressed database files and, once, about 29 MB of model and runtime. Every later visit starts from the browser caches with no network. Embedding a query takes on the order of 10 ms on a laptop CPU and the search a few milliseconds, and no note text leaves the device.

pitfalls.title: Everything on the main thread
pitfalls.fix: Run PGlite in a Web Worker with `PGliteWorker` (`@electric-sql/pglite/worker`) and the embedding model in its own worker. Pass vectors as transferable `Float32Array`s.

pitfalls.title: Two tabs, two databases
pitfalls.fix: Use `PGliteWorker`. Tabs with the same `id` elect one leader that runs PGlite; the others forward their queries to it. Handle `onLeaderChange` to re-run live queries after a failover.

pitfalls.title: OPFS that works only in some browsers
pitfalls.fix: Use `idb://` unless you control the browser. If you use `opfs-ahp://`, run it inside a worker and fall back to `idb://` on Safari.

pitfalls.title: Changing the model without re-embedding
pitfalls.fix: Store the model name with each vector, filter on it, and re-embed old rows in the background when the model changes.

keyPointers: PGlite 0.5.16: `pglite.wasm` 3.24 MB + `pglite.data` 1.85 MB + `initdb.wasm` 0.13 MB gzipped, about 5.2 MB before JS; `vector.tar.gz` adds 51 kB.
`dataDir`: `memory://` (default), `idb://name` (every browser), `opfs-ahp://name` (worker only, not Safari). A fresh cluster is about 40 MB of files.
One connection per database: share it across tabs with `PGliteWorker`, which elects a leader per `id`.
Transformers.js: `pipeline('feature-extraction', 'Xenova/all-MiniLM-L6-v2')` with `pooling: 'mean', normalize: true` gives 384-d unit vectors; about 29 MB to download once, then the Cache API.
Unit vectors: `<=>` = 1 + `<#>`, so rank with `<#>` and `vector_ip_ops`. Index basics are in [HNSW](/e1/hnsw); operators in [distance and exact search](/e1/distance-and-exact-search).

modules.title: Time-Series with TimescaleDB
modules.summary: Hypertables and chunks, time_bucket and gap filling, continuous aggregates, columnar compression and retention.

lessons.title: Time-series data on PostgreSQL
lessons.tldr: **Time-series data** is a stream of timestamped measurements that arrive roughly in time order, are rarely changed, are read by time range and are deleted when they age out. Plain PostgreSQL already handles it with **BRIN indexes**, **range partitioning** and `date_bin`, and **TimescaleDB** packages those ideas as an extension that automates partitioning, rollups, compression and retention.

visualizer.title: Why time order makes a 24 kB index work
visualizer.interaction: Drag the query window across 200,000 rows and watch which BRIN block ranges match. Switch to **Shuffled** to see the same index read the whole table, then open **What TimescaleDB adds** for the edition split.

presets.label: Physical order
presets.lookFor: `correlation` = **1** for `time`: physical order matches time order exactly, because rows were appended as they arrived. `sensor_id` is near 0.25, so BRIN would be useless on it.

presets.label: BRIN: one hour
presets.lookFor: `Heap Blocks: lossy=32` is one block range. BRIN knows only min and max per range, so it returns whole pages and **Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 1424** are filtered out.

presets.label: B-tree vs BRIN size
presets.lookFor: The B-tree has one entry per row (**4408 kB**). BRIN has one summary per 32 pages (**24 kB**, three pages). The B-tree is dropped again so later presets use BRIN.

presets.label: Bucket by hour
presets.lookFor: `date_bin` is the native `time_bucket`: it maps each timestamp to the start of its bucket. Each sensor reports 900 times per hour. The origin `2000-01-03` matches the TimescaleDB default.

presets.label: Shuffled: BRIN breaks
presets.lookFor: Same rows, random physical order: correlation is near **0**. Every range matches, so the plan reads **lossy=1280** blocks (the whole table) and rechecks away 196,400 rows.

presets.label: Latest reading needs a B-tree
presets.lookFor: BRIN can filter but cannot return rows in order, so "latest row" is a full scan plus a top-N sort. A B-tree on `time DESC` (the index TimescaleDB creates by default) turns it into a one-row index scan.

production.title: Keeping 30 days of 1 Hz sensor data in plain PostgreSQL
production.problem: The B-tree on `time` grew with every row and no longer fit in memory. The nightly `DELETE` rewrote nothing on disk: it left millions of dead tuples, autovacuum ran all day, and the table never shrank.
production.outcome: On 200,000 time-ordered rows, BRIN is **24 kB against 4408 kB** for the B-tree, about 180 times smaller, and still narrows a one-hour query to one 32-page range. Dropping a daily partition removes its files outright, so there are no dead tuples and no vacuum debt.

pitfalls.title: BRIN on data that is not physically ordered
pitfalls.fix: Check `pg_stats.correlation` for the column (near 1 or -1 is good). Use BRIN only on append-ordered columns, partition so each partition stays ordered, or use a B-tree.

pitfalls.title: Retention with DELETE
pitfalls.fix: Partition by time and drop whole partitions. With TimescaleDB, use `drop_chunks` (Apache 2 edition) or `add_retention_policy` (Community edition).

pitfalls.title: Expecting the full feature set on a managed service
pitfalls.fix: Run `SHOW timescaledb.license;` before designing around a feature. Use the Community edition (self-hosted) or Tiger Cloud, or the native equivalents shown in this module.

pitfalls.title: Monthly buckets with date_bin
pitfalls.fix: Use `date_trunc('month', time)` natively, or `time_bucket('1 month', time)` with TimescaleDB, which supports month and year widths.

keyPointers: Time-series = **append-mostly**, read by **time range**, deleted by **age**. Every tool in this module exploits one of those three facts.
**BRIN** stores min/max per block range: tiny, and only useful when physical order follows the column (`correlation` near 1). More in [BRIN indexes](/m4/brin).
Partition by time so queries **prune** to a few partitions and retention is a `DROP`, not a `DELETE`.
**TimescaleDB** is an extension loaded through `shared_preload_libraries`. Version 2.32 supports PostgreSQL 16 to 18.
**Apache 2 edition**: hypertables, `time_bucket`, `drop_chunks`. **Community edition**: continuous aggregates, columnstore, gap filling, policies and jobs. Neon offers only the Apache edition.

lessons.title: Hypertables and chunks
lessons.tldr: A **hypertable** is a table that TimescaleDB splits by time into child tables called **chunks**, creating each chunk automatically the first time a row needs it. Chunks let queries skip every time slice outside their WHERE clause (**chunk exclusion**) and let old data leave by dropping whole chunks, without anyone managing partitions by hand.

visualizer.title: Chunks appear as time advances
visualizer.interaction: Ingest data and watch chunks being created on demand, then add a late row and a row from a broken clock. Drag the query window to see chunk exclusion, and switch to **Native partitioning** to see what PostgreSQL does without the extension.

presets.label: List the chunks
presets.lookFor: Seven daily partitions of 1440 rows and 216 kB each. This is what `show_chunks()` and `timescaledb_information.chunks` report for a hypertable.

presets.label: Exclusion at plan time
presets.lookFor: Only `conditions_20260303` appears: the planner compared the constants with each partition's range and dropped the other six. TimescaleDB calls this **chunk exclusion**.

presets.label: Exclusion at run time
presets.lookFor: A generic plan cannot know `$1`, so pruning happens when execution starts: **Subplans Removed: 5**, two chunks scanned with 1440 rows each. TimescaleDB's ChunkAppend node does the same for values such as `now()`.

presets.label: No automatic chunks
presets.lookFor: Native PostgreSQL rejects the row: **no partition of relation "conditions" found for row**. After `ensure_chunk()` creates `conditions_20260308` the insert succeeds. A hypertable does that step for you, inside the INSERT.

presets.label: Unique keys need the time column
presets.lookFor: Uniqueness is enforced inside each partition, so every unique key must include the partition column. Hypertables have the same rule: `cannot create a unique index without the column "time"`.

presets.label: Space partitioning
presets.lookFor: This mirrors `add_dimension('readings', by_hash('device_id', 2))`: each time slice becomes two chunks. A filter on both columns prunes down to one (`readings_d1_h1`). The chunk count doubles, which is why the extra dimension is discouraged.

presets.label: Latest row vs latest per device
presets.lookFor: The first plan is an **ordered Append**: chunks are read newest first and the LIMIT stops after one row. "Latest per device" needs a Merge Append over every chunk. TimescaleDB's SkipScan (Community edition) speeds that up.

production.title: Turning a growing metrics table into a hypertable
production.problem: One huge table means one huge B-tree that no longer fits in memory, so inserts read cold index pages from disk. Hand-made partitions helped until a scheduled job that created them failed one weekend, and inserts stopped with "no partition found".
production.outcome: Inserts touch only the newest chunk's indexes, which stay in memory, and a one-day query reads one or two chunks. With 7-day chunks a year of data is about 52 chunks, far below the 1,000-chunk warning level.

pitfalls.title: Chunks that are far too small
pitfalls.fix: Size by the memory rule, not by query granularity. `set_chunk_time_interval` changes new chunks only, so fix history with a table-swap migration. Raise `max_locks_per_transaction` (restart needed) as a stopgap.

pitfalls.title: Unique key without the time column
pitfalls.fix: Include the partition column in every PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraint, for example `(device_id, time)`. Enforce global uniqueness of other ids elsewhere.

pitfalls.title: A bad clock creates future chunks
pitfalls.fix: Validate timestamps at ingest (for example a CHECK against `now() + interval '1 day'` in the application), and clean up with `drop_chunks(newer_than => …)`.

pitfalls.title: Space partitioning on one disk
pitfalls.fix: Use time-only partitioning plus a `(device_id, time DESC)` index. On a hypertable that already has data, `add_dimension` only partitions chunks created afterwards, and existing chunks keep covering the whole hash range.

keyPointers: A hypertable is a parent table, and **chunks** are child tables in `_timescaledb_internal`. Insert and query the parent only.
Chunks are created **on demand** by the INSERT. Ranges are aligned on the epoch; the default `chunk_interval` is **7 days**.
Size chunks so the **indexes of active chunks fit in about 25% of memory**; more than 1,000 chunks is a warning sign.
**Chunk exclusion** = partition pruning: at plan time for constants, at run time for parameters and `now()`. The native mechanism is covered in [partitioning and pruning](/m7/partitioning).
Hypertables, `show_chunks`, `add_dimension` and `set_chunk_time_interval` are **Apache 2 edition**; SkipScan and `reorder_chunk` need the **Community edition**.

lessons.title: time_bucket and gap filling
lessons.tldr: `time_bucket` maps every timestamp to the start of a fixed-width bucket, and `time_bucket_gapfill` with `locf` or `interpolate` adds rows for buckets that have no data. Charts and rollups need one row per interval, while real sensors report irregularly and go silent, so bucketing and gap filling turn raw readings into a regular series.

visualizer.title: Where bucket boundaries fall, and filling the holes
visualizer.interaction: In **Bucketing**, change width, origin, offset and time zone and watch readings regroup; pick 1 day in Berlin to see the 23-hour day. In **Gap filling**, step from plain buckets to gapfill, locf and interpolate.

presets.label: time_bucket = date_bin
presets.lookFor: `time_bucket('15 minutes', ts)` equals `date_bin` with origin 2000-01-03, a **Monday**, so weekly buckets start on Monday 2026-11-09. A Sunday origin moves them to 2026-11-08.

presets.label: Month buckets
presets.lookFor: `date_bin` refuses months: **timestamps cannot be binned into intervals containing months or years**. `time_bucket('3 months', t)` counts from origin 2000-01-01; month arithmetic reproduces it (April and October).

presets.label: Time zones and DST
presets.lookFor: 23:30 UTC on 28 March is already the 29th in Berlin. The day of the clock change lasts **23:00:00**. This is what `time_bucket('1 day', time, timezone => 'Europe/Berlin')` produces.

presets.label: Gap filling
presets.lookFor: Three rows become six: 01:00, 03:00 and 04:00 now exist with `NULL` average and `n = 0`. The series supplies the buckets that gapfill takes from the WHERE bounds.

presets.label: locf
presets.lookFor: `count(v)` only counts non-NULL values, so each NULL joins the group of the last real value, and `first_value` copies it forward: **11, 11, 20, 20, 20, 50**.

presets.label: interpolate
presets.lookFor: Linear interpolation needs the previous **and** the next real value: **15.5** between 11 and 20, then **30** and **40** on the way to 50. One `interpolate()` call replaces this whole query.

presets.label: first / last
presets.lookFor: These match `first(value, time)` and `last(value, time)`. The `array_agg` versions sort the whole group. PostgreSQL 18 has no `IGNORE NULLS`, which is why the locf preset needs the count() trick.

production.title: A dashboard that stopped drawing false lines
production.problem: The chart grouped by `time_bucket('15 minutes', time)`. Silent periods produced no rows, so the charting library drew a straight line across a two-hour outage, and "rooms out of range per hour" undercounted because missing hours were not rows at all.
production.outcome: Every room returns one row for every 15-minute bucket in the window (96 for a full, aligned day), so charts and per-hour counts line up. The `was_silent` flag keeps filled values distinguishable from measured ones.

pitfalls.title: Gapfill without an upper bound
pitfalls.fix: Always give both bounds in WHERE, or pass `start` and `finish` arguments explicitly.

pitfalls.title: Wrapping gapfill or filtering with HAVING
pitfalls.fix: Cast or round in an outer query, and filter filled rows in an outer CTE, not with HAVING.

pitfalls.title: Buckets aligned to UTC, not local midnight
pitfalls.fix: Pass the zone: `time_bucket('1 day', time, timezone => 'Europe/Berlin')`, or natively `date_trunc('day', time, 'Europe/Berlin')`. Expect a 23-hour and a 25-hour day each year.

pitfalls.title: Old code using time_bucket_ng
pitfalls.fix: Use `time_bucket`, which supports months, origin, offset and time zone.

keyPointers: `time_bucket(width, ts)` returns the bucket **start**. Default origin is **2000-01-03, a Monday** (2000-01-01 for month widths), aligned on UTC.

Natively: `date_bin(width, ts, origin)` for fixed widths, `date_trunc(unit, ts, zone)` for calendar units. `date_bin` cannot do months. Filling gaps by hand is a [gaps-and-islands](/f4/gaps-and-islands) pattern.
`time_bucket_gapfill` creates the missing buckets from the WHERE bounds; `locf` carries values forward; `interpolate` draws lines between them.
`time_bucket`, `first`, `last` and `histogram` are **Apache 2 edition**. `time_bucket_gapfill`, `locf` and `interpolate` are **Community edition** only.

lessons.title: Continuous aggregates
lessons.tldr: A **continuous aggregate** is a materialized view over a hypertable that TimescaleDB refreshes incrementally, recomputing only new time buckets and buckets whose raw data changed. Dashboards ask the same rollup questions every few seconds, and recomputing them from billions of raw rows is too slow, while a plain materialized view must be rebuilt in full on every refresh.

visualizer.title: Watermark, invalidation log and refresh window
visualizer.interaction: Advance time and watch the hourly policy materialize buckets behind the watermark. Backfill late rows to fill the invalidation log, compare one transaction with two, and switch on **real-time** to see buckets above the watermark computed live.

presets.label: A plain materialized view
presets.lookFor: An unpopulated matview raises **has not been populated**. `REFRESH` recomputes the entire query every time, however little changed.

presets.label: Concurrent refresh and staleness
presets.lookFor: `CONCURRENTLY` needs a unique index and still recomputes everything. The new 05:30 reading is invisible: the matview still says **50, n = 1** until the next full refresh.

presets.label: Build an incremental engine
presets.lookFor: A summary table (the **materialization hypertable**), an invalidation log fed by a statement trigger, and a refresh that handles whole buckets only. The window ends at 05:00, so 5 buckets are computed and the **watermark** moves to 05:00.

presets.label: Real-time view
presets.lookFor: This is `materialized_only = false`: stored buckets below the watermark, plus raw rows above it aggregated on the fly. The 05:00 bucket appears with **55, n = 2** (50 and 60) without a refresh.

presets.label: Backfill below the watermark
presets.lookFor: The late row is logged as **00:50 → 00:50**, but even the real-time view still shows **11** until a refresh. Refresh number 2 recomputes **1 bucket**, and the average becomes 40.67 (10, 12, 100).

presets.label: One transaction vs two
presets.lookFor: Only min and max are logged, so one write spanning 01:20 to 04:20 recomputes **4 buckets**, while two separate writes recompute **2**. TimescaleDB logs per transaction, so batch backfills by bucket.

presets.label: Rolling up without avg of avgs
presets.lookFor: A daily rollup of the hourly table (a **hierarchical** aggregate) must combine sums and counts: device 1 is **35.5**, while averaging the hourly averages gives a wrong 30.33.

production.title: Hourly dashboards over a year of per-second data
production.problem: The dashboard query aggregated raw rows on every page load, and a plain materialized view took longer to refresh than the interval between refreshes. Late readings arrive from meters that were offline for hours.
production.outcome: A daily dashboard for one meter reads 24 hourly rows instead of 86,400 raw rows, 3,600 times fewer. The policy refreshes each window in batches of 10 buckets (the default since 2.25), so each transaction stays small.

pitfalls.title: The last hour is missing
pitfalls.fix: Enable real-time aggregation if readers need fresh data, or shorten `end_offset` and `schedule_interval`.

pitfalls.title: Backfill never appears
pitfalls.fix: Run a manual refresh for that range, or add a second policy with a non-overlapping window for old data.

pitfalls.title: Retention deletes aggregated history
pitfalls.fix: Keep the retention interval longer than the refresh policy's `start_offset`, and give the aggregate its own, longer retention policy.

pitfalls.title: Averages of averages in a hierarchy
pitfalls.fix: Store `sum` and `count` in the lower level and divide in the upper one, or use Toolkit aggregates that support `rollup()` (`stats_agg`, `percentile_agg`).

keyPointers: A cagg stores finished buckets in a **materialization hypertable**. The **watermark** marks where materialized data ends.
Writes behind the invalidation threshold log **min and max time per transaction**. A refresh recomputes only new and invalidated whole buckets in its window.
Policy = `start_offset` / `end_offset` / `schedule_interval`. Leave the open bucket out, and expect data to lag by up to schedule + end_offset.
**Real-time** (`materialized_only = false`) unions live raw data above the watermark. It has been off by default since 2.13.
Continuous aggregates are **Community edition** only. Natively: a summary table, a trigger-fed invalidation log, a refresh procedure and a UNION view.

lessons.title: Compression and the columnstore
lessons.tldr: The TimescaleDB **columnstore** (Hypercore, formerly called compression) rewrites older chunks so that each batch of up to 1000 rows becomes one row of compressed per-column arrays with min/max metadata. Time-series values repeat and change slowly, so storing columns together with delta and XOR encodings shrinks old data by 90% or more and lets analytical scans skip and read only the columns they need.

visualizer.title: From 12 heap rows to a few compressed rows
visualizer.interaction: Step through the conversion of one chunk: group, order, batch, encode, then query and update it. Switch **segmentby** to see why a low-cardinality column groups well and a unique id ruins compression.

presets.label: The rowstore
presets.lookFor: 30,000 rows in 192 pages (**1568 kB**), 156 rows per page. Each row carries its own header and repeats the symbol text.

presets.label: Build columnar batches
presets.lookFor: 30 rows replace 30,000: **1568 kB → 216 kB** (7.3x) with only TOAST's generic compression. 1000 prices fit in about 282 bytes because they repeat. Real columnstore codecs do far better on timestamps.

presets.label: Skip batches by metadata
presets.lookFor: The segment value and min/max metadata pick **1 batch of 30** before any array is opened. `unnest` plays decompression and returns the 4 matching ticks.

presets.label: Why timestamps compress
presets.lookFor: Within one segment ticks arrive every 3 seconds, so **delta-of-delta is 0** for every row: a 64-bit timestamp shrinks to about a bit. Prices step by a constant 3, which run-length and delta encodings capture too.

presets.label: Choosing segmentby
presets.lookFor: No segmentby is about as small here, but a query for ETH must open **all 30 batches** instead of 10. A unique segment key makes 30,000 one-value batches: **4104 kB**, bigger than the rowstore.

presets.label: Changing one value
presets.lookFor: Changing one price writes a **new version of the whole batch row** (1000 values). TimescaleDB instead decompresses the affected batch into the rowstore part of the chunk, which is why large UPDATEs on compressed chunks are expensive.

production.title: Keeping a year of market ticks on one server
production.problem: A year of rowstore chunks filled the disk, and month-long scans read every column of every row even though they used only time and price.
production.outcome: Expect a reduction of around 90% on data like this; a sample crypto-tick hypertable shrinks from 194 MB to 24 MB, about 8 times (88%). Queries on one symbol open only that symbol's batches and only the columns they reference. Measure your own ratio with `hypertable_columnstore_stats`.

pitfalls.title: High-cardinality segmentby
pitfalls.fix: Pick the column you filter or group by most, with low-to-moderate cardinality (device, symbol). Settings apply only to chunks converted afterwards.

pitfalls.title: Big UPDATE on compressed chunks
pitfalls.fix: Batch the change, raise the limit for that session, or pause the policy, convert the chunk back with `convert_to_rowstore`, change it, and convert again.

pitfalls.title: Enabling the policy on a large existing table
pitfalls.fix: Limit chunks per run with the `maxchunks_to_compress` config key, and convert the backlog manually from parallel sessions.

pitfalls.title: Assuming one policy schedule
pitfalls.fix: Read the real value instead of assuming it, and set it explicitly if it matters.

keyPointers: Columnstore conversion: group by **segmentby**, sort by **orderby**, cut into batches of **up to 1000 rows**, store each batch as one row of arrays with min/max metadata.

Codecs: since 2.32 the **Adaptive Integer Compressor** picks run-length, frame-of-reference or dictionary per block for integers and timestamps (delta-of-delta, simple-8b and run-length before); XOR for floats; dictionaries for text.
Scans skip batches by segment value and metadata, and decompress only the columns they read. DML decompresses only the batches it touches.
Renamed in 2.18: `compress_chunk` → `convert_to_columnstore`, `add_compression_policy` → `add_columnstore_policy`, `timescaledb.compress` → `enable_columnstore`.
The columnstore is **Community edition** only. Neon does not support compression. The playground's arrays rely on [TOAST](/m2/toast) compression instead.

lessons.title: Retention, tiering and jobs
lessons.tldr: **Retention** in TimescaleDB drops whole chunks once their entire time range is older than a cutoff, and a built-in **job scheduler** runs that and every other policy on a schedule. Dropping a chunk removes files instantly with no dead tuples or vacuum work, and policies turn the chunk lifecycle (rowstore, columnstore, tiered, dropped) into configuration instead of cron scripts.

visualizer.title: The life of a chunk
visualizer.interaction: Advance day by day and watch chunks move from rowstore to columnstore and finally get dropped. Change `drop_after` and the continuous aggregate's `start_offset` until retention starts deleting aggregates, and try Tiger Cloud tiering.

presets.label: The chunks
presets.lookFor: Ten daily chunks of 1440 rows; the newest is half full (720). This is the table the retention job will trim.

presets.label: Retention with DELETE
presets.lookFor: Deleting one day writes **about 79 kB of WAL** for 1440 rows and leaves 1440 dead tuples for VACUUM. Rolled back, so the data is still there.

presets.label: A retention job
presets.lookFor: The cutoff is Nov 7 12:00, so the Nov 5 and Nov 6 chunks go, using a few kB of WAL for two whole days. Nov 7 stays because part of it is newer than the cutoff: the oldest row is **7 days 12:00** old.

presets.label: A tiny job scheduler
presets.lookFor: This mimics TimescaleDB's scheduler and `timescaledb_information.jobs`: job 1001 ran, dropped Nov 7 and Nov 8 (cutoff Nov 9 12:00), and its **next_start** moved one day ahead.

presets.label: A failing job backs off
presets.lookFor: A bad config fails twice. Each failure pushes `next_start` further out (12:05, then 12:15), the pattern TimescaleDB uses: consecutive failures × `retry_period`, capped at 5 × the schedule, plus jitter.

production.title: A 13-month lifecycle for fleet telemetry
production.problem: A nightly `DELETE … WHERE time < now() - interval '30 days'` ran for hours, generated gigabytes of WAL and left the table bloated. When someone added a retention policy, a continuous aggregate with a long refresh window silently lost its history.
production.outcome: Retention removes one chunk file per day instead of deleting millions of rows: dropping two daily chunks in the playground takes a few kB of WAL, while deleting one day row by row takes about 79 kB per 1,440 rows. The daily aggregate keeps 13 months of history after the raw data is gone.

pitfalls.title: Retention shorter than the refresh window
pitfalls.fix: Keep `drop_after` on the hypertable longer than the aggregate policy's `start_offset`, and give the aggregate its own, longer retention.

pitfalls.title: Data older than the cutoff is still there
pitfalls.fix: This is by design. Use a smaller chunk interval if the policy must be tighter, or filter in queries.

pitfalls.title: Replacing a job config by accident
pitfalls.fix: Merge instead of replace: `config_merge` (2.29+) or `config || '{…}'`.

pitfalls.title: Jobs that never run
pitfalls.fix: Raise `timescaledb.max_background_workers` and `max_worker_processes` (restart needed), check `SHOW timescaledb.license`, and on Neon use pg_cron while the compute is awake.

keyPointers: `drop_chunks` / `add_retention_policy` drop a chunk only when its **whole range** is older than the cutoff. One retention policy per hypertable.
Every policy is a **job**: see `timescaledb_information.jobs` and `job_stats`; change it with `alter_job`, run it with `CALL run_job(id)`.
Keep raw retention **longer than** any continuous aggregate's `start_offset`, and retain the aggregate separately.
Multi-node was removed in 2.14. Tiering to object storage is Tiger Cloud only; for sharding PostgreSQL see [Citus](/e3/sharding-citus).
`drop_chunks` is **Apache 2 edition**; retention policies, `add_job` and the scheduler are **Community edition**.

lessons.title: Hyperfunctions: time-weighted averages, candlesticks, percentiles and counters
lessons.tldr: **Hyperfunctions** from the TimescaleDB Toolkit extension (`timescaledb_toolkit`) are aggregates for time-series questions that plain `avg`, `percentile_cont` and `max - min` get wrong or cannot combine across buckets: time-weighted averages, OHLC candles, approximate percentiles and counters with resets. Each one builds a small **summary** that accessors read and `rollup()` merges, so a continuous aggregate can store it per bucket and still give correct answers for any larger time range.

visualizer.title: Four hyperfunctions, step by step
visualizer.interaction: Pick a hyperfunction and step through it. Switch **LOCF / linear** for time-weighted averages, watch ticks become candles, merge hourly sketches, and correct a counter that resets. Each summary is a model computed in the page; the Toolkit itself does not run here.

presets.label: avg() vs a time-weighted average
presets.lookFor: `avg()` says **25.125** because the 2-minute spike holds 2 of 8 samples. Weighting by duration gives **21.931** (LOCF, a step curve) or **23.043** (linear, straight lines between samples). The last reading has no duration, as in `time_weight`.

presets.label: Buckets: average vs interpolated
presets.lookFor: Per bucket: **20.8 / 23.269** using only points inside each bucket, and **20.833 / 23.167** once the edges are filled from the neighbouring bucket (21 from 08:25 to 08:30 in the first, 21 from 08:30 to 08:32 and 24 from 08:58 to 09:00 in the second).

presets.label: Roll up time-weight summaries
presets.lookFor: Averaging the bucket averages gives **22.035**. Merging the summaries, including the 21 × 7 minutes between 08:25 and 08:32, gives **21.931**: the same as the whole-hour query in the first preset.

presets.label: OHLC candles and their rollup
presets.lookFor: Two candles: VWAP **99.8767** and **101.2786**. Merged: open 100, high 102.3, low 99.2, close 101.8, volume 85, VWAP **100.5694**. The average of the two VWAPs (100.5777) is wrong because the minutes traded different volumes.

presets.label: Exact percentiles do not combine
presets.lookFor: Hourly p95: **58**, **838.65** and **78** ms. Their average is **324.88 ms**, but the true p95 is **77.05 ms**: the incident hour served 20 of 620 requests. The only exact fix is to keep and re-sort all **620** values.

presets.label: A mergeable log-bucket sketch
presets.lookFor: 12, 15 and 12 bucket counts replace 400, 20 and 200 values. Merged by summing counts, the sketch says p95 ≈ **77.663** ms (exact 77.05) and p99 ≈ **574.815** (exact 560.93), each within 5% of a real value.

presets.label: Counter resets with lag() and CASE
presets.lookFor: Raw arithmetic gives **−30** or **215**. Reset-aware: **310** requests, **2** resets, **0.0891** per second. Bucketed deltas are 145 + 140 = 285: the 25 between 09:25 and 09:30 need the neighbouring bucket, which is what `rollup()` keeps.

production.title: Latency and traffic dashboards that stay correct at every zoom level
production.problem: The hourly continuous aggregate stored `percentile_cont(0.95)` and `max(total) - min(total)`. Daily and weekly panels averaged the hourly p95s and summed the hourly deltas. After a short incident the daily p95 was several times too high, and every deploy, which restarts the counters, made that hour's traffic wrong.
production.outcome: On the playground's three hours of traffic, the old method reports a p95 of 324.88 ms against a true 77.05 ms. A merged sketch with a 5% error bound gives 77.66 ms. Each hourly sketch is bounded at 200 buckets however many requests it summarizes, and the counter delta stays correct across restarts.

pitfalls.title: Averaging irregular samples
pitfalls.fix: Weight by duration: `time_weight` with `LOCF` for report-on-change devices, `linear` for sampled signals. Use `interpolated_average` with `LAG`/`LEAD` for exact bucket edges. Natively, compute interval areas with `lead()`.

pitfalls.title: Averaging percentiles across buckets
pitfalls.fix: Store `percentile_agg` (or `uddsketch`/`tdigest`) per bucket and query `approx_percentile(p, rollup(sketch))`. All sketches you roll up must share `size` and `max_error`, and a mismatch is not always detected.

pitfalls.title: Ignoring counter resets
pitfalls.fix: Use `counter_agg`: `delta`, `rate` and `num_resets` account for resets. Combine buckets with `delta(rollup(cs))`, or `interpolated_delta(cs, bucket, interval, LAG(cs), LEAD(cs))` per bucket. For Prometheus-style rates, set bounds and call `extrapolated_rate(cs, 'prometheus')`.

pitfalls.title: Experimental functions change between versions
pitfalls.fix: Keep stable functions in caggs and views. Before an upgrade, list the dependent objects and save their definitions.

keyPointers: **Two-step aggregation**: an aggregate builds a summary, accessors (`average`, `vwap`, `approx_percentile`, `delta`) read it, and `rollup()` merges summaries. Store summaries in [continuous aggregates](/e2/continuous-aggregates).
`time_weight('LOCF' | 'linear', ts, v)`: the area under the curve divided by elapsed time. One point gives NULL; `interpolated_average` fills bucket edges from neighbours.
`candlestick_agg(ts, price, volume)`: open/close by time, high/low, volume and VWAP = Σ(price·volume) / Σvolume, all mergeable.

UddSketch buckets values at ⌈log_γ x⌉, so merging adds counts and keeps a relative error bound (0.001 for `percentile_agg`, which grows if 200 buckets overflow). Never average percentiles. `counter_agg` treats any drop as a reset to zero.

`timescaledb_toolkit` 1.27.0 supports PostgreSQL 16–18 under the Timescale License. It comes with Tiger Cloud and the `timescaledb-ha` image; self-hosted servers install it from packages (apt, yum, brew) or from source. Neon does not offer it.

modules.title: Distributed PostgreSQL
modules.summary: Why and how to distribute: sharding with Citus, distributed query execution and transactions, distributed SQL, multi-master and HA clusters.

lessons.title: Why and how to distribute PostgreSQL
lessons.tldr: PostgreSQL is a **single-node** database, and every "distributed PostgreSQL" adds one of three things around it: **replication** (copies), **distribution** (parts of the data on different machines) or **decentralization** (storage and compute on different machines). Each design buys scale or availability by adding network round trips and new failure modes, so the right choice starts from what one well-tuned node cannot do.

visualizer.title: Five architectures, one write, one read
visualizer.interaction: Pick an architecture, send a write and a read, then fail a component and send them again. The latency panel shows what each extra round trip costs.

presets.label: One node, one WAL stream
presets.lookFor: Every change becomes WAL records: a heap insert, a B-tree insert, a commit. A physical replica replays exactly this stream; a shared-storage system ships only this stream to its storage layer.

presets.label: Commit knobs: latency vs safety
presets.lookFor: `synchronous_commit` can change per transaction. With `remote_apply` a commit waits until a synchronous standby has replayed it. Here the standby list is empty, so nothing waits. `synchronous_standby_names` needs a reload, not a `SET`.

presets.label: A slot for a replica
presets.lookFor: A replica connects through a slot, so the primary keeps the WAL the replica still needs. `active = false`: no replica is connected to this single node.

presets.label: Distribution on one machine
presets.lookFor: Hash partitions on one node model shards: each tenant lands in exactly one part. A sharding extension puts those parts on different machines. Note the uneven sizes: 20 tenants do not split evenly 4 ways.

presets.label: Copies of a subset
presets.lookFor: Logical replication publishes chosen tables, columns and rows. It is the building block of multi-master systems. The warning says this node is not configured to send logical changes; the catalog entry still shows what would be published.

presets.label: Latency arithmetic
presets.lookFor: Same numbers as the visualizer: 5 statements at 70 ms round trip allow about 3 transactions per second per session. Distance, not CPU, sets the ceiling.

production.title: Choosing an architecture from measurements, not fashion
production.problem: Nobody knows whether reads, writes or one heavy tenant drive the load. A distributed design chosen blind would add round trips to every request and change uniqueness, sequences and joins for the whole application.
production.outcome: Reads were most of the load, so the team added two streaming replicas behind an HA manager and moved reporting to them. Each next step is now driven by a measured bottleneck, not by the architecture of the week.

pitfalls.title: Reading your own write from a replica
pitfalls.fix: Send reads that follow a write to the primary for a short window, or make that transaction commit with `remote_apply` to a synchronous standby. Load-balance only staleness-tolerant reads.

pitfalls.title: One synchronous standby blocks every commit
pitfalls.fix: Name at least two candidates and wait for one: `ANY 1 (s1, s2)`. Then one standby may be down without stopping writes.

pitfalls.title: Distributing a chatty application
pitfalls.fix: Cut round trips first: batch with multi-row `INSERT` or `COPY`, combine reads, move loops into a single statement or a function, and pool connections. Keep each transaction on one node or one shard.

pitfalls.title: Talking past each other about "cluster"
pitfalls.fix: Name the thing: "the instance", "the HA group", "the shard group". Write runbooks with host names, not "the cluster".

keyPointers: Three mechanisms: **replication** (copies), **distribution** (parts), **decentralization** (storage separated from compute). Real systems stack them.
A transaction costs **round trips × latency**: 20 ms per transaction caps one session at 50 transactions per second.

Replicas scale reads but are stale; shared storage gives durable quorum writes with one writer; sharding splits data by a key; distributed SQL runs Raft per tablet; multi-master accepts writes everywhere and resolves conflicts later.
**CAP**: under a partition choose consistency or availability. **PACELC**: otherwise choose latency or consistency, which `synchronous_commit` lets you pick per transaction.
Most workloads fit one large node plus [streaming replicas](/m7/streaming-replication) and an HA manager. Distribute when a measured limit says so.

lessons.title: Sharding with Citus
lessons.tldr: **Citus** is a PostgreSQL extension that hash-splits each distributed table by a **distribution column** into shards, ordinary tables spread over worker nodes, and routes or parallelizes queries from a coordinator. It exists to scale one database past one machine while keeping PostgreSQL itself, as long as the data model is built around a shard key such as the tenant id.

visualizer.title: A shard map: from a key to a worker
visualizer.interaction: Type a company_id or press Route next key. Change the worker count, break colocation for ads, or switch to reference and schema-based sharding.

presets.label: The shard map
presets.lookFor: This table models Citus's `pg_dist_shard` on one node: 32 ranges of 134,217,728 hash tokens each, placed round-robin. Citus itself is not installed here.

presets.label: Route a key to its shard
presets.lookFor: Hash the key, find the range that contains the token, read the node. Company 7 hashes to -978793473, which falls in shard 102048 on worker1: the same numbers the visualizer shows with 2 workers.

presets.label: Colocation: one company, one shard index
presets.lookFor: All three tables are split by the same key with the same modulus, so a company's rows always land in partitions with the same suffix. Citus colocation makes the same promise across machines.

presets.label: Unique keys must include the shard key
presets.lookFor: No single part can check uniqueness across all parts, so the key column is required. Citus applies the same rule to distributed tables: unique per tenant is easy, globally unique is not.

presets.label: Foreign keys inside a colocation group
presets.lookFor: The foreign key includes `company_id`, so the parent row is always in the matching part. In Citus this is the only way a distributed table may reference another one.

presets.label: Schema per tenant
presets.lookFor: Same table name, no tenant column: `search_path` chooses the tenant. Schema-based sharding in Citus distributes whole schemas like this one, each to one node.

production.title: Sharding a multi-tenant ad platform by company
production.problem: Primary keys are plain `id` columns, so nothing in the schema says which rows belong together. Distributing as is would make every join a cross-node join and every unique key unenforceable.
production.outcome: Each company's companies, campaigns and ads shards sit on the same worker, so dashboard queries filtered by `company_id` touch one shard, and foreign keys keep working. Adding a worker and rebalancing adds capacity without touching application queries.

pitfalls.title: A unique key without the distribution column
pitfalls.fix: Make uniqueness per tenant: `UNIQUE (company_id, email)`. If a value must be unique across all tenants, keep it in a reference table or a separate lookup table.

pitfalls.title: Distributing the child before the parent
pitfalls.fix: Distribute in dependency order: the referenced table first, then the tables that point at it, with `colocate_with`. Foreign keys from a reference table to a distributed table are never allowed.

pitfalls.title: A distribution column with few values
pitfalls.fix: Pick a high-cardinality key that matches how queries filter, usually the tenant id. Move one very large tenant to its own shard with `isolate_tenant_to_new_shard`.

pitfalls.title: The coordinator keeps a local copy
pitfalls.fix: Run `truncate_local_data_after_distributing_table('table')` once the copy is verified.

keyPointers: A distributed table is split by `hashint4`-style hashing of the **distribution column** into `citus.shard_count` (default **32**) shards, each an ordinary table named `<table>_<shardid>` on a worker.
`pg_dist_shard` stores each shard's token range, `pg_dist_placement` its node. The coordinator routes a query that pins the key to one shard.
**Colocated** tables share ranges and placements, so joins and foreign keys on the key stay local. **Reference** tables are copied to every worker and written with 2PC.

Primary keys and unique constraints must **include the distribution column**, the same rule as for [partitioned tables](/m7/partitioning). Foreign keys work between colocated tables on the key, or to reference tables.
Schema-based sharding (Citus 12+) distributes whole schemas, one per node, for apps with up to thousands of tenants and no tenant column.

lessons.title: Distributed query execution
lessons.tldr: A sharded query is planned twice: the **coordinator** decides which shards it needs and splits the work into **tasks**, and each worker plans and runs its task as an ordinary PostgreSQL query. How the query uses the distribution column decides its cost, from one round trip to one worker up to a full shuffle of rows between all workers.

visualizer.title: Five queries on four shard groups
visualizer.interaction: Pick a query type and step through it. Tasks fly out, partial results fly back with the real numbers of the playground data.

presets.label: Router: the key prunes to one shard
presets.lookFor: Partition pruning plays the role of the Citus router: only `ads_s3` is scanned, and company 7 has 100 ads there. This is a single-node model of the idea, not Citus.

presets.label: Fan-out: no key, every shard
presets.lookFor: An `Append` over all four parts: the single-node shape of a multi-shard query with **Task Count: 4**.

presets.label: Aggregates in two phases
presets.lookFor: `Partial Aggregate` per part and one `Finalize Aggregate` on top: the same split Citus makes between workers and coordinator. Both averages are 42.55.

presets.label: Colocated join, pushed down
presets.lookFor: Each `ads_sN` joins only `campaigns_sN`, and the grouping happens inside each pair. A colocated distributed join runs exactly like this, one pair per worker.

presets.label: Join without the key
presets.lookFor: Without `company_id` in the join, any part may match any part: one big join over two `Append`s. Even with a filter on `ads`, every `campaigns` part is scanned. In Citus the first query needs a repartition join.

presets.label: Move a shard
presets.lookFor: Copy, swap the new copy in, drop the old one, all in one transaction: the table never loses a row. A Citus shard move does the same across machines, with logical replication so that writes can continue.

presets.label: Split a hot shard
presets.lookFor: The largest part (1300 rows) becomes two parts of 900 and 400 by doubling the modulus for that slice. Splitting the hash range is how a sharded system relieves a hot shard.

production.title: A dashboard query that touched every shard
production.problem: The tile joined `ads` to `campaigns` on `campaign_id` only and filtered by `company_id` on one side. Citus could not prove that both sides were on one shard, so with repartition joins enabled for reporting it re-shuffled rows between all workers on each request.
production.outcome: The tile now sends one task to one worker instead of shuffling rows between all of them, so its latency no longer grows with the number of shards, and the workers stop running work that returns nothing.

pitfalls.title: Joins that need repartitioning
pitfalls.fix: Add the distribution column to the join, make the small side a reference table, or, for rare analytics only, enable repartition joins for that session.

pitfalls.title: Connection storms on the workers
pitfalls.fix: Pool clients in front of the coordinator, keep `citus.max_shared_pool_size` below the workers' `max_connections`, and lower the per-session pool size for many small queries.

pitfalls.title: A CTE that pulls everything to the coordinator
pitfalls.fix: Filter and aggregate inside the CTE so that it returns a few rows, or rewrite it so that it joins on the distribution column and can be pushed down.

pitfalls.title: Rebalancing a table without a replica identity
pitfalls.fix: Give every distributed table a primary key before rebalancing. Preview with `get_rebalance_table_shards_plan()` and watch `citus_rebalance_status()`.

keyPointers: **Router** query: the filter pins the distribution column, so one task goes to one worker and any SQL works, much like [partition pruning](/m7/partitioning) on one node.
**Multi-shard** query: one task per shard in parallel, merged on the coordinator. Aggregates split into worker parts and a final step (avg → sum + count).
Joins on the distribution column of **colocated** tables push down; other joins need a **repartition** shuffle, which is off by default.
EXPLAIN shows `Custom Scan (Citus Adaptive)` with `Task Count` and one sample task plan from a worker.
Rebalancing moves whole colocated shard groups, online through logical replication when tables have a replica identity.

lessons.title: Distributed transactions and consistency
lessons.tldr: A transaction that writes on several nodes needs an **atomic commit protocol**, usually **two-phase commit** (prepare everywhere, then commit everywhere), plus a way to order events across machines whose clocks disagree. Without them a crash can commit half a transfer, and the guarantees a single node gives for free (isolation, sequences, unique keys, foreign keys) each need a new answer.

visualizer.title: Two-phase commit, clocks and cross-node rules
visualizer.interaction: Step through three 2PC scenarios, including a coordinator crash after PREPARE. Then send messages between two skewed clocks, and click the matrix to compare systems.

presets.label: Two-phase commit, both phases
presets.lookFor: Between PREPARE and COMMIT PREPARED the balances still read 100 and 0: prepared work is invisible. After phase 2 they read 70 and 30, and nothing is left prepared.

presets.label: In doubt: locks with no session
presets.lookFor: The prepared transaction holds its locks with `pid` NULL: no session owns them. NOWAIT reports the lock instead of waiting, SKIP LOCKED leaves row 3 out, and `backend_xmin` is held at the prepared xid. The preset resolves it at the end.

presets.label: Recovery from the decision log
presets.lookFor: xfer-44 has a logged commit, so both halves are committed. xfer-45 never got a decision, so the safe choice is to roll it back. Any session may finish a prepared transaction.

presets.label: Two nodes, two clocks
presets.lookFor: One logical transfer left two local xids with two commit timestamps. Each node orders its own history; nothing on a node knows the other node's xids. That is why distributed systems need a shared timestamp such as an HLC.

presets.label: Sequences across nodes
presets.lookFor: Interleaved increments never collide, but every node must know the scheme forever. Snowflake ids embed time and node, so they sort roughly by time without coordination.

presets.label: Unique per node is not unique
presets.lookFor: Each node's unique index only sees its own rows, so the same email exists twice. A single table that owns the value turns the second claim into an error before anything is written.

production.title: An orphaned prepared transaction that stopped VACUUM
production.problem: A deploy killed the manager between the two phases. Weeks later table bloat grew on one shard, wraparound warnings appeared, and some account rows timed out on every update. A prepared transaction from that deploy still held its locks and its xmin.
production.outcome: With the orphan resolved, VACUUM caught up and the locks were released. The alert now fires within minutes, long before bloat or wraparound pressure can build.

pitfalls.title: Forgotten prepared transactions
pitfalls.fix: Monitor `pg_prepared_xacts`, resolve each GID from the transaction manager's log, and keep `max_prepared_transactions = 0` where nothing uses 2PC.

pitfalls.title: Assuming postgres_fdw commits atomically
pitfalls.fix: Do not rely on cross-server atomicity through FDWs. Use a coordinator that runs `PREPARE TRANSACTION` on each server, or design with an outbox and idempotent retries.

pitfalls.title: Prepared transactions on a standby
pitfalls.fix: Raise the setting on standbys first, then on the primary. If you use 2PC, set it at least as high as `max_connections`.

pitfalls.title: Read Committed code on a Snapshot-only system
pitfalls.fix: Enable the system's Read Committed mode where available (YugabyteDB: `yb_enable_read_committed_isolation`) and retry `40001` in the application in any case.

keyPointers: 2PC: **PREPARE TRANSACTION** on every participant, durably log the decision, then **COMMIT PREPARED** (or **ROLLBACK PREPARED**) everywhere. A failed PREPARE is a rollback.
If the coordinator dies after PREPARE, participants are **in doubt**: they hold locks and xmin until recovery reads the log and finishes. 2PC is a blocking protocol.
`max_prepared_transactions` is 0 by default, which disables 2PC. `pg_prepared_xacts` lists what is prepared, and any session can finish it.
A **hybrid logical clock** (physical, logical) orders causes before effects across nodes with skewed clocks. Commit timestamps decide "latest" in multi-master systems.

Across nodes, sequences, unique keys, foreign keys and [isolation](/m5/isolation-levels) all weaken unless the system adds global machinery for them. Old prepared transactions also block [wraparound protection](/m7/xid-wraparound).

lessons.title: Distributed SQL and multi-master
lessons.tldr: **Distributed SQL** systems such as YugabyteDB put a PostgreSQL-derived query layer on top of a sharded store where every shard (a **tablet**) is replicated with **Raft**, while **multi-master** systems such as EDB PGD and pgEdge Spock let every PostgreSQL node accept writes and replicate them to the others asynchronously. Both remove the single primary, but the first pays with a consensus round trip on every write and the second with **conflicts** that must be resolved after commit.

visualizer.title: Raft tablets and a multi-master conflict
visualizer.interaction: Write rows and fail nodes to watch tablet leaders move. Then make two nodes change the same row and pick a conflict resolution rule and a clock offset.

presets.label: Both nodes change the same row
presets.lookFor: Each node read 100 and committed its own change. The log shows what each would replicate: old value, new value and a commit timestamp (`track_commit_timestamp = on`). This models two nodes with two schemas on one server.

presets.label: Last update wins
presets.lookFor: The later commit timestamp wins on both nodes, so they agree on 120, and the +50 from node A is gone. That is the **lost update** of last-update-wins. The tie-breaker on origin covers equal timestamps.

presets.label: Delta-apply: replicate the difference
presets.lookFor: Each node adds the other's difference instead of copying its value: both reach 170. `session_replication_role = replica` is how an apply worker keeps triggers from logging the replicated change again.

presets.label: Different columns, same row
presets.lookFor: The two nodes touched **different** columns, yet a row-level rule keeps one whole row: the later balance survives and the rename is lost (`bo`, 55). Tracking a change time per column merges both edits (`bo k.`, 55). EDB PGD resolves per row by default and can switch a table to column-level detection, which needs `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`.

presets.label: A unique key on two nodes
presets.lookFor: Both inserts succeed locally. When A's row arrives at B, the email already exists with another id. PostgreSQL 18 counts such cases per subscription as `confl_insert_exists`, `confl_update_origin_differs` and five more.

presets.label: Replication needs a row identity
presets.lookFor: A table without a primary key cannot publish UPDATE or DELETE, so the error comes from the publishing node itself. Multi-master tools need a primary key on every replicated table to match rows at all.

presets.label: Hash ranges into tablets
presets.lookFor: YugabyteDB hashes the first primary key column into 0x0000–0xFFFF and gives each tablet one slice, as `SPLIT INTO 3 TABLETS` would. This uses PostgreSQL's own hash as a stand-in, so the counts show the idea, not YugabyteDB's exact placement.

production.title: Two regions, one wallet table
production.problem: A test with last-update-wins lost balance top-ups whenever a user's phone and a scheduled job changed the same wallet in different regions within a second, exactly the counter case.
production.outcome: Concurrent top-ups now add up on both nodes, and the few remaining overwrite conflicts are visible in the resolutions log instead of silently lost.

pitfalls.title: Last-update-wins on counters
pitfalls.fix: Write each counter on one node only, or use delta-apply columns (Spock), conflict-free replicated data types (EDB PGD ships counters such as `bdr.crdt_pncounter` and `bdr.crdt_delta_counter`), or an append-only ledger summed on read.

pitfalls.title: Clock skew deciding the winner
pitfalls.fix: Keep clocks synchronized tightly, monitor skew, and do not rely on last-update-wins for data where order matters.

pitfalls.title: Foreign keys and uniqueness during apply
pitfalls.fix: Route writes for one entity to one node, use global id generators (snowflake-style sequences or UUIDs), and audit cross-node uniqueness regularly.

pitfalls.title: Treating distributed SQL as plain PostgreSQL
pitfalls.fix: Keep hot transactions on one tablet (filter by the full hash key), colocate small tables, use a connection pooler, enable Read Committed and wait queues, and retry `40001`.

keyPointers: YugabyteDB: YSQL reuses PostgreSQL's query layer over **DocDB**; tables split into **tablets**, each a **Raft** group with one leader. A write commits on a majority; a lost leader is replaced within seconds (about 3 s with default heartbeat settings).
Hash sharding uses a 16-bit space **0x0000–0xFFFF**, and by default only the first primary key column is hashed. Range sharding (`ASC`/`DESC`) suits range scans but risks hot spots.
Multi-master (PGD, Spock) commits locally and replicates later, so conflicts are detected on apply, for example (in PostgreSQL 18 terms) insert_exists, update_origin_differs, delete_missing.

Resolution rules (`last_update_wins`, `keep_local`, `apply_remote`, `error`) trade correctness for availability; delta-apply fixes counters; global sequences fix ids. See [logical replication](/m7/logical-replication) for the building block.
Use multi-master only for simple, partitionable write patterns; use distributed SQL when you need strong consistency across regions and can pay the write latency.

lessons.title: High-availability clusters in practice
lessons.tldr: An HA cluster is a primary with standbys plus a manager such as **Patroni** that holds a **leader key** in a consensus store (etcd, Consul, ZooKeeper), promotes a standby when the leader stops renewing it, and lets a proxy route clients to whoever holds the key. PostgreSQL ships replication and `pg_promote()` but no failure detection or fencing, and getting those wrong means either long outages or two primaries.

visualizer.title: A Patroni failover, second by second
visualizer.interaction: Step through a crash, a network cut and a planned switchover. Move the ttl, loop_wait and retry_timeout sliders to see the timings change and the split-brain rule break.

presets.label: Am I the primary?
presets.lookFor: This is the first question every health check asks. A promoted standby starts a new **timeline**, visible in the first 8 hex digits of the WAL file name. This single node is a primary on timeline 1.

presets.label: One slot per member
presets.lookFor: With `use_slots` (the default) Patroni keeps a physical slot for each other member, so the primary retains the WAL a lagging replica still needs. Here no replica is connected, so both slots are inactive.

presets.label: How far behind is a replica?
presets.lookFor: Lag is a WAL distance in bytes. Patroni compares it with `maximum_lag_on_failover` before letting a replica take over, and HAProxy can exclude laggards with `/replica?lag=…`. The inactive slots keep growing until dropped.

presets.label: Synchronous commit, per transaction
presets.lookFor: `synchronous_standby_names` has context `sighup`: Patroni writes it into the configuration when `synchronous_mode` is on. Each transaction can still choose how long to wait. With no standbys listed, nothing waits here.

presets.label: Check the timing rule
presets.lookFor: Patroni requires `loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout <= ttl`; since 3.2 it lowers `loop_wait` (or `retry_timeout`) with a warning when the values break it. The "wrong" row breaks it: the old leader could still be primary when the key expires. The failover estimate adds an assumed 2 s promotion and two 3 s HAProxy checks to the TTL.

production.title: A three-node Patroni cluster with zero data loss
production.problem: Its first setup had one asynchronous standby and a script that promoted it when pings failed. A network blip produced two primaries, and a real crash lost the last seconds of orders.
production.outcome: A crash now costs well under a minute of write unavailability with the default timings (about 40 s in the worst case modelled above) and no acknowledged order is lost, because a commit returns only after a synchronous standby has it. The isolated old primary demotes itself before anyone else is promoted.

pitfalls.title: Split-brain from a home-made failover script
pitfalls.fix: Use a manager with a leader lock in a consensus store (Patroni + etcd), so a node that cannot renew the lock demotes itself. Add a watchdog for the case where Patroni itself hangs, and never promote by hand while the old primary may be alive.

pitfalls.title: Timings that break the fencing rule
pitfalls.fix: Keep `loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout <= ttl`. Change the values with `patronictl edit-config`; `bootstrap.dcs` only applies when the cluster is first created.

pitfalls.title: Synchronous mode with a single standby
pitfalls.fix: Run at least two replicas so another can become synchronous, or use quorum commit (`synchronous_mode: quorum`, `ANY n (...)`) so one standby can be down.

pitfalls.title: An old primary that cannot rejoin
pitfalls.fix: Enable `use_pg_rewind` (it needs `wal_log_hints = on` or data checksums), or rebuild the node from a fresh base backup. See [streaming replication](/m7/streaming-replication) for timelines and standbys.

keyPointers: Patroni keeps a **leader key** with a TTL in a DCS (etcd, Consul, ZooKeeper, Kubernetes). Only the key holder runs as primary; a holder that cannot renew it **demotes itself**.
Defaults `ttl` 30 / `loop_wait` 10 / `retry_timeout` 10, and the rule **`loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout <= ttl`**. A crash costs roughly the TTL plus promotion plus proxy checks.
HAProxy routes by HTTP checks against Patroni's REST API: `/primary` for writes, `/replica?lag=` for reads. A pooler such as [PgBouncer](/m7/connection-pooling) sits behind it or beside it.
`synchronous_mode` makes failover lose nothing acknowledged; asynchronous failover can lose the unreplicated tail.
Switchover is the planned, lossless version: rehearse it regularly. A returning old primary needs `pg_rewind` or a rebuild.

modules.title: Spatial Data with PostGIS
modules.summary: Geometry and geography, coordinate systems, spatial indexes, nearest-neighbour search and the spatial queries maps are built on.

lessons.title: Geometry, geography and coordinate systems
lessons.tldr: PostGIS adds two spatial types to PostgreSQL: **geometry**, measured on a flat plane in the units of its coordinate system (its **SRID**), and **geography**, measured on the curved Earth in metres. Every coordinate means nothing without its SRID, so picking the right type and coordinate system up front is what makes distances, areas and joins come out right.

visualizer.title: One pair of cities, three rulers
visualizer.interaction: Switch the ruler and watch the grid morph from longitude/latitude to Web Mercator. **Next city pair** moves north and south; the checkbox shows what swapped coordinates do.

presets.label: Make a point
presets.lookFor: The same point in four encodings. The default text output is **HEXEWKB**. `ST_MakePoint` alone has SRID **0** (unknown); `ST_Point(x, y, 4326)` sets it in one call.

presets.label: Coordinate systems
presets.lookFor: **8500** coordinate systems ship in `spatial_ref_sys`. 4326 is longitude/latitude on WGS 84, 3857 is Web Mercator, and 3035, 27700 and 32618 are local projections in metres.

presets.label: Three rulers
presets.lookFor: geometry in 4326 returns **3.63 degrees**. geography returns **343.9 km**. Web Mercator says 537 km, about 56% too long at this latitude. The local equal-area projection 3035 is within 0.5 km.

presets.label: Swap lat and lon
presets.lookFor: Latitude first puts "London" in the Indian Ocean, and the distance comes out as **402.7 km**, with no error. Out-of-range geography input is silently wrapped to `POINT(-160 80)`.

presets.label: Area by latitude
presets.lookFor: A 1° × 1° cell is **1 square degree** everywhere, but its true area falls from 12 309 km² at the equator to 6 123 km² at 60°. Mercator grows it to 25 168 km².

presets.label: Typmods guard the column
presets.lookFor: `geometry(Point, 4326)` rejects a wrong SRID and a wrong shape. A point that really is in 27700 must be **transformed**, not relabelled; the third insert works and lands on London.

presets.label: The antimeridian
presets.lookFor: Two points 1° apart across the date line. The plane thinks they are **359 degrees** apart; geography knows the Earth is round and says **111 km**.

production.title: A delivery app that measured in the wrong units
production.problem: Web Mercator stretches lengths by about 1/cos(latitude). At 51.5° N every distance came out about **1.6×** too long, so customers were overcharged. Moving the code to `ST_Distance(geom, geom)` in 4326 made it worse: the result was in **degrees**.
production.outcome: For London–Paris the three answers are 537.3 km (3857), 3.63 (degrees) and 343.9 km (geography). The fee now uses the 343.9 km kind of number, and the local projection agrees to within half a kilometre.

pitfalls.title: Latitude written first
pitfalls.fix: Always pass longitude first to `ST_Point`/`ST_MakePoint`. Add a check constraint for your region to catch swaps.

pitfalls.title: Reading degrees as metres
pitfalls.fix: Cast to geography for metres, or transform to a projected SRID whose unit is metres.

pitfalls.title: ST_SetSRID where ST_Transform was needed
pitfalls.fix: Set the SRID the data was really produced in, then transform.

pitfalls.title: Measuring in Web Mercator
pitfalls.fix: Keep 3857 for display. Measure with geography or with a local equal-area or conformal projection.

keyPointers: **geometry**: planar, units of its SRID, the richest function set. **geography**: spheroid, metres, the right default for lon/lat data spread over a wide area.
Coordinates are **(x, y) = (longitude, latitude)**. `ST_Point(lon, lat, 4326)` builds a point with its SRID in one call.
`ST_Transform` changes coordinates; `ST_SetSRID` only changes the label.
Use typmods such as `geometry(Point, 4326)` so the column rejects the wrong SRID or shape.
Next: how a spatial index answers "what is near here" in [Spatial indexes](/e4/spatial-indexes).

lessons.title: Spatial indexes
lessons.tldr: A PostGIS **GiST** index is an R-tree of **bounding boxes**: each page stores boxes, and each box covers everything beneath it. It lets a query skip whole regions with the cheap `&&` box test and run the exact, expensive geometry test only on the few rows that survive.

visualizer.title: Two-step filtering through a GiST tree
visualizer.interaction: Drag the ✕, set the radius, and step the phases. Then switch to **geom::geography** to see the same query lose its index.

presets.label: Box overlap: &&
presets.lookFor: `&&` is answered by the GiST index alone: **Bitmap Index Scan**, about 5 index buffers. The long hex string is the query box in WKB.

presets.label: ST_DWithin, indexed
presets.lookFor: Read the **Index Cond**: `geom && st_expand(…, 0.005)`. Two-step filtering in one plan. The radius is **0.005 degrees**, because the column is geometry in 4326.

presets.label: The geography cast trap
presets.lookFor: Metres at last, but the plan is a **Seq Scan** over the whole table: **19 995** rows removed by the filter. The index is on `geom`, not on `geom::geography`.

presets.label: Fix: expression index
presets.lookFor: Same query, now a **Bitmap Index Scan** on `places_geog_gist` with `_st_expand` on geography. A few index pages, 8 heap blocks, and only 3 rows removed.

presets.label: ST_Distance is never indexed
presets.lookFor: Same 5 rows, but **Seq Scan** even with the geography index: `ST_Distance` has no index support. Write radius filters with `ST_DWithin`.

presets.label: GiST vs SP-GiST vs BRIN
presets.lookFor: GiST 864 kB, SP-GiST 968 kB, BRIN **24 kB**. BRIN is tiny because it stores one box per range of 4 pages. Whether it helps depends on row order (next preset).

presets.label: BRIN needs sorted rows
presets.lookFor: On `places` the rows are scattered, so every range box covers the whole area: **lossy=171**, all pages. `ORDER BY geom` lays rows out along a space-filling curve, and BRIN then reads only about **16** pages.

production.title: A store finder that slowed down as it grew
production.problem: Latency grew in step with the table. `EXPLAIN` showed a **Seq Scan** with almost every row removed by the filter. The cast to geography made the filter an expression that the GiST index on `geom` cannot serve.
production.outcome: In the playground the same pattern goes from a Seq Scan that discards 19 995 of 20 000 rows to a Bitmap Index Scan that reads a few index pages and 8 heap blocks. The gap grows with the table: the seq scan is linear, the index descent is logarithmic.

pitfalls.title: Wrapping the indexed column in a cast or function
pitfalls.fix: Put the transformation on the **constant** side, or create an expression index that matches.

pitfalls.title: Filtering with ST_Distance
pitfalls.fix: Use `ST_DWithin(a, b, 500)`. It adds `&&` against the expanded box, so the index cuts the candidates first.

pitfalls.title: Using && when you mean "inside"
pitfalls.fix: Use `ST_Intersects` for the exact answer. It does the `&&` index step for you and then the exact test.

pitfalls.title: BRIN on unsorted or frequently updated data
pitfalls.fix: Use BRIN only for append-mostly data written in spatial order (or rewritten with `ORDER BY geom`). Use GiST otherwise.

keyPointers: Indexes store **boxes**; queries run in two steps: box filter (index) then exact test (recheck).
Index-aware: `&&`, `~`, `@`, `ST_Intersects`, `ST_Contains`, `ST_Within`, `ST_Covers`, `ST_DWithin` and friends. Not `ST_Distance`.
Casting the column (`geom::geography`) needs a matching **expression index** or the plan becomes a Seq Scan.
GiST is the default; SP-GiST suits points; BRIN is tiny but needs spatially sorted rows. Compare [GiST and SP-GiST](/m4/gist-spgist) and [BRIN](/m4/brin) internals.
Read the plan for `Index Cond` and `Rows Removed by Filter`, as in [EXPLAIN ANALYZE](/m4/explain-analyze).

lessons.title: Nearest-neighbour search
lessons.tldr: `ORDER BY geom <-> point LIMIT k` asks for the k nearest rows, and a GiST index answers it directly by returning rows in distance order. It exists because "the closest five" has no radius to filter on, and sorting every row by distance gets slower as the table grows.

visualizer.title: Best-first search through the index
visualizer.interaction: Pop entries off the priority queue and watch pages open and rows come out in order. Drag the ✕ or change **LIMIT k**, then compare the work with a full sort.

presets.label: KNN plan
presets.lookFor: **Index Scan** with `Order By: (geom <-> …)`. No Sort node: the index hands rows over already in distance order, after about 10 buffers.

presets.label: Degrees can mis-rank
presets.lookFor: The first five agree, but the 6th differs: ordering in **degrees** picks #9976 at 652 m, while the true 6th nearest is #11179 at **524 m**. At 51.5° N a degree east is shorter than a degree north.

presets.label: Geography KNN
presets.lookFor: Without a geography index the plan is **Seq Scan + Sort**. With the expression index it becomes an ordered Index Scan. Geography `<->` measures on a sphere, in metres.

presets.label: KNN with a filter
presets.lookFor: The index walks outward in distance order and the filter throws away non-pharmacies: **Rows Removed by Filter: 11**. A rare kind would mean walking much further.

presets.label: Nearest per row: LATERAL
presets.lookFor: For each rider, `r.geom` is a constant inside the subquery, so every probe is an index KNN scan: **Index Searches: 50**, one per rider.

presets.label: Trap: join without LATERAL
presets.lookFor: The distance is between two **columns**, so no index can order it: Seq Scan on `places`, then Sort. Rewrite with LATERAL or a scalar subquery.

presets.label: Radius and order
presets.lookFor: With a radius the planner filters through the index and **top-N sorts** the 14 survivors. `<#>` is box distance: 0 for a point inside a diagonal line's box, even though the line is 7.07 away.

production.title: Assigning the nearest courier
production.problem: The first version joined orders to couriers and sorted by `ST_Distance` with a 5 km `ST_DWithin` cap. On busy evenings every order computed distances to hundreds of couriers, and quiet suburbs found nobody inside 5 km.
production.outcome: Each order costs one short index descent instead of a scan. In the playground, 50 riders find their nearest pharmacy with 50 index probes in a few milliseconds. Taking 3 by degrees and re-ranking in metres fixes the degree mis-ranking.

pitfalls.title: <-> between two columns
pitfalls.fix: Use `CROSS JOIN LATERAL (… ORDER BY t.geom <-> outer.geom LIMIT k)`. Inside the subquery the outer value is a constant.

pitfalls.title: Nearest in degrees
pitfalls.fix: Order by geography (`geom::geography <-> $1::geography` with a matching index), use a projected SRID, or fetch a few extra rows and re-rank by `ST_Distance` on geography.

pitfalls.title: Ordering by ST_Distance
pitfalls.fix: Order by `geom <-> $1`; select `ST_Distance` in the column list for display.

pitfalls.title: A selective filter on top of KNN
pitfalls.fix: Use a partial index per hot filter value, or a separate table for the rare kind.

keyPointers: `ORDER BY geom <-> constant LIMIT k` is an **index-ordered scan**: rows leave the index already sorted, with no Sort node.
The scan is **best-first** over a priority queue: boxes are keyed by a lower-bound distance, rows by their exact distance.
geometry `<->` uses SRID units (degrees in 4326); geography `<->` gives metres on a sphere and needs a geography index.
